title: I believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Our sanctions aren’t about the Israeli people, but about the unacceptable policies of the Israeli government, and the suffering they cause Palestinians, says the UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: Our sanctions aren’t about the Israeli people, but about the unacceptable policies of the Israeli government, and the suffering they cause Palestinians, says the UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: The aftermath of an Israeli airstrike that targeted a nearby medical supplies and pharmaceuticals warehouse belonging to Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital, in Deir el-Balah, Gaza, 1 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of an Israeli airstrike that targeted a nearby medical supplies and pharmaceuticals warehouse belonging to Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital, in Deir el-Balah, Gaza, 1 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionPalestineI believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope aliveAndy BurnhamOur sanctions aren’t about the Israeli people, but about the unacceptable policies of the Israeli government, and the suffering they cause PalestiniansTue 8 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIn a difficult and dangerous world, a decade on from Brexit, there is a risk that Britain loses the confidence to lead and stand up for its values. I’m not prepared to let that happen. It is more important than ever that Britain stands for something.We have called for years for atwo-state solutionin the Middle East, but we must recognise that those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action.For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel. Today we are announcing carefully judged, targeted steps that are not aimed at the Israeli people, but at the unacceptable policies of the current Israeli government.The suffering of the Palestinian people is a scar on the conscience of the world. Innocent Palestinians, including children, continue to be killed inGaza. And there is still a humanitarian crisis, with far too little aid getting in.The scale of destruction is hard to comprehend. More than 70,000 people lie dead –at least 20,000 of them children. Families and communities have been torn apart. Millions displaced. And the population of Gaza is now penned into just one third of the territory.I know that people across the UK feel very deeply about this issue – and so do I.Israel to close UK consulate in Jerusalem after sanctions against illegal settlements – UK politics liveRead moreBefore I became prime minister, I said our country’s response had been too slow and simply not good enough. That’s why I committed to changing the government’s approach.I will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution – the best hope for peace and stability in the region – comes under attack.More settlements have been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years. The UN has reported more than 1,500 incidents of settler violence so far this year, aimed at driving out Palestinians. And the situation is growing worse, fast.The Israeli government has now approved 104 new settlements since it took office in December 2022, and ahead of the October elections in Israel, it is allowing tendersfor the construction of the E1 mega settlementto go ahead. This would cut a swathe through the heart of the West Bank – snuffing out the hope of realising a two-state solution. It cannot be allowed to happen.That’s why we are announcing a newpackage of tough measuresto put pressure on the Israeli government:First, we will ban the trade in goods with illegal settlements inPalestine.Second, we have formally changed the view of the British government to say for the first time that the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory is unlawful – independent of, but in line with, theconclusion of the international court of justice.And third, we will sanction individuals and companies that support, facilitate or profit from illegal settlements. That includes any businesses or investors that take part in the construction of the E1 settlement.In addition, we are announcing a new package of desperately needed humanitarian aid to Gaza.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe are taking these steps because it is the right thing to do.I have condemned the monstrous terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in the strongest possible terms – and continue to condemn Hamas. However, it does not justify the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza or the West Bank.The measures we are taking are about targeting illegal settlements and increasing the pressure on the Israeli government to change course. We are not imposing sanctions on Israel as a whole, which would punish the Israeli people, many of whom disagree with their government’s position.The Israeli people are not responsible for the actions of their government. And nor is the Jewish community in the UK. Blaming British Jews for the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple.I met the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society.The measures we are announcing today are about protecting the only solution that could see the Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security – something that people up and down the UK desperately want to see. The government I lead will keep working with our partners around the world to keep that hope alive.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: A constipated baby and a kid that looks like Boris Johnson: why would anyone bother stealing a Renoir? | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The chocolate boxiest of all the impressionists has long had his haters – even Manet thought he was rubbish. Little surprise then that the thieves ditched two works on the way out
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: The chocolate boxiest of all the impressionists has long had his haters – even Manet thought he was rubbish. Little surprise then that the thieves ditched two works on the way out
Content: ‘For the most part, the haters are right’ … Coco Lisant, 1905, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘For the most part, the haters are right’ … Coco Lisant, 1905, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: AlamyArt and designA constipated baby and a kid that looks like Boris Johnson: why would anyone bother stealing a Renoir?The chocolate boxiest of all the impressionists has long had his haters – even Manet thought he was rubbish. Little surprise then that the thieves ditched two works on the way outEddy FrankelTue 8 Sep 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStealing from the Louvre you can understand. I mean, who wouldn’t want a Géricault or Leonardo to hang in the downstairs loo? Same for the Musée d’Orsay too, even the Pompidou – they’re French museums absolutely rammed full of stunning art, all just begging to be audaciously heisted. But the Renoir Museum? It’s hard to see why anyone would bother.As French art fans reel at the news thattwo Renoir paintings were stolen from the Cagnes-sur-Mer museumthat bears his name this week, the rest of the art world has been saying really? Him? Renoir? He’s … awful. It’s like doing a heist of flares in the era of skinny jeans.Did the thieves know something the rest of us don’t? Or was this just a crime of opportunity, taking advantage of a regional art museum with shonky security?View image in fullscreenShonky security … police outside the gates of the Renoir Museum.Photograph: MAXPPP/AlamyPierre-Auguste Renoir was one of impressionism’s head honchos, a leading figure in one of 19th-century art’s most important movements. But time hasn’t been too kind to poor old Pierre. Where his contemporaries like Monet, Cézanne and Degas have been heralded as modernist revolutionaries, artists who shaped the future of western painting and helped set the path that all of their successors would soon follow, in recent years Renoir has been denigrated, mocked, protested and hashtagged.In 2015, a group who called themselvesRenoir Sucks at Paintingpicketed the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, and then protested outside the Met in New York, with placards that read “God Hates Renoir” and “ReNOir”, demanding the museums remove his work from display. And they had their sympathisers: the hashtag #RenoirSucksatPainting trended soon after, they sold hundreds of anti-Renoir T-shirts, and their Instagram was full of photos of people giving the finger to Renoir paintings or pretending to vomit in front of them.View image in fullscreenKitsch and chintziness … Renoir.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesAnd his crime? Kitsch and chintziness. His work is soft focus and gentle, his figures are plump and joyful, it’s all happy haze and night-time revelry. He lacks the hard-edged absolute dedication to angular, prismatic experimentation that made the impressionists so famous. He is the safest of the group, the chocolate boxiest, the easiest, the horniest. And that has made him the most hated.It’s not a new thing. Even his contemporaries disliked him. Édouard Manet said he had “no talent” and Mary Cassatt described his paintings of women as “the most awful of all”. Add to all of that a hefty dose of antisemitism (he refused to take part in exhibitions that featured Jewish impressionist Camille Pissarro), a big pinch of misogyny, and you’ve got a recipe of aesthetic distaste that can last centuries.However in PR terms, the timing of this latest in a long string of French art robberies couldn’t be better. The National Gallery is opening their majorRenoir and Loveexhibition next month, a show they hope will have the same blockbuster success it had at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris this summer.I want to defend Renoir, if only for the sake of debate, but I’ve hated his work for decades. I like him when he’s weird, when his nudes look like a super-psychedelic, ultra-horny version of Rubens with endless, surreal, undulating rolls of pink flesh. And I like a lot of his hazy, strange landscapes, though not as much as the work of any other impressionist. But for the most part, the haters are right.View image in fullscreenSoft focus … left, detail from Madame Colonna Romano; right, detail from Jeune Femme au Puits.Composite: Musée d’OrsayI mean look at the works the thieves made off with after cutting through the fence with bolt cutters in the early hours of the morning. The first isPortrait of Madame Colonna Romano, her tiny head dwarfed by shoulders so vastly broad she could play rugby for Saracens, all watched over by a tiny painting-within-a-painting of a constipated looking baby. The other,Jeune Femme au Puits, is an unfinished smudge of a woman pulling a bucket out of a well. An art detective said the thieves would “have no idea what to do” with the paintings, well, they probably have some idea, and it involves the dustbin.The best bit about this week’s heist on the Côte d’Azur is that the thieves actually took four paintings, but decided to leave two behind as they ran for it, including a portrait of a little boy who looks almost exactly like Boris Johnson. In all my years as an art critic, I’ve never managed a piece of criticism as incisive, cutting and direct as a bunch of criminals looking at a painting that they’d already nicked and thinking “leave it – it’s not worth it”.Explore more on these topicsArt and designArtPierre-Auguste RenoirArt theftFranceEuropeMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: America: the gulf, the lake and now the state – what’s next on Trump’s huge renaming spree?  | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: Farewell, New Mexico. The war isn’t going well and nowhere on Earth is safe from the US president’s favourite displacement activity, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: Farewell, New Mexico. The war isn’t going well and nowhere on Earth is safe from the US president’s favourite displacement activity, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Donald Trump on board Air Force One, 9  February 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump on board Air Force One, 9  February 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpAmerica: the gulf, the lake and now the state – what’s next on Trump’s huge renaming spree?Marina HydeFarewell, New Mexico. The war isn’t going well and nowhere on Earth is safe from the US president’s favourite displacement activityTue 8 Sep 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareBusy times for crayon-wielding US president Donald Trump, Earth’s most tireless freelance cartographer, who at the weekend celebrated the US labouring under thehighest diesel prices in its historywhile his “two-week” Iran war edges into its seventh month with a social media spree in which he pushed renaming New Mexico as New America.In some ways, it was a surprise to see Trump go for merely rebranding a state at this point, given that it was only so recently that he declared: “If you think about it,we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean.” This is believed to be a reference to the Gulf of America, formerly – and indeed currently, in every meaningful sense – the Gulf of Mexico. It was also a nod to Lake America, as precisely no one calls Lake Ontario despite Trump supposedly retitling it by executive order last month, in another fit of pique over his trade war with Canada. Candidates for this heavily trailed American Ocean clearly include the Pacific and the Atlantic – though why the other oceans should be locationally ineligible increasingly feels unclear. At this rate, geography exams in the US are also about to get a whole lot easier.In the end, you sense, most of the places in the US will go to the chop shop, and either have “America” bolted on the back, or have the Trump name fused on to them as a prefix. See the Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, or the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington DC. Or, indeed, the President Donald J Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida. A new class of warship may also be procured for naming privileges.As for potential rebrand candidates/victims, how your area votes clearly affects the order in which its landmarks – or itself in its entirety – will be slapped with a fun new identity. When proposing the New Mexico renaming, Trump casually noted that it was“one of the great vote-cheating states of all time”. I wouldn’t be feeling all that confident if I were the Georgia state capitol, or the Trump America capitol as it may imminently be known.Meanwhile, it must be said that all this frenetic activity does feel born of Trump’s conviction that it should surely be possible to shitpost his way out of anything, even a war. After all, the Iran war, which I seem to remember was won on day one, has now been going on for more than six months. This feels confusing. First it was going to be two weeks, then four to five weeks. Four days into Operation Epic Fury, Trump explained that the US was“already substantially ahead of our time projections”, while the secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, added: “It could move up, it could move back.” Having said that, evidence suggests it could only move up, although Trump wrapped up his first week of the conflict back in March by assuring the American people that his campaign continued “to totally demolish the enemy far ahead of schedule and at levels that people have never seen before”. Two days after that, the conflict was downgraded to “a short excursion”, with non-committal historical allies dismissed with a triumphant: “We don’t need people that join Wars after we’ve already won!” The war was “complete, pretty much”, he said two days later.View image in fullscreenMap of New Mexico renamed New America on Donald Trump’s social media.Illustration: @realDonaldTrumpAnd yet, was it? A couple of weeks in, Trump was explaining he’d know when the war should be over because he’d “feel it in my bones”. Alas, he seems to have failed to get the arthritic signal to pull out as late as three weeks in, despite assuring everyone that – contrary to appearances such as still bombing the shit out of things – the war had in fact been over “in two or three days”. Flash forward to a month in, and they were still “way ahead of schedule”, although once the five-week mark was hit Trump was dropping casual asides like “a whole civilization will die tonight”. Six weeks in, things were going “swimmingly”. Although, not to nitpick, but were they?That was April. In May, a deal with the Iranians could apparently “happen any day”. By the end of the month, it could have potentially happened “over the weekend”. Same thing a weekend later. A whole two months after that, unfortunately, Trump shifted from the war being over to declaring that his notional/imaginary agreements to end the war were in fact the thing that was “over”. He no longer wished to negotiate with Tehran. Jump ahead to the present day, in fact, and he has spent quite a lot of the past weekbombing the shit out of things again. Which is very much the behaviour of any state that won a war back in the first days of March. Unhelpfully, the former US defence secretary Leon Panetta estimated at the weekend that the war woulddrag on for another six months.All of which suggests there has really never been a better time to renameNew Mexico. Those eternal searchers for a so-called Trump doctrine are surely beginning to see that it essentially boils down to wimping out of the big, painful calls that could literally move the dial – for example, boots on the ground – and existing in an eternally figurative zone where you can simply post the problem away. Here, there is no better way to signal that the war is over than to unilaterally rename the strait of Hormuz either the strait of Trump, or the strait of America. As some psychologists like to say: you have to name it to tame it.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistWhat a Time to be Alive! by Marina Hyde (Guardian Faber Publishing, £20). To support the Guardian, order your signed copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal man | Movies | The Guardian
description: Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentary
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentary
Content: Charmless … Musk at a Trump campaign event in 2024.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenCharmless … Musk at a Trump campaign event in 2024.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APMoviesReviewMusk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manVenice film festival:Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentaryPeter Bradshawin VeniceTue 8 Sep 2026 08.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Elon is a nuke.” The speaker is Ashley St Clair, a former conservative Maga influencer and one of Elon Musk’s former girlfriends-slash-baby mommas.She is a fascinating expert witness in Alex Gibney’s four-hour epic study of the world’s richest and dullest man: the overgrown brattish South-African-born trillionaire plutocrat, ersatz visionary and Trump courtier who owns Tesla cars, SpaceX rocket ships, Starlink satellites on which nation states’ military capabilities are increasingly reliant, X (formerly Twitter) which shapes the collective “incel” id of billions and GrokAI whose vast server farms daily guzzle oceans of precious water.State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmRead moreAs head of Trump’s incompetent cost-cutting Doge (Department of Government Efficiency) unit, Musk actually increased the US deficit by sacking thousands of revenue officers whose job was to rake in tax – while reportedlyaccessing and improperly sharing Americans’ sensitive social security data.He does indeed look like a nuke, efficiently designed, destructive, seemingly unguided and uncontrolled.Gibney’s excellent film covers a lot of ground in its extraordinary story, although we don’t get to hear about the mysterious process that changed a balding youngster into a follicularly unchallenged mature man.Musk is a uniquely disquieting baseball-capped figure, grinning and giggling and smirking on a thousand sycophantic podcasts like a modern, hyper-evolved version of Anthony Trollope’s wealthy charlatan Augustus Melmotte in The Way We Live Now. But given Musk’s boyish love of space travel and sci-fi, Gibney wittily compares him to the hero of the 1936 film version of HG Wells’s The Man Who Could Work Miracles about godlike space aliens who capriciously confer supernatural powers on a banal, ordinary earthling.Gibney doesn’t get to talk to Musk (or Trump) though in the spirit of Musk’s AI interests, he creates a photorealistic CG avatar who mouths all the things the man himself is reported as saying (a rather contrived visual joke, actually, which the film didn’t need). He speaks to many professional colleagues, and to Musk’s formidably opinionated father Errol Musk who fills us in on Elon’s formative years in the tense world of South Africa in which young Musk was bullied and beaten up.Gibney speaks to Musk’s first wife Justine Musk (née Wilson), a passionate and intelligent woman who tells us about the tragedy of one of their infant children dying of Sids and then the hurt she felt when Elon felt the need to grandstand about this on social media, claiming the child had died in his arms (it was her arms, she says). And given that heart-wrenching death, how crass it was for him to announce later on social media that his trans daughter had “died” of “woke mind virus”. Much later, Musk showed a creepy enthusiasm for procreating many children with various women; Musk reportedlybuilt compounds for his extended familieslike something from The Handmaid’s Tale.Back in the 90s as a pushy, bright young tech innovator, Musk had started out by inventing and selling an online Yellow Pages-type site, got involved in Peter Thiel’s PayPal and cleaned up again when this was sold to eBay. He got involved in the electric automobile industry, giving us Teslas, whilemisleading the public about their range.Big tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?Read moreHis SpaceX adventure and his preposterous and ignorant effusions about colonising Mars were spectacular advertisements for his personal brand – so important for inflating stock market valuation – especially when he did indeed invent rockets that could be landed and re-used. But the question of how and when these rockets will carry us to inhabitable planets remains unanswered. Both his cars and his rocket ships got him on the receiving end of millions of dollars of federal money and lines of credit.And at the beginning of the 21st century he was still the darling of the liberal world and the Obama administration for an apparently compelling eco-vision for non-fossil-fuel cars.All this changed when Joe Biden seemed to be casting a cold eye on Musk’s businesses, and Musk went all in on promoting Trump 2.0 in 2024 and was rewarded with that grotesque Doge sinecure, damaging American public finances –from which he had benefited so lavishly.What is so absorbing about Gibney’s documentary is that it has the structure and rhetoric of a film that could be about, say, Elizabeth Holmes, disgraced inventor of the phoney blood-test, or Sam Bankman-Fried, the cryptocurrency fraudster, or Billy McFarland, promoter of the Fyre festival. All of these were media darlings in their day, supposed visionaries and feted disrupters, talking the talk in front of saucer-eyed believers.Unlike these illusionists Musk does have actual palpable success, with Tesla being a long-standing profitable company and Space X, among other things inventing successful re-usable rockets, allied with a skill they don’t have in moving on from commodity to commodity, while controlling the means of production in social media and cultivating the presidency. Just as well because, if Musk were ever to fall, it would truly send shock waves through Wall Street, Washington and Silicon Valley.Explore more on these topicsFilmElon MuskDocumentary filmsAlex GibneyDonald TrumpVenice film festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war | Meteorology | The Guardian
description: Experts helped guide weather scenes in Pressure – a film depicting dramatic buildup to 1944’s D-day landings
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Experts helped guide weather scenes in Pressure – a film depicting dramatic buildup to 1944’s D-day landings
Content: A scene from Pressure, with Brendan Fraser as Gen Dwight D Eisenhower, Andrew Scott as Capt James Stagg and Kerry Condon as Capt Kay Summersby.Photograph: Focus Features/PAView image in fullscreenA scene from Pressure, with Brendan Fraser as Gen Dwight D Eisenhower, Andrew Scott as Capt James Stagg and Kerry Condon as Capt Kay Summersby.Photograph: Focus Features/PAMeteorologyHow meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world warExperts helped guide weather scenes in Pressure – a film depicting dramatic buildup to 1944’s D-day landingsNicola DavisScience correspondentTue 8 Sep 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 15.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDressed in a Royal Air Force uniform and sporting a trim moustache,Andrew Scottlooks slightly queasy – as well he might. Behind him is a huge map of the Channel, and in front of him is Brendan Fraser, looming with a request: “I need a forecast,” he says.Starring in the film Pressure, based on a true story, Scott plays the meteorologist Gp Capt James Stagg – the man who must tell Gen Eisenhower – played by Fraser – whether conditions will be suitable for theD-daylandings scheduled to take place on 5 June 1944. But a large storm is approaching the Normandy coast.The film, showing in cinemas in the UK and Ireland from 9 September, unites two topics that ceaselessly fascinate the British: the second world war – and weather.It is also a rare treat for meteorologists, who are not hugely represented on the big screen and are delighted to be portrayed as the heroes of a film.Dr Stephen Burt of the University of Reading, an adviser for the film, said the challenge Stagg and his colleagues faced was enormous. “To do a forecast beyond 24 hours was, in the 1940s, like trying to land a man on the moon,” he said.Scientists had only recently started to use upper air data to predict the weather, he said, and largely relied on surface measurements of pressure, temperature, dew point, wind speed and direction, and experience-based intuition.One difficulty is that most of our weather comes in from the Atlantic. “Nowadays we have satellites and so on and we can see what’s coming, we have observations coming from the US,” he said. “But then there were … just a couple of ships, a couple of submarines maybe and some aircraft observations. And that’s it.”Crucially, the week before D-day was the hottest May week on record, Burt said – a high that was only broken this year. Then a huge storm blew up, with another close behind.View image in fullscreenBritish troops take positions on Sword beach during D-day on 6 June 1944, when there was a small window of clear weather.Photograph: Imperial War Museum/AFP/Getty ImagesProf Ed Hawkins of the University of Reading, an expert in historical weather data collection and examination, including D-day, explains that there were three teams working on the D-day forecasts – although only two are depicted in the film – all feeding into Stagg. Butthey took different approachesand produced different forecasts.It was up to Stagg to reconcile the results and present a recommendation to Eisenhower that would, ultimately, affect 160,000 Allied troops. “Stagg was in a very difficult position. He left his very pregnant wife to come and do this very important task,” Hawkins said.The teams were split about the forecast for 5 June – with Stagg concluding the conditions would be too perilous. The landings were postponed. But by the evening of 4 June a consensus emerged: there appeared to be a small but suitable window on 6 June. The invasion was back on.“They managed to do the forecast, and the invasion, and get away with it,” said Burt.Burt andhis colleaguesagree that even modern systems based on artificial intelligence have struggled to accurately predict conditions for 6 June 1944 using data available from the time.“[I’d] still have been chewing my fingernails on morning of the sixth,” said Burt.Catherine Ross, aMet Officearchivist, said film-makers used exact replicas of records from June 1944. “We were able to provide images of every single weather chart that was being produced at the time. We had codes and examples of how the observations were sent in and all sorts of documentation,” she said.She notes that even before modern technology, allied forecasters were on the front foot in terms of access to data. They already had data from the UK and across the Atlantic. “But because of Bletchley Park they had broken the Enigma code, so they had access to all of the German weather observations as well,” Ross said.While the German forces may have been aware of the storms, they were not aware of a potential break in the weather. “Sometimes there’s no Atlantic on the [German] chart, which is where the weather was coming from in early June 1944,” she added.It is no spoiler that D-day was a success for the British, but the film sheds new light on the drama that unfolded behind the scenes.“It’s the most famous forecast ever made by the Met Office. It’s probably one of the most important weather forecasts in history,” said Ross.This article was amended on 8 September 2026. The military rank given to James Stagg was that of group captain (Gp Capt), not captain as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsMeteorologyMet OfficeSecond world warD-dayAndrew ScottnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mr T: I Pity the Fool review – a rare chance with an electrifying star … and they blew it  | Television | The Guardian
description: The former A-Team legend tells his extraordinary story with endless charisma, but this show is so rushed that they even misspell his name. No wonder he isn’t happy with it
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The former A-Team legend tells his extraordinary story with endless charisma, but this show is so rushed that they even misspell his name. No wonder he isn’t happy with it
Content: A-Team player … Mr. T: I Pity the Fool.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenA-Team player … Mr. T: I Pity the Fool.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewMr T: I Pity the Fool review – a rare chance with an electrifying star … and they blew itThe former A-Team legend tells his extraordinary story with endless charisma, but this show is so rushed that they even misspell his name. No wonder he isn’t happy with itLucy ManganTue 8 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere’s a question: when was the last time you had as good a time as when you were watching The A-Team as a child? I know.Many of the best moments of the wholly unexpected documentary Mr T: I Pity the Fool recall his legendary turn as the soldiers of fortunes’ genius engineer, pugilist and instant fan favourite (not that we used the phrase then) BA Baracus. According to Mr T, the show was built around him; when you see now how well it plays to his talents and charisma – a proper tough guy, but shot through with warmth and humour, giving a perfectly outsize performance and never overplaying his hand – it makes a lot of sense, however much it would annoy George “Hannibal” Peppard to hear it.Mr T is now 74. Iknow. He looks a bit older, but the charisma is absolutely intact. He sits alone in a darkened room, occasionally being played old footage of his career’s highlights and lowlights, dressed in a stars-and-stripes boiler suit and bandana. You cannot take your eyes off him.Watch the trailer for the documentary.He has done very few public interviews since his heyday, but the clips they show from that period are electrifying, especially his thrillingly uncompromising one with David Letterman in which he unsmilingly explains his look to the increasingly cowed host. The Mohawk-style haircut and feathered earrings honour his African Mandinka warrior heritage. The gold chains are a transmutation of the shackles his ancestors were put in. He doesn’t get involved in “Black exploitation movies – no dope-dealing movies, no pimp roles … Give me the type of role you’d give Charlton Heston.” The audience laughs, not uneasily, missing and making his point.At the same time, his rise to fame and riches has an inescapably “only in America” feel to it. He was born Laurence Tureaud (spelled Tero throughout the documentary), one of 12 children to his loving and beloved mother Willa Lee, and brought up in an impoverished housing project in Chicago. He and his brothers worked on their fitness together – by the time he was 15, he already looked like an athlete-cum-bodybuilder.He renamed himself Mr T “so that the first word out of people’s mouths was always ‘Mister’”, after watching his father and brothers – including a Vietnam veteran – being habitually addressed as “Boy”. When his mother was robbed by local “thugs”, he went looking for them; although the story is left unfinished, it is implied that he carried out some serious physical damage. If so, it was a rare lapse in what seems to have been an otherwise hugely disciplined life.‘I don’t chase the dollar. I never did’: the astonishing hidden life of Mr TRead moreHe worked three manual jobs until bouncing gave way to bodyguarding and an entree into the world of television, which led to him being spotted by Sylvester Stallone and cast as the antagonist Clubber Lang in Rocky III. He turned up word-perfect to the audition – discipline again – met the ad-libbing requirements and worked on the accent the part originally required. The film was a hit – and so was Mr T.Then came The A-Team, enormous popularity and wealth (Mr T commercials and merch was everywhere), an almost inevitable inflation of ego – and then, in the mid-90s, a cancer diagnosis that, along with his increasing demands, caused his star to wane. Since then, he has become a man of God and finds fulfilment in good works and preaching.That, at least, is how the documentary tells it. In the accompanying publicity tour, Mr T has made clear that he finds the filmdishonest and unfair. He says that he wasn’t forced but chose to step out of the limelight, having fulfilled his ambition to set his mother up in comfort for the rest of her days. As a child, he had promised her a house and pretty dresses. “If that’s the lord’s willing,” she replied.Other objections include the time given to his former agent Peter Young (whom he says he had to sue and who is the main contributor of claims about Mr T’s diva behaviour and “bad decisions” professionally) compared with his longtime pastor, the Rev Henry Hardy, and the omission of counterweights to the hardman narrative.It is certainly a small, slight documentary. In a 50-minute runtime, some omissions are to be expected, but even without knowing about its subject’s resulting displeasure, the emphasis on the violent incident reads oddly and the misspelling of his name raises questions about the quality of the research. There is a sense of eagerness with which the picture of Mr T as a monstrous egomaniac is painted. At best, it feels like a rushed job. At worst, it feels like the imposition of another negative narrative on a Black man by fools who are more to be censured than pitied.Mr T: I Pity the Fool is available on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing | Israel | The Guardian
description: Ed Miliband announces sanctions on trade with settlers as PM says in the Guardian it is time to act
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Ed Miliband announces sanctions on trade with settlers as PM says in the Guardian it is time to act
Content: Palestinian landowners, journalists and protesters run from teargas fired by Israeli security forces blocking a road leading to a newly built Israeli settlement near Dura in the West Bank in June.Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPalestinian landowners, journalists and protesters run from teargas fired by Israeli security forces blocking a road leading to a newly built Israeli settlement near Dura in the West Bank in June.Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelUK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backingEd Miliband announces sanctions on trade with settlements as PM says in the Guardian it is time to actI believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy BurnhamPippa Crerar,Jessica ElgotandKiran StaceyTue 8 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 08.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSettler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank,Ed Milibandhas said, in the UK’s starkest condemnation since the foundation of the Israeli state.Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued,writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.In the Commons, the foreign secretary said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of theWest Bankwas unlawful in its entirety, as he announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.The dramatic shift in the UK’s position comes after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank, which has resulted in 12 nations – including France and Canada – announcing they would impose sanctions.In a joint statement Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney said: “The time has come to take further action to uphold our commitment to protect the two-state solution, our interests and to stand up for our values, before it is too late.”In response, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Saar, announced the closure of the UK consulate in Jerusalem and that 12 British MPs and activists – including Jeremy Corbyn and Labour MP Diane Abbott – would be banned from enteringIsrael.Saar accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”. Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, warned that the US could take retaliatory action over trade.However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Washington would “obviously” not follow the UK’s course of action, and did not want to see the West Bank destabilised, but declined to comment further. Burnham had briefed Donald Trump on the plan in advance.In his statement to parliament, Miliband said the UK government would enact:An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories and a new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK.Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence.A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.1:59UK foreign secretary announces sanctions on trade with Israeli West Bank settlements – videoThe foreign secretary said the UK’s actions would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice, and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whosehomes had been destroyedand from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment.The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.Ministers expect the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months, although they could be subject to legal challenge, which would result in a delay.Graph of demolitions in the West Bank since 2023Miliband stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, as some on the left have demanded, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts, but that there was evidence of “war crimes”.Speaking in the Commons, he said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.“All too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians.“I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”Graph of Palestinian civilian killings in West Bank since 2020Miliband suggested that Keir Starmer had been reluctant to take action against West Bank settlers during his time as prime minister. “I’ll say very bluntly we should have acted earlier. And it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation,” he told MPs.Burnham, whoapologised for Labour’s stance on Gazawhen he became prime minister, attempting to shore up votes on the party’s progressive flank, also said the previous government had been too slow to act.Writing in the Guardian , he said: “We have called for years for a two-state solution in the Middle East, but we must recognise that those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action. For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel.”Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust. “I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said.“And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state ofPalestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.”The foreign secretary said that to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.The action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine, he said, one that not only condemned but took action. “Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.”Burnham wrote that the British Jewish community must not be blamed for the actions of the Israeli government. “[It] is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple,” he said.“I met with the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society.”Far-right Israeli minister outlines plan for removal of all Palestinians from GazaRead moreThe shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said “illegal settlements are wrong” but suggested that Miliband was introducing policies the Foreign Office did not believe would work. Whitehall insiders denied this was the case.The senior Conservative MP also said there was a risk of harming Palestinians who worked in the West Bank and that “the economies of Palestine and Israel were too interconnected” for a ban on goods for illegal settlements to work.But the veteran Tory MP Edward Leigh gave full backing to the sanctions. “I am proud to say as the longest serving member of the Conservative Friends of Israel that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and justice for all people in this world,” he said.The move forms part of a broader attempt by Burnham’s government to reset British policy towards Israel, in part to regain the trust among Muslim and progressive voters in the UK they lost in the early days of the conflict.It was overwhelmingly welcomed by Labour MPs, many of whom have been struggling with the issue in their constituencies, although some sounded a note of caution about the potential impact on local Jewish communities.Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the foreign affairs select committee, said: “At last! I am so very happy to see a British government – a Labour British government – finally doing the right thing and taking a strong stance … no longer a bystander wringing their hands.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelForeign policyEd MilibandWest BankPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Far-right port protests: police told to improve intelligence gathering | Police | The Guardian
description: Whitehall officials ask why laws meant to clamp down on mask wearing at demonstrations were not used
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Whitehall officials ask why laws meant to clamp down on mask wearing at demonstrations were not used
Content: Anti-migrant protesters confront police at Portsmouth at the weekend.Photograph: Jamie Lashmar/PAView image in fullscreenAnti-migrant protesters confront police at Portsmouth at the weekend.Photograph: Jamie Lashmar/PAPoliceFar-right port protests: police told to improve intelligence gatheringWhitehall officials ask why laws meant to clamp down on mask wearing at demonstrations were not used​Vikram Dodd,Ben Quinn,Rajeev SyalTue 8 Sep 2026 15.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice have been told by the government they expect better intelligence gathering after masked far-right groups took to the streets at the weekend, the Guardian has learned, as the Kent force admitted mishandling warnings of potential trouble.Police in Kent on Saturday and thenPortsmouth, Hampshire, on Sunday said they were taken by surprise when hundreds massed to oppose what they say is illegal immigration via small boats.Both protests are believed by police to have been far-right inspired, with evidence emerging that those behind them were determined to avoid detection.Claims by Kent police since Saturday that they had no warning fell apart on Tuesday when the force admitted there werewarning calls to police on Friday eveningwhich were not acted upon.Kent police said: “The force had received non-emergency information late on Friday evening that a protest could take place in the town the following day. This information was not fully assessed.”The government’s view is that police actions once officers were faced by hundreds of men was reasonable.But there is dismay at how Kent police explained their decision-making afterwards, for instance viewing the gathered masked men outside the port of Dover as peaceful protesters, with one source describing it as “fucking crackers”.On Tuesday evening the prime minister, Andy Burnham, met police chiefs to discuss what had happened and preparedness for any further unrest.In Dover on Saturday, where hundreds of masked men in black converged undetected, police believe those taking to the streets used walkie-talkies to coordinate their actions.Police on the ground report the masked men had lawyers’ phone numbers and cited public order case law and were well briefed on how far they could go: “They toed the line perfectly to avoid arrest,” one source said.InHampshirepolice are investigating whether vehicles were deliberately left behind to block access roads.Police said the Dover gathering passed peacefully, while in Hampshire there were clashes, with the local Police Federation saying anger and violence was directed at officers.The Guardian understands that part of Hampshire police’s investigation will examine whether the gathering of 200 people was meant to harass or intimidate.A spokesperson added they are also hunting for those behind the violence, conducting “a thorough review of the body-worn video” to look for offenders.The protests are believed to have been coordinated on closed social media networks and not publicly advertised.Police are considering whether the threshold for warrants for covert tactics has been met, with one source warning that police were wary of criticism of using “police state tactics” against people portraying themselves as peaceful protesters motivated by a legitimate issue.The National Police Coordination Centre has intensified its monitoring.The action in Kent was organised by Daniel Thomas, a long-term associate of the far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known as Tommy Robinson. Thomas, who has established an umbrella grouping called Patriot Platform, was also linked to theblockade in Portsmouththe following day.Whitehall officials have asked police whytougher lawsin place since last year meant to clamp down on the wearing of face masks at protests were not used.The police view was that at Dover those gathered complied with requests from officers and dispersed after three hours. In Portsmouth, which was more heated, police prioritised a formal dispersal order which they think worked.Both police and government sources say the “optics” of masked men in black thronging the streets looked “intimidating”.Also on Tuesday it emerged that lifeboat staff who picked up 120 asylum seekers from a large dinghy in the Channel on Sunday were refused entry to two ports shortly before being harangued by right-wing protesters.Crew on two RNLI vessels were also threatened with legal action if they approachedSouthamptonPort and tried to bring the claimants ashore.They were forced to take the migrants several miles away to Eastney, where police, firefighters, Border Force and other officials faced protests by up to 200 people, most of whom wore balaclavas and black clothing.Peter Sparkes, the chief executive of the RNLI, said abuse of its volunteers is “wholly unacceptable in a civilised society”.He said recent protests had “generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding” about the charity, and condemned threats by “those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard”.Officials confirmed that a broadcast on an open marine VHF radio said Southampton Vessel Traffic Service and King’s Harbour Master Portsmouth denied the RNLI permission to enter their ports.The two RNLI rescue boats from Bembridge and Yarmouth had intercepted a “mega-dinghy” that had left Utah beach near Cherbourg in Normandy.A spokesperson for Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates the port of Southampton, said: “ABP did receive an enquiry about landing recovered migrants at the port of Southampton. We had to decline the enquiry as the port did not have suitable reception facilities available. If there had been a safety of life at sea issue where Southampton was the closest port or if we had received a formal direction from the relevant authority then we would have played a role. Neither was the case in this situation.”On Tuesday, anti-migrant protesters attempted to identify RNLI volunteers involved in rescuing those onboard the dinghy. Demonstrators named and shared pictures on X of two people they said were volunteers, claiming they had tracked down an address for one of the men.Sparkes’s words come after footage posted on social media showed volunteers labelled as “traitors”. In a statement issued on Tuesday, Sparkes said the misinformation led to “some of our volunteers and staff [being] the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse.“The RNLI’s people represent the very best in our society. They selflessly give up their time to keep others safe.“Yet they and their families are being threatened by those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard.“Their action, in contrast, is wholly unacceptable in a civilised society.“We will take whatever steps we can to care for and protect our people and their families.”Explore more on these topicsPoliceFar rightSouthamptonPortsmouthKentHampshireImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK air traffic control problem strands hundreds of thousands of passengers | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: More than 1,000 flights cancelled as airlines call for overhaul of ATC system after third incident in just over three years
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: More than 1,000 flights cancelled as airlines call for overhaul of ATC system after third incident in just over three years
Content: People queue at check-in desks at Heathrow terminal 5 after large-scale disruption caused by an air traffic control system glitch.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople queue at check-in desks at Heathrow terminal 5 after large-scale disruption caused by an air traffic control system glitch.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesAirline industryUK air traffic control problem strands hundreds of thousands of passengersMore than 1,000 flights cancelled as airlines call for overhaul of ATC system after third incident in just over three yearsUK airport disruption: what are your rights?Gwyn TophamTransport correspondentTue 8 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 10.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of thousands of air passengers had flights delayed or cancelled after another UK air traffic control technical glitch kept planes grounded for hours on Tuesday.Airlines demanded action after a “technical issue” at the air traffic control services provider Nats caused the third large-scale stoppage in just over three years.Flight monitoring website Flightradar24 said more than 1,000 flights had been cancelled at UK airports by about 8pm in an incident that started at about 1pm and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports, including Heathrow and Gatwick.Nats said on Tuesday evening that work was continuing to assist airlines and airports recover from the disruption, adding: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.”By the time Nats said it had identified and implemented a fix to restart its flight processing system almost four hours later, most flights scheduled to depart from theLondonairports and others were yet to take off. The disruption had spread to include incoming flights to much of southern England.Cancellations and delays were continuing well into Tuesday evening, andBritish Airwayssaid disruption would affect operations through Wednesday at least, with passengers offered free rebooking until Friday.Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed and 50 flights cancelled. The knock-on effects hit flights across Europe, according to easyJet. Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely until the evening.All London airports, as well as Manchester and Birmingham, were among the most directly affected. Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted.According to the flight monitoring website FlightRadar24, easyJet had 137 flights cancelled, British Airways 111, KLM 26, Eurowings 22 and Ryanair 21 by 5pm.View image in fullscreenPassengers stranded at London Gatwick’s south terminal.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PANats initially announced at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”. It later identified the problem in its flight processing system, and announced at 4.40pm that it had implemented a fix.A spokesperson said the fault was not the same as the ones that caused previous outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.They said the system was only “starting to recover”.“We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery,” they said. “We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.”The chief executive of Nats, Martin Rolfe, expressed his “huge sympathies to everyone who has been caught up in today’s disruption”.“We absolutely take responsibility for this,” he told Sky News.“We never want this sort of thing to happen. I completely understand how frustrating it is for passengers.”He claims, however, “these things are relatively rare”.“We resolved it to get back to our systems operating normally,” he added. “But of course, there’s a huge amount of disruption that’s now built up in the system.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’re working very closely now with airlines and airports to try to work through the night to make sure that we can get as many people travelling as possible.”The air traffic control problems follow an“isolated event” a year agothat caused widespread disruption, although it so far appears less severe than the fullgrounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.However, British Airways said that “the severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact for customers and colleagues”.“We were forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday afternoon, inconveniencing tens of thousands of customers,” a spokesperson said.“This incident was entirely out of our control and incredibly frustrating for our customers and colleagues, with aircraft and crews ending up out of place.”Heathrow said late on Tuesday that departures had resumed with disruptions but arrivals had been suspended for the rest of the night.Airlines renewed calls for Nats to be overhauled after the third incident ascribed to its systems in as many years.Ryanair repeated its calls for Rolfe to resign. The Irish airline’s chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Families travelling on holiday, people travelling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for Nats’ abhorrent failure.”He said the government should “stop making excuses for repeated Nats failures and appoint a new leader capable of running the UK ATC system”.Wizz Air said: “A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. Nats is simply not fit for purpose in its current form.”The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “I’m aware of a technical issue impacting flights at airports including Heathrow and Gatwick. Technicians have identified the issue and are fixing it as we speak. I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry.“I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job.”Explore more on these topicsAirline industryHeathrow airportGatwick airportLondonAir transportStansted airportTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two more people arrested over ‘mountain of illegal waste’ dumped in Oxfordshire | Waste | The Guardian
description: A total of six people apprehended as clean-up of rubbish stacked 10 metres high cost about £6m
Author: Charlie Moloney
Headline: A total of six people apprehended as clean-up of rubbish stacked 10 metres high cost about £6m
Content: Fly-tippers dumped hundreds of tonnes of waste in a field between the River Cherwell and the A34 near Kidlington, Oxfordshire, west of London.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFly-tippers dumped hundreds of tonnes of waste in a field between the River Cherwell and the A34 near Kidlington, Oxfordshire, west of London.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesWasteTwo more people arrested over ‘mountain of illegal waste’ dumped in OxfordshireA total of six people apprehended as clean-up of rubbish stacked 10 metres high cost about £6mCharlie MoloneyTue 8 Sep 2026 17.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men have been arrested after fly-tippers dumped a “mountain of illegal waste”, stacked 10 metres high, inOxfordshire.Hundreds of tonnes of rubbish appeared in a field between the River Cherwell and the A34 near Kidlington in November last year. The waste tip was so large that removing it could cost more than the local council’s annual budget, the area’s MP said.The clean-up operation, which concluded last month, took five months. An estimated 22,704 tonnes of rubbish were cleared, with the operation costing an estimated £6m.The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed on Tuesday that a 21-year-old man from Ashford in Surrey and a 43-year-old man from Stanwell in Surrey had been arrested.It brings the total number of people apprehended to six, after one arrest in February, two in January and one in November, the EA said.The watchdog shut down the Kidlington site in October after officers discovered continued criminal activity after the first report of dumping at the site in July 2025.Colin Chiverton, area environment manager for the Thames at the EA, said: “The dumping at Kidlington was abhorrent and had no regard for the local community.“We moved quickly to remove all illegal waste from the site and our teams continue to work tirelessly on this investigation. These arrests are another vital step in collecting new evidence and delivering justice for the residents of Kidlington.”Dame Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said: “This government said we’d take on waste criminals and that’s exactly what we’re doing.“These arrests are another step towards delivering justice for Kidlington residents, who have had to put up with the dumping of disgusting waste.“The years of waste crime being allowed to fester have ended. We are taking decisive action through our crackdown and putting more officers on the frontline to restore pride in our communities.”The two men have been released on conditional bail pending further investigations.The EA previously announced it was to spend millions of pounds to clear the enormous illegal rubbish dump, saying the waste was at risk of catching fire.Its policy is to refuse to clear up illegal waste dumps across the country, instead pursuing the perpetrators and landowners. But officials said they had taken the exceptional decision to clear up the waste outside Kidlington, which is next to the River Cherwell, because the scale of the fire risk set it apart from other illegal waste dumps in England and presented an overriding public imperative.The agency was given no extra money to clear the waste, and the EA said this would come from “making efficiencies in its operations”. The cost to the taxpayer would also include the payment of the landfill tax on the waste to the Treasury.The dumping in Kidlington took place under the noses of the EA, which was monitoring the site after being alerted to suspicious activity.Explore more on these topicsWasteEnvironment AgencyOxfordshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: British family of man abducted by Saudi Arabia speak out over nine-year ordeal | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Mira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Mira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017
Content: Rami Naimi with his son, Ali, his wife, Mira, and his daughters, Saria and Noor, in 2016.Photograph: Bring Rami Home Campaign/PAView image in fullscreenRami Naimi with his son, Ali, his wife, Mira, and his daughters, Saria and Noor, in 2016.Photograph: Bring Rami Home Campaign/PASaudi ArabiaBritish family of man abducted by Saudi Arabia speak out over nine-year ordealMira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017Geneva AbdulTue 8 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 10.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British woman has spoken out for the first time about the alleged abduction, torture and coercion of her husband at the hands of Saudi authorities, after nine years of “failed” quiet diplomacy.The businessman Rami Naimi was first abducted in Dubai in 2017 on his return from a trip to Australia with his father. After being tortured, he was released the following year.The father of three, who is the son ofAli Al-Naimi, a former Saudi oil minister and head of the state oil company Aramco, was detained again in 2022 and held for two years. Last year he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial.He was initially detained alongside 400 of the kingdom’s most powerful people in an infamous round-upat the the Ritz-Carlton hotelin Riyadh, which became the biggest and most contentious purge in the modern kingdom’s history.Speaking out for the first time after years of what they described as a failed diplomatic process, his family has alleged abduction, disappearance, torture and coercion at the hands of Saudi authorities.Naimi now faces a second trial for allegedly following certain accounts on X critical ofSaudi Arabiaand for attempting to leave the country without permission – both of which he denies.“The first thing I wanted to do was speak out, but I was told no,” said his wife, Mira Lozi, speaking alongside her son at acampaign launch to bring Naimi homein London on Tuesday.Lozi, currently fighting cancer, fought back tears as she said she had been encouraged to keep silent since 2017 to help secure his release.“For nine years my children and I have lived through a nightmare,” she said. “Saying the truth today is like a liberation, enough is enough and we’re just hoping that we can end this nightmare and all the governments will be able to help us.”View image in fullscreenMira Lozi with her husband, Rami Naimi.Photograph: Bring Rami Home Campaign/PANaimi left Saudi Arabia aged 13 and travelled for years between the UK, US and Middle East as a businessman. His family claim he was abducted in Dubai in 2017 after returning home from a book tour trip from Australia with his father.They say he was blindfolded and forcibly taken by car to Abu Dhabi and then by private jet to Saudi Arabia. He was surprised to find himself with the others who had been rounded up, his family said, as he is not a journalist, activist or politician.His abduction in 2017 came as the kingdom’s elite were detained at a five-star hotel in Riyadh during a purge in which princes, tycoons and ministers were stripped of their fortunes. Accounts later surfaced detailing torture and coercion, and the event preceded the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, whoseassassination at the Saudi consulatein Istanbul in 2018 sparked revulsion around the world.Naimi was held at the hotel and tortured, electrocuted, waterboarded and psychologically abused for three months, his family said. He was told, falsely, that his father was being tortured next door. He was released in January 2018 after signing a “settlement agreement”.He was subsequently forced to sign a document pledging to surrender 5bn Saudi riyals, later “discounted” to 1bn riyals (£200m) – which the family says neither he nor they possess. Naimi was placed under electronic surveillance and banned from leaving the kingdom.His family said he was disappeared again for nearly two years in 2022, and subjected to further torture, and emotional and psychological abuse. They said they had no idea if he was alive or dead, and learned only through the help of his legal team and diplomats that he was being held in Saudi’s notorious Al Ha’ir prison.It was after his release in March 2025, with an electronic tag and subject to a travel ban, that he learned of charges against him claiming he had “exploited” his father’s official influence. Naimi faced allegations he acted as an agent for a US company in Saudi Arabia and helped Aramco to secure a contract to provide technology to prevent diesel smuggling.After seven years without charges, Naimi, an EU citizen, was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial. Now he is unable to leave Saudi Arabia and his communications with his family remain monitored. He has no idea, the family said, of their decision to go public with his case.“Until today we have no idea why Rami was targeted,” said Lozi, who is too frightened to return to Saudi Arabia or travel to the United Arab Emirates.“It really is something out of a movie. It’s shocking and we just want to end this nightmare,” said his 21-year-old son, Ali, who was 12 when his father was abducted.In recent years the UK’s relationship with Saudi Arabia has come under scrutiny over the flow of arms between the two countries, Riyadh’s use of public executions and targeting of exiled activists and dissidents.“Any family making a decision like this needs to be supported by the government,” said human rights lawyer Caoilfhionn Gallagher KC, who is leading the case.As the family hopes to meet the new prime minister and foreign secretary, Gallagher said the recent appointmentof a special envoy for Britons detained overseasdid not go as far as campaigners, experts andparliamentarians had called for.Gallagher described it as: “Tea and sympathy for a very limited group of people.”Last month the Guardianreportedthat X had become the latest US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.The UK Foreign Office declined to comment. The Saudi embassy in London has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricaHuman rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Glastonbury tickets break £400 for first time as on-sale date is announced | Glastonbury festival | The Guardian
description: Tickets set to cost £408 at return for Somerset festival after a fallow year, a jump from £378.50 in 2025
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Tickets set to cost £408 at return for Somerset festival after a fallow year, a jump from £378.50 in 2025
Content: Glastonbury’s Pyramid stage, pictured in 2023.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGlastonbury’s Pyramid stage, pictured in 2023.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianGlastonbury festivalGlastonbury tickets break £400 for first time as on-sale date is announcedTickets set to cost £408 at return for Somerset festival after a fallow year, a jump from £378.50 in 2025Ben Beaumont-ThomasTue 8 Sep 2026 13.58 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a fallow year in 2026,Glastonbury festivalfans can start to get excited – and nervous – about tickets for 2027’s event going on sale.The price breaks £400 for the first time, at £408 including a £5 booking fee, a rise from the 2025 cost of £378.50. The usual scramble to acquire them – with all the attendant frantic spreadsheets and WhatsApp groups – will begin at 9am on Sunday 4 October.To encourage festival-goers to take more environmentally sound coaches rather than cars, tickets bundled with coach travel go on sale earlier, at 6pm on Thursday 1 October.Harry Styles is already much rumoured to be headlining, with the likes of Taylor Swift, Fontaines DC, Sabrina Carpenter and Fred Again among others mooted by the bookies.Organiser Emily Eavis scotched rumours that Madonna would play, saying: “No, it’s definitely not Madonna, I’ll tell you that. But we have got three [other] headliners and we’re very excited about it – it’s all coming together really well.”In 2025, the festival was headlined by the 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo, with the latter described as “the weekend’s best big set” in a five-star Guardian review.There were also secret sets from Pulp, Skepta, Haim and more, and acclaimed turns from Doechii, Alanis Morissette and others. But there was controversy around Kneecap’s appearance at the festival, as well as the act that preceded them:Bob Vylan, who led a chantof “death to the IDF”. Then-BBC director general, Tim Davie, said “I deeply regret that such offensive and deplorable behaviour appeared on the BBC,” and the furore led to an internal investigation.Since that previous edition, Eavis’s father, Michael, who founded the festival in 1970, has turned 90. Speaking to the BBC in October, he said: “It’s all been a long story of excitement. That’s probably what’s keeping me going.”He added: “I was always at war with the council and the village and the local magistrates and the police”, as he turned the festival from a gathering on his Somerset dairy farm into arguably the world’s greatest music festival. “And it came good. Which is extraordinary, really. The fight was really what made it work, there’s no doubt about that. It was certainly worth it.”The 2027 festival takes place between June 23-27. Anyone wanting to buy a ticket must register with the festival by 5pm BST on Friday 25 September. Tickets can be paid for in full or with a £100 deposit, with the rest paid off in the first week of April. Under-13s attend for free.Explore more on these topicsGlastonbury festivalFestivalsMusic festivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI claims to have solved maths problem that stumped humans for decades | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: Company behind ChatGPT says 10,000 of its AI systems cracked the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Company behind ChatGPT says 10,000 of its AI systems cracked the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours
Content: OpenAI denied that the company had used work from rivals to solve the notoriously difficult puzzle.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI denied that the company had used work from rivals to solve the notoriously difficult puzzle.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersMathematicsOpenAI claims to have solved maths problem that stumped humans for decadesCompany behind ChatGPT says 10,000 of its AI systems cracked the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hoursIan SampleandDan MilmoTue 8 Sep 2026 17.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI claims to have solved a major mathematics problem that has stumped humans for nearly a century after spending millions of dollars on the artificial intelligence-led endeavour.The company behind ChatGPT said it had cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven Millennium Prize Problemspublished by the Clay Mathematics Instituteto highlight some of the biggest unsolved puzzles in the field.However, the announcement swiftly became mired in controversy after mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, a professor at New York University, said OpenAI accelerated its work on the problem after hearing that he and another researcher at Anthropic, an OpenAI rival, were poised to announce their own breakthrough.Buckmaster had further concerns because the pair’s work in progress was stored in OpenAI’s Codex model, which is used for writing computer programs, potentially making the work visible to the OpenAI team.In a document posted on his website, he added: “I do not know what their model did, or how. I do not know whether our data was used. I am not accusing anyone of anything.”At a press briefing on Tuesday, OpenAI researcher Sebastien Bubeck denied that the company had used the pair’s work or accessed material shared with OpenAI’s servers.OpenAI’s announcement on the breakthrough gave more details, saying that the company was inspired to launch the effort after hearing rumours that two Millennium Prize Problems had been solved. It also said it could not rule out that data from the pair’s use of their products “helped improve our models.”OpenAI said it tackled theNavier-Stokes problemwith an internal OpenAI system that was more powerful than its latest GPT-6 Astra model. About 10,000 AI agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – worked on the problem at once and reached the solution in 88 hours.“A major goal of our work is to empower scientists to advance research and technology that benefits all of humanity,” OpenAI researcherswrote in a blog.“We believe it is important to inform the world about the pace of AI progress and what to expect from upcoming models”.OpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went rogueRead moreThe breakthrough is the latest to demonstrate how advanced artificial intelligence models consuming enormous amounts of computing power are encroaching on and reshaping the field of mathematics. In May, OpenAI claimed progress inanother mathematical problemfirst proposed 80 years ago, while Google DeepMind has alsoclaimed maths achievementswith its models.Bubeck said the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem was “a spectacular culmination of the arc we have seen over the past 12 months”.The Navier-Stokes problem asks whether equations that are used to describe the movement of fluids like air and water fail under particular conditions. OpenAI’s proof suggests that they do, with the equations occasionally “blowing up” with the speed of fluids becoming impossibly infinite. It took OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra about 17 hours to verify the solution.Mathematicians who solve any of the Millennium Prize Problems are in line for a $1m (£740,000) reward from the ClayMathematicsInstitute. OpenAI, which is preparing for a flotation that could value the business at around $1tn, said it did not intend to claim the prize.The clash with Buckmaster aside, the maths announcement also allows OpenAI to cast its technology in a positive light after a period of alarm over how safely it is being developed. OpenAI revealed in July that a swarm of agents hadhacked into Hugging Face, a third'-party software store, during a cybersecurity test.The incident, plus asimilar episode at Anthropic, has led to renewed calls for curbs on AI development, with US senators calling last week for apermanent ban of AI “superintelligence”– the term for systems that outperform humans in all cognitive tasks.Explore more on these topicsMathematicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAInewsShareReuse this content

title: Ed Miliband has overturned decades of Foreign Office inertia on illegal Israeli settlements | Israel | The Guardian
