title: Commons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Opposition to Miliband’s announcement of sanctions rings hollow – helped by fewer than 10 Tory backbenchers turning up to debate
Author: John Crace
Headline: Opposition to Miliband’s announcement of sanctions rings hollow – helped by fewer than 10 Tory backbenchers turning up to debate
Content: An Israeli military bulldozer uproots olive trees on a Palestinian farm in the village of Arraba, near the West Bank city of Jenin, on 2 September 2026.Photograph: Majdi Mohammed/APView image in fullscreenAn Israeli military bulldozer uproots olive trees on a Palestinian farm in the village of Arraba, near the West Bank city of Jenin, on 2 September 2026.Photograph: Majdi Mohammed/APThe politics sketchPoliticsCommons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlementsJohn CraceOpposition to Miliband’s announcement of sanctions rings hollow – helped by fewer than 10 Tory backbenchers turning up to debateTue 8 Sep 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareNobody can say they weren’t warned. The Andy Burnham government might have looked like Continuity Keir with more positive vibes for the first six weeks or so, but on Tuesday a new line was drawn. When Burnham said he felt Labour had not done enough on Palestine and Gaza, he had meant it. His decision to imposetrade sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bankwas to be his first break with the past.Some opponents chose to get their retaliation in early, beforeEd Milibandhad even stood up to make the announcement in the Commons on Tuesday. Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador, declared on Sunday that Ed was guilty of “hating Jews”. Which rather implied he thought Ed hated himself.Huckabee also wondered when we would get round to sanctioning Russia, China and North Korea. Er … We have, Mike. Try to keep up.The Israeli president, Isaac Herzog, insisted that “the UK would be on the wrong side of history” if the sanctions were imposed. Presumably that means that doing nothing asIsraeli settlers, with the explicit endorsement of the Israeli government, seize land, burn homes and kill children is the right side of history. It’s a strange world we live in.Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right security minister, went completely rogue. His take was that this made “Las Malvinas” Argentinian territory. As though it was the sanctions that were the nail in the coffin for the Falklands. Still, there was some consistency there. TheIsraelgovernment has never placed much weight on the rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination. So why should they bother to make an exception for the Falkland islanders?Nor was all the oppo to be found abroad. Kemi Badenoch wrote a piece for the Jewish Chronicle in which she insisted that the government was desperate to win back Islamists and that Jews would no longer be safe in this country. Bizarrely, though, she made no effort to engage with what the Tories proposed to do about the Israeli settlements. Presumably nothing. Just give another nod and a wink to Benjamin Netanyahu as yet more Palestinians are forced off their land. I mean, it’s not as if the diplomatic efforts until now have had much effect.By contrast, the Commons itself was an oasis of calm. Proof that just occasionally MPs are capable of behaving and arguing as adults. A proper debate with proper arguments, sincerely held. This could have been partly helped by fewer than 10 Tory backbenchers having bothered to turn up – we have to assume most of them don’t care much either way what goes on in theWest Bank– but the Labour benches were all but full. For most of them, this was a statement that was long overdue. Though there was little triumphalism to be seen. More like relief. Burnham even showed up to lend support.Milibandstarted by addressing his own Jewishness. He had reason to be grateful to Israel for providing a home to some of his relatives and he condemned all forms of antisemitism. But there was a separation to be made between the Israelis and the Israeli government. This was about righting a wrong, not giving in to hatred. And these sanctions would only apply to goods and services provided to or from the illegal settlements. This wasn’t a blanket ban on everything Israeli. It was about taking a moral stance. At no longer being a bystander while a foreign government broke the law. It was time to live our values and fight oppression and suffering. We were not powerless. It was the only way to maintain the dream of a two-state solution. Nor were we alone. France and Canada had also joined other countries in imposing sanctions.The tone of the debate was immeasurably improved by having Tom Tugendhat reply for the Tories. Had Priti Patel still been the shadow foreign secretary, it would almost certainly have become a lot more bitter. Although Tugendhat was clearly operating with one hand tied behind his back. It wasn’t immediately clear what Tom really thought about the sanctions, but he was under instructions from Kemi to say they were definitely a bad thing and they needed to be opposed. So that’s rather what he had to do.Tugendhat began with a long list of things with which he agreed in Miliband’s statement. That the settlements were illegal, that crimes had been committed, that Hamas were a terrorist organisation and that a two-state solution was the only workable outcome. You felt that in another world, Tom might have left it at that. But he had a job to do so he came out with a few comebacks. The sanctions wouldn’t work, British security would be compromised and 25% of the UK would die because we would no longer receive Israeli pharmaceuticals.As with Kemi, Tom couldn’t quite square all this away with his default position of doing nothing. Tugendhat considers himself a man of action. Someone who would much rather be seen to be doing something. Now he was left to endorse the option of continuing to let Netanyahu get away with allegations of literal murder. As if all our allies automatically got a free pass. An annual allowance of dead children. Up to 100 and we promise to look the other way.Much of the rest of the statement was taken withLabourMPs offering their appreciation to a government that had listened to their concerns. Nor was it just the home crowd. Edward Leigh declared he was the longest-standing member of the Conservative friends of Israel and he was 100% behind Miliband in this. Enough was enough. Kit Malthouse and Desmond Swayne felt much the same. When you have these three on your side, you’ve almost certainly more than made your case.Oliver Dowden was a little more reticent. Couldn’t we have waited just a little bit longer? Until after the Israeli elections. Then Netanyahu might be out of office and a more moderate government installed in its place. It was hard to know what he was getting at. It’s not as if any Israelis are in much doubt about the nature of their current government. Britain imposing sanctions isn’t going to sway some marginal voters into thinking that maybe they needed more illegal settlements after all. Maybe it was just Oliver’s way of thinking out loud. He’s easily confused after all.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsThe politics sketchEd MilibandAndy BurnhamLabourIsraelWest BankPalestinecommentShareReuse this content

title: Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’ | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Nothing good can come of ditching annual investor votes on remuneration reports or encouraging online-only shareholder meetings
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Nothing good can come of ditching annual investor votes on remuneration reports or encouraging online-only shareholder meetings
Content: The UK’s business department is launching a consultation on ‘modernising corporate reporting to support long-term economic growth’.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe UK’s business department is launching a consultation on ‘modernising corporate reporting to support long-term economic growth’.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPANils Pratley on financeBusinessYes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’Nils PratleyNothing good can come of ditching annual investor votes on remuneration reports or encouraging online-only shareholder meetingsTue 8 Sep 2026 13.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe government, like every other one in living memory, is on a mission to reduce red tape for business. The former chancellor Rachel Reeves promised“a blitz on bureaucracy” and “pointless admin”and here comes the business department witha 12-week consultationon “modernising corporate reporting to support long-term economic growth”.Never mind that cutting energy costs for business would, by an order of magnitude, do more to support growth than any bonfire of red tape ever will. The consultation is still worthwhile: clearing out accumulated clutter, exploring digital options and clarifying reporting “exemptions and exclusions” for small- and medium-sized companies could free up a bit of time for doing more business.But two ideas in this burden-lifting exercise are terrible because they involve an unacceptable loss of transparency.One is the idea of dropping annual shareholder votes on companies’ remuneration reports. The supposed justification is that, since a binding vote on a company’s overall remuneration policy would still be required on a three-yearly cycle, there is no point in having an annual advisory-only poll on how the policy has been implemented.Such a weaselly idea could only have come from those FTSE 100 companies that resent scrutiny of their directors’ mega-bucks pay packages. Too bad: annual votes are a modest (and mostly ineffectual anyway) check on runaway boardroom rewards. Obliging the non-executives on the remuneration committee to justify their decisions to the outside world, in the knowledge the owners will vote, is a bare minimum requirement for retaining a bit of accountability in the system. If the chief executive has to squirm when, say, 30% of shareholders rebel, so be it. By rights, any reform ought to be in the other direction: it would be better to make the annual poll binding.The government’s other bad proposal is to encourage the trend among quoted companies towards online-only annual shareholder meetings. It’s true that many such meetings struggle to attract attendances in double figures, so the desire to turn the thing into a glorified Teams call is vaguely understandable. But a well-established principle is at stake: even small investors in a listed company should have the right, once a year, to buttonhole the bosses and ask a question in the flesh.The best solution in a digital age is hybrid meetings – let the shareholders decide if they wish to turn up or dial in. It is hardly an onerous requirement on the company to make a meeting room available. Again, one suspects the dead-hand of corporate affairs departments at work: with honourable exceptions, they don’t like the hassle of dealing with retail investors or campaign groups. Sorry, but that’s life.One other piece of advice for the department: yes, it’s true that annual reports have grown monstrous in size – running to “98,000 words, longer than JRR Tolkien’s The Hobbit” on average,it complains. And, yes, burdensome reporting requirements explain part of the growth. But it’s also true that companies don’t help themselves by padding out their productions with acres of irrelevant corporate babble.If, as the consultation says, annual reports are “a document primarily intended for investors and creditors”, make them easy to use. Part of the corporate instinct to write at Tolkien-like length stems, one suspects, is from fear of being accused of leaving anything out. The result, too often, is unreadable guff that doesn’t offer a concise account of the directors’ view of how the company is run and the risks and opportunities it faces.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBy all means, reform some of the reporting burdens – there are probably plenty to go at. But don’t undermine the transparency offered by annual votes on pay and annual meetings. And don’t allow companies to use “regulatory requirements” as an excuse for boilerplate communication.Explore more on these topicsBusinessNils Pratley on financeCorporate governanceAnnual resultsFinancial sectorExecutive pay and bonusescommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s approval rating is plummeting – as his fortune grows and grows | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of living, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of living, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Altruism personified … Donald Trump this month.Photograph: Samuel Corum/EPAView image in fullscreenAltruism personified … Donald Trump this month.Photograph: Samuel Corum/EPAOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s approval rating is plummeting – as his fortune grows and growsArwa MahdawiThe US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of livingTue 8 Sep 2026 09.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIf I had a dollar for every time Donald Trump said something inane, I would be a very rich woman. But even with an income that steady, I could never hope to be as flush as the president.A Forbes calculationfrom March puts his net worth at about $6.5bn – and it’s growing rapidly. Trumpmade $2.2bnin 2025 via business interests that ranged from selling cryptocurrency andTrump Biblesto offeringearly accessto his (oftenmarket-moving) Truth Social posts.To be fair, Trump isn’t making all this money just so he can buy golf clubs and gold toilets. No, he’s amassing these billions for the good of the little people; it’s altruism, not avarice! “I do this for our Country, not myself,” the president wrote on Truth Social onSunday nightalongside an AI-generated picture of him trading Intel stock. “I’ve made Hundreds of Billions of Dollars on Stocks, and many other type Holdings, for the U.S.A., not myself, and all I do is get criticized by the Radical Left Dumocrats. Very unfair, but what can you do!”Oh, I have some ideas about what you can do, Mr President. Unfortunately, I can’t print most of them. I also can’t explain why Trump said he’s madehundredsof billions, apart from pointing to his propensity for exaggeration. It seems his post was referring to the fact that the US governmenttook a 9.9% stakein Intel last year. That stake was worth $8.9bn at the time and as of Friday is worth nearly five times as much.According to the Trump administration, this is a win for everyone. In May, the White Housereleased a statementcalling Intel’s surging stock price “a direct windfall for American taxpayers”. Weirdly, I seem to have missed my portion of that windfall. Intel’s stock price has had little impact on my life. Whatishaving an impact is the soaring cost of necessities such as electricity and groceries.But I shouldn’t be grumpy, should I? I should be grateful that our intrepid president is balancing the demands of the day job with stock trading for the good of the country. According toTrump’s latest government disclosure, he made more than 1,000 equity trades in June. And his picks are doing very well: a report published in August by Democrats on Congress’s joint economic committee argued that Trump’s holdings in oil and gas stockshad risen by nearly $16mbecause of the war with Iran. “Experts on government ethics have flagged how rare it is for presidents to hold and trade stocks in individual companies, especially since Trump’s war in Iran and his other favors to the oil industry have all pushed up the value of Big Oil stocks,” the report read.Trump’s shamelessness may be rare, but he isn’t the only politician with serious conflicts of interest issues apropos stock market dealings.A 2022 New York Times investigationfound that, from 2019 to 2021, 97 lawmakers or their family members traded financial assets in industries that could be affected by their legislative committee work. In 2020, for example, the wife of the now retired Democratic congressman Alan Lowenthal sold her Boeing shares a day before a House committee on which Lowenthal sat released a damning report about the company. Lowenthal told the Times that he was not involved in this trade at all, so I imagine it was just a funny coincidence.Still, these sorts of funny coincidences don’t do much to build up trust in the US government, do they? A majority of Americanssupport commonsense legislationto stop lawmakers and their family members from trading individual stocks. After a lot of resistance, a bill to this effect iswinding its way through Congress. The bill does not affect the president or the vice-president, however.Money can’t buy you everything, of course: while the president’s stock portfolio is rising, his personal stock is plummeting. According to an FT poll this week, Trump’s approval rating has hit a record low, with only 33% of registered voters saying they approve of his performance.But don’t take that as a sign that the US is coming to its senses or that Republicans are cognisant that dear leader’s war isbleeding the country dry: the same poll found that 72% of Republicans still approve of the president. That figure is down from 82% in May, but it’s still an awful lot of people. Either these Trump loyalists are bigoted fools or they are getting the Intel windfall checks that I’m missing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionStock marketsIntelOil and gas companiesEnergy industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: I am sending the assisted dying bill back to the Lords – and this time, peers must do the right thing | Lauren Edwards | The Guardian
description: The will of the elected chamber – and a popular, compassionate piece of legislation – must not be frustrated again by a small minority of peers, says Labour MP for Rochester and Strood Lauren Edwards
Author: Lauren Edwards
Headline: The will of the elected chamber – and a popular, compassionate piece of legislation – must not be frustrated again by a small minority of peers, says Labour MP for Rochester and Strood Lauren Edwards
Content: Dignity in Dying campaigners outside Westminster, London, in April 2026.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDignity in Dying campaigners outside Westminster, London, in April 2026.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockOpinionAssisted dyingI am sending the assisted dying bill back to the Lords – and this time, peers must do the right thingLauren EdwardsThe will of the elected chamber – and a popular, compassionate piece of legislation – must not be frustrated again by a small minority of peersLauren Edwards is the Labour MP for Rochester and StroodTue 8 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTShareIwas elected to Westminster two years ago, when the country was crying out for change and looking to parliament to tackle the big issues that had been forgotten for too long. When that change didn’t come fast enough, trust in politics once again started to ebb away. We have one last chance to prove we can deliver on people’s priorities.Assisted dying didn’t feature in the manifesto I was elected on. Nor should it have done. Matters of conscience such as this are rightly left to individual MPs to decide upon. There will always be a range of views within all political parties. But this issue has been supported by a substantial majority in the country for a very long time. Reputable independent polling has shown support for assisted dying consistently at about 75%. The latest British social attitudes survey from the National Centre for Social Research found that “it is clear we are observing a continued high level of public support for legal change to allow assisted dying in some circumstances”.Having examined the issue with great care, MPs decided in the last session to support the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill. On the Labour benches there was a clear majority in favour, as there was on the Lib Dems’. The Greens supported it unanimously. It is the most pressing, progressive reform of this parliament. But it wasblocked in the Lords earlier this yearby a small minority of peers, led in part by ex-Tory ministers such as Thérèse Coffey and Mark Harper.On Friday, I will be asking MPs to send the bill back to the Lords. There they can amend the bill if they choose, just like any legislation, and if the Commons agrees, that’s fine. But they should not be allowed to frustrate the will of the elected chamber a second time.I am not reopening divisions in the Labour party or in parliament, as some have claimed. Exactly the reverse is true. MPs have already made their decision. In a democracy, we settle our differences by voting on them. Last time, opponents in the Lords prevented a vote taking place on the bill’s provisions.The voters put us here to tackle the big issues they care about, not to constantly kick them down the road. After a shaky start, this parliament has the chance to show that it can deliver; that we won’t shirk our responsibilities and will start to restore the public’s faith in our democratic system.Other major social changes such as a woman’s right to choose and gay rights were bitterly contested at the time. But once passed, the reforms were quickly accepted and ceased to be controversial. It is time to do the same and give terminally ill people the choice to exercise some control over the manner of their deaths. We owe it to them, and to the vast majority of voters who support them, not to sit back and allow a minority of unelected peers to stand in their way.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLauren Edwards is the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood and has reintroduced the terminally ill adults bill in parliamentExplore more on these topicsAssisted dyingOpinionHouse of CommonsHouse of LordscommentShareReuse this content

title: Here in Liverpool, buses are back under public control – and that’s great for the only people who really matter | Steve Rotheram | The Guardian
description: For decades we were told that privatisation would deliver better services. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story, says Steve Rotheram, mayor of Liverpool city region
Author: Steve Rotheram
Headline: For decades we were told that privatisation would deliver better services. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story, says Steve Rotheram, mayor of Liverpool city region
Content: A Metro bus in Hanover Street, Liverpool, in June.Photograph: Alan Edwards/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Metro bus in Hanover Street, Liverpool, in June.Photograph: Alan Edwards/AlamyOpinionPublic transportHere in Liverpool, buses are back under public control – and that’s great for the only people who really matterSteve RotheramFor decades we were told that privatisation would deliver better services. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different storySteve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city regionTue 8 Sep 2026 08.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTShareOne of the best-known scenes from the TV series The Inbetweeners is the four angst-ridden teenage charactersshouting abuseat people queueing at a bus stop. Only losers take the bus, is the point – except they use a much ruder word. There’s also a statement, misattributed to Margaret Thatcher, that any man over the age of 26 using a bus was a loser. This idea is deeply ingrained.But when I was an MP it became obvious that there wasn’t the same stigma attached to jumping on the bus in London as there often was in other big cities. It often wound me up that the rest of the country was expected to accept a suboptimal public transport system – so much so that it could be joked that only losers would use it – while London retained its excellent bus service, which it ran under public control.And I remember thinking: why can’t we have something like this at home in Liverpool? Well, last weekend Liverpool city region combined authority began to roll back the Thatcherite belief that private was all good, while public was all bad. For the first time in four decades, buses in the Liverpool city region have begun to be brought back under public control,starting in St Helensin Merseyside before spreading across the rest of the region.What does this mean? Instead of private operators deciding where and when buses run, we will set the routes, fares and standards. Our franchised buses will still be operated by third parties. But we will set the rules, decide what kind of network our communities need and hold operators accountable for delivering it. It is the biggest change to public transport in our region for generations. Nobody standing at a bus stop at six in the morning cares about the finer points of franchising legislation. But they do care whether the bus turns up; whether they can get to work on time, get their kids to school or college, or make it to a hospital appointment.Public control means we can start putting passengers first, with more frequent services, more evening and weekend buses, better connections to hospitals and railway stations and simpler fares. And we have kept single bus fares capped at £2, the price they have been for the past four years.Change will be immediate. A new express service now connects St Helens directly withLiverpoolJohn Lennon airport. For a family heading on holiday, that may mean avoiding airport parking charges. For somebody looking to work at the airport, it could open up a job. These changes will make a massive difference to people’s lives.And, for me, that gets to the heart of the argument for public control. A bus route that helps somebody take a job, gets a student to college or allows an older person to remain independent has a value that won’t always show up on an operator’s balance sheet. Markets have their place. But public control allows us to ask not simply, “does this route make money?” but “do our people need it?”That principle doesn’t stop with buses. We have bought a£500m fleet of new trainsand are working towards bringing Merseyrail services intopublic ownership in 2028. In the coming weeks, theRoyal Daffodil– our first new ferry ’cross the Mersey in 60 years, built by a loyal local workforce – will make its maiden voyage.For decades we were told that privatisation and deregulation would inevitably deliver better services and that the government’s job was to get out of the way. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story.When he was mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham and I spent years working together to make that case and show what can be achieved when local leaders have the power to shape the services their communities rely on. Now we have a Labour government bringing our railwaysback into public ownershipandgiving local leaders more powerover the essentials that ordinary people depend on.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter decades in which the state steadily retreated from people’s lives, we have an opportunity to prove that active government can be a force for good again. That is what started in St Helens last weekend.I want the Liverpool city region to have the best public transport system in the country. I want people to come here, get on one of our buses, trains or ferries, see what we have built and go home asking the same question I used to ask in London: why can’t we have this at home?Steve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city regionExplore more on these topicsPublic transportOpinionLiverpoolBus faresLocal governmentTransport policyTransportRail transportcommentShareReuse this content

title: I went to Ikea with my son – and was confronted with my parenting failures | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: The pre-university shop is the moment you find out how much domestic wisdom you’ve managed to impart. In my case, none, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The pre-university shop is the moment you find out how much domestic wisdom you’ve managed to impart. In my case, none, writes Zoe Williams
Content: ‘I think you might be about to starve.’Photograph: Tony Still/Alamy (posed by models)View image in fullscreen‘I think you might be about to starve.’Photograph: Tony Still/Alamy (posed by models)OpinionParents and parentingI went to Ikea with my son – and was confronted with my parenting failuresZoe WilliamsThe pre-university shop is the moment you find out how much domestic wisdom you’ve managed to impart. In my case, noneTue 8 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 06.05 EDTShareIhave yet again found my ultimate tribe in a high-street shop, this timeIkea. As far as the eye could see, there were middle-aged women trying to choose kitchen essentials for their late-teenaged sons, for whom the next chapter of life, in which they move to another city and never once use a kitchen, cannot commence fast enough. I don’t know where all the girls were – did they do it all online? Have they been collecting teapots for years, as part of a wistful university trousseau?The negotiation started with a chopping board, which my son said he absolutely did not need or want. I said, “How are you going to chop vegetables?”, and he said he would cross that bridge when he came to it, and I said: “Oh my God, you’re going to get scurvy.” Behind me a woman and her son were arguing about whether or not he needed a cheese grater, which ended in her saying: “I think you might be about to starve.”The household-item shop is a uniquely confronting experience, I realised halfway through, and one I had in no way prepared for. It’s the moment you find out how much domestic wisdom you’ve managed to impart. When you get a question like “Can you wash sheets?”, it turns out the answer is: “None.” I remember going round a far larger Ikea with my own mother, when I was in my 30s and my youngest was a baby, and my mum noticing, on the way in, that my daughter had nits. I say “nits” – it was one tiny nit. “Give her a chance,” I said. “She’s barely got any hair.” My mum, taking this as proof that I wasn’t serious enough about hygiene, tried to buy every bath-related item in the shop – at the top of her voice. By the third hour, there was nobody in there who didn’t know about the nit.Ikea should have a sign at the door, saying: “Parents! If you’re having this conversation now, it’s already too late.” It would probably sound quite melodic in Swedish.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Britain’s new Middle East policy: an unlawful occupation must carry a price | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Ed Miliband has delivered Britain’s toughest indictment of Israeli conduct in Palestinian lands - and rightly says this has economic consequences
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Ed Miliband has delivered Britain’s toughest indictment of Israeli conduct in Palestinian lands - and rightly says this has economic consequences
Content: Ed Miliband addresses the Commons. ‘Mr Miliband has delivered perhaps the toughest official British indictment of Israeli conduct in recent history.’Photograph: House of Commons/PAView image in fullscreenEd Miliband addresses the Commons. ‘Mr Miliband has delivered perhaps the toughest official British indictment of Israeli conduct in recent history.’Photograph: House of Commons/PAOpinionPalestineThe Guardian view on Britain’s new Middle East policy: an unlawful occupation must carry a priceEditorialEd Miliband has delivered Britain’s toughest indictment of Israeli conduct in Palestinian lands - and rightly says this has economic consequencesTue 8 Sep 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareRarely in recent years has the Commons felt like the cockpit of history. On Tuesday it did. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, placed Britain at the head of a12-country coalitionconsidering economic restrictions on Israel’s illegal settlements, with the UK, France and Canada committing to national trade bans.The move comes after escalating numbers of attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the West Bank. International opinion seemed to shift decisively after Israel gave the go-ahead for 1,200 homes in theE1 settlementthat would cleave the West Bank into two – using illegal settlements to bury Palestinian statehood for good. Mr Miliband added that evidence of war crimes in Gaza was mounting, making the overdue case for Britain to recast its economic and military relationship with Israel.Mr Miliband, who is Jewish and lost more than 60 relatives at the hands of the Nazis, declared himself to be a friend of Israel. But clearly he thinks friends should talk straight to each other. Mr Miliband has delivered perhaps the toughest official British indictment of Israeli conduct in recent history, declaring that “ethnic cleansing” is taking place in the West Bank and accusing members of Israel’s government of supporting forced displacement.Probably the most consequential move by Mr Miliband is to formally declare the occupation of the Palestinian territories unlawful, in line with theinternational court of justice’s 2024 opinion. The import ban logically follows. But private acts will have to change too. British companies could soon have to ask whether they are profiting from – or helping to sustain – an illegal occupation.To emphasise this point, the foreign secretary also promised to take action against those providing construction, infrastructure and financing services, because a goods-only ban would leave untouched the commercial activity sustaining unlawful settlements. He also committed to target extremist settlers and to refuse to license arms sales that “contribute to the occupation”. By simultaneously sanctioning Iran and Hezbollah, the UK is signalling that it recognises the threats Israel faces while opposing its illegal actions.No one can accuse Mr Miliband of ducking a fight. His statement will be pored over by the Trump administration, which has supported Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Being part of an international coalition will help to shield Britain from US ire. However, Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel,warnedthat some US states such as Florida could impose penalties against foreign governments deemed to be boycotting Israel.Britain’s intervention comes in the midst of an Israeli election campaign. Opinionpollsgive neither Mr Netanyahu’s far-right coalition nor the opposition a sustained lead. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, a figure expected to be above the fray, absurdly claimed that Mr Miliband was interfering in the elections – as if the campaign itself could excuse ethnic cleansing. Israel closed the UK consulate in Jerusalem as a first response.Tuesday’s announcement deserves a welcome. Mr Miliband has been characteristically brave. But the test is not what he said, but what he enforces in the weeks and months ahead. He promises a “sanctions regime” to take action against“companies and individuals”aiding settlements. Britain has accepted the principle that it must sever the business ties that uphold an unlawful occupation. The test is whether Mr Miliband can turn that into a comprehensive embargo, rather than a symbolic blacklist.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on English schools: teachers and pupils should be proud of bucking a downward trend  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: International comparisons suggest that some things are being done right in England’s classrooms
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: International comparisons suggest that some things are being done right in England’s classrooms
Content: ‘Many [schools] are meeting the demands of a challenging curriculum.’Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Many [schools] are meeting the demands of a challenging curriculum.’Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamyOpinionSchoolsThe Guardian view on English schools: teachers and pupils should be proud of bucking a downward trendEditorialInternational comparisons suggest that some things are being done right in England’s classroomsTue 8 Sep 2026 13.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareTeachers, headteachers, children, parents and politicians should all feel proud of England’s schools, which havebucked a disappointing international trend. Results from 15-year-olds in reading, maths and science have held up well compared with 90 other countries, according to the programme for international student assessment (Pisa). Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland did not match England’s success in reading and maths, although all four UK nations scored well in science.Worries aboutchildren reading fewer booksthan in the past should be dispelled to some degree by England’s results, which show no decline in capability since 2022, when the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) last published results. The decision to place more emphasis on science, technology, engineering and maths (Stem), both at primary and secondary levels, has seemingly borne fruit.Pisa scores do not record everything that schools are doing, and a positive set of results doesn’t mean that all is suddenly right with the system. The focus on Stem was partly at the expense ofarts subjects, which were wrongly excluded from the Ebacc suite of favoured GCSE subjects promoted by the Conservatives. This is due to be scrapped by Labour, following the recommendation of Prof Becky Francis’s review. Prof Francis was also right to highlight the demoralising effect of compulsory maths and English GCSE retakes. The education secretary, Lucy Powell, has cited thedevelopment of modular replacementsas a priority, along with improved technical qualifications, some of which she has suggested could take the form ofnew GCSEs.Reform of special educational needs provision, and the laws surrounding it, is arguably the aspect of schools policy that will end up absorbing most ministerial attention. Earlier this week, the Guardian reported on asurge in applicationsfor the education, health and care plans that compel councils to provide a specified level of support to individuals. The government must also find ways to addresstroublingly wide regional disparities. But concerns about attainment gaps and inequalities, and about the dismayingly high number of pupils who do not thrive at school, should not detract from schools’ striking successes. Many are meeting the demands of a challenging curriculum.The stagnation and decline in other countries should not be viewed simply as a backdrop for England’s success. Andreas Schleicher, the OECD’s director for education, believes there are weaknesses in how schools adapt to technological change and has questioned whether heavy smartphone use is “compatible with sustained academic attention”. This echoes theconcerns of academicswho believe that overreliance on screens in schools is undermining learning. While other experts believe that the evidence points to more nuanced conclusions, it seems clear that caution is needed when assessing the role of technology in classrooms as well as in children’s lives in the round.It would be overly simplistic to blame a poor set of international results on smartphones. After all, English teenagers use them too. But Prof Francis is right that England’s scores suggest there are “important things our education system is getting right”. Her review was aimed at avoiding too much disruption, given the impact on teacher workloads and morale. Further changes should not be rushed into – even by a new education secretary keen to make a mark. England’s schools deserve some praise.Explore more on these topicsSchoolsOpinionEducation policyeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Neither political donations nor special interest groups should dictate policy | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to George Monbiot’s article on Andy Burnham and political donations
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to George Monbiot’s article on Andy Burnham and political donations
Content: ‘Leaders of any party must endeavour to serve not some, but all – without fear or favour – including those who didn’t vote for them.’Photograph: James Willoughby/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Leaders of any party must endeavour to serve not some, but all – without fear or favour – including those who didn’t vote for them.’Photograph: James Willoughby/SOPA Images/ShutterstockParty fundingLettersNeither political donations nor special interest groups should dictate policyReaders respond to George Monbiot’s article on Andy Burnham and political donationsTue 8 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTShareGeorge Monbiot condemns Andy Burnham for his alleged subservience to the interests of the wealthy (Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations, 2 September). If true, I agree. But the same could be said of any interest holding sway in our politics. Lobbying groups, activists, unions, thinktanks, people who obsess about this, that or the other. It is surely not OK for our democracy – at local or national level – to have its priorities dictated by those with the shrillest voices, as well as those with the deepest pockets.Speaking from Scotland, I think that our public realm is a case in point. It seems special interest groups are, to all intents and purposes, the main driver of government policy now. And all too often, said influence is framed by an ideological mission that does not necessarily align with that boring, broad swathe of folks who don’t follow politics closely, and don’t see government as a means to progress personal hobbyhorses or single-issue causes.The latter are, in their own insidious way, as injurious to democracy as the whispers of the wealthy in the ears of politicians. So too is turning a blind eye to such undue influence because its aims chime with your own beliefs. Leaders of any party must endeavour to serve not some, but all – without fear or favour – including those who didn’t vote for them. Not easy. No guarantee of success. But abandoning that principle makes our politics all the poorer.Colin MontgomeryEdinburghI was surprised to see George Monbiot paying feasance to that liberal shibboleth, “the general interest”. If a society is fractured by inequalities of class, race, gender, sexuality, etc, then there can be no “general interest” until these are overcome. Ensuring trade union influence overLabourpolicy through the continuation of union donations acts as leverage against policy being captured by the likes of Lord Alli and Lord Sainsbury.When Monbiot goes on to say that “Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers”, he misses the obvious point that the way, then, to protect benefit claimants is to organise them. Unite, for instance, already has a community membership for students, claimants and pensioners, and has organised days of action against benefit cuts and sanctions. Monbiot’s proposal would not strengthen the power of benefit claimants, it would simply weaken the power of trade unions.Nick MossLondonGeorge Monbiot is right; Andy Burnham lacks the courage to take on vested interests, and nowhere is this more apparent than over climate breakdown. During an extensive Panorama interview with Laura Kuenssberg, the climate crisis was not mentioned once, despite record temperatures, drought affecting half the country and unprecedented wildfires raging throughout Europe. The cap on bus fares will be financed by abandoning international climate payments; and now Burnham wants to take a “pragmatic” approach to drilling in the North Sea.Next year we will breach the 1.5C limit stipulated in the Paris agreement, and this will be followed by the disappearance of coral reefs and the eventual disintegration of the Western Antarctic ice sheet – irreversible events that will undermine the marine food chain and raise sea levels by six metres. Andy Burnham’s lukewarm approach won’t look so pragmatic to our descendants when coastal cities worldwide are under water.Dr Robin Russell-JonesFounder, Help Rescue the PlanetHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Save our seabirds from the huge windfarm due to be built near Bass Rock | Birds | The Guardian
description: Letter: The offshore windfarm at Berwick Bank is predicted to kill more than 4,000 birds in its first year alone – among them gannets, puffins and kittiwakes, writes Ashley Davies
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: The offshore windfarm at Berwick Bank is predicted to kill more than 4,000 birds in its first year alone – among them gannets, puffins and kittiwakes, writes Ashley Davies
Content: ‘I support windfarms, but the location of this one is deadly, cruel and shortsighted.’Photograph: Sally Anderson/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘I support windfarms, but the location of this one is deadly, cruel and shortsighted.’Photograph: Sally Anderson/AlamyBirdsLettersSave our seabirds from the huge windfarm due to be built near Bass RockThe offshore windfarm at Berwick Bank is predicted to kill more than 4,000 birds in its first year alone – among them gannets, puffins and kittiwakes, writesAshley DaviesTue 8 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareLev Parikian paints a vivid picture of the gannets of the Bass Rock and the impact that avian flu has had on their numbers (Country diary, 31 August). There’s another threat, though, and it’s one that puts some supporters of renewable energy like me in a novel situation: protesting against the construction of a windfarm.Berwick Bank will be one of the biggest offshore windfarms in the world – a few kilometres from the Bass. This is perilously close, and theRSPBhas calculated that it will kill more than 4,000 seabirds in its first year alone, among them gannets, puffins and endangered kittiwakes.I support windfarms, but the location of this one is deadly, cruel and shortsighted, and thousands of us want it to be moved further out to sea. Stick up for these seabirds atstopberwickbank.co.uk.Ashley DaviesNorth Berwick,East LothianHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Black-clad mobs and the puzzle of two-tier justice | Far right | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to reports and commentary on far-right groups of masked vigilantes causing unrest in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to reports and commentary on far-right groups of masked vigilantes causing unrest in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend
Content: Far-right anti-migrant protesters in Dover on Saturday 5 September.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeView image in fullscreenFar-right anti-migrant protesters in Dover on Saturday 5 September.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeFar rightLettersBlack-clad mobs and the puzzle of two-tier justiceReaders respond to reports and commentary on far-right groups of masked vigilantes causing unrest in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekendTue 8 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIn Dover and Portsmouth at the weekend, mobs of masked vigilantes in balaclavas acted in an intimidating and racist manner (‘Army of Christian patriots’: how a black-clad vigilante group swarmed Portsmouth, 8 September). Critical infrastructure was blocked, with roads, boats and transport disrupted. Police officers were injured and vehicles damaged. Permission for the orchestrated demonstrations was not sought or granted. Arrests? None.Imagine if this had been a masked pro-Palestine protest or an unauthorised environmental action disturbing the flow of traffic, intimidating the public and injuring police officers. There would have been hundreds of arrests. So, we have an extraordinary example of “two-tier policing”, with the police service being tough on Palestine and climate protesters while going easy on anti-immigrant demonstrations.To be consistent, it’s time to call for extremist racist organisations such as Patriot Platform to be designated as “terrorists”. Or, at the very least, for the government and police to use the many powers they have to take robust action against the participants of this kind of shocking whipping up of hatred that has already led to racist pogroms in many parts of the UK.Gideon Ben-TovimUniversity of LiverpoolZoe Williams is right to expose the hollowness of the hard right’s claim to “protect … our women” (Why does the hard right have such a high tolerance for domestic abusers in their midst?, 7 September). Last year, I was one of a number of women in a group protesting against Tommy Robinson’s Unite the Kingdom march. As we waited for our train home, our group was attacked by some of his supporters. I was punched in the face. I am due to give evidence in the resulting court case.The contradiction is hard to miss. A movement that presents migrants and refugees as a threat to women can apparently tolerate intimidation and violence against women who stand in its way.There is another disturbing contrast. I am due in court myself, charged under the Terrorism Act after sitting peacefully in Trafalgar Square holding a placard saying: “I oppose genocide, I supportPalestine Action.”Masked far-right protesters can march through our streets intimidating refugees, migrants and Muslims, while peaceful protesters face prosecution under terrorism legislation. If the phrase “two-tier justice” means anything, surely this deserves scrutiny.Name and address suppliedIt’s right that to undercut support for racism (Editorial, 7 September), an end to 15-plus years of austerity must be called not just in theory but in practice. That means spending on public services and infrastructure, not cuts, and wages at least keeping pace with inflation.There is also an immediate task. The far-right mobilisations in Dover and Portsmouth represent an attempt to build a fascist street force fuelled by the words of Reform UK and Restore Britain. As we approach the 90th anniversary of thebattle of Cable Street, the lesson remains clear. They must not pass.Keith FlettTottenham, LondonMy response to the horrifying sight of masked thugs parading in Dover? title: Blake’s townhouse could be open to all  | William Blake | The Guardian
description: Letter: Directors of the William Blake Congregation respond to an editorial and a letter about writers’ homes
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Directors of the William Blake Congregation respond to an editorial and a letter about writers’ homes
Content: William Blake’s home in Felpham, West Sussex, photographed in 2015.Photograph: Blake Society/PAView image in fullscreenWilliam Blake’s home in Felpham, West Sussex, photographed in 2015.Photograph: Blake Society/PAWilliam BlakeLettersBlake’s townhouse could be open to allDirectors of the William Blake Congregation respond to an editorial and a letter about writers’ homesTue 8 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareWe were pleased to see your editorial about writers’ houses (18 August), and the response from Richard Clemmow, a trustee of the Blake Cottage Trust (Letters, 25 August). However, we must disagree with Clemmow’s statement that William Blake’s cottage in Felpham, Sussex, is the only one of his residences that could ever open to the public. The other surviving house where Blake lived, 17 South Molton Street in London, is not “disappearing behind new development”, but is at present being carefully restored by its owner, the Grosvenor Estate. With inspired support, the leasehold could be acquired and it could be made into a culturally significant museum.TheWilliam BlakeFellowship has been in negotiations with the Grosvenor Group/Grosvenor Property UK about this project for several years, and has the support of Sadiq Khan, Tate Britain, the V&A, English Heritage and thousands of Blake lovers, artists, poets and musicians who have signed our petitions and our letter to the Duke of Westminster, and sent messages of support. This project is gaining momentum and may even, with luck and vision, also be able to open to the public for the bicentenary of Blake’s death on 12 August next year.Helen Elwes and Stephen MicalefThe William Blake CongregationHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Real Madrid somehow cling on to beat Inter on José Mourinho’s big night | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Two goals in the first 23 minutes secured Real Madrid a 2-1 victory against Inter, who had pulled one back through Carlos Augusto, in the Champions League
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Two goals in the first 23 minutes secured Real Madrid a 2-1 victory against Inter, who had pulled one back through Carlos Augusto, in the Champions League
Content: Fede Valverde (left) is congratulated by Kylian Mbappé after scoring Real Madrid’s second goal.Photograph: Juanjo Martin/EPAView image in fullscreenFede Valverde (left) is congratulated by Kylian Mbappé after scoring Real Madrid’s second goal.Photograph: Juanjo Martin/EPAChampions LeagueReal Madrid somehow cling on to beat Inter on José Mourinho’s big nightSid Loweat the BernabéuTue 8 Sep 2026 17.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes football is silly, sometimes it doesn’t make much sense, and sometimes it’s fun for it. On a night when there were 37 shots and the goalkeepers shared 13 occasionally absurd saves between them, José Mourinho’s current side beat his former team Inter on hisChampions Leaguereturn to Real Madrid. Just don’t ask exactly how. Except perhaps to cite Thibaut Courtois, whose astonishing 89th-minute stop from Henrikh Mkhitaryan explained much and allowed them, just, to hold on to the first-half lead they had been given by goals from Kylian Mbappé and Fede Valverde.Haaland double gives Manchester City ideal Champions League start in PortoRead moreBy Mbappé, Valverde, and Inter themselves, that is. You might be tempted to say the Italians had shot themselves in the foot, only if they tried Courtois would probably save that too. “If he wasn’t voted man of the match tonight, he never will be,” Mourinho said. It took 77 minutes for him to be beaten, Carlos Augusto’s goal giving this match a frantic last 15 minutes and Inter hope of justice, but it didn’t happen again. So a game that could have had any scoreline – “5-1 to us, 6-6, I don’t want to say they could have won,” Mourinho suggested – actually ended 2-1. Madrid’s manager called it “mad, and not a madness I like.”This wasn’t always good from Madrid, in fact at times it was terrible. There was a void where the midfield should be, Mourinho thanking Trent Alexander-Arnold for filling in a “specific” midfield role that’s not for him. The intensity in the press high up was matched by a passivity elsewhere. Inter played through and round them, clocking up twice as many attacks and passes. At the end the Santiago Bernabéu whistled; Vinícius Júnior in particular felt their frustration. Yet their team, who also could have won by more – Jude Bellingham said he had missed “two sitters” – have started with a win.View image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho makes his point against the team with whom he won the treble.Photograph: Diego Souto/Getty ImagesThe irritation had grown. When Madrid scored the first, this placed cheered but they might have laughed too. That Madrid led didn’t make sense; not when it came to the goal, not when it came to the game either. It had taken Madrid four minutes to get a meaningful touch, and by then Courtois had already made a superb save from Marcus Thuram. But this is Madrid in the Champions League and now somehow they led. Ninety minutes later, they still did, which didn’t compute either.Quick GuideDortmund's Karetsas taken to hospitalShowBorussia Dortmund's Konstantinos Karetsas was taken to hospital after slumping to the turf 25 minutes into his Champions League debut against Villarreal.“Konstantinos Karetsas had to leave the field due to circulatory problems,” Dortmund said in a statement. “Kosta is doing well under the circumstances and is on his way to the hospital for further tests.”The 18-year-old Greece international passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass. Karetsas was treated laying down then taken away on a stretcher. The score was 0-0 at the time.Dortmund went on to win 3-2 at home. Renato Veiga’s 53rd-minute own goal put the Bundesliga side ahead before Santiago Mouriño equalised in the 66th. Serhou Guirassy restored the lead in the 80th minute and scored the third with an 84th-minute penalty, before scoring an own goal in added time while trying to help in defence.Real Betistwice came from behind to beatLille3-2 away, ⁠with Marc Bartra scoring in the 34th and 49th minutes before Troy Parrott’s 54th-minute winner.Lille ​scored their opener in the 12th minute ‌and regained the lead through ‌Alexsandro in the 37th. The hosts later had Ethan Mbappé sent off for an elbow to ‌the face of an opponent.AEK Athens​made a winning start, beating the Austrian sideLASK1-0 in Greece thanks to Romanian midfielder Razvan Marin’s curling free-kick midway through the first half.AgenciesWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Inter had been playing with what looked like ease until suddenly even the simplest things looked complicated. Hakan Calhanoglu and Lautaro Martínez had just fired off the third and fourth shots without reward when it happened. Inter had enjoyed 65% of possession so far but gave it up in a way that was comic. Curtis Jones struggled with the first ball, playing to Yann Bisseck who fatally lost his bearing and his footing. Stumbling like someone attached his legs the wrong way round, he gave it to Brahím Diaz who sent Mbappé away to score.It was Madrid’s first shot and the opening goal. If that was silly, what came next was even more ridiculous. What is it Madrid do to goalkeepers in this competition? Receiving on his line, Josep Martínez saw Valverde steaming in and tried a drag back, which failed. A flick of the ankle and the Uruguayan had scored. Twenty-three minutes, two shots, 2-0. “That was not chance,” Mourinho said and the lead might have grown when another robbery saw Vinícius dashing away. Bissek, this time, made a fantastic saving challenge. For all the fortune this felt like a plan now: force the mistake, punish it. Madrid forced more too, which they didn’t punish.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKylian Mbappé opens the scoring for Real Madrid in the 14th minute.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersInter recovered and reasserted themselves, a calmness in possession at one end that contrasted with the calamitousness further back. Curtis Jones, Lautaro Martínez and Augusto virtually walked into the area, where Jones’ effort smashed the crossbar. Then another gift, from Benjamin Pavard, saw Madrid escape just before the break. Bellingham was denied by a wonderful stop from JosepMartínez and Díaz hit the post. Inter led 12-3 in shots, boasted 70% possession and had completed 125 final third passes to Madrid’s 13. Madrid, though, led.Those numbers evened as the game opened, the second half beginning with Josep Martínez coming out to stop Mbappé before Inter came back at them. Courtois saved from Jones, Nicolò Barella shot wide and Thuram scooped over. The roar that then greeted an outrageous Courtois double stop spoke of disbelief, although the flag was up. The feeling was similar when Josep Martínez scrambled across his line to stop Bellingham after Díaz’s glorious scoop over him and into the Englishman.A competition built between the keepers. Madrid could have killed this, many times. Inter could have revived it. Courtois saved from Alessandro Bastoni. Josep Martínez saved from Mbappé with his legs. That was 6-5 to Courtois. There were whistles, frustration, but chances too: the 20 seconds or so between Lautaro Martínez being blocked at one end and Díaz slotting wide at the other told a tale. Inter finally scored when another incisive exchange saw Lautaro Martínez pull back for Augusto to score. There were f15 minutes left and a game on, but that, somehow, was that. Which didn’t make sense either.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueReal MadridInternazionalematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Haaland double gives Manchester City ideal Champions League start in Porto | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Erling Haaland scored at the beginning and end of the second half to give Manchester City a 2-0 win in Porto, despite tempers flaring
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Erling Haaland scored at the beginning and end of the second half to give Manchester City a 2-0 win in Porto, despite tempers flaring
Content: Erling Haaland scores Manchester City’s second against Porto.Photograph: Luis Vieira/APView image in fullscreenErling Haaland scores Manchester City’s second against Porto.Photograph: Luis Vieira/APChampions LeagueHaaland double gives Manchester City ideal Champions League start in PortoJamie Jacksonat Estádio do DragãoTue 8 Sep 2026 17.08 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca admitted a liking for the “boom-boom” of house music in the buildup to this match, then enjoyed the sweet notes of victory having overseen a gritty performance from hisManchester Cityside in incessant rain.City had lost six of their past nine away games in the competition, and been beaten in the 2021Champions Leaguefinal at this venue, so to beat Porto and claim three points is a fillip for the manager’s nascent project.Mbappé and Valverde fire Real Madrid to Champions League win against InterRead moreA bust-up at half-time as the players and staff neared the tunnel may bring Uefa scrutiny, though. Images showed Rúben Dias placing a hand on what appeared to be Francesco Farioli, thePortohead coach. The defender did so as tempers frayed after a clash between Marc Guéhi and Gabriel Veiga that left the latter with a head injury, though he continued.Informed of Dias’s act, Maresca was visibly angered when asked if his captain will be spoken to, as it could cost City. “Probably, anyway you can ask what you want but how many times you see me or my bench or the guys that work with me stand up on the bench. Zero, for 95 minutes. How many times you see their bench?” he said.Overall, the Italian should feel exuberant. All four of his opening games have been won – maybe more than even the 46-year-old could have hoped for, Erling Haaland’s double maintaining the perfect start. The goalscoring phenomenon is now third on City’s all-time chart with 167 goals after only four years, with 59 in 59 Champions League matches.Haaland said: “Amazing game, against the champions of Portugal. We have to deliver on the biggest stage and we did that tonight.”Maresca gave Ayyoub Bouaddi a full debut, alongside Enzo Fernández in midfield, and the 18-year-old Moroccan impressed, though a failure to find Haaland brought a reprimand. “I told the chairman [Khaldoon al-Mubarak] we’ve got a gem there,” said Haaland. “But he should’ve played me through in the second half, I was all alone. I was a bit angry so I’ll tell him right now – but he played a good game, except that pass.”Initially, Porto could allow City to pitter-patter passes about as there was no quickness or penetration. Farioli’s men offered an example of how when Guéhi’s ball short-changed Bouaddi, possession was nabbed, and suddenly William Gomes had to be stopped on the edge of City’s area. Earlier, Veiga sliced through and had Gianluigi Donnarumma saving: the offside flag went up but here were two warnings.Quick GuideDortmund's Karetsas taken to hospitalShowBorussia Dortmund's Konstantinos Karetsas was taken to hospital after slumping to the turf 25 minutes into his Champions League debut against Villarreal.“Konstantinos Karetsas had to leave the field due to circulatory problems,” Dortmund said in a statement. “Kosta is doing well under the circumstances and is on his way to the hospital for further tests.”The 18-year-old Greece international passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass. Karetsas was treated laying down then taken away on a stretcher. The score was 0-0 at the time.Dortmund went on to win 3-2 at home. Renato Veiga’s 53rd-minute own goal put the Bundesliga side ahead before Santiago Mouriño equalised in the 66th. Serhou Guirassy restored the lead in the 80th minute and scored the third with an 84th-minute penalty, before scoring an own goal in added time while trying to help in defence.Real Betistwice came from behind to beatLille3-2 away, ⁠with Marc Bartra scoring in the 34th and 49th minutes before Troy Parrott’s 54th-minute winner.Lille ​scored their opener in the 12th minute ‌and regained the lead through ‌Alexsandro in the 37th. The hosts later had Ethan Mbappé sent off for an elbow to ‌the face of an opponent.AEK Athens​made a winning start, beating the Austrian sideLASK1-0 in Greece thanks to Romanian midfielder Razvan Marin’s curling free-kick midway through the first half.AgenciesWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Discard the ponderous pace might have been Maresca’s message because when Phil Foden switched flanks from the right and accelerated, Porto were splayed, and Haaland’s header from the cross required Diogo Costa to keep the contest goalless.A near-carbon copy arrived when Antoine Semenyo popped the ball over from the left but, this time, Haaland’s header sailed over. City were warming up: Foden, Rayan Cherki and Haaland all being denied, as Porto were caught in a chokehold around their area.At Leicester and then Chelsea Maresca drew criticism for a quasi-sideways style. Yet tonight’s XI had become direct and a threat, as when Bouaddi chipped the ball left from near halfway, it went forward at speed, and a panicked Porto cleared.Now, when Veiga went down after the challenge with Guéhi, the match was halted and the discord that continued to the tunnel area started up.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet following the seemingly de rigueur fireworks before every Champions League game, Porto had begun with sky-high confidence after winning all of their five Primeira Liga outings, so when wandering off they remained content.The mood changed instantaneously on their return. City, at last, showed the ruthlessness needed at this level. Cherki, broke into the area, swerved left, leaving Costa stranded. He fed Fernández and Haaland headed the delivery into the turf and home and the visitors had a priceless lead.What would be Porto’s response? To rove upfield and go close to the equaliser, was the answer, a corollary of City’s openness, as when André Silva had an age to dip right and let fly, the former Portugal forward’s attempt hitting the side netting.View image in fullscreenErling Haaland outjumps Jakub Kiwior to head City into the lead.Photograph: Clive Brunskill/Getty ImagesThe lead was slender, as it was in Saturday’s 1-0 win over Coventry. Maresca acted when the hour passed, removing Cherki and Semenyo for Elliot Anderson and Iliman Ndiaye: two attackers for one forward and a holding player in Anderson whose role was to exert control and aid Bouaddi in snuffing out any Porto threat.A second goal would also stymie the hosts, so Ndiaye skipped across the grass and unloaded, but the effort went straight into Costa’s clutches. Foden, too, tried to break in behind, but the ball was shepherded back to the Porto keeper.Whenever Farioli’s team moved forward City remained vulnerable, despite Anderson’s presence. At the death, though, Haaland’s right-footed finish made sure of victory and meant that even when tempers flared again it was of zero import to Maresca’s team, who had emerged victorious on a difficult evening.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeaguePortoManchester CityEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy protection as it looks to ‘begin the next chapter’ | LIV Golf Series | The Guardian
description: Saudi investors stopped backing LIV Golf this year although top players like Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cam Smith are still involved
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Saudi investors stopped backing LIV Golf this year although top players like Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cam Smith are still involved
Content: Jon Rahm was one of LIV’s highest-profile recruits but his future on the breakaway tour has not been confirmed.Photograph: Justin Casterline/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJon Rahm was one of LIV’s highest-profile recruits but his future on the breakaway tour has not been confirmed.Photograph: Justin Casterline/Getty ImagesLIV Golf SeriesLIV Golf files for bankruptcy protection as it looks to ‘begin the next chapter’Saudi investors stopped backing LIV this yearRahm, DeChambeau and Smith among the creditorsAgence France-PresseTue 8 Sep 2026 17.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 20.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLIVGolf, the breakaway tour that spent billions of dollars luring top players away from the PGA and triggered bitter divisions within the sport, has filed for bankruptcy protection in the US.The filing at a New Jersey court indicates LIV, which abruptly lost its deep-pocketed Saudi investors earlier this year, intends to restructure and return in a new form.LIV Golf to lay off majority of staff amid ‘compressed timeline’ for new investorsRead moreBut documents show LIV owes between $500m and $1bn in estimated liabilities to at least 1,000 creditors, including star players like Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm and Cam Smith.The future of those popular players remains deeply unclear; they are now faced with deciding whether to remain with the tour in its new guise, or leave and attempt to pursue the millions of dollars they are owed in court.“This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf,” said the chief executive, Scott O’Neil, whose organisation had already laid off the majority of its staff this month.O’Neil said LIV still intends to return in a new form next year “built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem”. But “no definitive decisions regarding the 2027 schedule or individual events are being announced at this time,” the statement added.Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) had spent an estimated $5bn on the tour before abruptly pulling the plug this year. LIV Golf is also seeking recognition of the US bankruptcy filing in England and Wales to cover its international assets and operations.LIV officials have pledged that a “2.0” version of the tour will re-emerge under new investors next season, with a shorter schedule and reduced prize money. Much will depend on whether the top stars of the tour remain. Tuesday’s statement said “the company remains in advanced discussions”with players, including on “creating an ownership structure aligning players’ interests with the League’s long-term success”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWidespread reports have linked several LIV stars with returns to the PGA Tour and other series, though the PGA said it has no plans to offer LIV players a pathway back.Explore more on these topicsLIV Golf SeriesSaudi Arabia and sportGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: England seek calm end to chaotic Test summer against penitent Pakistan | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Late-night drinking incidents and a post-Bazball reboot have given the hosts plenty to think about, while the tourists have their own problems to sort out
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Late-night drinking incidents and a post-Bazball reboot have given the hosts plenty to think about, while the tourists have their own problems to sort out
Content: Joe Root has seen his batting average drop below 30 in recent months as bowlers have been on top in the series.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenJoe Root has seen his batting average drop below 30 in recent months as bowlers have been on top in the series.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAEngland v Pakistan 2026England seek calm end to chaotic Test summer against penitent PakistanLate-night drinking incidents and a post-Bazball reboot have given the hosts plenty to think about, while the tourists have their own problems to sort outAli MartinTue 8 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are some chilly white-ball games still to come this month and with it the sight of Kevin Pietersen back in England training kit for the first time in 12 years. KP is down with the kids these days,6/7 memes and the like, and starts a new life as the “specialist mentor” to Harry Brook’s young thrusters.But the final Test of the summer that starts at Edgbaston on Wednesday does feel like an end of sorts, or at least one last push before a breather for the side that has undergone the more significant recalibration. And that is before we get on to Pakistan and a tour that has descended into a bonfire of players and aphone-snatching investigation into “discipline and conduct”.Joe Root backs ‘always brilliant’ Pietersen to bring best out of England playersRead moreNone of what has transpired on the English side of the ledger was the plan back in March, save for sitting 2-0 up with one to play in this second home series. Ben Stokes has left the building, while Brendon McCullum has been boxed off into white-ball specialism. And as the Test team await Stephen Fleming’s arrival as head coach, those operating under the rebooted captaincy of Joe Root have been slowly deprogrammed from some of the extremes of the Bazball era.All of this has taken place in a season where late-night drinking incidents have generated copious headlines and, more relevant to the Test cricket witnessed, the Dukes ball has dominated the bat. Wobble seam has been calling shots and awicket has fallen every 40 deliveries on average. Not since the 1880s has this figure been lower for a summer in England which, given this has also been the hottest since the days of WG Grace, has been quite something.It has been a far cry from 12 months ago, certainly, when all five Tests against India went five days, batters loosened their belts, and fast bowlers walked off at stumps with blood in their boots. Instead, Ollie Robinson has breezily nipped out 23 victims at eight runs apiece, while Ben Duckett’s 113 at Trent Bridge remains the only century to have been scored by an England player.Root was keen to stress this context a day before the toss and not simply because his own average this season sits just under 30 amid a growing pattern of lbw dismissals. The last Test of summer is traditionally when players state their case to make the winter tours and Root was keen to assure his fellow batters that the dominance of the bowlers will be factored in when plans are drawn up for their next assignment in South Africa this December.While Jacob Bethell will create a logjam in the top seven when he returns to fitness after knee surgery, players such as Emilio Gay, Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence have instead been encouraged to focus on this week alone, the completion of a 3-0 clean sweep, and to consider the team’s needs at any given moment. “It’s understanding that the game is bigger than you and your individual achievements,” Root said when asked about Gay. “It is what you do collectively that matters.”View image in fullscreenPakistan will be hoping the likes of Saim Ayub will seize their chance in the team after making sweeping changes to their lineup.Photograph: Stefan Gosatti/AAPWhether a late outbreak of runs occurs on an Edgbaston surface that is brown and light on grass remains to be seen. And there may be more factors at play. This is the first time the ground has hosted a Test in September, while this is the 47th pitch out of 48 that has been prepared this year. The ball has swung during the recent County Championship fixtures also, with the increasingly autumnal overheads potentially more relevant than a tired surface.As well as a desire for greater adaptability and nuance with the bat, rather than the prescriptive attacking mantra of before, another change from the previous England regime has been the return of the sports psychologist David Young this series. A key part of the setup that won the World Cup in 2019, and still contracted for 50 days a year overall, Young was not required by the Test team under McCullum because the head coach himself was the resident shrink.Quick GuideThird Test teamsShowEngland (likely):Emilio Gay, Ben Duckett, Jordan Cox, Joe Root (c), Harry Brook, Dan Lawrence, Jamie Smith (wk), Gus Atkinson, Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh TonguePakistan (possible):Azan Awais, Saim Ayub, Shan Masood, Abdullah Shafique, Babar Azam (c), Saud Shakeel, Ghazi Ghori (wk), Mohammad Ali, Razaullah, Ubaid Shah, Mohammad AbbasUmpires:Chris Gaffaney and Paul Reiffel.Third Umpire:Allahudien Paleker.Fourth Umpire:Russell Warren.Match Referee:Ranjan MadugalleWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Although, one wonders whether Pakistan are in greater need of Young’s services given how messy their tour has become this past week: seven players and two coaches have been shown the door, the same number have walked through it in the other direction. Even by Pakistan’s standards, it has been chaos; the kind that makes England’s Ashes calamity last winter look like a minor blip.In Pakistan’s favour is the fact that the only way is up.
