And with Root admitting his backroom staff are slightly light on info about the newcomers, there is the element of surprise. For Babar Azam, who notably distanced himself from the mid-tour overhaul and the disciplinary issues that have since emerged, this Test is simply a “golden chance” for the next generation to make their mark.Among them are Ubaid Shah and Razaullah, two young seamers who should bring a bit more zip in support of Mohammad Abbas, while the opener Saim Ayub offers a part-time spin option that could allow Pakistan to match England’s four‑pronged pace attack. Whether all this is enough to see the home side’s summer of unplanned recalibration finish on a bum note is another matter.Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: First-half treble powers Aston Villa to Champions League win at Club Brugge | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Goals from John McGinn, Emiliano Buendía and Nicholas Jackson secured Aston Villa a 3-2 victory against Club Brugge in their Champions League opener
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Goals from John McGinn, Emiliano Buendía and Nicholas Jackson secured Aston Villa a 3-2 victory against Club Brugge in their Champions League opener
Content: Nicolas Jackson takes the ball past Yann Sommer before scoring Aston Villa’s third goal.Photograph: Aston Villa/Aston Villa FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNicolas Jackson takes the ball past Yann Sommer before scoring Aston Villa’s third goal.Photograph: Aston Villa/Aston Villa FC/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueFirst-half treble powers Aston Villa to Champions League win at Club BruggeBen Fisherat the Jan Breydel StadiumTue 8 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAston Villa were 3-1 up after 43 minutes but were made to sweat for their first win of the season, emerging victorious from an entertaining Champions League opener with Club Brugge. John McGinn, who struck the only goal when Villa belatedly got their season up and runninglast September against Bologna, opened the scoring before Emi Buendía and a first goal for Nicolas Jackson in claret and blue appeared to put Villa out of sight at half-time.The Belgian side have become familiar foes since Villa returned to the big time, the glitziest club competition of them all; a freakish Tyrone Mings handball gifted the hosts a penalty, andsubsequently victory, in 2024-25 and on this occasion Aaron Wan-Bissaka conceded a second-half penalty to plunge a seesawing contest back into the balance.Mbappé and Valverde fire Real Madrid to Champions League win against InterRead more“Today was a very important step forward, being resilient when we were struggling,” said Unai Emery. “It is very important to start with three points. Hopefully it gives us confidence for the next matches, in the Premier League this Saturday against Nottingham Forest.”Emery had been at pains to radiate positivity despite another slow start – Villa picked up their first point of the Premier League season at the weekend and these goals represented their first of the campaign – but he was typically animated on the touchline in Brugge. He was particularly agitated midway through the second half when he felt, not for the first time this season, his substitutes were not ready for action. AtHull last weekend, it was Tammy Abraham and Wan-Bissaka, and a few days earlier Alejandro Garnacho against Arsenal.This time the culprits were Alysson, Ross Barkley and Lamare Bogarde. “In the dressing room at half-time we were speaking about some players who were tired, [Boubacar] Kamara, Wan-Bissaka,” Villa’s manager said. “I tried to keep [them on for] 15 minutes, but when I asked the players to replace [them] they were talking through the set pieces, sorting individual issues, but I needed quickly their impact on the field, and they did afterwards.”Quick GuideDortmund's Karetsas taken to hospitalShowBorussia Dortmund's Konstantinos Karetsas was taken to hospital after slumping to the turf 25 minutes into his Champions League debut against Villarreal.“Konstantinos Karetsas had to leave the field due to circulatory problems,” Dortmund said in a statement. “Kosta is doing well under the circumstances and is on his way to the hospital for further tests.”The 18-year-old Greece international passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass. Karetsas was treated laying down then taken away on a stretcher. The score was 0-0 at the time.Dortmund went on to win 3-2 at home. Renato Veiga’s 53rd-minute own goal put the Bundesliga side ahead before Santiago Mouriño equalised in the 66th. Serhou Guirassy restored the lead in the 80th minute and scored the third with an 84th-minute penalty, before scoring an own goal in added time while trying to help in defence.Real Betistwice came from behind to beatLille3-2 away, ⁠with Marc Bartra scoring in the 34th and 49th minutes before Troy Parrott’s 54th-minute winner.Lille ​scored their opener in the 12th minute ‌and regained the lead through ‌Alexsandro in the 37th. The hosts later had Ethan Mbappé sent off for an elbow to ‌the face of an opponent.AEK Athens​made a winning start, beating the Austrian sideLASK1-0 in Greece thanks to Romanian midfielder Razvan Marin’s curling free-kick midway through the first half.AgenciesWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.In the end, it was a blend of old and new faces that got Villa over the line. Zion Suzuki made a couple of fine saves, João Gomes put in a typically tigerish performance and Jackson got the goal an encouraging all-round display deserved. The 19-year-old George Hemmings did not look out of place on hisChampions Leaguedebut. “The old players need to keep our standards high, to show everybody this is the only way we can achieve the process in our objectives and targets,” Emery said. “I am so happy.”Pau Torres was the unlikely catalyst for two of Villa’s three first-half goals. McGinn’s opener was a product of the centre-back roaming unchallenged to the edge of the box. Presumably it crossed Torres’s mind to shoot, though just as he was getting giddy, he spread play to McGinn, who guided a superb first-time, left-foot strike into the far corner of Yann Sommer’s goal. In starting on Tuesday night, the Swiss became just the second goalkeeper to represent five clubs in the Champions League, but it was a night to forget for the 37-year-old.View image in fullscreenJohn McGinn punches the air after giving Aston Villa an 11th-minute lead.Photograph: PA Wire/PAClub Brugge replied when the lively Jan Virgili found a way past Wan-Bissaka – who was making his full Villa debut – and located Hugo Vetlesen in the box, the Norway midfielder sending a crisp finish beyond Suzuki. The hosts were level for less than three minutes, a slick Villa move culminating in Buendía wheeling away in celebration. Jackson’s deft backheel supplied Gomes, who twisted inside the box and then picked out Buendía who did the rest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVilla’s third arrived a few minutes before the interval. Emery punched the air, his delight at establishing a two-goal advantage plain to see. Torres collected the ball on the edge of the Villa 18-yard box and, after shifting the ball out of his feet, he sent a lofted pass spinning into the opposition half, where Jackson got in between the opposition centre-backs, Lee Han-beom and Brandon Mechele. Enter Sommer, who raced about 40 yards from goal. Jackson swiped the ball cleanly and then was too strong for Lee before passing into an empty net.Things appeared rosy, but Villa had to withstand heavy pressure after a video assistant referee review led the Swiss referee, Sandro Schärer, to penalise Wan-Bissaka for handball in the box. Nicolò Tresoldi sent Suzuki the wrong way from the penalty spot and a few minutes later Suzuki pushed another shot on to the post.Victor Lindelöf tested the nerves of Emery, slicing a routine clearance when attempting to relieve the pressure. Villa, too, had chances, Jackson getting a shot away after latching on to a McGinn pass and Bogarde had a shot cleared off the line by the home full-back Joaquin Seys.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueClub BruggeAston VillaEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Newcastle progress as Joe Willock strikes late to see off Millwall | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Joe Willock’s goal gave Newcastle a 1-0 win at Millwall that puts them into the fourth round of the Carabao Cup
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Joe Willock’s goal gave Newcastle a 1-0 win at Millwall that puts them into the fourth round of the Carabao Cup
Content: Joe Willock turns the ball into the net to win the game for Newcastle.Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoe Willock turns the ball into the net to win the game for Newcastle.Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty ImagesCarabao CupNewcastle progress as Joe Willock strikes late to see off MillwallBarney Ronayat the DenTue 8 Sep 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNewcastle did just enough in south-east London to progress to the next round of theCarabao Cup. Joe Willock scored the only goal of this boisterous, fun, slightly vague cup tie against a spirited Millwall team that was not so much down to the bare bones, as the bones beneath the bones.By the end there was a sense both sets of fans were more or less happy.Millwallfor the vigour of the performance and Newcastle for the result, the clean sheet and any signs of early progress in the dawning of the age of Jaissle-ball.Real Madrid cling on to beat Inter on Mourinho’s big Champions League nightRead more“We were worth it, we faced it, we did it,” was Matthias Jaissle’s verdict, having sent out a strong team, Jacob Ramsey coming in on the right for the early-season hot-hands Anthony Elanga. This was a significant win for Newcastle, who have been excitingly direct at times under their twinkly new manager, with his much-trailed blueprint for rapid transition, hyper-vertical attack and getting it forward quick-smart to the lads up front, but who still need to groove that system.Millwall also are not sure what they are yet this season, although this is more to do with injuries. They have 13 players out, which is at least an improvement on the previous 15. Absurdly, Alex Neil has already come under some pressure after a couple of losses. Football needs its irrational edge, but there is also a limit.Quick GuideCarabao Cup roundup: Rose gets his first winShowRyan Christie hit a hat-trick as Marco Rose celebrated his first win asBournemouthmanager with a 4-0 demolition ofLincolnin the Carabao Cup third round. Substitute Rayan completed the scoring against the Championship Imps at the Vitality Stadium.Jørgen Strand Larsen struck twice to propelCrystal Palaceto a 3-0 success overMiddlesbroughat Selhurst Park. Strand Larsen nodded home in each half before substitute Daichi Kamada lobbed Boro goalkeeper Sol Brynn to seal victory.Chemsdine Talbi scored the only goal to earnSunderlanda 1-0 win against Premier League rivalsHullat the Stadium of Light.Bradfordcame from behind to win 3-1 at fellow League One clubLeyton Orient. Goals from Will Swan, Stephen Humphrys and Nick Powell overturned a Macaulay Gillesphey own goal.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.At kick-off the sky was still a deep blackish blue above the lip of the Dockers Stand, the lights of the south London trains trundling past the unfilled corners of the ground. The Den was its usual self, a place that always manages somehow to generate that unique crackle of nonchalant hostility, no matter how midweek the crowd (and this one was a near-full house).View image in fullscreenIt was a pretty busy night down at The Den.Photograph: Ashley Western/Colorsport/ShutterstockNewcastle had most of the ball early on, but looked like what they are, a team still finding its shapes and rhythms. “They are PONY, Wall!” was one measured home fan assessment of the Jaissle project at this early stage.It is a fair point perhaps. Newcastle’s manager does have a very precise idea of the patterns and tempo-shifts he wants from his team. This sort of systems-football can lead to periods of drift while players learn the brief.Newcastle settled and began to dominate possession. Willock had the first real chance, snatching the ball from Romain Esse deep in the right-back zone and shooting powerfully but too close to Filip Marschall.In return Millwall offered graft, full-stretch defence and two deep banks of four in the classic old-school style. With 36 minutes gone Caleb Taylor headed just wide charging on to a nicely flighted free-kick, their first effort at goal. By half-time this had become something more like a cup tie as Millwall created pressure down the left, ratted and pressed nicely in midfield, and delivered some potent set pieces.Tino Livramento came on for Amar Dedic at the break. But it was Millwall who began at a clip, a zinging low cross from the right creating a scramble close to the Newcastle goalline, the ball eventually falling to Jenson Metcalfe, who shot with power just over the bar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter which it was more diffuse pressure from Newcastle. Most teams would feel the absence of a midfielder of Bruno Guimarães’ passing quality. This one definitely does.View image in fullscreenMillwall’s Tairyk Arconte hits the post shortly before Newcastle’s goal.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersFor a while the game looked like it was, an early season cup distraction for two chop and change teams, no lack of energy, but all feints and ducks and grapples, like a boxer warming up in the mirror. By the hour mark Newcastle had 70% possession plus 17 shots at goal, but somehow Millwall’s collection of hurled together parts still looked more likely to create a telling chance.Elanga came on, a measure of Newcastle’s desire to get this done. Millwall had the best chance of the game up to that point on 79 minutes, Taïryk Arconte, a real menace on the right, hitting the post with a shot that pinged back on to Lukas Hornicek’s body but somehow stayed out.Moments later Newcastle scored with their first real moment of quality near goal. It was a lovely move to make it. Matias Fernandez-Pardo produced the key pass, a cute little shimmy and nudge outside to Lewis Hall. His cross found Willock in the centre, who finished it with a smart side-foot shot across the face of goal.Millwall continued to press, without finding much penetration and by the final whistle there was a concerted wave of noise coming from the full half-end of Newcastle fans, for whom the journey home into Wednesday morning would at least be a happy one.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupMillwallNewcastle Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Championship roundup: West Ham go top after Bowen double sinks Bolton | Championship | The Guardian
description: Captain Jarrod Bowen scored twice as West Ham’s 3-2 win over Bolton took them top of the Championship on goal differenc
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Captain Jarrod Bowen scored twice as West Ham’s 3-2 win over Bolton took them top of the Championship on goal differenc
Content: Jarrod Bowen races away after hitting what proved to be the winning goal for West Ham at Bolton.Photograph: Paul Currie/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJarrod Bowen races away after hitting what proved to be the winning goal for West Ham at Bolton.Photograph: Paul Currie/ShutterstockChampionshipChampionship roundup: West Ham go top after Bowen double sinks BoltonEngland forward scores twice in 3-2 victorySouthampton 3-1 Swansea; Watford 2-1 PrestonPress AssociationTue 8 Sep 2026 17.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCaptain Jarrod Bowen scored twice asWestHam’s 3-2 win overBoltontook them top of theChampionshipon goal difference. The England international opened the scoring after 13 minutes and earned his side a first win at Bolton for 31 years with his second 13 minutes from time.In between, Wanderers, beaten for a fourth successive outing, equalised through midfielder Ethan Erhahon’s maiden goal for the club and they looked on course for a ninth successive league victory over the Hammers when Ruben Rodrigues converted a 27th-minute penalty. Instead, Konstantinos Mavropanos levelled with a 31st-minute header and Bowen completed the comeback.Real Madrid 2-1 Inter, Millwall 0-1 Newcastle: Champions League and Carabao Cup – as it happenedRead moreCyle Larin scored his fifth goal of the season asSouthamptonbeatSwansea3-1 to beat the side who were top of the table for the second home match in a row. Larin, who is the joint-top scorer in the Championship, found the net either side of Finn Azaz and Leo Scienza strikes to make it 13 games unbeaten at St Mary’s.Watfordshook off an awful first-half display to grab a 2-1 victory overPreston, who suffered their fifth defeat in six league games. Callum Lang had put the visitors ahead in the sixth minute as they threatened to overrun the Hornets, who hit back with two second-half goals in seven minutes from Edo Kayembe and Mamadou Doumbia.Wrexham’s wait for a home win goes on after they were held to a 1-1 draw by winlessBurnleywho sit one place off the bottom of the table. Jacques Ekomie headed in his second goal for the club since joining in a £7m deal from Angers, cancelling out Zeki Amdouni’s first-half effort for the Clarets who at least ended a run of seven straight away defeats dating back to last term.But it was a result that does little to help either side in their pursuit of promotion, withWrexhamhaving lost the momentum they carried into last season while Burnley face bigger problems after relegation from the top flight, having won only one league game since October. Former England striker Jamie Vardy joined this week, but the 39-year-old was suspended for this match as a result of yellow cards collected during his time with Italian side Cremonese.SheffieldUnitedreturned to winning ways after a display of ruthless finishing secured a 2-1 win atBlackburn. All the goals came in a first half that Rovers dominated and deservedly took the lead in through Kristi Montgomery’s first goal for the club on 20 minutes. The Blades turned the game on its head with goals from their only two shots of the half as Tom Cannon stroked home a second on this ground in two weeks in the 35th minute. Sydie Peck rifled home his first of the season a minute before the break to complete the turnaround.Cardiff’s winless start to the season continued asStokeheld on for a 1-1 draw in the Welsh capital and their first away point since January. Stoke had hope of an away-day success after a run of nine straight Championship defeats when Ben Johnson scored midway through the first half. But the Potters came under fierce pressure in the second half and Joel Colwill’s headed home for Cardiff hosts who hit a post three times. The draw – Cardiff’s fourth in six games – was enough to take the home side out of the relegation zone, while Stoke slip to 15th.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipBlackburn RoversSheffield UnitedCardiff CityStoke CitySouthamptonSwansea CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Vuelta a España: Matthew Brennan follows Van Aert’s lead to complete four-timer | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Matthew Brennan enhanced his status as the standout sprinter at the Vuelta a España by winning a fourth stage on his Grand Tour debut
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Matthew Brennan enhanced his status as the standout sprinter at the Vuelta a España by winning a fourth stage on his Grand Tour debut
Content: Matthew Brennan celebrates after winning stage 16 of the Vuelta a España.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMatthew Brennan celebrates after winning stage 16 of the Vuelta a España.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesVuelta a EspañaVuelta a España: Matthew Brennan follows Van Aert’s lead to complete four-timerBriton powers to victory in sprint finish on stage 16Mas remains in red jersey as race enters final weekAssociated PressTue 8 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 18.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatthew Brennan enhanced his status as the standout sprinter at theVuelta a Españaby winning a fourth stage on his Grand Tour debut.The 21-year-old British rider was delivered to the front of the bunch with 100 metres left by an ideal leadout from Wout van Aert, his star teammate at Visma-Lease a Bike who had already won two stages at this race.Crossing the line, Brennan raised his right hand with four fingers out in a victory salute. Bryan Coquard was second and Vito Braet third. Van Aert was sixth at the end of a 181km ride in blazing heat from Cortegana to Palos de la Frontera.“It’s unbelievable. Four stages and the plan was for one,” Brennan said. “As a team we’re on six, I’ve lost count.” Of Van Aert’s work setting up the win, Brennan said: “It’s incredible that he can bring you in such a perfect position in such a chaotic race.”After 16 stages, the overall leader, Enric Mas, retained his advantage in the red jersey of 2min 6sec ahead of Felix Gall. Primoz Roglic is four seconds further back in third.View image in fullscreenThe peloton in action during the stage.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAWednesday’s stage is another flat ride into Seville before a 32.5km time-trial on Thursday that could be key for Roglic’s hopes. The Vuelta finishes on Sunday in Granada.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump renames places and poses as superhero in bizarre social media blitz | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Trump passed the long weekend posting a torrent of memes and musings on his Truth Social platform
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Trump passed the long weekend posting a torrent of memes and musings on his Truth Social platform
Content: Donald Trump makes remarks at a Steel Across America Event on the Ellipse in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDonald Trump makes remarks at a Steel Across America Event on the Ellipse in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/UPI/ShutterstockDonald TrumpTrump renames places and poses as superhero in bizarre social media blitzTrump passed the long weekend posting a torrent of memes and musings on his Truth Social platformLucy CampbellTue 8 Sep 2026 13.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe long weekend may have proved too long forDonald Trump, who passed the time by musing about annexing other countries, unilaterally renaming places he’s not allowed to rename and turning himself into a superhero.Amid the torrent of memes and posts by the president on his Truth Social platform over the Labor Day holiday weekend wasa bizarre AI-generated videodepicting Trump as the Green Lantern DC superhero, wielding a glowing green power ring to erect his border wall, illuminate an “American manufacturing” scene, and command a fleet of warplanes and warships behind him.Trump’s controversial forays into AI-generated images have seen him depict himself asa Christ-like figure,the pope,Atlas from Greek mythology,as Superman, and many others.Over the weekend he also shareda mapwith a US flag emblazoned over most of North America and several countries in Central America, as well as Greenland, Iceland and many islands in the Caribbean. Iceland hassummonedits US ambassador over the post. Trump also separately claimedthe moon.The president has spent much of his second term taunting Canada repeatedly with the suggestion of making ita 51st US statewith “economic force”, and aggressively pushingfor the annexation of Greenland, a self-governing Danish territory, which has sparked a major geopolitical row. He has also threatened military action inMexico,CubaandColombia, threatened to seize the Panama Canal, and casuallymusedabout taking over other countries including Micronesia and the Marshall Islands.Also in the flurry of Labor Day posts wasa mapof the US state of New Mexico with the word “Mexico” crossed out and replaced with “America”. A few hours later, he posted what seems to bean AI videoof him sticking an “America” label over the word “Mexico” on a “Welcome to New Mexico” road sign.Trump’s suggestion that New Mexico should be renamed to “New America” comes as tense trade negotiations ⁠with Mexico ramp up. It also comes hot on the heels of Trumpsigning an orderdirecting the federal government to change Lake Ontario’s name to “Lake America” amid his escalating trade war with Canada after negotiations last month failed to produce a deal.He has alsojokedabout renaming either the Atlantic or Pacific oceans, along with the strait of Hormuz, which has been central to his disastrous war against Iran, to “Trump strait”. Hedeclinedto elaborate on that latter idea when asked by a reporter in the Oval Office last week.In the case of New Mexico, whose name predates the founding of the United States and is explicitly enshrinedin its constitution, Trump has no legal authority to rename it – or indeed any US state. Any change to its name would have to come from the state itself and would require a formal constitutional amendment.While his “Lake America” order directs federal agencies to adopt the name-change on US maps, documents and databases, Trump has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake, nor to compelCanada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS politicsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to force Apple and Google to block explicit images on children’s smartphones | Internet safety | The Guardian
description: Lisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthrough
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Lisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthrough
Content: Lisa Nandy says the government will start work on an act of parliament to prevent under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.Photograph: EMS-FORSTER-PRODUCTIONS/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLisa Nandy says the government will start work on an act of parliament to prevent under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.Photograph: EMS-FORSTER-PRODUCTIONS/Getty ImagesInternet safetyUK to force Apple and Google to block explicit images on children’s smartphonesLisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthroughDan MilmoandKiran StaceyTue 8 Sep 2026 14.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple andGooglewill be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said.The legislation commitment puts ministers on a collision course with two of the biggest players in Silicon Valley, months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s.Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, said the government would start work on an act of parliament to stop under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.Talks with Google andApple, whose operating systems dominate the smartphone market, had not reached agreement as a three-month deadline passed on Tuesday.Nandy told the House of Commons the tech companies could still reach a deal but it was “almost certain” groundbreaking legislation would be required.“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from some of the worst harms,” she said. “And to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace that we need it to, while harm is being done now.”The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the protections would be “built into the device and switched on by default”, and tech companies will be required to verify an adult user’s age before they are allowed to take, view or send nude images. The government also wants the restrictions to apply to apps used by children, which will require further legislation.Nandy said: “This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.”Sources familiar with progress in the talks have said there iwas a desire to reach a deal on both sides but significant hurdles remained including privacy concerns on the tech side.Jess Phillips, the Labour MP and former safeguarding minister, said the legislation would stop the UK from producing self-generated child sexual abuse material, where children are duped or groomed into sharing explicit images of themselves.However, she urged the government to ensure the UK was followed by other countries and to make sure that “while we lead the world, we’re not standing alone for too long”.Hannah Swirsky, head of policy at the Internet Watch Foundation, which monitors the online spread of child sexual abuse material [CSAM], said: “It is deeply disappointing that tech firms have failed to act in full, but we are pleased that the government is now taking decisive legislative action to keep children safe.”Last year the IWFsaid a quarter of the images or videos of CSAMit recorded were self-generated, representing more than 140,000 pieces of content over a 12-month period.One of Keir Starmer’s final acts as prime ministerwas to give Apple and Google three months to stop under-18s from generating, sending or seeing nude images on their devices, by activating built-in features on the hardware or other technological solutions. Between them, Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android smartphone operating systems dominate the mobile phone market.The nudity block implies the use of “client-side scanning”, where content is scanned by software on the device before it is encrypted or sent.“Client-side scanning is the least evil approach,” said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow in cybersecurity and privacy at Kings College London. “That said, it does put in place an infrastructure to scan content of messages.”Privacy campaigners have also warned that adults would have to verify their age before switching off any nudity-blocking features. In June, the government said the proposals would “not affect the use of devices owned and used by adults who verify their age”.Google said it was “pleased to have made progress” in talks with the government and was “fully committed” to working with legislators, experts, app developers and device manufacturers to “keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information”.An Apple spokesperson said the company was preparing to strengthen its “communication safety” feature, which warns children when they are receiving or sending nude images and videos.“We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen communication safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”Explore more on these topicsInternet safetySmartphonesGoogleAppleChildrenLisa NandynewsShareReuse this content

title: Anti-AfD protests sweep Germany as far right closes in on two more states | Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) | The Guardian
description: Alarm that Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may fall next after party’s Saxony-Anhalt election victory
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Alarm that Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may fall next after party’s Saxony-Anhalt election victory
Content: Protesters rally in central Berlin on Monday against the AfD win in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAView image in fullscreenProtesters rally in central Berlin on Monday against the AfD win in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)Anti-AfD protests sweep Germany as far right closes in on two more statesAlarm that Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may fall next after party’s Saxony-Anhalt election victory‘It breaks my heart’: victory sparks dismayEurope live – latest updatesDeborah Colein BerlinTue 8 Sep 2026 08.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of Germans have staged protests against the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) after the party’s watershed victory in a state election, warning it posed a danger in two more polls this month.Demonstrators at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate held a peaceful pro-democracy rally denouncing the anti-immigrant, pro-Russian AfD, which has called for mass deportations of asylum seekers and a rollback of state support for renewable energy and public broadcasting.The party captured itsbest-ever state resultin the former communist eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, with clear momentum heading into regional elections in the capital and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic coast, on 20 September.Police reported 5,000 protesters, while organisers said they drew more than 14,000 people in a campaign to mobilise voters against the AfD. Posters in the crowd read: “Fascism is no alternative”, “Stop the Nazi AfD: end racism and cuts to social services” and “History has its eyes on us”.With less than two weeks to election day, demonstrators at the Berlin rally cautioned against resignation and cynicism after Sunday’s shock result.The AfD’s nearly 44% vote in Saxony-Anhalt, thebest for a nativist party since the Nazi period, is a “disgrace that makes you furious and stunned”, Jens-Christian Wagner, the director of the memorial at the former Nazi concentration camp Buchenwald, said from the stage.View image in fullscreenProtesters throng the roads around the Brandenburg Gate, Berlin, on Monday after the AfD victory.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyWagner sounded the alarm that the AfD, although it fell just short of an absolute majority, was on the brink of taking power in Saxony-Anhalt, a first for the far right since the second world war. That “should not be accepted in silence”, he said.Max Schneller, 17, a member of the far-left Linke, from Saxony-Anhalt, said activists in the state would fight any attempts by an AfD government to target minorities. “We will not start categorising our neighbours according to their origin, religion or skin colour – we are too humane to hate,” he said to loud applause.The AfD is three votes short of the support necessary to form a government under its candidate, the media-savvy firebrand Ulrich Siegmund, who hopes to peel off dissenters from the remaining parties willing to play kingmaker.Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has since 2023 listed the state chapter of the party as rightwing extremist, saying it poses a threat to democratic norms.Hundreds of anti-AfD protesters also gathered in Potsdam, near Berlin, with rallies also organised in Münster, Göttingen, Dresden, Aachen, Bamberg, Darmstadt, and Halberstadt, in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD captured nearly half the votes, local media reported.View image in fullscreenA protester in Berlin on Monday.Photograph: Maryam Majd/ReutersIn Halle, the region’s second largest city, leftist groups and civil society organisations have been staging a protest camp since election day.The AfD is leading in voter intentpolls in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, with about 35%. However, the centre-left Social Democratic party (SPD) of the state premier, Manuela Schwesig, mounted a remarkable comeback over the summer and is now scoring above 30%.In Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the picture is more mixed, withseveral parties jockeying for first place. It is governed by a coalition of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the SPD.The CDU, the party of chancellor Friedrich Merz, whoserecord unpopularity is reported to have weighed heavily with voters in Saxony-Anhalt, holds a wafer-thin lead in the capital, with about 20%.Hot on its heels is the Linke, which has focused on soaring housing costs in its campaign, and the AfD, followed by the SPD and the ecologist Greens, both polling in the mid-teens.Merz has vowed to stay in officeand fight for a signature package of painful reforms, arguing the only way to defeat the AfD is to get Europe’s top economy moving again and repair its creaking social welfare system.However, the SPD, his junior coalition partner, has indicated its willingness to backtrack on some of the most unpopular measures to shore up support for the embattled government.Analysts say the dispute could further destabilise the shaky coalition.Explore more on these topicsAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)GermanyThe far rightFriedrich MerzEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk told ex-girlfriend he needed ‘a legion of children before the civil war’ | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Ashley St Clair was speaking at the Venice film premiere of Alex Gibney’s documentary Musk, where she warned of his dangerous influence
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Ashley St Clair was speaking at the Venice film premiere of Alex Gibney’s documentary Musk, where she warned of his dangerous influence
Content: ‘He is causing deliberate division that may be catastrophic’ … Ashley St Clair at a photocall for Musk at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Independent Photo Agency Srl/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘He is causing deliberate division that may be catastrophic’ … Ashley St Clair at a photocall for Musk at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Independent Photo Agency Srl/AlamyVenice film festivalElon Musk told ex-girlfriend he needed ‘a legion of children before the civil war’Ashley St Clair was speaking at the Venice film premiere of Alex Gibney’s documentary Musk, where she warned of his dangerous influenceMusk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manPhilip Oltermannin VeniceTue 8 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Musk is sowing “deliberate division” via his social media platform X that will be catastrophic unless regulated, the mother of one of the 14 confirmed children fathered by the world’s richest man has warned.In Musk, a new documentary by veteran film-makerAlex Gibney, former Maga influencer Ashley St Clair says Musk told her in a text message he wanted to have a child with her because he needed to have “a legion of children before the civil war”.State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmRead moreThe couple had a son in 2024 but have since separated. St Clair says Musk’s team offered her a $40m lump-sum payment and a monthly stipend of $100,000 in return for her signing a non-disclosure agreement but withdrew the offer after she refused to sign it.Asked at the documentary’sVenice film festivalpremiere whether her ex-partner was just scared of a civil war or actively trying to stoke one, St Clair said: “Whatever it is, what he’s doing with this platform on X cannot be ignored, because he is stoking flames that don’t exist in the real world.”Elon Musk’s ex-girlfriend accuses him of sowing ‘deliberate division’ on X - video“He is creating something that is causing real world effects with all of these inputs on X,” said the former Trump supporter, who also said she now regrets her former political activism. “I do believe that he is causing deliberate division that may be catastrophic if it’s not regulated or tamed, or if we don’t do our part in putting it down.”Since acquiring the site formerly known as Twitter in 2022, Musk has used the platform to amplify his personal political views. On Monday, he celebrated the strong result for Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, writing “Well done!” in response to co-leader Alice Weidel’s acclamation of the lead candidate.Film-maker Gibney, whose previous subjects include Enron, Vladimir Putin and the US military, said Musk’s preoccupation with civilisational collapse was probably rooted in his childhood in South Africa.Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manRead more“He had a childhood that was very difficult and traumatic,” Gibney said in Venice. “To some extent he’s now playing out that trauma on the rest of us, if I were to psychoanalyse the situation.”The four-hour documentary, which Gibney filmed over three years, paints a comprehensive portrait of Musk’s rise from software start-up tech bro to engineering entrepreneur selling rockets and electric cars to Maga acolyte.“What I discovered was that the story of Musk was not a new tech story,” said Gibney. “But his story is the story of an old wine in a new bottle. His story turns out to be the story of the confidence man, the stock pumper. His wealth and power comes from inflating stock.”Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalElon MuskAlex GibneyFestivalsDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ikea wins right to launch legal action against Belgian far-right party | Ikea | The Guardian
description: EU’s highest court allows Swedish furniture firm to begin proceedings after Vlaams Belang used its trademarks in immigration campaign
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: EU’s highest court allows Swedish furniture firm to begin proceedings after Vlaams Belang used its trademarks in immigration campaign
Content: The Flemish nationalist party Vlaams Belang used Ikea’s branding in political material published in 2022.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Flemish nationalist party Vlaams Belang used Ikea’s branding in political material published in 2022.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockIkeaIkea wins right to launch legal action against Belgian far-right partyEU’s highest court allows Swedish furniture firm to begin proceedings after Vlaams Belang used its trademarks in immigration campaignRob DaviesTue 8 Sep 2026 14.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIkea has won the right to take legal action against a Belgian far-right political party that parodied the Swedish flatpack furniture firm’s branding in its anti-immigration campaign.In a ruling on Tuesday, Europe’s highest court said that Ikea had the right to oppose the use of its trademarks and distinctive graphics by Vlaams Belang, a rightwing Eurosceptic political party that advocates for an independent Flemish state.The court found that Vlaams Belang’s use of Ikea’s trademarks to illustrate its policy on asylum and immigration could “cause significant detriment to the repute” of the company.The party, which has called for a near total stop to immigration and limitations on the building of mosques, had used Ikea’s branding in political material published in 2022.One image featured characters modelled on the cartoon people used in Ikea instructions, one carrying a flag featuring a lion – the symbol of Flanders – and another holding a shield in Ikea’s distinctive blue and yellow livery.The image was titled “Ikea plan” with the subtitle “Immigration really can be different.”After Ikea issued proceedings against Vlaams Belang, the party argued that its freedom of expression should override the Swedish company’s rights over its brand.But the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice of theEuropean Unionruled on Tuesday that Ikea could proceed with legal action against Vrijheidsfonds, the association behind the party.In a statement, the court said “it does not appear that the use of the Ikea trademarks for the sole purpose of taking advantage of their reputation to reinforce a political message and increase its dissemination, takes precedence over the rights and interests of the proprietor of those trademarks.”However, it said a final decision on the dispute could only be made in subsequent legal proceedings in a Belgian court.Pauline Piernez, a trademark and design associate at Marks & Clerk, an intellectual property law firm, said: “While the CJEU rightly confirms that political parody is not prohibited, it also makes clear that freedom of expression is not a blank cheque to appropriate the identity of a famous brand simply to amplify a message.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In this case, the court found that the use of the Ikea trademarks was liable to damage their reputation and was primarily intended to take advantage of their notoriety in order to increase the reach of a political message entirely unrelated to Ikea itself.“The decision should be welcomed as an important safeguard for the system of protection afforded to reputed trademarks.|“Inter Ikea fully believes in – and deeply respects – freedom of expression,” the company said in a statement. “At the same time, it cannot accept the use of the Ikea trademarks in ways that damage their reputation or distinctive character, particularly when such use serves no other purpose than to free-ride on the reputation of the Ikea brand.”​Vlaams Belang ​said its campaign association had taken note of the judgment and that it “will thoroughly study its scope in the context of the further legal proceedings”.Explore more on these topicsIkeaCourt of justice of the European UnionEuropean UnionIntellectual propertyEuropeRetail industryInteriorsShareReuse this content

title: California confirms rare sighting of gray wolf in Mendocino national forest | California | The Guardian
description: Officials say sighting a sign species – driven to extinction in state before reintroduction in 2011 – expanding its range
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Officials say sighting a sign species – driven to extinction in state before reintroduction in 2011 – expanding its range
Content: A photo from a Facebook post showing a gray wolf.Photograph: Lake County Supervisor Brad Rasmussen via FacebookView image in fullscreenA photo from a Facebook post showing a gray wolf.Photograph: Lake County Supervisor Brad Rasmussen via FacebookCaliforniaCalifornia confirms rare sighting of gray wolf in Mendocino national forestOfficials say sighting a sign species – driven to extinction in state before reintroduction in 2011 – expanding its rangeDani AnguianoTue 8 Sep 2026 18.09 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA gray wolf has recently been seen in California’s Mendocino national forest for the first time since the species returned to the state 15 years ago, state wildlife officials confirmed.Officials in Lake county, which is about two hours north of San Francisco, said last week the California department of fish and wildlife (CDFW) had received reports of sightings in the forest in late August. The agency verified the presence of a wolf in the far north end of the county, county supervisor Brad Rasmussen said in astatementon social media.The CDFW confirmed the sightings in a statement, telling the Guardian it had received two separate reports from an area where Mendocino, Glenn and Lake counties meet. The agency received photos and were on the ground to confirm the presence of the animal the following day, said Alicia de la Garza, the CDFW deputy director of public affairs.“The sighting was verified by a CDFW wolf biologist who confirmed the validity of the photos, conducted surveys in the area and confirmed wolf tracks where one of the sightings was reported,” de la Garza said.A century ago hunters and settlers drove wolves in California to extinction, but the animals returned to the state in 2011 and havesignificantly expandedtheir presence over the last decade, largely in the rural and remote north-east. There are at least 50 documented wolves in California.The recent appearance in the Mendocino national forest, which was first reported byMendoLocal.Newslast week, is significant.It represents the only confirmed sighting west of the Sacramento Valley, Axel Hunnicutt, the state gray wolf coordinator for the CDFW, told theSacramento Bee, and is a sign the species is expanding its range.“Evidence of wolves in that part of the state is a good thing,” he said.The return of the animal has not been without controversy. Ranchers have expressed frustration that there is little they can do when wolves kill their livestock – the species is protected in California and under the federal Endangered Species Act. Donald Trump has sought to change that.Last week the president signed anexecutive order, titled “Supporting America’s Ranchers”, that directs the interior department to look at removing gray wolves from the Endangered Species Act, and to loosen restrictions for “lethal removal”.The US Fish and Wildlife Service has sought to de-list the gray wolf, but the matter is still unfolding in court. Meanwhile, the act protects the wolves that are across the majority of the lower 48 states under a 2022 federal court order.Environmental groups condemned Trump’s order.“Once again, we see this administration attempting to override the checks and balances provided by bedrock environmental laws like the Endangered Species Act in order to create industry carveouts and distract from other bad policies that are proving unpopular,” said Leia Barnett, New Mexico conservation lead for WildEarth Guardians.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaAnimalsWest CoastConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: One in 12 golf clubs in England broke water extraction rules in past five years | Water | The Guardian
description: More than 140 clubs breached licences, with a third caught taking water illegally, analysis shows – but no fines issued
Author: Emma Howard
Headline: More than 140 clubs breached licences, with a third caught taking water illegally, analysis shows – but no fines issued
Content: Clubs use water to maintain and irrigate their courses and grounds. There are 1,735 golf clubs in England, according to England Golf.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenClubs use water to maintain and irrigate their courses and grounds. There are 1,735 golf clubs in England, according to England Golf.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesWaterOne in 12 golf clubs in England broke water extraction rules in past five yearsMore than 140 clubs breached licences, with a third caught taking water illegally, analysis shows – but no fines issuedEmma HowardTue 8 Sep 2026 08.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 140 golf clubs inEnglandhave breached their water extraction licences in the past five years, according to data analysis by the Guardian.More than a third of these clubs were caught taking water illegally from the environment, either by taking more than permitted or by removing it outside the permitted period.In most of the other cases, the breaches were the result of golf clubs that were either not reporting or monitoring their water usage properly, or were not reporting and monitoring it at all.Although 100 of the golf clubs breached their licences in a way that put the environment at risk, none of the infringements have led to a prosecution or fine.Amy Fairman, head of campaigns at the campaign group River Action, described the figures as “absolutely unacceptable”. “It suggests that there are no meaningful consequences for breaching licences. Monitoring and enforcement must be significantly strengthened.”TheEnvironment Agency(EA) told the Guardian that it had increased its ability to monitor and detect breaches of abstraction licences. A spokesperson said: “Our first response is to work with abstractors to bring them back into compliance, however we won’t hesitate to take further action if necessary.”Over 70% of England is nowin droughtafter a summer of back-to-back heatwaves, which the Met Officehas just declaredto be the UK’s hottest on record. The previous record was set just last year. Nine major reservoirs are classed as having exceptionally low storage, and farmers have warned that the droughtcould leadto food shortages.The Guardian obtained the data, which covers the period from 2021 to 2025, from the EA via an environmental information request (EIR). The overall number of breaches has more than doubled in that time, probably largely because of the digitisation of records and improved monitoring.Over the five-year period, golf clubs breached their licences 279 times, accounting for about 6% of the total breaches. Of these, 175 were category 2 or 3 breachesmeaning thatthey posed the threat of a “reasonably foreseeable” impact on the environment, human health or quality of life.Although the figures do not relate to the 2026 drought, they do include breaches that occurred during the droughts of 2022and 2025.Fairman said: “As we face increasingly climate stressed conditions, we need to look at who is prioritised to extract our water and that should be essential services, not golf clubs. Demand and competition for water is going to increase so the government needs to take this issue really seriously and put in place a national plan for water resilience.”In England, the removal of water from rivers, lakes and boreholes in the ground is governed by a system of abstraction licences, held by public water companies, farmers and many other businesses. The licences place conditions on where, when and how much water businesses can remove, as well as how they must monitor and report their usage.Dr Megan Klaar, an associate professor in hydroecology at the University of Leeds, told the Guardian that breaches of abstraction licences were “bad news for the environment”.“If the water level gets too low this can increase the temperature, concentrate effluent and other pollutants and dry out the river. There needs to be enough water so that species such as fish have enough habitat to exist in.”The Environment Agency checks compliance through a mix of inspections and desk-based assessments, including use of satellite data. Where breaches occur, the agency can respond with advice, a warning letter, a fine or a prosecution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGolf clubs use water to maintain and irrigate their courses and grounds. There are 1,735 golf clubs in England, according to data from EnglandGolf, meaning that roughly one in 12 have breached a water abstraction licence in the past five years.‘It’s all right for them’: private schools and golf courses stay green despite England’s hosepipe bansRead moreWhile some clubs abstract water using their own licence, others havecome under criticismfor using mains water in areas where householders have had to comply with a hosepipe ban.Guy Shrubsole, an environmental campaigner and author of The Lie of the Land, called for courses to be rewilded. “Golf’s purpose seems to be to spoil a good walk – and now it turns out golf clubs are stealing our water, too. As the climate crisis accelerates, the last thing we need is this wasteful, water-guzzling, land-hungry extravagance,” he said.Fairman suggested that clubs should retain more water on their land by creating their own small-scale reservoirs or wetlands.England Golf, which represents golf clubs in England, told the Guardian that it provided guidance to clubs on managing water shortages. Its head of sustainability, Kirstin McEvoy, said: “Our objective is to work with all clubs who need help, to ensure that they are making the necessary steps to be sustainable when it comes to their water usage … we recognise these are increasingly challenging times.”An Environment Agency spokesperson said: “Abstraction licences have strict conditions to protect the environment and are reviewed regularly. We expect all abstractors, including golf clubs, to comply fully with these licence conditions to help protect our rivers and groundwater.”Explore more on these topicsWaterEnvironment AgencyGolfDroughtEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: US federal court says no constitutional right to clean water in Mississippi case | Mississippi | The Guardian
description: Appeals court dismisses lawsuit from Jackson residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their rights
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: Appeals court dismisses lawsuit from Jackson residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their rights
Content: Residents of Jackson, Mississippi, say that they have long reeled from water crises.Photograph: Ben Hasty/Reading Eagle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenResidents of Jackson, Mississippi, say that they have long reeled from water crises.Photograph: Ben Hasty/Reading Eagle/Getty ImagesMississippiUS federal court says no constitutional right to clean water in Mississippi caseAppeals court dismisses lawsuit from Jackson residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their rightsVictoria BekiempisTue 8 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US appellate court hasdecidedthat the federal constitution does not guarantee a right to clean water.That legal opinion came in the form of a decision on Friday from the fifth circuit court of appeals to uphold a lower court’s dismissal of a 2022lawsuitfrom several Jackson, Mississippi, residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their constitutional rights.Those residents of Mississippi’s capital city contended that their local drinking water was unsafe to drink because of high lead levels and other contaminants.The New Orleans-based fifth circuit’s majority opinion held that the residents wanted “recognition of two new constitutional rights lacking any foundation in the history and tradition of our nation” – those being “the right to be free from exposure to contaminated water and the right to accurate information from public officials”.In the majority’s view, residents should have gone about their legal fight for clean water another way, such as pursuing “tort claims” or by “electing representatives who will better manage the public-water system, and petitioning their representatives for other remedies”.Tort claims allege “harms caused by others” while seeking “to impose liability on parties responsible for the harm, and to deter others from committing harmful acts”, according toCornell University’s law school.Friday’s decision also said that state and federal officials were working hard to improve the majority-Black city’s drinking water. The residents who filed suit alleged that public authorities had for years failed to mitigate lead levels and failed to inform them about an increase.“Plaintiffs have not been left to go at it alone,” the court said. “The State of Mississippi and federal government have worked for years, and continue today, to improve the city of Jackson’s drinking water quality through regulations, investigations, and compliance plans.”Meanwhile, the opinion also said: “It is undisputed that the Constitution does not guarantee clean water.”The opinion also held that a state does not have a constitutional duty “to provide substantive services for those within its border absent a special relationship”. And municipalities are not constitutionally obligated to provide sewerage, water treatment or waste management services “in a reasonably competent fashion”, the decision said.The decision nonetheless said that the majority of the court recognized the allegations of “serious government misfeasance” and was “sympathetic to the injuries [the plaintiffs] may suffer as a result”. But, the court’s ruling said “our sympathies cannot be the basis” for converting tort claims into constitutional issues.“These deprivations, while grievous, do not infringe upon any deeply rooted constitutional right,” the fifth circuit’s opinion said.Attorneys for the plaintiffs could not immediately be reached for comment. John Horhn, the Jackson mayor, said in a statement: “We are pleased that the fifth circuit upheld the dismissal of these claims.“The City remains committed to the health, safety, and well-being of every Jackson resident.”Jackson residents say that they have long reeled from water crises.The NAACP filed acomplaintin September 2022 alleging that Mississippi state authorities violated civil rights law by repeatedly sending federal money earmarked for drinking water safety to white communities rather than Jackson. Such diversion of funds constituted racial discrimination, the complaint said.“The result is persistently unsafe and unreliable drinking water and massive gaps in the access to safe drinking water that are intolerable in any modern society,” Jackson residentssaidin a complaint to the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). “Nearly all of the residents of Jackson have watched brackish, dirty, impure, and undrinkable water trickle from their taps. At times, some have had no water at all.”The NAACP’s Jackson branch sued over the diversion of these funds in August 2025. The suit against several Mississippi state officials alleged that they “intentionally deprived [Jackson] residents … of access to federal relief funds … which were promised to Jackson in order to address the water infrastructure crisis”.The lawsuit asked for a judge to declare that this diversion of money “is both facially discriminatory and the result of discriminatory purpose” – and to bar officials from permanently siphoning that money away from Jackson.Explore more on these topicsMississippiWaterUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Global move away from oil could lead to conflict and migration, experts say | Oil | The Guardian
description: Researchers urge governments to help worst afflicted countries, such as Nigeria and Algeria, which rely on oil revenues for public services
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Researchers urge governments to help worst afflicted countries, such as Nigeria and Algeria, which rely on oil revenues for public services
Content: Two men walk past gas flares belonging to the Agip Oil company in Idu, in the Niger Delta area of Nigeria.Photograph: Sunday Alamba/APView image in fullscreenTwo men walk past gas flares belonging to the Agip Oil company in Idu, in the Niger Delta area of Nigeria.Photograph: Sunday Alamba/APOilGlobal move away from oil could lead to conflict and migration, experts sayResearchers urge governments to help worst afflicted countries, such as Nigeria and Algeria, which rely on oil revenues for public servicesFiona HarveyEnvironment editorMon 7 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 04.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConflict, migration and economic upheaval will accompany the global move away from oil, unless governments act urgently to help the worst afflicted countries to cope, research has found.Nigeria, Iran, Angola and Algeria are among the countries that will be severely affected, as they rely strongly on oil revenues for their government and provision of public services, but have little diversification and too little capital to cushion the blow.Oil use is already waning in many countries, with the growth of renewable energy, and has been hastened by theeffects of the Iran war, which has constrained supply and sent prices soaring, triggering high inflation and political instability.Global demand for oil is forecast to plateau in the coming decade, with a peak likely in the early 2030s, which will force producers to chase a shrinking pool of buyers. Many will try to hang on to their resource revenues as long as possible, according toresearchfrom the E3G thinktank published on Tuesday, but the cheapest producers with abundant resources – such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – are likely to win against those with less advanced infrastructure.The example of Venezuela, which wassuffering collapse and have had a partial takeover of government by the US, now shattered further by theimpact of earthquakes,should warn countries of what is at stake, the report’s authors found.“Governments are not thinking about and not prepared for [these outcomes],” said Beth Walker, co-author of the report. “The transition becomes riskier for everyone when oil producers are left to adjust on their own, and oil markets left to manage themselves. Producer fragility becomes a global security risk.”Graph showing how mid-tier producers are more exposed to declining oil revenuesPutting off or slowing down thetransitionis an even worse option than confronting it, however, as the climate crisis is rapidly worsening. “None of this is an argument for slowing the transition,” said Maria Pastukhova, a co-author of the report. “A slow but chaotic transition can be just as destabilising as a fast one, maybe even more so.”E3G compiled the report over two years, in part through “war-gaming” various scenarios for declining oil demand with more than 100 public servants and experts from around the world.Bob Ward, policy director at the Grantham Research Institute at the London School of Economics, who was not involved in the report, said developed countries would also be affected. “Many oil producers have been in denial about the pace and scale with which both demand and supply will have to fall if we are to avoid dangerous climate change,” he said. “We should be clear that the highest-cost producers will likely be the first to feel this shock. TheNorth Seahas high operating costs and so is unlikely to be economically viable once demand starts to fall sharply and market prices reduce.”Income from oil makes up more than 40% of the revenue to governments in 17 countries around the world, and in some cases is overwhelmingly the biggest source of income, for instance in Iraq and Libya, where it represents 70% to 90% of government revenues.But this revenue will fall rapidly from 2030: E3G forecasts that Algeria will experience an 87% drop in revenue and Nigeria more than 60%. Algeria in particular was “one to watch” said Walker, with its position near the borders of Europe and almost total reliance on the EU for its exports.This will leave countries with big gaps to fill in providing basic services, which will destabilise social structures. Debt will be an increasing burden – already, Angola and Mexico spend more than a quarter of their government revenue in servicing public debt, the report found.Walker said: “This isn’t one dramatic global oil or security crisis, it’s a series of national fiscal crises that could turn into very different security problems: unrest and migration in Algeria; a much more brittle settlement in Iraq with spillover into Gulf regional stability; weaker state capacity in the most populated country in Africa, Nigeria, with spillovers across the continent; military competition over oil infrastructure in Libya with heightened security risk in Europe. Most of these problems are a much larger scale than Venezuela, and they could all unravel just as the UK and Europe’s capacity to contain live conflicts is drained.”Any attempt to remedy this situation will require organisations such as the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, private sector financial institutions and governments to work together.“Much of the toolkit already exists, but in separate policy boxes that need to work together,” said Pastukhova. “Major demand powers need to coordinate and communicate more clearly about their future demand. They need to produce adjustment not just as part of their development assistance or climate policy, but as part of their foreign and economic security policy, given the consequences that otherwise might follow.”China was the dominant source of increasing oil demand over the past few decades, but itsoil consumption is now on a downward path, in part owing to the rapid uptake of electric vehicles.India’s future direction is less certain, and the country could become pivotal to whether demand declines in time to stave off some of the worst impacts of climate breakdown.Explore more on these topicsOilEnergyFossil fuelsClimate crisisMigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Curbs on vertical drinking in Soho pubs to go ahead as Khan criticises council’s ‘breathtaking arrogance’ | London | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: London mayor accuses council of ‘ignoring’ responses to a consultation
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Exclusive: London mayor accuses council of ‘ignoring’ responses to a consultation
Content: People drinking outside a pub in Soho. Westminster council has proposed that new licences should be granted to pubs and bars in which people are seated rather than standing.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople drinking outside a pub in Soho. Westminster council has proposed that new licences should be granted to pubs and bars in which people are seated rather than standing.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesLondonCurbs on vertical drinking in Soho pubs to go ahead as Khan criticises council’s ‘breathtaking arrogance’Exclusive: London mayor accuses council of ‘ignoring’ responses to a consultationHelena HortonTue 8 Sep 2026 08.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 15.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSadiq Khan has criticised the “breathtaking arrogance” of Westminster council, which has kept restrictions on vertical drinking in Soho and an effective ban on new bars and pubs in the area.The mayor of London has accused the Conservative-led council of “ignoring” the responses to a consultation into its new licensing policy. The vast majority of respondents, 81%, disagreed with the council’s “cumulative impact zone” which decrees that applications for bars and pubs in theWest Endof London, one of Europe’s most famous nightlife districts, will be refused unless in exceptional circumstances. Eighty-four per cent said the licensing policy would be bad for business.Respondents also criticisedthe council’s position on “vertical drinking”, which is standing up to have a beverage, a common practice in British pubs. The council proposed, to widespread outcry, that new licences for pubs and bars should be granted to those venues which have table service instead of ordering at the bar, and those in which people are seated rather than standing.The mayor had responded to a consultation held this summer by the council and ordered them to scrap the cumulative impact zone and allow pubs and bars to have space for vertical drinking. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, also waded into the row, saying vertical drinking is “British life”.Despite this, the council is continuing with both the vertical drinking policy and the cumulative impact zone, and said that those who wrote to complain did so because they did not understand the terminology in its licensing document.Khan told the Guardian: “The arrogance of Westminster council is breathtaking. By ignoring all those who oppose their plans and viewing hospitality in the heart of our capital city as a problem, they are letting down businesses, residents and our economy. They would rather see nightlife die than thrive.”Tim Barnes, Westminster city council’s deputy leader, said the issue was a policing one and called for more resources for the area. He added: “Beyond disagreements over policy jargon there are serious issues acting as a drag on our hospitality industry.“A lack of investment in policing has left the Met objecting to many licensing applications over public safety concerns.”But the final licensing policy keeps restrictions on vertical drinking. It reads: “When considering new licence applications, discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high volume vertical drinking.”In the revised policy, the council says it did approve a new pub in the cumulative impact zone recently – The Lady in Covent Garden. However, most of the space in this pub is for a sit-down restaurant. The document states that the bar on the bottom floor of the pub would not usually be allowed, but in this case it is because it will “only operate in association with the restaurant use”.The government is due to grant new powers to Khan, allowing him to “call in” local council decisions he opposes.He said: “London’s famous hospitality and nightlife sectors are vital for our economy, and one of the reasons our capital is so special.“Running our world-famous nightlife district with a nimby village-hall mindset is simply not sustainable. This is why the government was right to give me new powers to help ensure our fantastic hospitality and nightlife can flourish, helping create more jobs and ensure we stay a vibrant global city.”Data shows that only 3.5% of applications that went to a licensing subcommittee in Westminster were approved exactly as applied for between 2023 and 2026. Pub and wine bar applications were down 80% in 2022-24.The Soho Society, a group established in 1972 aimed at “preserving the character of Soho”,voted in its AGM earlier this summer for a new licensing mandate, meaning it will challenge all new applications for bars and restaurants in the area, including reviews of existing licences. It will also object to any venue that wishes to open beyond “core hours”, which Westminster council decrees end between 10.30pm and midnight, depending on the business and day of the week.Explore more on these topicsLondonHospitality industrySadiq KhanPubsWest EndnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK government pays highest interest rate on 30-year bond since 1998 | Government borrowing | The Guardian
description: High yields threaten to wipe out at least half of the £24bn headroom John Healey was expecting to have for his budget
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: High yields threaten to wipe out at least half of the £24bn headroom John Healey was expecting to have for his budget
Content: The Bank of England’s governor, Andrew Bailey, said the latest oil price rises were also putting pressure on inflation and interest rates.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Bank of England’s governor, Andrew Bailey, said the latest oil price rises were also putting pressure on inflation and interest rates.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAGovernment borrowingUK government pays highest interest rate on 30-year bond since 1998High yields threaten to wipe out at least half of the £24bn headroom John Healey was expecting to have for his budgetHeather StewartEconomics editorTue 8 Sep 2026 13.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 15.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government was forced to pay the highest interest rate for a 30-year bond since 1998 on Tuesday, underlining the fiscal challenges facing the chancellor, John Healey.Echoing the global bond market sell-off that has driven up yields, or interest rates, on government borrowing across the main markets, the Treasury paid 5.82% to borrow £4bn.That was the highest rate since the Debt Management Office, which is responsible for financing government borrowing, was established in 1998. Healeyused a speech in Coventryon Monday to stress that he was determined to balance the books.Markets have been spooked by fears of a fresh rise in inflation after the resumption of the Middle East conflict increased oil prices, and investors fretting about the risks of rising public debt.When the Office forBudgetResponsibility does its latest forecast before the budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on government borrowing are expected to wipe out at least half of the £24bn headroom that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, built up at her spring forecast in March.‘There’s no plan’: as instability in global bond markets rises, what are the knock-on effects?Read moreNews of the costly debt auction came as the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, told MPs the latest rise in oil prices were also putting pressure on inflation and interest rates.“The risks, I’m afraid, are on the upside,” he said. “And that’s really the risks coming from energy prices.”Bailey insisted there was no secret plan to raise interest rates, however, and stressed that higher borrowing costs had already had an impact on consumers without the Bank having to take action.“UK mortgage rates now are typically at the moment about a three-quarters of a percent higher than they were at the point when the conflict broke out,” he said. “I think with the possible exception of Japan, although that’s a little hard to map, that’s the largest increase in mortgage rates in the G7.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBrent crude was trading at about $97 a barrel on Tuesday. Bailey said the oil price could be higher still with the strait of Hormuz still largely closed to tanker traffic and Ukraine attacking refineries in Russia.The governor was appearing at the Commons Treasury select committee alongside three fellow members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee, which will meet next week to set interest rates.Megan Greene, who was in the minority voting for a rate rise in July, said she remained concerned about the risks of acting too late against inflation, but Dave Ramsden and Alan Taylor, who didn’t back a rate rise, suggested prices had risen less than feared as a result of the Iran war.Explore more on these topicsGovernment borrowingBondsGiltsEconomic policyEconomicsBudgetEconomic growth (GDP)newsShareReuse this content

title: Channel 4 to axe about 300 jobs in biggest layoffs in its history | Channel 4 | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Staff expect ‘brutal’ cutbacks as broadcaster seeks to reduce costs amid advertising slowdown
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Exclusive: Staff expect ‘brutal’ cutbacks as broadcaster seeks to reduce costs amid advertising slowdown
