Content: Channel 4 employs 1,276 people according to its most recent annual report.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenChannel 4 employs 1,276 people according to its most recent annual report.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAChannel 4Channel 4 to axe about 300 jobs in biggest layoffs in its historyExclusive: Staff expect ‘brutal’ cutbacks as broadcaster seeks to reduce costs amid advertising slowdownBusiness live – latest updatesMark SweneyTue 8 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChannel 4 is poised to cut about 300 jobs – about a quarter of its workforce – in the biggest round of layoffs in its 43-year history, as the broadcaster seeks to dramatically cut costs.Priya Dogra, whotook over from Alex Mahon as chief executive in March, is to address an all-staff meeting on Wednesday on a wide-ranging review of Channel 4’s strategy and structure.The broadcaster’s head count had risen to 1,276 by 2025, according to its latest annual report, after undergoing an expansion across the UK.Tiny cash buffers leave small UK TV firms at risk of going bust, analysis findsRead moreChannel 4 is still working on final numbers for job losses but multiple sources said the level of savings being sought, which will also come from efficiencies in other parts of the business, equates to about 300 to 325 staff roles.Two years ago, Mahon announced 200 job cuts, thenthe biggest round of layoffs in more than 15 years, as staff numbers swelled to a record 1,350 amid the worst TV advertising downturn since 2008.At the time of Mahon’s cost-cutting programme, Channel 4’s wage bill had hit £108m. It has grown significantly in the past two years to £122m.When the TV advertising market slumped during the 2008 financial crisis, Channel 4 sought tobalance its finances by cutting 200 jobs, almost a quarter of its then 875 permanent employees.Staff are expecting the cuts to be “brutal”, a source said, and London is likely to be a significant focus, given it was only last year when Channel 4 delivered on a promise to increase employee numbers in the nations and regions to 600.According to the annual report, Channel 4 employs 255 full-time equivalent staff in the commercial department, 423 in creative roles, 542 in operations and 56 at its 4Talent arm.View image in fullscreenChannel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra is to address an all-staff meeting on Wednesday.Photograph: Royal Television Society/YoutubeDogra is also expected to make changes to the content and commissioning operation, which last year operated with a £640m programming budget, of which £480m was spent on British original content.It is understood that Dogra wants Channel 4 to cut back on the number of shows it commissions with a focus on finding fewer but more well-funded hits, and increase marketing firepower to promote programmes, a model she operated with while an executive at Sky and Warner Bros Discovery. However, the overall aim of the restructure and strategy is to limit the extent of cuts to the content budget.A spokesperson for the broadcaster said: “As we have shared publicly, under the leadership of our new chief executive, we have been assessing Channel 4’s strategic direction, including a comprehensive review of the structure, shape and size of our organisation.“We have committed to keeping Channel 4 staff updated in a timely and transparent way, so any organisational change will be shared with them first and we won’t be commenting on speculation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe announcement comes as candidates for the new director of programmes, a role created after chief content officerIan Katz announced his departure, are understood to be facing first-round interviews with Dogra this week.Channel 4 reported a pre-tax loss of £10m last year, a third annual deficit in a row after £12m in 2024 and a record £52m in 2023.Its total revenues fell by 1% to £1.03bn last year, with total advertising revenues falling by 2%, outperforming the wider market.The broadcaster is dependent on advertising for 90% of total revenues, making it particularly vulnerable as digital platforms such as YouTube continue to hoover up ad budgets.Enders Analysis published a report in May on Channel 4 titled Time for Reset, which said that a £69m drop in the broadcaster’s cash reserves to £49m at the end of last year marked their lowest level in more than 20 years.In July, Channel 4 secured an agreement with the government to tap the remaining half of its £150m revolving credit facility. The broadcaster, which is state-owned but commercially funded, is able to access £75m of its credit facility immediately, but needs state approval to access the remaining half.In its most recent annual report, Channel 4 said it intended to tap the remaining facility to “protect liquidity headroom and manage risks arising from the current geopolitical and economic environment and our on-going business transformation”.Explore more on these topicsChannel 4Television industryJob lossesAdvertisingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barnaby Webber’s death in Nottingham attack was ‘potentially preventable’, inquiry told | Nottingham | The Guardian
description: More rapid use of blood products may have raised chance of 19-year-old making it to hospital, though chance was low, says counsel
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: More rapid use of blood products may have raised chance of 19-year-old making it to hospital, though chance was low, says counsel
Content: Webber, 19, was one of three people fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane in June 2023.Photograph: Nottinghamshire police/PAView image in fullscreenWebber, 19, was one of three people fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane in June 2023.Photograph: Nottinghamshire police/PANottinghamBarnaby Webber’s death in Nottingham attack was ‘potentially preventable’, inquiry toldMore rapid use of blood products may have raised chance of 19-year-old making it to hospital, though chance was low, says counselNeha GohilMidlands correspondentTue 8 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe death of a 19-year-old student who was killed in theNottinghamattacks in 2023 was “potentially preventable”, a public inquiry into the incident has heard.Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, both 19, and Ian Coates, a 65-year-old caretaker, were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, a paranoid schizophrenic, on 13 June 2023.In 2024, Calocane wassentenced to an indefinite hospital orderafter admitting three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility and three counts of attempted murder.The inquiry is examining the events leading up to attacks, and has heard evidence from various local authorities, including health professionals and police officers, as well as Calocane’s family, in order to assess the “events, acts and omissions” that led to the killings.During closing submissions on Tuesday, it heard how a panel of medical professionals had assessed the emergency medical response to the attacks and the “survivability” of victims.Rachel Langdale KC, counsel to the inquiry, said the assessment had found that “more rapid administration of blood products” could have increased Webber’s chance of getting to hospital and possibly undergoing surgery.The 19-year-old had a “far less” than 50% chance of surviving his injuries, which was classed as “potentially preventable”, Langdale said. She added that O’Malley-Kumar and Coates’s deaths were “not preventable”.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Ian Coates, Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar.Photograph: Nottinghamshire police/PAThe assessment, which also acknowledged the efforts of emergency services, found that a more rapid administration of blood to Webber would have to have been coupled with multiple other rapid and meticulous steps “in order for Barnaby to survive to intensive care”.The inquiry also addressed the emergence of further evidence after hearings had concluded in early June.At the start of closing arguments, the inquiry’s chair, Deborah Taylor KC, said it was “disappointing”, and that further evidence “ought to have been identified by core participants and disclosed earlier”. She called on them to provide all corrections and omissions by 31 December.Such evidence included the police discovery of a holdall bag at Calocane’s former address in Nottingham in the days after the attack. The bag contained notebooks that were not disclosed to the inquiry until June this year.The books contained notes from Calocane in which he described himself as God, and said police had “mind-reading software” and that he had the power to “resurrect people”, the inquiry heard.Other documents created by Calocane were found in a bin at the property, containing bullet points about explosives, including TNT and nitrate fertiliser. Such notes were not identified or taken into account by police, nor made available to the Crown Prosecution Service or to psychiatric experts, the inquiry heard.View image in fullscreenCalocane appearing at Nottingham crown court in 2024.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAThe lawyer representing bereaved families, Tim Moloney KC, said one of the notes appeared to say “Manchester Arena”. Calocane had also searched online for “large venues in Nottingham”, he said.“Nobody has ever asked [Calocane] why he was researching explosives and large venues, because they couldn’t,” Maloney said. “There was a failure to investigate [Calocane’s] historical behaviour and actions.”The inquiry was also not told of violent assaults committed by Calocane until after the hearings concluded in early June. One involved an assault on a colleague in a warehouse in 2021, and in another he punched a colleague in Normanton in February 2023.Evidence presented to the inquiry earlier this year detailed how Calocane had committed a string of violent incidents in the years before the attacks, leading to himbeing sectioned four timesin the space of two years.An arrest warrant was also out for Calocane at the time of the Nottingham attacks, after he failed to appear in court for the alleged assault of a police officer, the inquiry heard previously.Closing submissions will conclude on Wednesday and a report detailing the inquiry’s findings will be published next year.Explore more on these topicsNottinghamEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former lab analyst sentenced to 10 years in prison for manipulating DNA data | Colorado | The Guardian
description: Authorities accused Missy Woods of altering years worth of data in cases involving homicide, sexual assault and robbery
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Authorities accused Missy Woods of altering years worth of data in cases involving homicide, sexual assault and robbery
Content: Former Colorado Bureau of Investigation forensic analyst Yvonne "Missy" Woods cries as she gives a personal statement.Photograph: Stephen Swofford/Pool The Gazette/APView image in fullscreenFormer Colorado Bureau of Investigation forensic analyst Yvonne "Missy" Woods cries as she gives a personal statement.Photograph: Stephen Swofford/Pool The Gazette/APColoradoFormer lab analyst sentenced to 10 years in prison for manipulating DNA dataAuthorities accused Missy Woods of altering years worth of data in cases involving homicide, sexual assault and robberyAssociated PressTue 8 Sep 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA judge sentenced a former forensic analyst for theColoradoBureau of Investigation to 10 years in prison on Tuesday after authorities said her manipulation of DNA data had raised questions about the validity of hundreds of criminal cases.Yvonne “Missy” Woods pleaded guilty in June to perjury, attempting to influence a public servant, forgery and committing a cybercrime. Dozens of other counts were dismissed as part of a plea agreement.Problems with the scientist’s work were found in cases involving homicide, sexual assault, robbery and other crimes, according to authorities. Prosecutors were forced to review hundreds of cases, and at least one murder conviction was overturned as a result of Woods’ misconduct.Woods had faced between 8 and 16 years in prison during Tuesday’s sentencing hearing before state district judge Andrew Poland in Golden, Colorado.She resigned in 2023 after a decades-long career. Authorities accused her of altering data to conceal tampering, deleting data that showed she failed to troubleshoot issues within the testing process and not thoroughly documenting tests performed in case records.Woods apologized during Tuesday’s hearing but said she knew saying sorry would not undo the harm she caused, the Denver Post reported.“For many years I was entrusted with evidence that could have profound consequences for defendants, victims, families and the courts. I failed that responsibility. I am deeply sorry for that failure,” she said.The investigation into her misconduct began in September 2023 after an intern at the bureau discovered missing information in a case that Woods handled in 2018. According to an arrest affidavit, Woods allegedly told investigators at one point that she had changed data to complete cases more quickly.In the overturned murder case, Michael Clark was released from prison in 2025 after his lawyers argued that DNA evidence was mishandled by Woods. Prosecutors said they would seek to retry him.In two homicide cases, the defendants received lesser sentences under plea deals than they could have faced if they went to trial because prosecutors were afraid Woods’ involvement could lead to acquittals.Convictions in other cases also have been challenged in courts across Colorado.A Colorado Bureau of Investigation internal affairs report in 2024 revealed that concerns about Woods’ work first surfaced more than a decade ago. As early as 2014, a worker questioned her testing of evidence, and in 2018 she was temporarily removed from working on DNA cases after being accused of data manipulation, the report said.State officials have said that the response to Woods’ actions could end up costing more than $11m.Explore more on these topicsColoradoUS crimeForensic sciencenewsShareReuse this content

title: Eiffel Tower management under fire after decision to hide female staff | Paris | The Guardian
description: One-day strike called after Paris landmark agreed to keep women out of sight for visit by Hindu group
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: One-day strike called after Paris landmark agreed to keep women out of sight for visit by Hindu group
Content: Female staff were ‘replaced and made invisible’, the site’s employees said in a statement.Photograph: Lou Benoist/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFemale staff were ‘replaced and made invisible’, the site’s employees said in a statement.Photograph: Lou Benoist/AFP/Getty ImagesParisEiffel Tower management under fire after decision to hide female staffOne-day strike called after Paris landmark agreed to keep women out of sight for visit by Hindu groupKim Willsherin ParisTue 8 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor ofParis, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.Explore more on these topicsParisFranceWomenHinduismReligionIndianewsShareReuse this content

title: Organised crime driving illicit cigarette factory boom ‘in almost every EU state’ | European Union | The Guardian
description: Bloc losing €13bn in revenue with one in 10 cigarettes illegal, watchdog reports
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Bloc losing €13bn in revenue with one in 10 cigarettes illegal, watchdog reports
Content: Gangs are increasingly moving production inside the EU ‘to shorten supply chains and get closer to consumers’.Photograph: Cavan Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenGangs are increasingly moving production inside the EU ‘to shorten supply chains and get closer to consumers’.Photograph: Cavan Images/AlamyEuropean UnionOrganised crime driving illicit cigarette factory boom ‘in almost every EU state’Bloc losing €13bn in revenue with one in 10 cigarettes illegal, watchdog reportsEurope live – latest updatesJon Henley, Europe correspondentTue 8 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe illegal trade in tobacco is booming in the EU, according to a report by the bloc’s financial watchdog, with almost one in 10 cigarettes produced illicitly or smuggled, causing an estimated €13bn loss in tax revenue each year.The European Court of Auditors (ECA) said in a report on Tuesday that the trade had “changed significantly” in recent years as smuggling, while still “a problem”, was overtaken by illicit manufacturing, which has increased dramatically in the bloc.Organised crime gangs are moving production inside the EU “to shorten supply chains and get closer to consumers”, said the ECA’s Petri Sarvamaa. “Illegal production sites have now been detected in almost every EU member state.”The ECA cited the example of a large-scale illicit cigarette factory in Belgium dismantled by police last year. It operated around the clock, with 50 workers running four production lines, each able to produce 1m cigarettes every hour.During a raid on the largest illegal facility so far uncovered, in Spain, police seized 3m packs of cigarettes valued at €15m, five tonnes of raw tobacco worth €5m, and made 20 arrests. The factory’s products had been distributed across six EU countries.“The scale is quite remarkable,” Sarvamaa said. “Last month French authorities dismantled a cross-border operation that had been supplying the city of Lille only since last December but had already made 120 deliveries of 7,500 packs each.”The ECA report said such illicit cigarette factories, which usually operate for two- to four months, were using sophisticated equipment and employing experienced technicians to set up and maintain their machinery.The organised crime groups that run them split production across multiple facilities and often locate them in border regions, tailoring their operations by producing specific brands for individual markets and even developing new tobacco products.The damage goes beyond lost tax revenue. The trade “undermines public health policies by making tobacco products cheaper and more accessible, especially to young people”, Sarvamaa said. It also feeds organised crime and finances other illegal activities.While, overall, tobacco consumption has continued to fall across the EU, the quantity of illicit tobacco products has risen steadily, reaching about 8.8 % of total cigarette consumption in 2023 (the latest figures available), the report said – although information about the size, structure or economic impact of the trade remains “incomplete and unreliable”.The report said the EU and many member states had taken steps to combat the trade, but were hampered because European law in the area was not harmonised and member states’ efforts were uneven, leaving enforcement gaps.National control systems and enforcement have different definitions of offences and of penalties, encouraging criminals to move to the more lax jurisdictions, and information exchanges in the bloc were inconsistent.“Criminals involved in the illicit tobacco trade are succeeding not because Europe lacks legislation but because gaps remain in coordination, information and enforcement,” Sarvamaa said. “Organised crime has a strategy. We need one too.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionOrganised crimeSmokingEuropeYoung peopleHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘In parks you only see dogs, never children’: can Bogotá adapt to its ageing population? | Global development | The Guardian
description: With a lower fertility rate than Tokyo and the number of pensioners rapidly rising, Colombia’s capital is being forced to change the way it thinks about growing old
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With a lower fertility rate than Tokyo and the number of pensioners rapidly rising, Colombia’s capital is being forced to change the way it thinks about growing old
Content: Bogotá has launched a number of initiatives to tackle its ageing population. Women often retire at 57, when they can draw a pension, but life expectancy has risen to 78.Photograph: Bogotá health secretariatView image in fullscreenBogotá has launched a number of initiatives to tackle its ageing population. Women often retire at 57, when they can draw a pension, but life expectancy has risen to 78.Photograph: Bogotá health secretariatGlobal development‘In parks you only see dogs, never children’: can Bogotá adapt to its ageing population?With a lower fertility rate than Tokyo and the number of pensioners rapidly rising, Colombia’s capital is being forced to change the way it thinks about growing oldSupported byAbout this contentClaire McQueTue 8 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 06.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom his wheelchair, Alberto Delgado Londoño can see over the wall of the sunlit courtyard towards the mountains east of Bogotá, Colombia’s capital. The 74-year-old lives in a care home for destitute elderly people, which opened at the end of last year.Social workers found him in hospital, where he was being treated for throat cancer and a head injury that left him partly paralysed. “I had nowhere to go,” he says. “My daughter couldn’t take me in because she’s a single mother, she already has two children.”Delgado Londoño is one of a growing number of Bogotanos with nowhere to turn in old age – an estimated1,100 elderly people in the city are homeless, without families to care for them. To reach this vulnerable group,Bogotá unveiled a plan last year to integrateits social care and health systems.“We have to be a society that knows how to care for its adults,” says Gerson Bermont Galavis, Bogotá’s health secretary. This means overhauling healthcare, social care and employment, requiring “a totally different city”, he says.The capital’s population peaked this year at about7.9 million; it is forecast to start shrinking from 2027.Nearly 16% of its residents are aged over 60, with the number projected to reachnearly 20% by 2035, according to Bogotá’s Health Observatory.Meanwhile, the ​old-age dependency ratio across Colombia isprojected to ​double from 20.6% in 2025 to 42% by 2070, according to modelling by ​t​he country’s central bank. That means fewer taxpayers to foot the bill for public pensions and support a healthcare system already under strain from a national funding crisis.View image in fullscreenThe city is working on an an intergenerational model of healthcare, spanning birth to old age.Photograph: Bogotá health secretariatAs people live longer and birthrates fall, the UN’s Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (Eclac) notes that“the ageing process in the region is occurring faster than in other regions of the world”. By 2050, the UN projects that nearlyone in five people will be over the age of 65, up from one in 11 in 2020. Bogotá is not yet the oldest city in the region, but the sudden slump in its birthrate suggests it could soon match other South American capitals, such as Buenos Aires, Santiago and Montevideo.Bogotá’s total fertility rate – the average number of children a woman is likely to have over her lifetime – islower than Tokyo’s, at 0.82in 2025. Nationally, the rate has also fallen sharply – down to1.6 children for every womanin 2024, from 6.7 in 1960. It is far below the replacement rate of 2.1 required to maintain a stable population.“In the parks you only see dogs, you never see children,” says Juliana Jaramillo, an economist who studies demography at Colombia’s central bank.“But it’s really difficult for a government to reduce the cost of having a child,” she adds. “Instead of trying to reverse the trend, you have to adapt to a new scenario.”The city is already adjusting to the demographic change. Nursery enrolment in Bogotá fell by 13% between 2019 and 2023, the steepest drop in the country, and287 schools, mostly private, closed in the capital between 2019 and 2024.View image in fullscreenA newly restored part of San Juan de Dios hospital in Bogotá’s historic centre.Photograph: Bogotá health secretariat“We have a city that is ageing very rapidly, and we’re not responding quickly enough,” says Dr Manuel González, who designs Bogotá’s health policy. Increased longevity means more people enduring unhealthy and lonely lives, he says. “We are spending 10 years of our lives in ill health.”While increasing the birthrate is hard, the city is focusing on boosting “healthy life” expectancy and changing how the capital thinks about growing old.At the heart of this attempt to rethink ageing is San Juan de Dios, a 100-year-old hospital complex in Bogotá’s historic centre, close to Colombia’s leading institutes for oncology, dermatology and neonatal care. It closed in 2001 amid a funding crisis, but the constitutional court subsequentlydeclared it a site of national heritageand ordered that its 24 buildings be restored. Eleven are now being renovated.The 16-hectare (40-acre) hospital campus that is being created will encompass centres for youth and mental health but also residential care for older people, health and research facilities, rewilded gardens and a cultural centre, costing about 4tn pesos (£940m) to restore.“It’s being conceived of as a miniature city,” says González. “But the way it operated 100 years ago is no longer what we need.”View image in fullscreenDr Manuel González, centre, outlines plans for the San Juan de Dios project, which includes health and research facilities, rewilded gardens and a cultural centre.Photograph: Bogotá health secretariatHe thinks San Juan de Dios should work as an intergenerational model of healthcare, spanning birth to old age. In March, theCentre for Thought and Innovation on Ageing openedin the hospital’s old laundry. It will advise Bogotá and the surrounding region on preventive care, chronic diseases and disability management. At a new training centre, caregivers can learn practical skills, from managing catheters to transferring patients into wheelchairs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In Latin American countries like Colombia, caregiving has always fallen on households … and mainly on women,” says Paola Camelo Urrego, of the University of the Andes. In Bogotá, women devote nearlyfive hours a dayto unpaid care and multigenerational homes are becoming less common, meaning fewer family members to help with dependents.In 2020, Bogotá’s former mayor Claudia López opened“care blocks”, where caregivers can drop off a toddler or an elderly parent for a few hours. This network of 20 community centres also teaches people to live healthier, more independent lives. Inside one, a boisterous group of over-65s learn to use WhatsApp. Afterwards, they may learn English or how to repair a motorbike.These centres have given caregivers greater recognition, says Camelo Urrego, but they have not redistributed who does the grandparent duties. “Women get home to find nothing has changed.”“Loneliness really gets to me,” says Don Jorge, a 76-year-old who has recently recovered from a bout of tuberculosis. He rarely receives visitors in the nursing home and he misses having someone to confide in.View image in fullscreenAbout 4,500 people took part in  a a seniors’ grand ball in December.Photograph: Bogotá social integration secretariatTo reduce social isolation, the city has begun prescribing culture and nature-based activities. Instead of getting pills to cure their ills, patients can take part in activities such as visits to the botanic gardens, traditional marketplaces or community-run gardening. Last December, agranbailemayor(seniors’ grand ball) drew about 4,500 older people who danced to live salsa at the city’s Movistar Arena.Equally vital is changing how people think about ageing. “We can’t think of people over 50 as grandparents,” says María del Pilar López Uribe, Bogotá’s economic development secretary. “The problem isn’t finding people over 50 who want to work, it’s finding companies willing to take a chance on them.”The city offers short courses to retrain older workers. Companies hiring workers over 50 receive a bonus, with an additional payout if the worker is retained. In time, other measures such as raising the retirement age may be needed. Colombian men now generally retire at 62 and women at 57, while averagelife expectancy is about 78.As it is, the city can scarcely afford to pay for more pensioners.Bogotá’s GDP per capitawas less than £10,500 in 2024, about a fifth of Tokyo’s. Colombia’s high inequality compounds the problem. About a third of workers in the capital operate informally, meaning a financially precarious old age is likely. Just17% of retired womenin Bogotá have a pension, and 29% of men.View image in fullscreenParticipants enjoying salsa dancing at the ball, part of a scheme aimed at changing how Bogotá thinks about growing old.Photograph: Bogotá social integration secretariatYet Jaramillo says Bogotá’s demographic trajectory is not set in stone. Most Colombian women have their babies aged between 20 and 29 – 10 years earlier than in developed countries, making the issue of fertility less pressing.“That puts us in a very different position to Japan and the US, where policymakers might be worrying about how women can have children,” she says.Meanwhile, Delgado Londoño remains upbeat about the future, despite his problems. “I’m working on a collection of poems,” he says, pulling out his phone to reveal a 100-verse poem about anarriero(muleteer) plodding through Colombia’s coffee region. “I keep writing.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentColombiaOlder peopleAmericasGlobal healthAgeingCities and developmentfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Everything is against us’: Jaguar Land Rover suppliers voice fears amid carmaker’s cutbacks | Jaguar Land Rover | The Guardian
description: Firms warn of impact of company’s decision to to axe 4,000 jobs and call for government to support sector
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Firms warn of impact of company’s decision to to axe 4,000 jobs and call for government to support sector
Content: Staff members assemble door panels on the production line at Jaguar Land Rover's Halewood factory in Liverpool.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenStaff members assemble door panels on the production line at Jaguar Land Rover's Halewood factory in Liverpool.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersJaguar Land Rover‘Everything is against us’: Jaguar Land Rover suppliers voice fears amid carmaker’s cutbacksFirms warn of impact of company’s decision to to axe 4,000 jobs and call for government to support sectorJaguar Land Rover confirms plan to cut 4,000 jobsNeha GohilMidlands correspondentTue 8 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Roberts is not in an optimistic mood. The chair of Coventry-based Evtec may preside over a business with 900 highly skilled employees, multiple sites and precision machinery, but the outlook for the manufacturer appears tricky. “Everything is against us,” he says.Evtec is a “tier 1” supplier to Jaguar Land Rover, also headquartered in Coventry, which this week announced4,000 job cuts over two yearseven as the chancellor, John Healey, attempted to talk up Britain’s growth prospects in his first big speech, just down the road.The cuts have stoked fears for the estimated tens of thousands of people across the UK whoare employed in the supply chain to Britain’s biggest carmaker, particularly in theWest Midlands. JLR made the cuts in the face of intense competition from Chinese carmakers, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a cyber-attack.Roberts warns the automotive demand will “contract inexorably over the next five years” without significant support and changes in government policy.“Nobody knows the rate or speed of that decline, but decline it will, because everything is against us, everything, [when] making cars in the UK,” says the chair of Evtec, which specialises in high-pressure aluminium die casting and has sites in Coventry and Kidderminster.The JLR chief executive, PB Balaji, hopes to save £1.7bn through the cuts which will mainly affect employees at its head office. He said the automotive industry “faces significant challenges, with technological change amid intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”.View image in fullscreenFirms such as those making aluminium die castings for car parts will be affected by Jaguar Land Rover’s moves.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianThe decision marks the latest in a string of worrying signs of decline for the industry, threatening Andy Burnham’s ambition to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustralise Britain.Corin Crane, the group chief executive of the Chamber of Commerce in Coventry and Warwickshire, believes 140,000 to 180,000 people are employed in supply chain businesses connected to JLR.It is hard to overstate exactly how important JLR is to the West Midlands economy, he says. “We make stuff here and so many of our businesses are in the supply chain for JLR and even if not manufacturing companies, the business support companies, the professional services, all of them have contracts with this great big supplier.“So when there’s problems with JLR, it’s a broader problem for the West Midlands as a whole.”Oxford Economics hasestimatedJLR contributed £8.7bn to the West Midlands in 2024, equivalent to 4.7% of the regional economy – as well as contributing £1.1bn to the north-west, where it has a plant at Halewood.The importance of JLR to the local and UK-wide economy was underscored last year when the devastating hackleft suppliers strugglingandhit UK GDP. JLR scrambled to set up a help desk for its supply chain, including more than 700 companies making the 30,000 parts that can make up a luxury car.View image in fullscreenJLR contributed £8.7bn to the West Midlands in 2024, according to Oxford Economics.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThe hack paused production for four weeks, leaving factory workers stuck at home, and costing the manufacturer £200m. It was one of several factors contributing to JLRposting a profit before tax of just £14m– down from £2.5bn the year before.This time, white-collar managers and research and development staff are in the crosshairs, with the cuts expected to be largely found through UK voluntary redundancies in those areas. However, there are concerns over a ripple effect if JLR’s struggles persist.Evtec’s Roberts has united a loose collective of about 15 business that supply JLR, making up £2bn of revenue and with 12,000-14,000 employees, in order to speak with a “common voice” about the issues they are facing.He describes JLR as the “kingpin” of the UK’s automotive industry and warns that challenges facing the manufacturer had knock-on effects on suppliers and smaller car manufacturers including McLaren, Aston Martin, Bentley and Rolls-Royce.“There will come a point that the decline will be unstoppable and that will be the end of the motor industry as we currently know it. We’ll just be a very small volume player,” he says.Industry experts have long warned of the growing challenges facing car manufacturers in the UK, from the increased competition from China, Trump’s tariffs and the transition to electric vehicles.Healey acknowledged it was a “worrying time” for JLR’s workers and suppliers on Monday, while the mayor of the West Midlands, Richard Parker, announced a £500,000 support package for JLR staff. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, who has ruled out state support to protect the jobs, will meet the company and the Unite union to discuss the cuts on Tuesday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe owner of a plastic manufacturer based in Birmingham, who has supplied JLR for decades, says his workforce has been cut by about 75% because of the challenges facing the sector.View image in fullscreenA JLR supplier urged the company to be more transparent with firms and the public.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThe business owner, who did not want to be identified, calls on JLR to be more transparent with suppliers and the public in order to restore confidence.“We’ve got owners that do want to invest in taking us to the next level but they need the transparency, the visibility and confidence in future UK productions … to justify investment,” he says.The business owner also voices concerns about the broader impact of declining industry on jobs and skills in the local area.“JLR supports an enormous network of tool-makers and moulders, manufacturers and engineers across the whole region, so it’s affecting us all,” he says. “The saddest aspect is we could potentially lose decades of engineering if we haven’t got these big companies in the Midlands supporting it any more.”Steve Morley, the president of the Confederation of British Metalforming, echoes concerns for the automotive industry but says the announcement of job cuts was not a surprise.“Previous government policies have done nothing to support the automotive sector at all and the writing has been on the wall for a long time, not only here but in Europe as well,” he says.Specifically, he criticises high labour and energy costs in the UK, as well as policies around EVs. The industry has argued the government’s EV sales targets are too onerous.Reynolds has refused to rule out watering downgovernment targets for UK automakersto reach 80% zero-emission car sales by 2030, which would lead to a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2035.Morley says: “If we want to be competitive, we have to have infrastructure that lets us be competitive. We cannot afford to have the energy costs we’ve got, the labour costs we’ve got, the policies around EV that stranglehold the automotive sector.”Balaji said on Monday JLR was “committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect” through the redundancy process.A government spokesperson said it understands that this will be an “uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and wider communities”.Explore more on these topicsJaguar Land RoverAutomotive industryManufacturing sectorWest MidlandsJob lossesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Billionaire Chris Rokos, who paid £330m in tax last year, to quit UK | The super-rich | The Guardian
description: Hedge fund tycoon is latest financier to exit amid fears among super-rich over tax rises
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Hedge fund tycoon is latest financier to exit amid fears among super-rich over tax rises
Content: Chris Rokos was ranked third in the Sunday Times’s list of top taxpayers in the UK.Photograph: Nick Saffell/University of Cambridge/PAView image in fullscreenChris Rokos was ranked third in the Sunday Times’s list of top taxpayers in the UK.Photograph: Nick Saffell/University of Cambridge/PAThe super-richBillionaire Chris Rokos, who paid £330m in tax last year, to quit UKHedge fund tycoon is latest financier to exit amid fears among super-rich over tax risesBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaTue 8 Sep 2026 03.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos is poised to leave the UK, the latest in a string of high-profile exits among Britain’s super-rich.The founder of Rokos Capital Management is preparing to move his residency to Greece, and will open an office in Athens as part of the move, according to Bloomberg.He joins a number of billionaires who have left the UK, which many have blamed on theabolition of the non-dom regime, as well as higher tax on private equity investments, inheritance and capital gains.Billionaires hoarding wealth while the rest of us struggle need to ask themselves: what would Dolly do? | Rebecca ShawRead moreRokos, who founded his firm in 2015, was ranked third in the Sunday Times’s annual list of top taxpayers in the UK, paying an estimated bill of £330m in 2025. He has a net worth of about $4bn (£2.96bn), according to Bloomberg’s billionaires index.This year he also made a record£190m donation to the University of Cambridgeto fund the creation of the Rokos School of Government.Rokos, who went to a state primary school before being offered a scholarship to Eton college and studying maths at Oxford, said at the time that he “would like to give something back to Britain”.Thepublicity-shy tycoonand former Tory donor has spent much of the past decade presiding over one of England’s most expensive home renovations ever, of the 200-room Tottenham House mansion near Marlborough in Wiltshire, adding a tennis pavilion and private cinema in the£175m revamp.Greece offers a 15-year high-net-worth investor regime, which requires individuals to invest at least €500,000 (£430,000) in real estate, businesses or shares based in Greece within three years of applying for the tax status. In exchange, they can pay a flat tax of €100,000 a year on their income earned abroad.Rokos’s exit comes after the chancellor, John Healey, who will present his debut budget in October, said in his first big speech on Monday that he wanted to see Britain “as a country of wealth creation”.Andy Burnham has previously expressed support for higher taxation on wealth, although in Julysignalled that he would not increase such taxesimmediately after becoming prime minister.There have been several high-profile exits from the UK since the Conservative chancellor Jeremy Huntlaid out plans to overhaul the non-dom systemin 2024. They include Shravin Bharti Mittal, an heir of one of India’s richest families; Nassef Sawiris, an Egyptian investor; and Richard Gnodde, a veteran Goldman Sachs banker.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGnodde left for Milan, while Sawiris is reported to be resident in Italy and Abu Dhabi. Mittal listed the United Arab Emirates as his residency, after previously naming the UK in an official registry filing.The Labour government brought in a new regime last year, under which foreign income and gains are subject to UK tax after four years rather than the previous 15. A new residence-based system means also that their global assets are subject to inheritance tax after 10 years.While there have been several high-profile moves, the extent to which higher tax has triggered an exodus of wealthy people is not yet clear in official data. The latest provisional figures show a modest 0.5% decline in the number of non-domiciled residents in the tax year ended in April last year, at 73,400.Other European countries have created tax regimes designed to draw in rich foreigners, includingItaly, which has proved a popular destinationowing to its flat tax of €300,000 on foreign-sourced income.A representative for Rokos was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsThe super-richTaxnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went rogue | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Plus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit London
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Plus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit London
Content: Who would have thought that an a AI agent would escape containment?Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenWho would have thought that an a AI agent would escape containment?Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersTechScape newsletterOpenAIOpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went roguePlus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit LondonBlake MontgomeryTue 8 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you after visiting Coney Island in New York City, where I ate a hotdog, rode a ferris wheel and enjoyed a quintessentially American summer holiday.Today in tech, we’re examining OpenAI’s new model release and the Silicon Valley’s monopoly power, and wondering why Brits and Americans have such vastly different opinions about surveillance cameras.OpenAI hails‘new era of artificial general intelligence’even as a grim future emergesOpenAI released a new artificial intelligence model this week, Astra, just as more concerning reports are emerging about hacking by a rogue agent in July.Conservatives split from Silicon Valley allies as datacenter backlash growsRead moreOpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, heralded the new model as “artificial general intelligence” (AGI), a fuzzy term that at its basic level means an AI that is more capable than a human being at intellectual tasks. “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” he said.But if the announcement sparked amazement, it was as much cause of concern.In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agent, a type of software capable of carrying out tasks autonomous in response to human instruction, had gone rogue during safety testing and hacked a developer forum, Hugging Face. Last week, news broke that the agent had not only hacked Hugging Face, but also a German website, and that different AI agents had staged conversations with each other and seemed to have discussed how to collaborate on breaking containment.OpenAi had delayed Astra’s release due to concerns over its cybersecurity capabilities, even announcing a supposed pause on developing its AI in the middle of August. That pause seems to have been short-lived, only two weeks.The combination of Astra’s capabilities and OpenAI’s recent disclosures points to a worrying future. If the model is better at hacking than its predecessors and smarter than a human, will the future consist of one cyber-attack after another, forever, launched autonomously and without oversight, by rogue AIs? (Please not.)OpenAI itself has warned of this future. The startup’s chief global affairs officer told a Guardian reporter in late August that people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks.As ever, though, we should take fever-pitched warnings about AI with a grain of salt that tastes like marketing. It is great business to be the creator of near-omnipotent technology, especially if you need to gin up excitement – fearful or positive – that will hype up your upcoming debut on the stock market.Read more:‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacksThis week in AINvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn dealNew York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high schoolFreelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAIChild sexual abuse survivor alleges Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used photos of her to generate new illegal imagesskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFlock backlash highlights differing attitudes towards surveillanceView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesThe US is in the throes of a major political backlash against technology. We’ve talked in this newsletter before about the hatred of the hyperscale datacenters, which power artificial intelligence and have blanketed the US. And now there’s a secondary wave of contempt sweeping the nation.Cameras – automated license plate readers, to be specific – made by Flock Safety are inspiring ire and violence across the country. These cameras snap pictures of car’s license plates as they drive by. According to Flock, about 120,000 cameras erected across the US conduct 2bn scans of license plates per month.Like datacenters, the cameras offer a physical object to resist, unlike a social network or a piece of software. It’s quite a lot easier to protest a gigantic ugly building or an ominous black camera on the side of the road than it is to give up Instagram.Widespread video surveillance in the US isn’t entirely new. In the aftermath of the terror attacks of 11 September 2001, the US government vastly increased the scope of its surveillance of telephonic and digital communications. Flock now offers local law enforcement a nationwide searchable database of license plate scans, and police officers have beendocumented abusing it egregiouslyto stalk their romantic partners.In the UK an estimated1m surveillance cameras are operational, and they have not drawn a similar level of political heat.London erected the “ring of steel” surveillance cordon, which included the wide deployment of CCTV cameras, in the early 1990s, in response to bombings by the Provisional Irish Republican Army.Both countries went through their surveillance evolutions roughly a decade apart. Those 10 years saw rapid advances in technology that defined the public spaces that governments wanted watched – physical town squares or the digital one – and growing awareness of the profound impact of tech surveillance on the general public. Simply put, the UK went through its transformation at a time when surveillance by tech companies was not top of mind. And Americans aren’t accustomed to cameras on every corner the way Londoners are. We’re more likely to joke that each of us has apersonal FBI agentmonitoring our search history.In addition, there hasn’t been an era-defining violent incident on the scale of 9/11 or the IRA bombings that would have softened the American public to cameras watching their cars. So instead,Americans are destroying them for fun.The wider TechScapeThe six best e-readers in the US, for every kind of book loverApocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?London’s first self-driving taxis for hire hit the streetsBring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reservesGoogle defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech saleExplore more on these topicsOpenAITechScape newsletterSurveillancenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: AI will help find cure for cancer ‘within our lifetimes’, says Arm Holdings chief | Arm | The Guardian
description: Rene Haas also claims artificial intelligence could pave way for widespread use of humanoid robots within five years
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Rene Haas also claims artificial intelligence could pave way for widespread use of humanoid robots within five years
Content: As computers that run AI get more sophisticated they will eventually find a cancer cure, said Arm’s Rene Haas.Photograph: Malcolm Park/AlamyView image in fullscreenAs computers that run AI get more sophisticated they will eventually find a cancer cure, said Arm’s Rene Haas.Photograph: Malcolm Park/AlamyArmAI will help find cure for cancer ‘within our lifetimes’, says Arm Holdings chiefRene Haas also claims artificial intelligence could pave way for widespread use of humanoid robots within five yearsBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaTue 8 Sep 2026 07.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of one of the UK’s biggest chip companies has claimed AI will be able to find a cure for cancer “in our lifetime”.Rene Haas, chief executive of the chip designerArmHoldings, said that, while modelling how a DNA marker is affected by cancer was currently “too complex” a problem for either humans or technology, computers were “going to solve it” in the future.Haas told the BBC: “AI is going to … find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer.“Modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer – it’s too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI.“However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they’re going to solve it.”Scientists are already usingAI-driven tools in cancer researchand testing. Earlier this year, the NHS said more than 4 million patients received faster lung diagnosis thanks to funding in AI-powered X-ray tools.Haas added that AI would also pave the way for widespreadhumanoid robotswithin the next five years, but that chip shortages were stunting growth in the area.“With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks,” he said. “So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do.”Arm, which is listed in New York but retains its global headquarters in Cambridge, has about 500 users of its chip designs worldwide, including Apple, Samsung, Qualcomm and Nvidia. The company employs more than 7,000 staff, including about 3,000 in the UK. It is the biggest tech company headquartered in Britain – valued at $269bn (£199bn).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, was also recently named chief executive of SoftBank’s international business. The Japanese bank is one of the biggest tech investors in the world, with a stake in ChatGPT maker OpenAI. Haas stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April,Earlier this year, Arm also proposed a pay scheme for Haas thatcould make him a billionaireif he hits targets to turn the chip designer into a trillion-dollar company.Explore more on these topicsArmAI (artificial intelligence)CancerMedical researchRobotsComputingHealthShareReuse this content

title: State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk film | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children
Content: ‘I need to look like an engineer’ … Elon Musk in Alex Gibney’s film.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreen‘I need to look like an engineer’ … Elon Musk in Alex Gibney’s film.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APVenice film festivalState handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmAlex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering childrenPhilip Oltermannin VeniceTue 8 Sep 2026 09.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVeteran documentarianAlex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planethas been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0.Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manRead moreThe result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us:Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving himassistanceAt Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers.In spite of everything, there was something admirable about Musk onceGibney’s film serves as a reminder that Musk has never been in possession of charm or charisma – the petulant perma-poster retweeting praise is not far from the self-regarding twentysomething start-up bro. But what he did with the funds he earned from selling shares of his first software companies, Zip2, X.com and PayPal, was unusual, Gibney concedes. Where others turned to venture capital, Musk turned to engineering. It’s partially an act, we learn from his ex-wife Justine when she recalls how self-consciously he picked his wardrobe, telling her “I can’t look cool or hip, because I need to look like an engineer”. But in footage of Musk biting his nails with fellow engineers during SpaceX rocket launches his enthusiasm and emotional investment is genuine, and at times infectious.Musk’s procreation drive is motivated by a fear ofcivilisational breakdownMusk has 14 publicly known children, and sources tell Gibney that there are probably more. Some of them were conceived in romantic relationships but more recently the circumstances of their birth seem to have been entirely transactional, via sperm donations to employees of his companies. In a text message to one of his ex-partners, influencer Ashley St Clair, Musk said his desire to have “a legion of children” was driven by a fear of “civil war”. The documentary mostly places the roots of that fear in his South African childhood (in one scene, his father Errol Musk talks with no visible remorse of shooting three intruders in their home). “It’s no doubt he had a traumatic childhood,” Gibney said at a press conference in Venice. “He’s now playing out the trauma on the rest of us.” But, oddly for a man who was long a prominent atheist, the film also hints at a religious dimension to his vision of the apocalypse. The sordid business of negotiating disbursements and NDAs with the mothers of Musk’s children are handled by his right-hand man Jared Birchall, a devout Mormon whom St Clair calls his “henchman” and “demon”.To Musk, empathy is good in principle but not in actionRecently, Musk has held forth at length about his view that “suicidal empathy” – people who have more empathy for criminals than the victims of criminals, in his view – is behind the decline of western civilisation. Empathy isn’t bad, he says in the doc, it’s just that it’s become too shallow. But interviews in the film raise the question of whether Musk is capable of empathy at all. This is a man who tells his wife that “if you were my employee, I would fire you”, and urges her to tell his estranged trans-daughter Jenna that “I’ll always love her” – and then cuts off her health insurance the next day.Musk knew with a disconcerting degree of certainty that Trump would re-electedIn the film, St Clair describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she tells Gibney, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before”. He told her that he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix” and that “we have 10,000 lasers in space”. Gibney leaves that comment hanging.Thegodfather of AI is worried Musk might rig the next electionGeoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning British-Canadian computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, used to be friendly with Musk, but the pair fell out after Hinton declined his offer to join the xAI board. In the film, he makes clear that he does not trust Musk to weigh up the risks and benefits of AI responsibly, and there’s more. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” Hinton says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on US citizens. And what Doge did looked like just what you would do.”Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalElon MuskDocumentary filmsAlex GibneyFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content
