title: Bunker review – Cruz and Bardem just can’t dig Florian Zeller’s shallow thriller out of a hole | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: An architect (Javier Bardem) alienates his book editor wife (Penélope Cruz) when he agrees to build a luxurious bunker for a tech billionaire
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: An architect (Javier Bardem) alienates his book editor wife (Penélope Cruz) when he agrees to build a luxurious bunker for a tech billionaire
Content: Power couple in crisis … Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem in Florian Zeller’s Bunker.Photograph: Tamara Arranz/Blue Morning Pictures/Mod Producciones/Pathé FilmsView image in fullscreenPower couple in crisis … Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem in Florian Zeller’s Bunker.Photograph: Tamara Arranz/Blue Morning Pictures/Mod Producciones/Pathé FilmsVenice film festivalReviewBunker review – Cruz and Bardem just can’t dig Florian Zeller’s shallow thriller out of a holeVenice film festival:An architect (Javier Bardem) alienates his book editor wife (Penélope Cruz) when he agrees to build a luxurious bunker for a tech billionairePeter Bradshawin VeniceTue 8 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven the formidable pairing of Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem can’t save this new movie from writer-director Florian Zeller – his first created directly for the screen, and not adapted from his own stage original. It’s shallow and unsatisfying, a drama without the intimate, authentic passion of his previous movies likeThe Father(2021) orThe Son(2022).Bunker has nothing that interesting or original to say about its metaphorically showcased theme of alienation and inequality; the central relationship is left unexplored in favour of so-so home-invasion suspense styling – although one extended marital-argument scene showed what might have been achieved if their relationship was the film’s point – and the violent finale ending is outrageously glib, silly and unconvincing. An off-camera paramedic or doctor actually has to be heard explaining in a brief sentence afterwards what is supposed to have happened. Very lame.Cruz and Bardem are Sofia and Miguel, a stylish Spanish couple with two teen daughters; the family has moved to London so that Sofia, a book editor, can take up a job managing a UK publisher’s foreign literature in translation list.Miguel is a world-famous architect (what other sort is there?) who cordially tells an interviewer that he can work in any city. It seems as if he might himself have designed the huge, modernist rear extension to their handsome Victorian terrace house.Their relationship is perfectly happy until Miguel is approached by a tech billionaire (Paul Dano) to design for him a luxurious survivalist mega-bunker in Hawaii, what his beady-eyed agent (Mark Gatiss) calls a “pharaonic” project. Sofia hates the idea of taking cash from the kind of arrogant plutocrat who has caused the very problems that he now wants to be insulated from.But to Sofia’s rage, Miguel is tempted by the colossal fee: is he the man she fell in love with? In her depression, she finds herself becoming friendly with a handsome young author (Patrick Schwarzenegger). Meanwhile, Miguel has got into a serious row with their chippy, stroppy working-class neighbour (Stephen Graham) who has built a window overlooking Miguel’s garden without permission.Could it be that Miguel is already getting walled up in his own petty bunker of snobbery and emotional seclusion? Yes it very much could.Zeller says he was inspired by Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman in Kubrick’s Eyes Wide Shut; I wonder if he also had somewhere in the back of his mind the icy ordeal of Daniel Auteuil and Juliette Binoche in Haneke’s Hidden.There are certainly some amusing incidental touches:Eileen Atkinshas a crisp cameo and we get some boisterous comedy when security conscious Miguel is persuaded to install “fog cannon” in the house, which supposedly smother intruders in smoke. A fat lot of good they turn out to be.Gatiss’s agent is intensely frustrated and irritated by Miguel’s squeamish hesitation – and of course we can see how the right thing for Miguel to do would be to turn it down and go back to his worthy but dull project of designing a hospital in Munich. But something in me agreed with Gatiss’s snappish rebuke: “Think big!” Perhaps this film could have thought a bit bigger: a more direct engagement with the iffy tech oligarch, a more explosive confrontation in the marriage, a more explicit on-camera account of what is supposed to happened in that final climax. This is a disappointment.The Bunker screened at the Venice film festivalExplore more on these topicsVenice film festivalPenélope CruzJavier BardemDrama filmsThrillersFlorian ZellerMark GatissreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The L Word: 22 years on, the sexy lesbian series remains a cornerstone for modern sapphic culture | The L Word | The Guardian
description: Made in response to the success of hetero Sex and the City, the groundbreaking show follows queer women navigating love and life in perpetually horny LA
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Made in response to the success of hetero Sex and the City, the groundbreaking show follows queer women navigating love and life in perpetually horny LA
Content: ‘It’s impossible to exist even on the periphery of lesbian culture and not know the show’s core references’. Pictured: Leisha Hailey as Alice and Katherine Moennig as Shane in The L Word (2004).Photograph: PictureLux/The Hollywood Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It’s impossible to exist even on the periphery of lesbian culture and not know the show’s core references’. Pictured: Leisha Hailey as Alice and Katherine Moennig as Shane in The L Word (2004).Photograph: PictureLux/The Hollywood Archive/AlamyStream teamThe L WordThe L Word: 22 years on, the sexy lesbian series remains a cornerstone for modern sapphic cultureMade in response to the success of hetero Sex and the City, the groundbreaking show follows queer women navigating love and life in perpetually horny LALucille MacKellarTue 8 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 19.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI recently posted a simple question on Instagram: “Attention queer people in my phone: what is your relationship toThe L Word?”A few people responded with names of the characters: Bette, Shane, Dana. Others lamented over storylines that should have been: Kit was supposed to be a leather dyke journalist but apparently they wrote it out; why did they let Alice and Tasha stay together for so long? Many gleefully commented on the amount of sex the show has. One well-meaning gay man said it takes him a while to say The L Word in a relationship, then he immediately realised I was talking about the TV show and retracted his statement. Overwhelmingly, however, was the variation on one take: It’s so terrible and I love it so much.Waking Life: Richard Linklater’s genre-defying indie is a kaleidoscopic masterpieceRead morePremiering in 2004, The L Word follows a group of queer women in their mid 20s to 30s as they navigate relationships, careers, sex and friendships against the backdrop of the permanently sunny and perpetually horny Los Angeles. Created by Ilene Chaiken, the show was based on her own experiences of flings, heartbreak and stereotypes as a lesbian, and was positioned as a response to the success and heterosexuality of Sex and the City, which was its own media mammoth by the early 2000s. The L Word’s first season tagline was simply: “Same sex. Different city.”View image in fullscreen‘I was immediately enamoured by the reality of a show following a group made up of entirely queer women who aren’t automatically likable or agreeable.’Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyRunning for six seasons, the show ended in 2009, yet remains a cornerstone for modern sapphic culture and discourse. It’s impossible to exist even on the periphery of lesbian culture and not know the show’s core references from the infamy of “the chart” (a massive web of names and lines connecting every queer woman in The L Word universe by who’s hooked up with who displayed permanently on a huge whiteboard in a character’s home), or the irresistibility of Shane (the group’s resident womaniser who has a Don Draper tendency to effortlessly hook up with every woman she meets).Tipping the Velvet to Top of the Pops: your favourite LGBTQ+ TV shows everRead moreDespite proudly calling myself a lesbian for nearly 10 years, I had never seen The L Word until a few months ago. From the pilot, I was immediately enamoured by the reality of a show following a group of entirely queer women who aren’t automatically likable or agreeable. In the decades following The L Word’s premiere, queer characters on screen have increased significantly, but they are still usually only one or two out of a cast, more often than not paraded out for a serious identity storyline or sardonic comic relief. As the seasons of The L Word go on, the extreme interpersonal drama enters an almost soap opera landscape, with the situations these women find themselves in ranging from an alleged murder plot, a burned-down hair salon and a Hollywood film set sabotaged by rival lesbian nightclub owners, all the while participating in some of the most explicit lesbian sex scenes in television history.View image in fullscreen‘The treatment of the only trans masc character, Max [played by Daniel Sea, right], is difficult to watch and widely regarded as a stain on the show’s legacy.’Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyIn 2026, the enjoyment of seeing unapologetically queer women navigating off-the-wall scenarios works overtime to offset the aspects of the show that have spoiled with age. The treatment of the only trans masc character, Max, is difficult to watch and widely regarded as a stain on the show’s legacy. Max constantly brushes off transphobic comments and behaviour, and is exempt from the loyalty and compassion extended to everyone else. This ridicule seems vitriolic even for the time, and it’s confounding to witness a show discuss a wide berth of taboos around queerness but draw the line at transness. The cast is also overwhelmingly white, despite taking place in a hugely diverse city like LA, and clunkily navigates the inherent differences of lived experience in interracial relationships with an emphasis on the white partner’s discomfort.In The L Word, queerness doesn’t equal moral goodness. These characters make all the wrong choices, communicate in the worst possible ways and never become better people, and that complexity is why it endures. It has all the hallmarks of other lost media relics of the 2000s: cringe-inducing takes on gender, an overwhelming sea of thinness, white washing, bizarre fashion choices – but, as displayed by the passion and numbers that blew up my Instagram, it is far from forgotten. The emotional anchors of the show, the characters and their relationships, paired with absurd plotlines perfectly engineered for maximum drama, creates an authenticity that encapsulates the idiosyncrasies of lesbian culture without ever feeling like the butt of the joke.The show knows queer people aren’t ethical angels; we can be mean, selfish, greedy and delusional, and that’s its superpower. In the words of the theme song, The L Word persists because “this is the way that we live and love”.The L Word is available to stream via Stan in Australia and the US, and via Prime Video in the UK.Find more recommendations ofwhat to stream in Australia hereExplore more on these topicsThe L WordStream teamTelevisionDramaSexualityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Company review – Casey Affleck entertains us with creepy campfire tales | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Affleck’s third film as a director is a diverting gothic anthology about mysterious strangers, murder and – pointedly – wronged men
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Affleck’s third film as a director is a diverting gothic anthology about mysterious strangers, murder and – pointedly – wronged men
Content: One dark and snowy night … a still from CompanyView image in fullscreenOne dark and snowy night … a still from CompanyVenice film festivalReviewCompany review – Casey Affleck entertains us with creepy campfire talesVenice film festival:Affleck’s third film as a director is a diverting gothic anthology about mysterious strangers, murder and – pointedly – wronged menXan Brooksin VeniceTue 8 Sep 2026 15.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGather ye ’round the glowing screen for aCasey Affleckcampfire tale. It contains superstitions and murder and human oddities of all stripes. An old hermit in his shack. Something nasty in the woodshed. If you like the first tale, fill your boots, settle back, because here comes another and another; each sparked by the embers of its neighbour and playing out with the same deliberately theatrical panache. Affleck’s picture roams and rambles like a creepy cracker-barrel Jackanory.Actually there is much to relish in Company, Affleck’s third film as a director, even if many of its elements feel like off-the-peg eccentricities; a little too laundered and self-consciously strange. It begins in tried and tested fashion with the arrival of a mysterious stranger on a dark winter’s night. The stranger takes a seat and spins a tale, at which point December 1975 melts into 1953, then 1903, before finally the film crosses the ocean to Europe at the tail end of the plague. Nick Nolte is a hermit pining for his lost daughter, whileBen Mendelsohnplays a mean, mordant farmer who reaches for his handgun too readily. Both men, one suspects, are destined for a bloody end.Where is it leading, this tale of a woman who tells a tale of a woman? Into the woods and through the darkness, of course, although the film’s centrepiece story, set in the Rockies at the turn of the 20th century, provides a torch to dimly light our way. Here Adelaide Clemens and Scoot McNairy play Rebecca and Emmett, a hard-bitten farming couple who discover a teenage boy, Caleb, lying prostrate in the snow. Caleb is played by Atticus Affleck, the director’s youngest son, with a vulpine gaucheness which grows more assured and compelling the longer he’s on screen. Caleb tells Rebecca that he is much older than he looks; that he’s been “hither and yon” and visited Argentina and London. When she starts to suspect the boy may be behind a spate of grisly local killings, Caleb’s bleak pronouncements seem hardly designed to dissuade her. “This whole world is tall grass,” he explains. “You have no idea of the dangers underfoot.”Affleck co-scripted Company alongside Ron Hansen, the author of The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford, which was made intoa fabulous 2007 filmby Andrew Dominik. Affleck co-starred as Ford, a snivelling beta male with dark dreams of glory, unsure whether he wants to befriend or kill his idol, and there is a similar scary ambivalence to the character of Caleb, who settles in at the farm and appears in no hurry to leave. Caleb might be a fantasist, bumming for work in the mountains. He might be a demon, blown in from the backwoods or beyond.As for Affleck, his career has peaked and troughed since those heady days of Jesse James. He won the best actor Oscar forManchester by the Seaand cropped up as an army intelligence man in Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer. Off-screen, though, he has been dogged by accusations of sexual harassment (subsequently settled out of court) and it is perhaps no coincidence that his passion project is occasionally afflicted by pangs of self-pity and features men who have been wronged and weren’t believed by their peers. The hermit’s wife was killed by an errant, unrepentant physician. Emmett witnessed his father shot dead by a well-connected landowner. The law is a joke; the innocent are kicked to the curb. But these jarring asides stray too close to special pleading. They add little to the narrative; he could have easily cut them out.Company is better – more satisfying – when it circles back to the fire and picks up the main thread; when it is sticking most closely to reliable American Gothic tropes. Affleck clearly loves this dark sub-genre and elects to play it straight, and his enthusiasm is infectious and embeds us in the yarn. His film is a diversion. Maybe it doesn’t wholly add up. But it contains a ripe gamey flavour with a crunch of buckshot in every bite. Don’t step into the woods after dark, it advises. And if a mysterious stranger taps at your door before dinner, think very carefully before introducing them to your guests.Company screened in competition at the Venice film festivalExplore more on these topicsVenice film festivalCasey AffleckNick NolteBen MendelsohnDrama filmsHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Just an Illusion review – Louis Garrel and Camille Cottin sizzle as an 80s couple in crisis  | Movies | The Guardian
description: The directing duo behind uplifting mega-hit Intouchables return for this heartwarming coming-of-age drama, but it is the parents in the story who pull focus
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: The directing duo behind uplifting mega-hit Intouchables return for this heartwarming coming-of-age drama, but it is the parents in the story who pull focus
Content: Funny and charismatic … Louis Garrel and Camille Cottin in Just an Illusion.Photograph: Manuel MoutierView image in fullscreenFunny and charismatic … Louis Garrel and Camille Cottin in Just an Illusion.Photograph: Manuel MoutierMoviesReviewJust an Illusion review – Louis Garrel and Camille Cottin sizzle as an 80s couple in crisisThe directing duo behind uplifting mega-hit Intouchables return for this heartwarming coming-of-age drama, but it is the parents in the story who pull focusCath ClarkeTue 8 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlivier Nakache and Éric Toledano are the French directors who created theuplifting mega-hit Intouchables, about a wealthy quadriplegic and his carer. Now the pair bring their brand of squishy heartwarming charm to the 1980s, with this nostalgic movie about a 13-year-old boy growing up in the Paris suburbs. It’s funny and sweet but I couldn’t help feeling the film-makers missed a trick; their coming-of-age plot is all very well, but Louis Garrel and Call My Agent! star Camille Cottin give such funny and charismatic performances as the boy’s bickering parents, a portrait of their marriage in crisis would have been 10 times more entertaining.‘I don’t care if I look good’: French heartthrob Louis Garrel on fashion, fatherhood and his radically dorky new roleRead moreThe film opens with Vincent (Simon Boublil) preparing for his barmitzvah against a fractious atmosphere at home. The country is gripped by recession and money is tight. His dad, Yves (Garrel) was laid off months ago, but every morning puts on a suit and pretends to go out to work; Garrel is terrific, likable but fundamentally unreliable. Vincent’s mum is a go-getting secretary, who can see that the future is technology and signs up for an IT course. At school, Vincent has a massive crush on a girl who cannot remember his name, or chooses not to – she calls him “Thingummy”.The period details are fondly remembered; a massive IBM computer arrives at the family’s flat from Sandrine’s work. Meanwhile, Vincent gets into an assortment of harmless scrapes, like renting a soft porn movie from the video shop that ends up in the hands of the rabbi. But these moments feel a bit B-game next to the scenes of his parents’ marriage in crisis. In the 80s women were told they could be having it all. The reality, for many like Sandrine, was that they were doing it all, working then coming home to cook and clean, with no expectation men would lift a finger. But times are a-changing, and negotiating this, Cottin and Garrel sizzle together; they’d be the perfect pairing for a Woody Allen-ish relationship comedy.Just an Illusion is in UK and Irish cinemas from 11 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsDrama filmsFranceComedyEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Freiburg Baroque Orch/Rattle/Faust review – ‘problem’ Schumann works shine in exceptional evening | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Simon Rattle, guest conducting the period instrument ensemble, brought insights and detail to these three lesser known works by Schumann. Isabelle Faust was a spirited and graceful soloist in the Violin Concerto
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Simon Rattle, guest conducting the period instrument ensemble, brought insights and detail to these three lesser known works by Schumann. Isabelle Faust was a spirited and graceful soloist in the Violin Concerto
Content: Isabelle Faust and Simon Rattle with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou /BBCView image in fullscreenIsabelle Faust and Simon Rattle with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou /BBCProms 2026ReviewFreiburg Baroque Orch/Rattle/Faust review – ‘problem’ Schumann works shine in exceptional eveningRoyal Albert Hall, LondonSimon Rattle, guest conducting the period instrument ensemble, brought insights and detail to these three lesser known works by Schumann. Isabelle Faust was a spirited and graceful soloist in the Violin ConcertoClive PagetTue 8 Sep 2026 08.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSimon Rattle sure loves a challenge. This all-Schumann evening featured three “problem” works: the overture to a failed opera, a violin concerto deemed sufficiently disappointing that the composer’s executors ordered it locked away for a century, and a symphony written in the depths of depression. What’s more, he was conducting the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra in an acoustic hardly conducive to the soft-grained tones of period ensembles. In the event, we needn’t have worried, but you have to admire his pluck.The overture to Genoveva got off to a moody start. Rattle and the Freiburgers drew the listener in by tapping into the musical storytelling – the quartet of horns was especially striking – rather than relying on sheer volume. Closer to Mendelssohn than Wagner, it must have felt old hat in 1848, but here came up bristling with romance and chivalry.Isabelle Faust was the soloist for only the sixth Proms performance of Schumann’s Violin Concerto (by comparison,the previous nightsaw the 103rd outing for Dvořák’s New World Symphony). Conducting without a podium, Rattle was an attentive partner, leaning into the first movement’s dark urgency while deftly shadowing Faust whose subtle rubato afforded a degree of flexibility to her otherwise determined sense of the work’s thematic architecture. Dynamic shading and delicate trills decorated the line as she calmly overcame a host of technical challenges. Sailing through the Elgarian central movement, she slid gracefully into a spirited yet wistful account of the polonaise finale. Rattle and the orchestra accompanied her with elfin lightness.Schumann’s Second is the Cinderella among his four symphonies. Rattle didn’t shy away from the opening movement’s gloomier moments, or indeed its turbulence, but on the whole, this was a crisp reading where sunshine outweighed the showers. In the scherzo, conductor and orchestra highlighted the obsessive nature of the nagging principal theme, which in turn emphasised the Jekyll and Hyde nature of the contrasting trio. The slow movement, an endless flow of melody, exuded a noble melancholy before the curiously structured yet ultimately celebratory finale carried all before it. Exceptional playing, insightful and affectionate conducting, and not once did the period-instrument blend blur or smudge.Available onBBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicPromsSimon RattlereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Castle by Jon Ronson review – bizarre tales of modern masculinity | Society books | The Guardian
description: A journalist embarks on a wild goose chase that might – or might not – be informative about the male condition
Author: Anthony Cummins
Headline: A journalist embarks on a wild goose chase that might – or might not – be informative about the male condition
Content: Chris Mark’s castle in Woodstock, Connecticut.Photograph: Tyra PachecoView image in fullscreenChris Mark’s castle in Woodstock, Connecticut.Photograph: Tyra PachecoSociety booksReviewThe Castle by Jon Ronson review – bizarre tales of modern masculinityA journalist embarks on a wild goose chase that might – or might not – be informative about the male conditionAnthony CumminsTue 8 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 05.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRecovering from surgery at home in upstate New York in 2023,Jon Ronsonawoke to a string of texts from his adult son about a weird evening he just had at a stranger’s castle in Connecticut. Having gone along with a friend who’d been invited to a party there, he arrived to find a few lost-looking young women with the sixtysomething host, Chris Mark, a steel heir filming a reality show about “101 princesses” whose first rule was “Never say no to King Chris”.As a parent, Ronson is worried; as a reporter of more than 30 years on the cranks-and-crooks beat, he’s already on the clock. After trawling online whispers of sinister goings-on at the castle, he decides to pay a visit to Mark, who proudly shows off the stalactites and waterfall in his “cave-themed” bedroom before explaining how he picks up women on dating apps to “adapt” them to life as “princesses”. “The only girls that really work are drug addicts ... they don’t know what’s going on,” he says. Almost touchingly, Mark asks Ronson to sign an NDA, and the book describes Mark flooding his phone with threats when he declines.Ronson knows he has a story on his hands; but what is it? A disenchanted associate leaks Mark’s private messages, revealing plans for a $2,500-an-hour floating brothel lit up in purple LEDs, and suggesting that Mark once paid for a woman to fly into the US from Poland, only for authorities to send her home in fear for her safety. Further dirt is dished by an ex-fiancee after Ronson two-facedly tells her he’s “really, really sorry” their relationship collapsed (he already told us “a break-up can be good news for a journalist”). As allegations mount, he imagines – perhaps even hopes – that Mark murdered his own father, who drowned in a boating accident in 2009.While Ronson ends up satisfied Mark didn’t do that, the author’s willingness to guy his own ego – he wants “to be better than every other nonfiction writer” – adds a vital measure of comic charm to this creepy wild-goose chase. But gonzo sleuthing is only one ingredient of The Castle: the subtitle, Adventures in a World of Unravelling Men, hints at its ultimately piecemeal nature, as Ronson zigzags around case studies designed to illustrate the plight of the post-industrial male, simultaneously exhorted to open up and be vulnerable while pressured to avoid giving women “the ick” by snoring or failing to spot a beard crumb.Boo hoo, one might counter, yet Ronson is persuasive on the problems of casting masculinity as original sin. He talks to an Australian man whose teacher rounded up every boy in his school to make them “apologise for rape”, and meets a lone father courted by YouTube for the lucrative videos he posted of his daughters’ food fights, then dropped when online Sherlocks wrongly accused him of kidnap.Ronson makes these and other bizarre tales feel emblematic of topsy-turvy times, but when he says Chris Mark is just one of many men “discovering there were things they’d once done that they couldn’t do anymore”, you sense an over-caffeinated logic at work. “I was reminded a little of America in Iraq,” he tells us, when Mark can’t decide what to do with his castle, torn between housing OnlyFans models or setting up an orphanage. Mark’s “insatiable ... self-gratification” prompts a segment on the controversial actor Armie Hammer, seemingly mentioned only so Ronson can let us know Hammer gave him a tell-all scoop interview he didn’t publish.Ronson’s reflexive parallels don’t always help us understand his slippery subjects. Mark also puts him in mind of the Father Ted co-creator Graham Linehan, an ex-friend whose online posts about transgender people Ronson compared to bullying, whereupon, he tells us, Linehan began subjecting him to multiple abusive messages. Ronson interviews him to try to fathom what fed his obsession, but it’s typical of The Castle’s jittery analytical style that Ronson’s eventual summing-up rests less on their six hours of video calls than on a tenuous analogy he detects in the tragic case of Brandi Bragg, a West Virginian teenager who fatally overdosed in 2004 after a lottery win plunged her into paranoia.Near the end, he recounts thefatal shootingof Renée Good by an ICE agent who muttered “fucking bitch”. It isn’t clear why he brings this up, until he notes that Linehan – the only man in the book described as “unravelling” – apparently took to X to repost a tweet that called her “the face of chaos” and “the epitome of the modern-day liberal white woman”. “Graham’s plummet into disinhibition, his obsessive anti-wokeness, had evidently become so overwhelming it eclipsed his role as a self-appointed defender of women.” The gotcha, slipped into a footnote seven pages from the end, leaves you wondering if The Castle has been constructed not simply as an exploration of 21st-century maleness but as an act of slow-brew payback – though maybe it tells us something about men either way.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The Newer World by Sebastian Barry review – a near-miracle of storytelling | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The third in a loose American trilogy follows the epic journey of a formerly enslaved man in the aftermath of the civil war
Author: Sara Collins
Headline: The third in a loose American trilogy follows the epic journey of a formerly enslaved man in the aftermath of the civil war
Content: Unrelenting lyricism … Sebastian Barry.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The ObserverView image in fullscreenUnrelenting lyricism … Sebastian Barry.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The ObserverBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Newer World by Sebastian Barry review – a near-miracle of storytellingThe third in a loose American trilogy follows the epic journey of a formerly enslaved man in the aftermath of the civil warSara CollinsTue 8 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 02.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBut is not the story as good as the truth?” asks Tennyson Bouguereau, the narrator of Sebastian Barry’s The Newer World. Tennyson, a formerly enslaved man in post-civil war America, recounts his life story in ways that call to mind the age-old debate about whether it’s better to get our history from novelists or historians. While historians might argue that there is no contest, the question hints knowingly at the novelist’s counter-argument. It sent me searching for a line from Barry’s 2008 Costa-award winning novel,The Secret Scripture, in which the narrator describes history as “a fabulous arrangement of surmises and guesses held up as a banner against the assault of withering truth”.In her Reith Lectures, Hilary Mantel suggested that history is “what’s left in the sieve when the centuries have run through it”, but I tend to think of it as more of a butterfly net. Historians chase after and capture the things they deem significant. They leave things out, often deliberately. Barry’s entire body of work is a prime example of fiction’s ability to fill history’s gaps, merging personal tragedies with national ones in ways that (dare I say) demonstrate the supremacy of the form – especially for those of us descended from people for whom history never cared one whit. I was therefore intrigued to learn that he had set out to write the story of a man like Tennyson. Barry’s earlier novels refracted Irish history through the lens of two fictional Irish families, the Dunnes and the McNultys. His first foray into this period of American history inDays Without End, for which he won his second Costa award, also followed one of the McNultys – Thomas McNulty flees the Irish famine for America, where he finds himself drawn into the genocidal work of clearing Native Americans off their land, and then, together with his lover and fellow soldier, John Cole, adopts a Lakota girl, Winona, whose family they have helped slaughter. Barry picked up Winona’s story inA Thousand Moons, published in 2020, which follows her fortunes as she, Thomas and John settle on the same farm outside Paris, Tennessee that is occupied by Tennyson and his twin sister Rosalee among others.double quotation markIn Barry’s hands, language attains registers that can only be described as soaring; a vertiginous high wire of proseWith the publication of The Newer World, it seems a loose trilogy has taken shape, hinting at possibilities for future expansion: the authorial hand nudging Tennyson from the background into centre stage and for the time being leaving the McNultys behind. This passing of the storytelling baton – an Irish refugee ceding the floor to a Native American woman, who then does the same in favour of a formerly enslaved man – feels as urgently contemporary as the best historical fiction always does, relevant to “the writer’s now”, to borrow John Fowles’s phrase. So too does the description of a postbellum Tennessee landscape in which the Confederates may have been defeated but their ideologies are still virulently alive: “All their intent was to shove us back into the hog pen and put the hasp on tight as they could, against any further straying”.Part Bildungsroman, part picaresque, Tennyson’s account of himself moves from the American civil war, when “the end of the world had come”, to its immediate aftermath, “a time of guns and watchfulness”. He describes himself and Rosalee, enslaved orphans in childhood, “freed but not free” in adulthood, as “nothing people”. It’s reminiscent of Winona’s description of herself as “just the cinders of an Indian fire”, and Thomas’s of the ships bringing “ruined people” from Ireland to Canada: “The point is, we were nothing. No one wanted us.” The thing I like best about a Barry novel is how he gives a voice to the “nothing people” of history. It’s like pulling up a rocking chair on a shaded porch and listening as the narrator, usually in retrospective mode, attempts to reckon with what they did and what was done to them. It’s an astonishing effect, especially when you consider the near-miracles Barry performs with language. In his hands it attains registers that can only be described as soaring; a vertiginous high wire of prose. Here, for example, is Tennyson describing a reunion with his sister at sunset, after many years: “The harbour of my brave sister. The darkness growing in courage and, since it met no enemy, having its little victory everywhere. Pleasing darkness, in its way. There was bliss in those long moments”.Putting this kind of arresting language into the mouths of “nothing people” makes it impossible to overlook them, as if only in fiction can they be given their due. And there is also a compelling point in using language from the poetic realm to reveal rather than cloak atrocities, its rhythms building to an unrelenting lyricism, a juggernaut that gains power precisely because it is not just set alongside brutality but entwined with it. Here is a siege, after Tennyson has enlisted in the army: “Men cried out as the life was lifted from them. All in the cruel dark.” Cruelty is endured and inflicted by the same people. In Days Without End, Thomas McNulty, an Irish famine victim, takes part in slaughtering Indigenous Americans; in The Newer World, Tennyson, an African American victim of enslavement, does the same. It is “never enough for Americans to live in their American paradise. There had to be blood and chaos all the while too.” What does it mean to be part of a “killing machine” where “[e]ven one death was a personal matter”?I can think of no other writer who could, as Barry does, describe blood and chaos in language that reaches for such a high register, as if at the same time invoking paradise, in an attempt to answer that question. I can also think of few whose natural writerly empathy, evidenced by such an impressive body of work, pre-empts the otherwise inevitable discussion about cultural appropriation. Any writer has the right to imagine any point of view, but few truly earn it.The Newer World by Sebastian Barry is published by Faber (£20).
