title: ‘We all have an expiry date’: Kimberly Akimbo, the achingly funny musical about a teen with a 64-year-old body | Musicals | The Guardian
description: The uplifting, award-winning show about a girl aging four times too fast electrified New York. As it hits the UK, co-creator Jeanine Tesori talks about being inspired by the Aids crisis and all her friends who died young
Author: Emma John
Headline: The uplifting, award-winning show about a girl aging four times too fast electrified New York. As it hits the UK, co-creator Jeanine Tesori talks about being inspired by the Aids crisis and all her friends who died young
Content: ‘Your one wild and precious life?’ … Maria Friedman and Gilli Jones in Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreen‘Your one wild and precious life?’ … Maria Friedman and Gilli Jones in Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerMusicalsInterview‘We all have an expiry date’: Kimberly Akimbo, the achingly funny musical about a teen with a 64-year-old bodyEmma JohnThe uplifting, award-winning show about a girl aging four times too fast electrified New York. As it hits the UK, co-creator Jeanine Tesori talks about being inspired by the Aids crisis and all her friends who died youngTue 8 Sep 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJeanine Tesori is thinking about her mother back home in the US. “She’s 95,” says the composer, “and she’s not been well. But she would look in the mirror and be like, ‘I can’t believe I’m old.’ It’s always a surprise, always. There’s an interiority about ageing, especially as women. You stay playful and you stay curious, but the world has other ideas.”Ageing – and growing up, which is not necessarily the same thing – are a central consideration in the musical that Tesori has been rehearsing. Kimberly Akimbo, which the composer developed with David Lindsay-Abaire from his play, follows a teenage girl with a rare genetic condition that causes her to age at four times the normal rate. Its London debut stars the 66-year-old Maria Friedman as Kimberly. “And she has such a bright young energy,” says Tesori as we chat in a rough-and-ready rehearsal room in London, “that she doesn’t have to do anything to play 16.”double quotation markMy dad was a man of science who really wanted to be a fisherman. He wanted sons and got daughtersIf a story about a girl with a life-shortening condition sounds like a tragedy, don’t be fooled. Kimberly Akimbo is a comedy about a chaotic family (from a hypochondriac mother to a criminal aunt) and a tender teenage romance. Uplifting and achingly funny, the original New York production was the biggest winner of the 2023 Tony awards. Tesori watched the London cast rehearse its bittersweet ending with her lips zipped firmly shut: “David and I know the show so well that we have to just let people interpret it their own way.”For Tesori, a protagonist who knows she may not reach adulthood raises the question of how we use our time. “We all have an expiry date,” she says, recalling the line from Mary Oliver’s poem, The Summer Day:what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life? “I lost so many friends during the Aids crisis. I’m from that generation of watching these incredible people, mostly men, disappear. You become aware of how you live.”At 64, her own life looks a fulfilled one: mother, teacher, legend of her industry. Her compositional dexterity and range, combined with an extraordinary ability to turn playwrights into lyricists and librettists, has produced everything from fun-packedBroadwayshows (Thoroughly Modern Millie, Shrek), to complex, thought-provoking musicals (Soft Power, Caroline, or Change) and avant garde operas about police racism, drone pilots, and Eugene O’Neill’s marital rows.“Everybody knows she’s a brilliant composer,” says Lindsay-Abaire, when he swings by rehearsals during lunch. “But she’s also one of the most insightful dramatists – she understands story structure and character and things that not all composers do or are even interested in.”What Tesori’s projects have in common is her laser-sharp focus on emotional truth, be it in the powerfully orchestral blues and spirituals of Caroline, or Change – or the intimately interwoven harmonies and counterpoint of the three-handed chamber piece, Fun Home. Aproductionof that last one – an adaptation of Alison Bechdel’s celebrated autobiographical graphic novel – ran at Manchester’s Royal Exchange Theatre this summer and its director, Sarah Frankcom, calls it “a masterpiece”, adding: “Jeanine is able to express moments of profound change in people, in what is a very spare musical. The motifs coalesce and consolidate and lead you towards a last 15 minutes that are absolutely shattering.”View image in fullscreen‘We both like inappropriate comedy’ …Jeanine Tesori and David Lindsay-Abaire during rehearsals for Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerTesori admits she’s drawn to dad-daughter stories, which are at the heart of Fun Home, Caroline, or Change and Kimberly Akimbo. Her own father died more than 20 years ago, but “the story lives on, and I think it helps me process – you try to answer the unanswerable question. My father was a very complicated man: a man of science who really wanted to be a fisherman. He wanted a simple life and he got anything but; he wanted sons and he got daughters.”Tesori’s upbringing in a chaotic, multi-generational Italian family helped inspire some of Kimberly Akimbo’s scenes. (Her three sisters sound a hoot: not long ago one of them stole a picnic table from a park in broad daylight to prove that older women are invisible). It also played its part in her musical development. Tesori’s grandfather was a band arranger and violist who emigrated from Sicily – she still has his baton – and one of her sisters played piano while another had a vast record collection. “We listened to everybody from Stevie Wonder and Aretha Franklin to the Stones and the Beatles, Led Zeppelin, Carole King. Cat Stevens was huge in our house.”That breadth of repertoire – encouraged by her first piano teacher – led Tesori outside the confines of classical academe, and fostered a musical versatility that has become the hallmark of her career. A recent trip to Jesus Christ Superstar blew her away, although she says it can be hard to relax and enjoy musical performances because her brain insists on analysing the scores. Instead, she has spent these weeks dipping into plays and comedy in off-West End and fringe venues: “That’s my favourite kind of theatre, to go in not knowing anything and just discover it.”View image in fullscreen‘Jeanine is able to express moments of profound change in people’ … Harriet O’Shea and Alex Young in Fun Home.Photograph: Johan PerssonWhat about Broadway, whichAndrew Lloyd Webberrecently pronounced to be “in dire danger”? Tesori says she finds the capitalisation of its business models “scary” and feels a responsibility to find solutions for its increasing costs. “My job is to make things work better than when I leave – that’s the job of everybody who has been rewarded by the industry. When I started doing shows they were tearing Broadway houses down, because there were not enough shows to fill them. So I’ve always heard this chorus of ‘Broadway’s in trouble’, but for different reasons.”She is a dedicated mentor (“I take that job seriously”) at a time when performing arts space in the US is being threatened and politicised. “It’s really frustrating,” she says, “and it’s very easy to feel hopeless. But I don’t. You could throw up your hands – but our job is to write.” She typically has three to four projects on the go, and has recently been researching a story in Naples, but never writes music for anything she doesn’t believe in. “Any show I do is going to be five years of concentrated work. That’s like graduate school plus a year. If I don’t understand it, I can’t say yes to it.”She adds: “I love working with playwrights who are looking at the global conversation.” And her deep friendship with Lindsay-Abaire is obvious. “We both have a similar sense of humour,” he says. “We like dark, inappropriate comedy, which is why this show is funny and sad at the same time.”Kimberly Akimbo is atHampstead theatre, London, until 7 NovemberThis article was amended on 8 September 2026. In an earlier version, the recent production of Fun Home at Manchester Royal Exchange was referred to as the first time it had been performed in the UK. In fact, it was performed at the Young Vic, in London, in 2018.Explore more on these topicsMusicalsTheatreBroadwayWest EndHampstead theatreAgeinginterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not good to walk through the world feeling like prey’: Thelma & Louise’s writer on turning a movie classic into a musical | Musicals | The Guardian
description: It was her very first film and it won her an Oscar. But can Callie Khouri now make it work on stage with songs? She talks about the outrages that made her write it – and how little has changed since
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: It was her very first film and it won her an Oscar. But can Callie Khouri now make it work on stage with songs? She talks about the outrages that made her write it – and how little has changed since
Content: ‘Nothing’s ever come as easily’ …Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis in the 1991 film.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Nothing’s ever come as easily’ …Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis in the 1991 film.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyMusicalsInterview‘It’s not good to walk through the world feeling like prey’: Thelma & Louise’s writer on turning a movie classic into a musicalLyndsey WinshipIt was her very first film and it won her an Oscar. But can Callie Khouri now make it work on stage with songs? She talks about the outrages that made her write it – and how little has changed sinceTue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Ihave a world-class case of beginner’s luck,” says Callie Khouri, who won an Oscar for her very first screenplay,Thelma & Louise. She also scored a hit with her first TV series,Nashville, which lasted six seasons. And at 68, she is taking on another first by penning a musical theatre version of Thelma & Louise, hoping her luck hasn’t run out. “I hope that this is not the end of that streak,” she laughs. “That I don’t hit a wall here and slide down it like Wile E Coyote.”Thelma & Louise isn’t an obvious bet for a musical. A story that features an abusive marriage, attempted rape, murder and double suicide doesn’t scream “jazz hands”, and Khouri had turned down offers before. “My agent said, ‘There’s a guy who wants to meet you to talk about doing Thelma as a stage musical,’” says Khouri. “And I just thought, ‘Well, that’s nuts!’” But the iconic 90s film – starring Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis (and a young Brad Pitt) – is an ultimately triumphant piece of cinema: a feminist road movie driven by the power of female friendship, which still captures imaginations. Khouri was eventually convinced. It’s been a decade in the pipeline, but things took off when uber-producer Sonia Friedman came on board, and now it has premiered at London’sYoung Vic, starring Rachel Tucker and Amy Lennox.double quotation markScenes would wake me up in the middle of the night – it was the easiest job I ever didI meet Khouri at a south London studio during one of the summer’s heatwaves. She is dressed in airy, white cotton, looking like an elegant lady who might be tending her garden in the American south – which is what she spends a lot of her time doing these days at home in Nashville, Tennessee, with husbandT-Bone Burnett. When Khouri floated the idea for the musical at home, it was record producer Burnett who immediately suggested a composer, the American singer-songwriterNeko Case.View image in fullscreen‘It’s a completely different telling’ … Amy Lennox as Thelma and Rachel Tucker as Louise.Photograph: Tea Films“As soon as he said it, I heard this giant click,” says Khouri. “I love her music so much and it’s such a different approach to a musical. She is truly a poet, but her songs are very tactile – I don’t know exactly the right word – and she’s got this voice that’s like a clarion call.” Choreography is by Bobbi Jene Smith with her husband Or Schraiber, whose dance you could also describe as tactile – and sensuous, mercurial, deeply feeling. “I’m on my knees with gratitude that Bobbi’s part of our team,” says Khouri. The director is Trip Cullman, whoseBecky Shawplayed on Broadway earlier this year.The musical version of Thelma & Louise is being tweaked to suit the 21st-century stage, but it’s not set in the modern day: no mobile phones, Khouri tells me. “It’s a completely different telling of this same story,” is how she puts it. There are scenes that are from the movie and new ones that aren’t, but Khouri is reluctant to give much more away. “I don’t want to reveal magic tricks,” she says. “One of the things I really enjoyed about the movie was that people walked in having no idea what to expect, and I think that’s still really important for this story.”It’s true that back in 1991, when the film was released, nobody had any expectations of Khouri, a complete unknown who was living in Santa Monica working in production on music videos for big-haired rock bands. She had studied theatre at university but didn’t want an actor’s life, as “I didn’t like being looked at”, she says. “I just kept thinking, ‘There’s something I’m supposed to be doing and this is not it.’” It was the beginning of the MTV era and there was “a lot of really intense talent” making music videos, including Hollywood-bound directors such asDavid Fincher. “There was also a lot of not really intense talent,” she says – guys who were writing scripts and getting jobs who didn’t seem much smarter than she was, which is what gave Khouri the confidence to have a go.View image in fullscreen‘I had friends who had bad experiences’ … Khouri with Davis and Sarandon at a 30th-anniversary screening of the film in 2021.Photograph: Amy Sussman/Getty ImagesAt 29, she began the script for Thelma & Louise in secret between freelance jobs. “You know, while I was writing it, scenes would wake me up in the middle of the night. It was the easiest job I ever did,” she says. “Nothing’s ever come as easily.” She showed it to a friend, and via a chain of friends and colleagues the script eventually got into the hands ofRidley Scott, who decided to direct it himself. “It was really such an improbable journey every step of the way,” says Khouri.Khouri never would have thought she’d still be talking about this story 35 years later. In the film, a girls’ weekend spirals out of control when Louise shoots Thelma’s would-be rapist and the pair end up on the run. Inspiration came in part from Khouri’s own experiences, having twice been mugged in LA, once at gunpoint. “When you feel your life being threatened …” she starts. “It’s not a good feeling to walk through the world as a prey animal, which is how you start to feel. I had friends who had really bad experiences – I feel like I was one of the lucky ones.”There is sadness in her voice that the elements of the film, from casual sexism to serious assault, seem just as prevalent all this time later. “I wish so much that it wasn’t,” she says. “Honestly, I wish the world had made that shift to be a more hospitable place for women, and especially for young women. I think our expectations got really high, and they rolled the clock back. We’ve lost rights in the States, and it’s dangerous.” She calls the rollback of abortion rights in the US “barbaric”.She does think her own industry is more welcoming to women than it used to be. “But then you look at the backlash from #MeToo and that’s real,” she says. “The Epstein files have not been fully released. Bill Cosby’s out of jail.” Did she think #MeToo was going to make a genuine change in Hollywood? “I never feel like anything’s going to make a tectonic shift. I know how slow change is,” she says. “To me, equality is the obvious goal for all of society, but there are a lot of people that don’t think that, and they don’t want to let go of it, and they’ll fight. And so will we.” She is as incensed by the deaths of young men in “wars that are fought over money” as she is about the assault on women’s rights. “It seems like the world keeps giving way too much power to psychopaths.”View image in fullscreen‘I was called to tell this story’ … rehearsals for the musical.Photograph: Helen MurrayKhouri may rage at the state of the world, but in her own little horticultural corner of it she has “a beautiful life”. She got into Gardeners’ World during the pandemic. “That’s my crack,” she says with relish. And she has nothing to prove these days. “I still have to work,” she says, “but I like to work.” And she is finding this foray into theatre “so much fun”, especially compared with her usual beat. “The film and television business has gotten really hard,” she says. “Everybody feels like we’re working for an algorithm. It’s not about original ideas as much as it once was. It’s a lot about IP and sequels and tent-poles [the blockbuster franchises that prop up the studios], and those aren’t really the kind of movies I’m interested in, especially at this age.”Thelma & Louise at 30: a groundbreaking road movie that still strikes a nerveRead moreOf course, you could say Thelma & Louise is a powerful piece of IP, on which Khouri is still trading. She has written other films, and directed too (Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood; Mad Money), but never topped her first time. “It’s always lucky when you get called to something, and I feel very much like that’s what happened,” she says. “I was called to tell this story and I didn’t really have a great desire to tell it again. But once we started the musical, I could see a whole new way. Everybody – Neko, myself, Trip – we are all finding ways to elevate it to being worthy of being on a stage.”Thelma & Louise is at theYoung Vic, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicalsTheatreYoung VicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Three people die at Burning Man this year, tripling average number of deaths  | Burning Man festival | The Guardian
description: Rise in fatalities comes amid news reports that the average age of Burning Man attendees is increasing
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: Rise in fatalities comes amid news reports that the average age of Burning Man attendees is increasing
Content: A satellite image of Burning Man in Black Rock City, Nevada, on 31 August 2026.Photograph: Vantor via ReutersView image in fullscreenA satellite image of Burning Man in Black Rock City, Nevada, on 31 August 2026.Photograph: Vantor via ReutersBurning Man festivalThree people die at Burning Man this year, tripling average number of deathsRise in fatalities comes amid news reports that the average age of Burning Man attendees is increasingLois BeckettTue 8 Sep 2026 19.08 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree men over 50died atBurning Manthis year, tripling the average number of deaths in connection with the annual festival that brings tens of thousands of people to build a temporary utopian community in the brutal conditions of theNevadadesert.The increase in fatalities comes asnews reportshave highlighted that the average age of Burning Man attendees is increasing, with fewer participants in their 20s, and more in their 40s and 50s.“Although we average one death a year at the festival, we have had two so far this year within the confines of the festival and I have received information regarding a third who died in transit to a hospital in Reno,” the Pershing county sheriff, Jerry Allen, told theReno Gazette-Journal.The festival, which has attractedupwards of 70,000 peoplein recent years, ended on 7 September. Founded in San Francisco in 1986 as a genuinely countercultural event, in which local artistsbuilt effigies and then set them on fire, Burning Man has increasingly become a jet-setting destination for the global tech elite.Data from the annualBlack Rock City censusfound that the estimated number of Burning Man participants in their 20s dropped from about 30% of total attendees in 2014, to only 10% in 2025, while the percentage of attendees in their 40s and 50s rose.The first person who died this year was a man in his “mid-50s”, the second was 51,and third was 60, according to the Washoe county medical examiner’s office andtheSan Francisco Chronicle.“We are saddened to have learned that a Burning Man participant who experienced a serious medical emergency in Black Rock City during the early hours of Friday September 4 and immediately received on-site lifesaving measures later passed away after being transported to Reno for medical care,” a spokesperson for the Burning Man organization said on Tuesday.Local authoritiesconfirmed that there were no signs of foul play with thethree deaths, twoof which occurred directly at the festival held in theBlack Rock playa, an arid stretch of federally managed land about 120 miles from Reno.Last year, a37-year old manwas found dead in a pool of blood on the final day of the festival, in what authorities said they wereinvestigating as a homicide. The case, which was thefestival’s first known homicidein nearly four decades, remains unsolved, theReno Gazette-Journal reported.The Pershing county sheriff’s office said this year’s first death was reported in the early evening of 3 September, at Rampart, the temporary hospital in the festival’s Black Rock City. A man had been found on the street within the festival and had been given CPR for several minutes before a doctor pronounced him deceased, the sheriff’s office said.The second death occurred in an ambulance in the early hours of 4 September, as a 51-year-old man was being transported away from Burning Man to receive more serious medical care, according to the Washoe County regional medical examiner’s office.The thirddeath was reported in the afternoon of 5 September, when a man was reported to have been found deceased in his trailer he was sharing with his significant other, according to the Pershing county sheriff’s office.More information on the deaths will be available in approximately six to eight weeks, after autopsies and toxicology reports are completed, the Pershing county sheriff’s office said in a statement.Explore more on these topicsBurning Man festivalFestivalsNevadanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cantona’s a Kwengletarian!’ Inside the maximalist, magical mentality of rising London Irish rapper Kibo | Music | The Guardian
description: The masterful ​Harrow MC behind the year’s funniest, most inventive UK rap debut explains how his parents sparked his ravenous outlook – and why he’s wrestling his peers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The masterful ​Harrow MC behind the year’s funniest, most inventive UK rap debut explains how his parents sparked his ravenous outlook – and why he’s wrestling his peers
Content: ‘I ain’t fucking bluffing / You’re not a bad boy, you’re an Egg McMuffin’ … Kibo.Photograph: SwurlaView image in fullscreen‘I ain’t fucking bluffing / You’re not a bad boy, you’re an Egg McMuffin’ … Kibo.Photograph: SwurlaMusicInterview‘Cantona’s a Kwengletarian!’ Inside the maximalist, magical mentality of rising London Irish rapper KiboHugh MorrisThe masterful ​Harrow MC behind the year’s funniest, most inventive UK rap debut explains how his parents sparked his ravenous outlook – and why he’s wrestling his peersTue 8 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 12.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew Guinnesses into an interview in his local Irish boozer, and 26-year-old Harrow rapper Kibo is cooking. We’re talking football. As a kid, he preferred playing Fifa Street – where ordinary players backflip off walls to score incomprehensible bicycle kicks – to regular realistic Fifa. “If I’m gonna play a video game, I want to do some shit I can’t do in real life,” he says. He’s drawn to similarly miraculous footballers:Balotelli, Drogba in his Chelsea days, Ronaldinho and his dad’s favourite, Eric Cantona: “Oh God, with his collar popped, looking like Kanye West?” Kibo then recites Cantona’s2019 Uefa president’s award speech– a mash-up of King Lear and philosophical musings on war and science – to near perfection.Magic is at the heart of Kwengletarianism, “the idea of being in a place that’s very grey, and trying to find a prismatic iridescence in it”, that underpins Kibo’s sensational album Kwengletaria: Ragamyff. (Cantona? “He’s a Kwengletarian to the nth degree.”) During his long rise through London’s rap scene, canonised by co-signs from Skepta, JME and Dave, Kibo has become a rare MC from Harrow, the town that produced Kate Nash and Jai Paul but no rappers of note. “It’s awesome,” he says of its lack of rap tradition, “a complete blank slate” to be as imaginative as he wants. Kwengletaria finds the myth in the mundane: on the track Bakerloo Dragon, a normal tube journey becomes a cruising broken-beat roller aboard a fire-spitting Bakerloo line train. I tell him my train to Harrow was one of these flame-graffitied dragons. “But did you get any sparks?” he asks enthusiastically. “You get sparks after Stonebridge Park!”We meet midweek, and Kibo tells me he’s heading to a wrestling match in Dublin at the weekend. I ask him who he’s watching. “No,I’mwrestling,” he fires back: he’s up against Irish rapper Lil Skag, “to see who really is ready to hold the responsibility of being the champion of Ireland”. Kibo is 6ft 4in tall, possessing Irish heritage, a goatee, a mane of hair straight from a fantasy film, and a sackful of devastatingly rude bars: “I’ll take your mum Butlin’s / And I ain’t fucking bluffing / You’re not a bad boy, you’re an Egg McMuffin.” You’d back him to win a match on aura alone.Add in references to anime, Pokémon, chicken shops and X-wing fighters, combine it with 16 producers making beats spanning garage, R&B, donk, grime and jungle, and you get a sense of Kwengletaria: Ragamyff’s scale. “I’m quite a maximalist guy, and a lot of the artists that I gravitate towards – Ghostface Killah, MF Doom, Yung Lean – it’s all about asking, how much can you stuff into one thing?” he says.The all-you-can-eat impulse comes from growing up online – “I was a kid with a million tabs open, trying to speak with a level of eloquence” – and the Kwelengletarianism concept stems from when Kibo’s schoolmates began trading pirated Yu-Gi-Oh! cards. “They would slap even more glitter and shine on it, to make it look like it was the most valuable shit ever,” he says. “Like, I know this is fake, but this shit looks awesome. It’s the first thing I remember in my life where I was looking at something and knowing it was valuable.”Kibo nods to his grime forebears on the album, sampling from Dizzee Rascal’s Boy in da Corner on closer Our War Game. “My absorption of grime was very retroactive,” he says. “Going back into Dizzee, Flirta D, Skepta, and D Double E … even though it was very local, it felt like discovering Three 6 Mafia, or old Memphis rap: like, this is awesome, but it’s nothere.” Where those older acts felt remote to Kibo, Novelist, the Lewisham MC behind grime’s modern resurgence and Kwengletaria’s only guest, was “the first time I was able to tune into grime sets live and feel like I was present for this thing,” Kibo says. “It’s always felt like he was bringing grime backandpushing it forward.”View image in fullscreen‘Charm from ma, swag from dad’ … Kibo.Photograph: SwurlaWhat’s impressive is how clear, satisfying and relentlessly funny Kibo’s path through the melee is. He shouts out Fiona Templeton, an academic at Brunel University (where he got a first in film, drama and media) for giving him a word for what he was doing: hyperdiction. “It was like someone showed me a brain scan,” he says. These collisions – of genres, references and words – create a new meta-language of smashed together non sequiturs in his work, such as “Courvoir-Sierra Leone”, or “Dimitar Burberrytov”. They’re also stamina-boosting power-ups. On Chancer, the album’s midpoint mellow grime flexer, Kibo’s criss-cross patterns unfold over three beat switches and five relentless verses.On Bakerloo Dragon, Kibo says he gets the “charm from ma, and the swag from dad”. Eileen of Limerick fell swiftly in love with John, a drummer from Harrow, when he was over in Ireland for a holiday. They navigated a two-year long-distance relationship before she moved to England. “There was one phone box in her whole village, so it would be like, ‘You must be here at 7 o’clock.’ My dad used to work at the BT phone line so he was able to wrangle a few things.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I’ve rebranded as a stoic. It’s my ting now!’ The crime and punishment of Pozer, UK rap’s fastest, fiercest talentRead moreIt made Kibo a true believer in romance. “It’s Kwengletarianism!” he says. “You’ve got to believe in something, you’ve got to believe there’s light at the end of the tunnel.” Kibo is a third generation member of Harrow’s Irish community, and there’s a distinctly Irish feeling to a project about belief, myths, good craic and finding the magic in ordinary objects.Kwengletaria: Ragamyff is about celebrating where you’re from, but it’s also about feeling stuck in a place that, once the iridescent sheen has faded, is still grey and boring. Off the back of the album, and a medley of viral live clips, Kibo has his sights set beyond Harrow. “I feel like I finally got a grip of London. [The track] Red Starz is like, I’ve completed London, right? It’s almost like the post-credit scene is Ryanair: oh shit, there’s 200 other countries? Damn. There’s a crunch point there, between leaving home and returning. But if you find the magic and the pride in your base, you can always come back to that and recharge. Home is like your charging point.”Kibo plays Bristol (28 October), London (30 Oct) and Manchester (1 November)Explore more on these topicsMusicRapinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I suggested maybe a lighter touch’: William Shatner on Star Trek at 60 | Star Trek | The Guardian
description: The actor and others involved with the phenomenon speak about the legacy and progressivism of a much-loved science fiction TV series as it reaches an important milestone
Author: David Smith
Headline: The actor and others involved with the phenomenon speak about the legacy and progressivism of a much-loved science fiction TV series as it reaches an important milestone
Content: William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy in Star Trek.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyView image in fullscreenWilliam Shatner and Leonard Nimoy in Star Trek.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyStar Trek‘I suggested maybe a lighter touch’: William Shatner on Star Trek at 60The actor and others involved with the phenomenon speak about the legacy and progressivism of a much-loved science fiction TV series as it reaches an important milestoneDavid Smithin WashingtonTue 8 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 08.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘The mystery of time,” musesWilliam Shatner, and for a moment we are back on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise listening to one of Captain Kirk’s philosophical tag-line speeches. “Not just the passage of time and our perception of it, but what is time? What does 60 years mean? It really is meaningless, isn’t it, 60 years, in terms of what time is? On the other hand, Dolly Parton just died. It brings up the whole concept of the passage of time and what that means.”Seam me up, Scotty! After 60 years, Star Trek has had a muppet takeover. About time tooRead moreIn an episode called The City on the Edge of Forever, Shatner’s Kirk travelled back in time and fell in love with a pacifist (Joan Collins) only to discover that she must die to prevent Nazi Germany winning the second world war. Such ethical quandaries help explain why Star Trek willcelebrate its 60th anniversaryon 8 September not just as a force in US culture but a mirror held up to the country’s politics.Born in the idealism of the 1960s, the show offered a utopian vision of the future in which humanity sought to explore rather than conquer. Diversity, empathy and reason had triumphed over tribalism, superstition and greed. Big government and big tech were liberators from scarcity and inequality. Star Trek’s fans includedMartin Luther Kingand his wife, Coretta, who said it was the only programme they allowed their little children to stay up and watch.But six decades on, the Enterprise is encountering some cosmic turbulence. Donald Trump’s America is convulsed by polarisation, culture wars and the retreat of liberal democracy, along with anxiety over artificial intelligence and climate catastrophe. Paramount,merged with Skydance Mediafor $8bn, promptly cancelled the latest Star Trek series amid claims that it was too “woke”.The rightwing complainers yearn for a return to the days of Iowa-born Captain Kirk, who fits their conceit of an all-American hero, even though Shatner is Canadian. When he was hired in 1965 after NBC rejected Jeffrey Hunter’s dour pilot performance asCaptain Pike, he brought an athletic, theatrical charisma that lifted the cerebral storytelling.“I saw the film and I thought it was really interesting, a little ponderous,” Shatner, a sprightly 95, recalls of the original pilot via Zoom from his home in Los Angeles, with his dogs sleeping nearby. “So I suggested maybe a lighter touch, and we made another pilot and it sold.”That lighter touch did not prevent Shatner from making history. In 1968, he and Nichelle Nichols, who played Lt Nyota Uhura, shared television’s first high-profile scripted interracial kiss in the episodePlato’s Stepchildren. Was he aware of its groundbreaking importance?View image in fullscreenLeonard Nimoy, DeForest Kelley, Nichelle Nichols and William Shatner.Photograph: Paramount/Sportsphoto/Allstar“I was told,” he says, sounding reluctant to be cast as a civil rights activist. Shatner muses about “infrequent hates” that are “dramatised by documentary filming” to shock audiences and contends: “The vast majority of us just want to live and have your barbecue and live in peace and quiet and go do what you want to. You believe what you wanna believe and, if you don’t bother me, I won’t bother you. I think most people want to do that and if we could elevate those people to express themselves more, we’d discover that humanity really just wants to be human.”Star Trek is still pushing boundaries, much to the chagrin of unlikely fan Stephen Miller, the deputy White House chief of staff and driver of Trump’s extremist immigration policy. In January Miller cited a social media account called End Wokeness that mocked the newest Star Trek series, Starfleet Academy, as “Beyond parody”.Miller himself wrote: “Tragic. But it’s not too late for @paramountplus to save the franchise. Step 1: Reconcile with @WilliamShatner and give him total creative control.”Shatner laughs at the idea of White House aides spending their days picking holes inStar Trek. “Can you imagine they’re watching TV, criticising TV. I mean, it’s bizarre! I don’t understand it. I don’t know why they don’t – I don’t want to be political. I’m Canadian in America but it’s enthralling.”He rejects Miller’s notion that Star Trek’s inclusiveness has gone too far. “I don’t know what going too far is. Where’s the demarcation line? Who drew that line? ‘Now you’ve gone too far.’ Excuse me, I didn’t realise that. Where should I have stopped? And by the way, what is ‘woke’?”In creator Gene Roddenberry’s 23rd-century vision, nation-states no longer exist and planets have banded together to form a sort of United Nations in space. Poverty, disease and hunger have been eradicated, currency has largely disappeared from Federation life and citizens pursue self-improvement rather than private accumulation. To some, it might sound likeJohn Lennon’s Imagine. But others would rather not imagine it.In 2017 the billionaire investor Peter Thieltold Maureen Dowdof the New York Times: “I like Star Wars way better. I’m a capitalist. Star Wars is the capitalist show. Star Trek is the communist one. There is no money in Star Trek because you just have the transporter machine that can make anything you need. The whole plot of Star Wars starts with Han Solo having this debt that he owes and so the plot in Star Wars is driven by money.”Shatner, whotravelled into space for real aged 90, sounds wryly amused. “Peter Thiel must be a very bright, creative man, full of opinions and he’s made a lot of money which should indicate he’s very self-sufficient and has ideas. He talked about money. Well, that’s one aspect. You need money to live. But you need other things as well and the other things are represented by Star Trek. I’d love to talk to him. I’d love to get into a discourse on the differences between Star Trek and Star Wars.”One difference has been articulated by Shatner’s friend, the astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson,who argues that Star Trekadheres more closely to real science. Another can be traced to the franchises’ origins: whereas Star Wars draws on the classic hero myth outlined by scholar Joseph Campbell, Star Trek was forged in the horrors of the mid-20th century.Roddenberrywas a decorated second world war bomber pilot who later survived a harrowing commercial plane crash in the Syrian desert. His writing partner Gene Coon had served in the marines and received training as a war reporter during the Korean war era.View image in fullscreenJoan Collins and William Shatner in Star Trek.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesMark Altman, co-author of The Fifty-Year Mission and director of a new documentary,The 60-Year Mission, says via Zoom from Los Angeles: “Their approach to Star Trek was they had lost a lot of friends and had seen war up close and they didn’t romanticise it. They knew the cost of war. They weren’t changing the name of the Department of Defense to the Department of War. They loathed war.“That’s something I find shocking, these deeply conservative fans like Stephen Miller say, ‘I’m a huge fan of Star Trek.’ How is that possible? Did they miss the memo thatin reality, Star Trek abhorred war, and it always said that talking is the way to resolve conflict?”Nowhere was that clearer than in the1967 episode Arena, in which Kirk refuses to execute the monstrous Gorn that has obliterated a Federation outpost. “Kirk makes this decision not to kill this alien creature that has annihilated our base and killed his friends,” Altman notes. “Some people look at it and say, ‘Oh, it’s this goofy monster in a suit.’ But there’s a reason an episode like that becomes so iconic: it’s the message as well as the visuals.”Viewers in the late 1960s were accustomed to all-white TV westerns. On Star Trek, they encountered a meritocracy: an African American woman, Nichols’s Uhura, answering communications with unflappable authority (she was poised to quit after one season butKing persuaded her to stay); George Takei’s Sulu piloting the flagship barely two decades after Japanese Americans had been interned; and an alien second-in-command, Leonard Nimoy’s Mr Spock, acting as what Altman calls “the ultimate immigrant”.Altman points out that this integration extended beyond the main bridge crew: “What about the diversity in the guest characters? In one episode you have Captain Kirk answering to his superior, Commodore Stone, played by the latePercy Rodriguez. Many years before Colin Powell, Kirk is answering to an African American who’s his boss. That stuff resonates too.”The original series ran from 1966 to 1969, crashing headlong into the Vietnam war, racial violence and the assassinations of John F Kennedy, King and Robert F Kennedy. Animated seriesand films followed. Then came The Next Generation (1987–1994), starring the Shakespearean actorPatrick Stewartas Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Deep Space Nine (1993–1999), Voyager (1995–2001) and several subsequent iterations.View image in fullscreenThe cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation.Photograph: Cine Text/Sportsphoto/AllstarAltman regards Kirk as an analogue for John F Kennedy, the young president who had pledged to reach the moon before the decade was out. “The final frontier isthe New Frontier. Kirk is very much a Kennedy-esque liberal. He’s liberal on social issues but more hard-nosed on defence. It’s more of a traditional moderate than what we see with democratic socialists today. It’s a meritocracy; it believes everybody needs to start from the same starting line but then it’s about your gifts and you have ability.“But if you look atThe Next Generation, it’s a very George HW Bush vision: consensus-building, a thousand points of light. Kirk has a line: ‘When this becomes a democracy, I’ll let you know.’ Picard was more of a consensus builder who had a lot of meetings to get a lot of input from people. It was more of an HW Bush thing.“You can extend that to a lot of Star Trek shows which were clearly influenced, if not necessarily by the president, by the tenor of the times.Deep Space Ninewas heavily rewritten in the aftermath of the Los Angeles riots and the beating of Rodney King. It was all about rebuilding and asking, can’t we all just get along? It has one of the great Star Trek quotes: ‘It’s easy to be a saint in paradise.’ When you’re on a starship and everything’s great, it’s easy to be a saint in paradise. But on a station, there’s more of a struggle and more conflict.”The latest series,Starfleet Academy, starred Oscar-winner Holly Hunter as the captain and a chancellor alongside Paul Giamatti as its central antagonist. The show boasted the largest and most expensive physical set in the franchise’s history. Set in a distant future where young cadets rebuild the Federation following an apocalyptic event, it was designed as an allegory for institutional renewal.But following Paramount’s merger with Skydance, which is led by David Ellison, who is the son of Trump ally Larry Ellison,Starfleet Academy was cancelled,with its forthcoming second season set to be its last. Miller had been joined by tech billionaire Elon Musk in a Maga pile-on denouncing the show’s alleged wokeness.View image in fullscreenPaul Giamatti and Holly Hunter in Star Trek: Starfleet Academy.Photograph: Brooke Palmer/ParamountAltman is scathing of the rightwing crusade. “How can you criticise Starfleet Academy on the ground that it’s too diverse? It’s absolutely ridiculous, and particularly if you’re someone who’s claiming to be a Star Trek fan who needs to understand that diversity is in the DNA of Star Trek.“Diversity as a strength is something that’s celebrated as a through-line in all the Star Trek series. The series can be very different but one thing that has never changed from 8 September 1966 is the value of diversity in making these crews stronger. If they were all homogeneous, they would not be able to as effectively deal with the challenges they face in the cosmos.”That sentiment is shared by the veteran actorRobert Picardo, who spent seven seasons playing Voyager’s Emergency Medical Hologram and reprised his role in Starfleet Academy. Speaking by phone, the 72-year-old does not mince words: “Let’s face it: when someone that high up in the administration and also Elon Musk piled on the same day, do I think it’s a coincidence that the new owners of Paramount cancelled our show the first moment they could have? We did not get a fair shake.We were killed in the cradle.”Picardo adds: “Yes, there was the fact that we hada gay Klingon. Did a lot of people get over-exercised about that? My feeling is, get over yourself! There seems to be a movement to drive us back to the 1950s. Star Trek is all about the future, not about returning.“In that climate the core values of Star Trek – science and also diversity and inclusion – are going to get lumped in with what is under attack. Some people say, do you feel that it was at all current politics that had to do with your cancellation? If we caught the same flu thatStephen Colbertand the editorial freedom of CBS 60 minutes caught then we’re in excellent company.”If Star Trek’s social politics were prescient, its engagement with science and technology was frequently uncanny. Decades before smartphones, tablets, automated doors and voice-activated digital assistants, the Enterprise was operating with personal access display devices, communicators and talking mainframes. But it also interrogated the ethics of innovation.View image in fullscreenRobert Picardo in Star Trek: Starfleet Academy.Photograph: Miller Mobley/ParamountFor Picardo, who spent seven years embodying a holographic doctor wrestling with sentience and civil rights on Voyager, current debates aroundSilicon Valley’s generative AI boomfeel oddly familiar. “The explosion of the technology and the pace at which it is happening is something nobody could have predicted.“It’s a useful tool but it’s raised all sorts of issues. We actually did episodes on Star Trek where my character wrote a book and then there was the question of whether an artificial intelligence could have intellectual property rights. We did the whole issue of whether an artificial intelligence can have an original idea or if it can only slice and dice human ideas scraped from the internet, from everything ever written.”Sixty years on, Star Trek’s faith in a United Federation of Planets that has outgrown bigotry, racism and nationalism feels perversely quaint in an era that has seen Trump champion “America first”,deride the UNand denigrate the very concept of empathy. The show, whose future is uncertain as Paramount’s new owners focus on a proposed $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros, offers utopia in a time of dystopia.Picardo observes: “Post-9/11, a lot of science fiction has become very apocalyptic. It’s in some hellscape future with a few straggler survivors and Star Trek is the opposite of that. But to me, the biggest damage that’s been done in current politics is the destruction the idea of truth or that there is such a thing as a fact and our word does matter. I worry about Star Trek’s survival in a post-truth, post-literate world.”Explore more on these topicsStar TrekWilliam ShatnerUS televisionScience fiction TVTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Garfield takes on Sam Altman in creepy first teaser for Artificial | Luca Guadagnino | The Guardian
description: Luca Guadagnino-directed film will be released by Neon after being dropped by Amazon amid OpenAI partnership
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Luca Guadagnino-directed film will be released by Neon after being dropped by Amazon amid OpenAI partnership
Content: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenAndrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonLuca GuadagninoAndrew Garfield takes on Sam Altman in creepy first teaser for ArtificialLuca Guadagnino-directed film will be released by Neon after being dropped by Amazon amid OpenAI partnershipBig tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?Owen MyersTue 8 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first teaser trailer ofLuca Guadagnino’s Artificial has been released.Afterbeing droppedby Amazon MGM Studios in June, the biopic of theOpenAItech executiveSam Altmanwill be released in the US on 25 December by Neon after it premieres at the New York film festival this October.In the trailer,Andrew Garfieldas Altman walks down the staircase of a luxurious mansion before entering a basement containing dozens of machine guns.Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman movie dropped by Amazon after it announces OpenAI partnershipRead more“The future’s inevitable,” says Altman as ominous electronic music plays. “Countries will fall. Industries are gonna collapse. And we get to be the ones to shepherd people into this new world.”In a statement earlier this summer,Amazonsaid that it believed “Artificial will be better served if it were released by a different studio and are working closely with the film-making team to find the film a new home”.Amazon’s deal with OpenAI will see the Jeff Bezos-owned companyinvestingas much as $35bn in the AI company in the coming months following an initial $15bn investment.On 30 June, Neon announced that it had acquired Artificial and that the film would be joining its awards season slate. The film follows the abruptfiring and reinstatementof Altman as OpenAI’s CEO amid a fight over who gets to control the technology.The film also features theAnoraactor Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever, the co-founder of OpenAI; Ike BarinholtzasElon Musk; andMonica BarbaroandCooper Hoffmanas other Altman colleagues at the company. The ensemble will also includeJason Schwartzman,Chris O’Dowd,Zosia Mamet, Cooper Koch and Billie Lourd.“I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield recently toldEsquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a company or a technology that is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.”In a recent red carpet interview with Variety, Hoffmansaidthat he was not surprised that Amazon dropped the film. “I’m shocked they picked it up in the first place,” he said. “When they dropped it, it was kinda like, ‘Oh, yeah, that kinda actually makes sense,’ but then it got picked up by Neon, which I’m so happy about.”Neon has emerged as a dominant force in awards season in recent years and has helped films includingParasite,Anatomy of a FallandAnoraon their paths to Oscar glory. This year, their awards season slate also includes Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’OrwinnerFjord, the James Grey dramaPaper Tigerand Ryusuke Hamaguchi’sAll of a Sudden.Explore more on these topicsLuca GuadagninoAndrew GarfieldSam AltmanOpenAIAmazonAI (artificial intelligence)Jason SchwartzmannewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘So big and so close’: spotting endangered bears on a trip to northern Spain | Spain holidays | The Guardian
description: Conservationists have helped Cantabrian brown bears claw their way back from the edge of extinction in the beautiful mountains of Asturias – and carefully controlled nature tourism allows visitors to see them
Author: Stephen Phelan
Headline: Conservationists have helped Cantabrian brown bears claw their way back from the edge of extinction in the beautiful mountains of Asturias – and carefully controlled nature tourism allows visitors to see them
Content: A Cantabrian brown bear in Somiedo natural park in Asturias.Photograph: Lucas Vallecillos/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Cantabrian brown bear in Somiedo natural park in Asturias.Photograph: Lucas Vallecillos/AlamySpain holidays‘So big and so close’: spotting endangered bears on a trip to northern SpainConservationists have helped Cantabrian brown bears claw their way back from the edge of extinction in the beautiful mountains of Asturias – and carefully controlled nature tourism allows visitors to see themStephen PhelanTue 8 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnce upon a time, in the woods outside Pola de Somiedo, lived a family of Cantabrian brown bears. The villagers reported sightings of a mother bear who had lost a leg to a hunter’s trap, her two cubs and two adult males, either of which might have been the father. In those days, at the end of the 1980s, they seemed to be the last of their kind in this part of Asturias. Meanwhile, the wider population dropped to about 60 bears across the surrounding Cantabrian mountain range that gave the species its name.They have since clawed their way back from the edge of extinction here in northern Spain, and nature guide Luis Frechilla believes their numbers may now be upwards of 500 again. “They’re still classed as endangered,” he tells me, until the official count hits 1,000. But relative abundance makes them much easier to see today inSomiedo natural park– one of Spain’s first such protected areas, established in 1988.View image in fullscreenSomiedo natural park.Photograph: Biosphoto/AlamySetting his scope on a tripod in a steep-angled pasture, Frechilla spots a bear almost as soon as we start looking. A juvenile, apparently, which means the animal is old enough to be foraging alone, but it’s still too small, and too far away, for him to tell if it’s a male or female. Another bear-spotter standing near us seems more willing to take a guess.“Ooh, look at his little ears,” she says delightedly, beaming behind binoculars. No expert myself, I watch that distant fuzzy shape move across the viewfinder and along the sharp ridges opposite, blinking in and out of sight like a cursor on the trend line of a graph. I’m not sure that we are close enough to call this an encounter, but it is an experience.double quotation mark‘They can’t be too heavy because they have to climb,’ says our guide. Their paw prints look big enough to meThe sun drops behind the peaks; the birds sing a dusk chorus in the birches and oaks; cowbells ring through the valley from the dairy herds that help this region of so-called “Green Spain” look and sound like the Swiss Alps. It gets cold at night up here, and it’s been known to snow in summer, though my own visit in late spring sees the mountaintops looking whiter than anyone around here can remember so deep into May.That weather, and the sheer calorific spend of living and working at a median altitude of 1,300 metres, has made the traditional cuisine much sturdier here than elsewhere in Spain.Down at the village inn,Casa Miño, we share a bottle of regional cider and acachopo(beef fillet topped with serrano ham, peppers and goat cheese, and pounded into a single solid unit the size of a solar panel). I wantfabada,too, the famous Asturian stew of white beans, pork belly and blood sausage. Frechilla says it’s a winter dish, customarily eaten for lunch – too heavy for the body to process later in the day. But I would orderfabadaat midnight in a heatwave, and keep eating it even while they loaded me into the ambulance.View image in fullscreenThe Lake of the Valley.Photograph: Manu Garcia/AlamyThe bears, meanwhile, don’t have much to feed on at the moment. They only woke from hibernation a few weeks ago, explains Alicia Madrid the next day, on a forest trail above the century-old hydroelectric power station at La Malva. A biologist with the conservation groupFundación Oso Pardo, Madrid tells me that Cantabrian bears don’t hibernate as long or deeply as other brown bears and are generally smaller and lighter than American grizzlies.“They’re adapted to this terrain, and they can’t be too heavy because they have to climb a lot,” she says. Their paw prints in the mud look big enough to me, and the bite marks where they chewed clumps of long grasses, and the hairs shed where they scratched their backs against trees. Madrid shows us, too, the hefty rocks they overturned looking for insects. Further into the summer, there’ll be plenty of berries, acorns, chestnuts and maybe some meaty carrion to fatten them up.The foundation has played a major role in the regrowth of bear populations, building bio-corridors with strategic placements of trees and bushes full of all the things they like to eat. Another key factor is the hunting ban, introduced in 1973. The trick now, says Madrid, is coaxing isolated cohorts to breed with other groups and boost genetic diversity.double quotation markEveryone is watching a large male bear as he lopes across a meadow to take a splash in the riverAlso: managing the tourists who come to see them, and balancing ecological imperatives against financial incentives. Later, after a long hike through the Valley of the Lake to reach the aptly named Lake of the Valley, I overhear Frechilla fielding the related concerns of two local women. Against a backdrop of blue sky, bright wildflowers and silver waters, the women seem to argue that conservation efforts amount to commercial exploitation. Frechilla gently insists that Somiedo natural park is a model of good practice in Spain. Much of the bears’ territory is closed to the public, and spotting expeditions are only permitted in the company of licensed guides. Nature tourism, he says, keeps villagers in jobs where farming culture cannot, and is proving vastly more sustainable than hunting bears for sport. As for protecting humans, there has been only one bear attack in recent memory, on an elderly lady whose evening stroll led her between a mother and cubs. She survived.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor now, at least, most residents seem willing to share the bears with outsiders. That evening, a small crowd gather by the side of a winding back road near Saliencia, some sitting comfortably on camping chairs with spotting scopes in their hands. Everyone is watching a large male bear – so big and so close that they don’t need the viewing equipment – as he lopes across a meadow to take a quick splash in the river. Another male is spotted in the treeline above, and the two circle each other at a distance for a while. There is some speculation that they might fight for this turf, and a man with two leashed greyhounds seems ready to take bets on it. Frechilla shakes his head.“Maybe later in the season, when they’ve gained enough weight.”View image in fullscreenA bear in Somiedo  natural park.Photograph: Lucas Vallecillos/AlamyThese bears are doing better now, but it’s still a tough life. The reality of their ongoing baby boom is that only 30% of juveniles will survive on their own, after a year of maternal supervision. This is surely why I find it so moving when we follow reports of another sighting in the twilight: a mother and her two young cubs have been seen climbing a slope called El Diente,or “The Tooth”.It’s getting dark and cold, but we can see them through the scopes, about a mile away from us across the high mountain pass at La Peral. I watch the mother bear waiting and cajoling as needed while the siblings struggle up the vertical planes of rock like toddlers trying to climb a baby gate. On the ridgeline, they turn to silhouettes, play-fighting against a white sky.They disappear over the far side, but then a little one comes back, seeming to wave goodbye with both front paws in the air. I remember a story I read to my daughter once, which put a poignant time limit on the usual fairytale ending: “And they all lived happily together, for as long as they could.”The trip was provided by theSpanish Tourist Office,Turismo AsturiasandCasa Miñoin Pola de Somiedo. Bear-spotting tours with nature guide Luis Frechilla can be organised throughWild Spain Travel. For more information on the Cantabrian brown bear and related conservation efforts, visitFundación Oso PardoExplore more on these topicsSpain holidaysEurope holidaysWildlife holidaysWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cockroaches were everywhere – even on our wine glasses | Insects | The Guardian
description: In a cheap London flat with no heating, dozens of the insects swarmed, leading to a Valentine’s Day that still makes me break out in a cold sweat
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: In a cheap London flat with no heating, dozens of the insects swarmed, leading to a Valentine’s Day that still makes me break out in a cold sweat
Content: We thought the bedbugs were bad …Composite: Guardian design;StellaNature/Alamy; ansonsaw/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWe thought the bedbugs were bad …Composite: Guardian design;StellaNature/Alamy; ansonsaw/Getty ImagesThe pest I’ll never forgetInsectsThe pest I’ll never forget: the cockroaches were everywhere – even on our wine glassesIn a cheap London flat with no heating, dozens of the insects swarmed, leading to a Valentine’s Day that still makes me break out in a cold sweatTim JonzeTue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 00.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdon’t know if cockroaches really could, as we’re often told, survive a nuclear apocalypse, but I can tell you this with certainty: they can definitely survive pest control. “Hopefully that should be a bit better now,” said the friendly exterminator after his first visit to our flat. By the third visit he was speaking more honestly. “The only way to get rid of your cockroaches,” he said, “would be to burn this whole block of flats to the ground.”It was January 2003 when I moved with my girlfriend Helen into our first London flat. It’s fair to say there were red flags we probably should have spotted. It was suspiciously affordable – £140 a week for a place less than a minute’s walk from Finsbury Park tube station? Sure, the place looked pretty skanky, but it was still spacious for a studio flat. We put the price down to the fact there was absolutely no way of heating the property and signed up.That winter was bleak – we were freezing cold and, worse, waking up each morning with lines of red bites down our arms and legs. It took us a while to work out the culprits: bedbugs.Bug spray was deployed, but it just made them angrier – the bites actually got worse. We replaced the mattress and that problem disappeared. (Despite not having encountered bedbugs anywhere since, Helen still checks down the the headboards in every hotel she stays at and won’t let her kids leave their bags on the floor.) The true horror, though, was yet to come.The lack of central heating wasn’t all bad: as it turned out, it had been keeping another set of houseguests out of sight. Now, with spring approaching, they began to make themselves known. At first it was just in the night. The odd one darting across the bathroom when you turned on a light. But soon we were spotting cockroaches on a daily basis – huge, black and shiny. By April, turning on the light in the middle of the night meant bracing yourself as dozens scurried to safety.I’d read somewhere that squishing a cockroach simply dispersed their eggs across the room to hatch elsewhere (a myth, it turns out, although they do apparently release dying chemicals that attract more cockroaches to the spot). We took to trapping them under glasses and bowls instead, then waiting for them to die that way. Our living space ended up littered with various pieces of roach-covering crockery. No, we didn’t have people round for dinner.We did have a particularly memorable Valentine’s Day dinner, though – not for any romantic effort on my part, sadly, but because at one point Helen reached for her wine and ended up grasping the shell of a massive roach that had climbed on to the stem of her glass.The landlord refused to accept we had an issue. Only when a traumatised Helen resorted to bringing dead bugs to his office in an empty takeaway box did he reluctantly send for the aforementioned pest guy. Although the guy couldn’t fix the problem, he was keen to inform us that we had oriental cockroaches – black rather than brown, and apparently much bigger and harder to kill than the more common German ones. His eyes lit up a bit when talking about it. At least someone was enjoying themselves.Mercifully, our rental agreement was only for six months. The feeling of living without cockroaches was overwhelming and joyful – although it wasn’t total freedom. I retained a fear that one of them might have snuck into a suitcase and followed us to the next property. For a while I saw pointy little antennae everywhere. I’ve still not totally shaken it.Explore more on these topicsInsectsThe pest I’ll never forgetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best beauty Advent calendars in 2026, tested – yes, we know it’s early! | Christmas | The Guardian
description: Christmas might be months away, but beauty Advent calendar waiting lists are filling up fast. From cult favourites to cruelty-free picks, here are the ones worth buying
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: Christmas might be months away, but beauty Advent calendar waiting lists are filling up fast. From cult favourites to cruelty-free picks, here are the ones worth buying
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterChristmasReviewThe best beauty Advent calendars in 2026, tested – yes, we know it’s early!Christmas might be months away, but beauty Advent calendar waiting lists are filling up fast. From cult favourites to cruelty-free picks, here are the ones worth buyingDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereSarah MatthewsTue 8 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs I write, an ice-cream van has just parked outside my flat. It’s the middle of this year’s umpteenth heatwave, and I’m finally understanding the appeal of a cold shower. That can only mean one thing: it’s time to start testing the best beauty Advent calendars.I wish I was joking, but many beauty brands and retailers have been curating their 2026 beauty Advent calendars since before last Christmas. And since these calendars offer a selection of high-end cosmetics, bestsellingbeauty staplesand new launches at far less than their usual combined price, they’ve become a festive staple for beauty fanatics.But as early as it might be, jingle bells wait for no one. Waiting lists for the most popular Advent calendars have already opened, and while many are yet to be released, some will sell out long beforeWhamageddonclaims its first victim. That was true of my favourite calendar last year, which sold out before the end of September.So, much as it pains me to say it, now might be a good time to buy one. Below, you’ll find my favourites, from bargain beauty Advent calendars under £50 to three-figure luxuries. I’ve tested 20 to find calendars packed with cult-favourite products suitable for a whole spectrum of skin types and preferences. I also looked at the packaging and broad appeal of each calendar to help minimise waste.If nothing tickles your fancy just yet, don’t panic. More calendars get released in the lead-up to December, and I’ll keep updating this article as soon as they drop.At a glanceBest beauty Advent calendar overallCult BeautyAdvent calendar Signature Edition£245 at Cult BeautyBest value beauty Advent calendarAnthropologie24 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£98 at AnthropologieBest beauty Advent calendar for high-end productsSpace NKBeauty Advent calendar£275 at Space NKBest beauty Advent calendar for familiesLushAdvent calendar£210 at LushBest Advent calendar for cruelty-free skincareLiz Earle12 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£79 at Liz EarleBest beauty Advent calendar for teens and tweensW7Beauty Blast Advent calendar£22 at W7Why you should trust meI test beauty products for a living, which means I’ve worked my way through more skincare, makeup, hair care, perfume and nail care products than I dare to count. Working in this industry has shown me the very best and absolute worst of what’s out there. I know how to spot a good product when I see one, even if it’s tucked away in the corner of a beauty Advent calendar.I also have a certification in cosmetic science, so I know how to identify products suited to different skin and hair types. I’ve struggled with sensitive skin for years, so I keep a close eye out for ingredients that might irritate. The calendars below are all full of products suitable for most people to minimise waste.How I testedView image in fullscreenBehind the doors: calendars were judged on the range and usefulness of their contents, as well as the packaging they came in.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianHeaps of Advent calendars are released every year. To help find the best calendars, I longlisted 30 before testing the 20 that offer the best range of products and value for money. I’ll continue to update this page with new options in the run-up toChristmas.Testing them lets me assess the quality of each calendar and its contents, as well as the packaging it arrives in. If the calendar itself is recyclable but arrives shrouded in plastic bags and polystyrene, it’s a non-starter. I also check that each calendar is made from packaging that is recyclable at home or genuinely reusable.It’s impossible to test every product inside every calendar – I only have one face, after all – but I judge each calendar based on the range, quality and usefulness of the products inside. Broad appeal is key to avoiding wasted products, and luckily, this is how most Advent calendars are designed.I look for a good mix of skincare, makeup, body care, hair care and nail care, unless a calendar is specifically dedicated to a certain product type. I also check how easy it is to incorporate each product into a typical routine. Too many harsh treatments or bold makeup shades would be less appealing than a calendar with a more approachable lineup.This helps me assess how broadly usable the contents are and how much is likely to go to waste. While beauty Advent calendars can’t be considered eco-friendly, it’s important to minimise waste where possible.Each year I end up with far more products than one woman can reasonably use. This year, I donated the contents of the calendars to theRedbridge Reach Outservice, which supports anyone experiencing domestic abuse.Our favourite beauty Advent calendars in 2026Best beauty Advent calendar overall:Cult Beauty Advent calendar Signature EditionCult BeautyAdvent calendar Signature Edition£245£245 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveHigh-end skincare and makeup in a beautiful designWhat we don’t loveMinimal hair care; a daring blush shadeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£245 at Cult BeautyStatus:launchedIf you’re hunting for a beauty Advent calendar filled with high-end makeup and skincare, this year’s Cult Beauty Signature Edition is my top pick. I’ve tried and recommended many of the products inside over the past year, while others are established favourites. There’s very little to dislike, and with 33 products inside, 19 of which are full-size, that’s no mean feat.What we loveWhile I’m most excited about the contents of this calendar, it’s also my favourite design. It opens like a book and features detailed illustrations of lipsticks and makeup brushes hidden among festive flowers and foliage. The white, sage green and gold colour scheme should work well with most Christmas decorations. And, when the countdown is complete, the box can go in your household recycling bin, while the gold ribbon can be reused.The skincare inside also has broad appeal. I tested the Medik8 Advanced Pro Collagen peptide cream for my recent roundup offace moisturisers, and its light texture and peptide formula made it my top choice for anti-ageing. You’ll also get a 15ml size of the eye-wateringly expensive Augustinus Bader the Rich Cream, which I found amazing for nourishing dry winter-stressed skin.There are just two skincare products you’ll need to be a little careful with: the Paula’s Choice Retinaldehyde treatment and the Allies of Skin Azelaic serum. Both contain ingredients used to target anti-ageing, acne and hyperpigmentation, but add them to your routine gradually and separately to reduce the risk of irritation.Makeup-wise, there’s a lot to like too, with a full-size Saie liquid blush and Westman Ateliermascara, both high-end products loved by many beauty enthusiasts. You’ll also find a travel-size Charlotte Tilbury setting spray and Milk Makeup Hydro Grip primer, both of which are top picks in my upcoming primer and setting spray tests.Topping things off with hair care, you’ll find the Fable & Mane HoliRootshair oil, which helps to promote stronger strands and increase hydration without using silicones. But the hair-care highlight for me is the travel-size Gisou Honey Gloss ceramide shampoo and conditioner, which smell divine and are from the same range as my favouritehair mask.It’s a shame that …only four of the products are hair care, and there’s no perfume included. And the Patrick Ta blush duo is almost highlighter pink; you’ll need a light hand, but the shade itself may not be for everyone.Claimed overall value:more than £1,100Number of products:19 full-size, 14 mini (33 in total)Calendar shell:recyclable card with reusable gold ribbonsStandout products:Westman Atelier Eye Want You mascara, Charlotte Tilbury Airbrush Flawless Finish setting spray,Patrick Ta Major Headlines Double-Take cream + powder blush duo, Saie Dew blush, Medik8 Advanced Pro Collagen peptide cream, Augustinus Bader the Rich CreamCult BeautyAdvent calendar Signature Edition£245£245 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveHigh-end skincare and makeup in a beautiful designWhat we don’t loveMinimal hair care; a daring blush shadeBest value beauty Advent calendar:Anthropologie 24 Days of Beauty Advent calendarAnthropologie24 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£98£98 at AnthropologieWhat we loveClassic, usable beauty treats at a good priceWhat we don’t loveOnly one makeup product insideView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£98 at AnthropologieStatus:launched for preorderSome beauty Advent calendars cost the world and then leave you wondering what on earth to do with all the products inside. That is not true of the Anthropologie calendar for 2026. There are 25 little luxuries behind 24 doors, and all are staples that should fit easily into an existing beauty routine. Small upgrades for a sensible price.What we loveThere isn’t too much skincare in this calendar, but you will find a full-size Grown Alchemist Regenerating serum worth £60. This has a light gel texture and contains rambutan, polysaccharides and plant peptides to help smooth the appearance of fine lines, hydrate and promote smooth skin.You’ll find the Espa Clean & Green Detox mask, which has a cream clay formula containing vitamin E.There are three fragrances included: the Malin+Goetz strawberry perfume oil, Phlur Father Figure, and a 10ml bottle of Floral Street Wild Vanilla Orchid. The latter is a light, floral fragrance that’s wearable and uplifting but not sickly sweet, and it’s one of my favourite new perfumes.The hair care highlights include the Superfoods prewash oil from Hair Syrup, which I’ve tested before and enjoyed using. You’ll also find a silk scrunchie from Slip, which I found snagged less than standard hair ties, creating less breakage. Be warned – I haven’t been able to go back to normal hair ties since trying these.The calendar also includes a few wellness treats, such as the This Works Deep Sleep pillow spray, a L’Occitane hand cream and a mini candle from Plum & Ashby.It’s a shame that …there’s only one makeup item inside, and Trip electrolytes sachets don’t feel like an exciting beauty treat. The Malin+Goetz strawberry perfume oil is also an acquired taste.Claimed overall value:£400Number of products:17 full-size, 8 miniCalendar shell:recyclableStandout products:Grown Alchemist Regenerating serum, Espa Clean & Green Detox mask, Hair Syrup Superfoods prewash oil, Slip silk skinny scrunchie, Floral Street Wild Vanilla Orchid eau de parfum, This Works Deep Sleep pillow spray, Phlur Father Figure eau de parfum, L’Occitane Amande (almond) Sublime hand cream, Neal’s Yard Wild Rose beauty balm, Manucurist Active Shine polishAnthropologie24 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£98£98 at AnthropologieWhat we loveClassic, usable beauty treats at a good priceWhat we don’t loveOnly one makeup product insideBest beauty Advent calendar for high-end products:Space NK Beauty Advent calendarSpace NKBeauty Advent calendar£275£275 at Space NKWhat we loveGreat product range for treatmentsWhat we don’t loveMostly anti-ageing skincareView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£275 at Space NKStatus:waiting list openThe Space NK calendar was my top pick last year, and this year’s curation is also strong. It was only pipped to the post because its skincare selection leans a little too heavily towards anti-ageing. Still, it’s a strong option if you’re a fan of high-end beauty and want to try a range of products.What we loveThis calendar has the most full-size products included of any here; there are 26, with nine minis. The full-size Skin Rocks cleansing balm effortlessly removed stubborn makeup. There’s also a full-size Medik8 Exo-PDRN Prismatic+ serum, which is one of the best PDRN serums I’ve tried for rejuvenating and improving skin tone, while supporting the skin’s barrier. Most of the headline skincare products are tailored toward anti-ageing, such as the La Mer moisturising cream and Caudalie Vinoperfect Brightening dark spot serum.For hair care, Space NK has skipped the basics and gone straight for treatments. There’s a K18 heat protectant, a leave-in treatment from Color Wow, and an Olaplex treatment, all of which are full-size. It’s good to see a daily essential like heat protection in there, as well as treatments that should suit a range of hair types.I’m also excited by the Kulfi lip stain oil, which is a moisturising, slightly glossy stain in a neutral rose designed to suit a range of skin tones. Likewise, the perfumes have broad appeal. I’ve tried Phlur Missing Person and the Gisou hair perfume before, but I was surprised by the velvety scent of the DS & Durga Debaser in Bloom perfume. All could be layered with the Saltair Salt Water Vanilla body oil, which has a deep, warm vanilla fragrance and feels light on the skin.It’s a shame that …all of the makeup inside is cream- or liquid-based, so if you prefer powder formulations, this won’t be for you. There’s also no nail care included. And, as mentioned above, most of the skincare is focused on anti-ageing. They’re all high-end brands, but the calendar may not include enough basics for younger people or those who prefer a simpler routine.Claimed overall value:more than £1,200Number of products:26 full-size, 9 miniCalendar shell:recyclableStandout products:La Mer Crème de la Mer moisturising cream, K18 HeatBounce conditioning heat protectant, Color Wow Carb Cocktail, Olaplex No3 Plus Complete Repair treatment, Augustinus Bader the Body Cream, Caudalie Vinoperfect Brightening Dark Spot serum, Kosas Soulgazer mascara, Kulfi Lassi lip staining oil, Medik8 Exo-PDRN Prismatic+ serum, Naturium the Booster hyaluronic acid body wash, Refy Lash Sculpt, Saltair Salt Water Vanilla body oil, Skin Rocks the Cleansing BalmSpace NKBeauty Advent calendar£275£275 at Space NKWhat we loveGreat product range for treatmentsWhat we don’t loveMostly anti-ageing skincareFor more, read Sali Hughes’s guide to thebest anti-ageing creams, serums and treatmentsskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox.
