Lush offers two stocked-up Advent calendars every year:one filled with bath bombs and bubble barsand another with the brand’s wider beauty offerings. This reusable hamper is the latter, filled with veganand cruelty-free festive bath bombs, creams, perfumes and a lip scrub to appeal to all ages.Why we love itThat distinctive Lush smell hits as soon as you open this hamper. This will either delight or repulse you, although presumably if you’re considering this you’re in the former camp. Inside, you’ll find 25 treats spread across two 12-day halves that save you a bit of rummaging around.Starting with bath products, you’ll find festive-food-themed bombs and bubble bars, including an orange, a candied pear, a candy cane, a carrot for Rudolph and a Christmas tree. There are also picks from Lush’s standard range, such as the Sleepy bubble bar. And the sweet theme doesn’t stop at bath time, thanks to the sticky dates, s’mores, and chocolate orange shower gels. You can even eat the Hot Chocolate Orange lip scrub, which tastes just as delicious as it sounds.Out of the bathroom, the calendar comes with two exclusive fragrances. The mini Santa’s Favourite body spray smells like soft florals and settles into a light grapefruit. Or, for something stronger, the Snowcake and Rose perfume smells like warm marzipan and feels more grownup. You’ll also find hand soaps, a dusting powder, a body butter, a candle and a cosy pair of Lush socks.Lush scores highly on sustainability: the hamper is made by a B Corp-certified manufacturer, and there’s adetailed breakdown onlineon the other packaging and how to recycle it. The packing peanuts can be placed in your food or garden waste bin, and when you’re finished with the bottles and tubs, you can return them to Lush using theBring it Back schemefor money off your next purchase.It’s a shame that …unlike previous years, there are no inserts to refill last year’s Advent calendar chest. While the new hamper design is a little more reusable day to day, this change seems counterproductive from a sustainability perspective, since part of the appeal of last year’s calendar was that you’d be able to refill it. I’m hoping this version will be refillable for years to come. For a completely refillable option, Lush is launching a fabric calendar this year for you to fill yourself, which will allow you to fill it with products you know you love.Claimed overall value:not listedNumber of products:24 full-size, 1 mini sizeCalendar shell:biodegradable and recyclable cardboard inserts, reusable wicker hamperStandout products:Hot Chocolate Orange lip scrub, Sleepy bubble bar, Sticky Dates shower gel, Honey Bear bath bomb, Once Upon a Time candle, Dream Cream body lotion, Honey I Washed the Kids body scrub, Christmas tree bath bomb, Snowcake and Rose perfumeLushAdvent calendar£210£210 at LushWhat we loveGreat mix of products for all ages to enjoyWhat we don’t loveThe fragrances are characteristically sweetBest Advent calendar for cruelty-free skincare:Liz Earle 12 Days of Beauty Advent calendarLiz Earle12 Days of Beauty Advent calendarfrom£79£79 at Liz Earle£79 at LookfantasticWhat we loveCruelty-free; luxury skincare; generous ‘minis’What we don’t loveFragranced; only 12 daysView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£79 at Liz Earle£79 at LookfantasticStatus:in stockLiz Earle is known for affordable luxuryand this 12-day calendar brings together a selection of its skincare and body care, from facial toners to rich creams. Its presentation box is recyclable; I found everything inside useful; and the selection isn’t overwhelming. It’s also Leaping Bunny certified.Why we love itIt wouldn’t be a Liz Earle Advent calendar if it didn’t include the Cleanse & Polish hot cloth cleanser. This is massaged on to dry skin, then gently “polished” off using a warm, damp washcloth (also included). The warmth makes the cleansing ritual feel spa-like.I’ve used this cleanser many times and always find the process enjoyable and oddly meditative. Add the large 75ml Superskin moisturiser, and you’ve already got the foundations of a good routine.Unlike in larger calendars, the “mini” products don’t feel like an afterthought. The Smooth & Glow exfoliating tonic, Instant Boost Skin tonic and Eyebright soothing lotion all come in matching 50ml bottles, which are larger and more high-end-looking than typical minis. The full-size body wash, body cream and hand cream come in a limited-edition fragrance, Mandarin & Nutmeg, which smells clean and uplifting, with a touch of festive warmth.It’s a shame that …much of the skincare here is fragranced, and there’s only 12 days’ worth, rather than 24. A24-day calendaris available, but it’s more than twice the price, and its vast range of skincare could easily feel overwhelming.Claimed overall value:£203.50Number of products:3 full-size, 1 supersize, 8 miniCalendar shell:recyclableStandout products:Cleanse & Polish hot cloth cleanser, Skin Repair hydrating night cream, Mandarin & Nutmeg body cream, Smooth & Glow exfoliating tonic, Eyebright soothing eye lotionLiz Earle12 Days of Beauty Advent calendarfrom£79£79 at Liz Earle£79 at LookfantasticWhat we loveCruelty-free; luxury skincare; generous ‘minis’What we don’t loveFragranced; only 12 daysBest beauty Advent calendar for teens and tweens:W7 Beauty Blast Advent calendarW7Beauty Blast Advent calendar£22£22 at W7What we loveAffordable; all the skincare and makeup basicsWhat we don’t loveMostly minis; no luxury touchesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£22 at W7Status:launchedNot all beauty Advent calendars require you to take out a loan; this W7 one costs less than the average takeaway and contains 24 makeup and beauty products. Last year’s W7 calendar was brilliant, and this year’s is even better suited to beautynewcomers.Why we love itStarting with skincare, this calendar contains a gentle cleanser, hydrating toner, moisturiser, lip mask and bronzing drops. Makeup-wise, there are two primers, plus a bronzer, blush, highlight and setting powder. For eyes and lips, there are two lip glosses, a lipstick and two lip liners, as well as shiny and matt eyeshadows and an eyeliner. It’s a good starter kit for tweens and teens dipping their toes into the beauty world, or anyone starting to build a beauty routine without spending a fortune.And, while the packaging isn’t high-end, the lip liners, H2O hydrating powder and setting spray are particularly good. That’s what you’d expect for a calendar at this price, but don’t expect a luxury finish here.Claimed overall value:not statedNumber of products:6 full-size, 3 accessories, 15 miniCalendar shell:recyclableStandout products:W7 Double Draw lip pencils, H2O hydrating powder, W7 Golden Glow Drops, Sugar Cookie overnight lip maskW7Beauty Blast Advent calendar£22£22 at W7What we loveAffordable; all the skincare and makeup basicsWhat we don’t loveMostly minis; no luxury touchesThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Will fit easily into most beauty routines’: the No7 25 Days of Beauty Advent calendar.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianNo7 25 Days of Beauty Advent calendarNo725 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£65£65 at BootsWhat we loveFull-size makeup; broad skincare rangeWhat we don’t loveMainly mini skincareView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£65 at BootsBest for:breaking a beauty rut rather than the bankStatus:in stockIf you want to switch things up in your beauty routine, this great-value calendar is a safe bet. It feels like the grownup equivalent of the W7 calendar above; it’s more luxurious, with a larger proportion of skincare, including products with retinoids and exfoliating ingredients.All the full-size products are makeup, aside from one lip balm. These include a cool-toned light brown matt lipstick and liner, a lip oil with a punchy fruity taste, a pink liquid blush, an eyeliner pencil and a black tubing mascara. All of this is simple to use, wearable and will fit easily into most beauty routines.The calendar includes skincare from several No7 ranges, including Radiance+ and Future Renew. There are serums, aneye cream, day and night creams, cleansers and a toner. These are all minis, but this does allow you to sample a range of products before deciding whether to buy full-size versions. There’s also a £5 voucher for selected No7 Future Renew products.It didn’t make the final cut because …while the calendar has a diverse range of things to try, it’s limited to No7, so there isn’t as much choice as other calendars. Also, it’s mostly skincare, so it may be less appealing if you already have a routine you’re happy with. None of the skincare products are full-size, either, except the lip balm.Claimed overall value:£248.93;number of products:24 including 8 full-size £5 voucher;calendar shell:recyclable;standout products:No7 Pro Artist Luxe liquid blush, Pro Artist lip shine oil, Pro Artist That’s a Wrap tubing mascara, No7 Future Renew Damage Reversal body serum, No7 Future Renew SPF40 day cream, No7 Radiance+ Vitamin C Glow tonerNo725 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£65£65 at BootsWhat we loveFull-size makeup; broad skincare rangeWhat we don’t loveMainly mini skincareJurlique Beauty Advent calendarJurliqueBeauty Advent calendar£110£110 at JurliqueWhat we loveB Corp-certified botanical beauty; reusable boxWhat we don’t loveNearly all minis; face oils won’t suit everyoneView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£110 at JurliqueBest for: B Corp-certified botanical beautyStatus:launched for preorderAustralian B Corp-certified skincare brand Jurlique makes lovely botanical skincare. This year’s 24-day calendar features a selection of its bestsellers, many of which contain ingredients grown on the brand’s farm in Australia. So, if you’re ethically conscious and a fan of botanical beauty, this might fit the bill.There’s a blend of essential oils, including mandarin, ylang ylang and geranium, designed for use in a diffuser for some calm during the Christmas period. You’ll also find products from the brand’s rose collection, including a face cream, hand cream, face mist, body lotion and shower gel, as well as its rose face oil. There are also products from its calendula range, along with serums and a hydrating face mask and cleanser.Like last year’s calendar, this comes in a gorgeous reusable box that’s just big enough to store trinkets without taking up too much space; I’m still using my 2025 calendar to store extra makeup.It didn’t make the final cut because …there’s only one full-size product, which feels a little disappointing. The essential oil needs adiffuser, so it’s not as versatile or useful as a full-size skincare product. The four face oils won’t suit everyone, and there are two identical mini rose hand creams. I’d prefer 24 different products rather than repeats. It’s also skincare-only, so makeup fans should look elsewhere.Claimed overall value:£280;number of products:1 full-size, 23 mini;calendar shell:recyclable inserts with reusable box;standout products:Balance Pure essential oil blendJurliqueBeauty Advent calendar£110£110 at JurliqueWhat we loveB Corp-certified botanical beauty; reusable boxWhat we don’t loveNearly all minis; face oils won’t suit everyoneWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenHigh-end beauty Advent calendars tend to have more luxury and full-size products than more affordable versions.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianAre beauty Advent calendars worth it?This depends entirely on your beauty routine and how much you enjoy experimenting with new products. If you like high-end, luxury beauty, then beauty Advent calendars can be a great way to get expensive products bundled together for a lower cost. It’s also an opportunity to try luxe brands without committing to buying full-size products.The first risk is you end up spending a lot of money on products you won’t use. To avoid this, think about the elements of your beauty routine that you like to switch up. If there’s anything you’re staunchly loyal to, for example your skincare, think twice before buying a skincare Advent calendar.There’s also the environmental impact of any products you don’t use, so it’s worth considering either donating them unopened to charity or giving them to any other beauty lovers in your circle.How much should you expect to spend?There is a huge range of beauty Advent calendars available, from below £20 to over £500. That chasmic difference in cost makes a big difference to the products inside. Entry-level calendars offer mostly mini-size products from high-street beauty brands. Some more affordable calendars also offer 12 doors, for the 12 days of Christmas, rather than 24.With the £20-£60 bracket covered by budget brands, the mid-range contenders sit somewhere between £61 and £150. These calendars tend to offer more full-size products than lower-price calendars, from mid-range brands. Unless you’re a big fan of one particular brand, the best way to try lots of new skincare, makeup and hair care is to choose a calendar from a beauty retailer such as Anthropologie, which offers curated calendars with a selection of brands. Most beauty fans will find something suitable in this price bracket.Spend between £151 and £250 and you can expect to find calendars filled with mainly full-size products, whether from mid-range or luxury brands or higher-end beauty retailers such as CultBeautyand Space NK.If you’re hoping for full-fat luxury at full-fat prices, you can spend over £250 and grab a calendar from super-high-end retailers such asSelfridgesandLiberty, or premium brands such asDiptyque. These tend to contain higher-value products, with some brands claiming a total value of more than £1,000. Just be sure to triple-check the contents all appeal to you before spending this much.Why are beauty Advent calendars released so early?Unlike edible Advent calendars, which can be packed up and filled with the same chocolates year after year, beauty Advent calendars take months of planning and coordination. As you’re opening the 2026 calendar, most brands will already be deep in planning on what to include in 2027.By opening waiting lists early, brands are able to better plan the number of calendars they need to make, and ensure they have enough time to send them out before 1 December.Starting your Christmas shopping early? title: Why bother deseeding tomatoes? | Chefs | The Guardian
description: It all depends on the variety of tomato and the dish you’re making, says our panel of experts
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: It all depends on the variety of tomato and the dish you’re making, says our panel of experts
Content: More often than not, a pasta sauce will work better if the tomatoes are deseeded.Photograph: Dan Matthews/The Guardian. Food styling: Lola Faura @ Style Department.View image in fullscreenMore often than not, a pasta sauce will work better if the tomatoes are deseeded.Photograph: Dan Matthews/The Guardian. Food styling: Lola Faura @ Style Department.Kitchen aideChefsWhy bother deseeding tomatoes?It all depends on the variety of tomato and the dish you’re making, says our panel of expertsAnna BerrillTue 8 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy do recipes often say to deseed tomatoes? Isn’t that where the flavour is,especially since the seeds don’t make much difference to a sauce’s texture?Catriona, by email“It all depends on the variety of tomato,” saysthe Guardian’s Rachel Roddy, “because some are much seedier than others. Sicilian varieties that require little watering, for example, have loads of little bitter seeds, which do need flicking or sieving out.” If, however, Catriona had some vesuvio tomatoes destined for a salad, Jay Patel, co-owner of Italian restaurantLegarein London, wouldn’t bother: “Those are generally pretty meaty and don’t have many seeds, so I’d just slice and dress them generously with olive oil and salt, and you’ll have something pretty special.” And that’s the crux of the matter: as well as the type of tomato, the answer hinges on what you’re planning to do with them, too. “If you’re making a salad with watery winter tomatoes, say, there’s a purpose for those seeds,” Patel adds, “because they provide a lovely pop as well as acidity.”The most common deseeding scenario is for pasta sauces, but even that comes with a caveat, Patel says: “If I’m going for a slow-cooked sauce, it’s tinned chopped tomatoes, seeds and all. But if I’m after a lighter, fresher tomato sauce, I’ll quickly blanch, peel and deseed fresh tomatoes myself.” Nick Molyviatis ofZyliain London, meanwhile, scoops out the seeds with a teaspoon or he grates his tomatoes instead – “the skin acts as a protector, a glove” – while Roddy’s “best defence against seeds” is a food mill: “Seeds don’t contain flavour as such, but the fleshy gel around them does, which is why a food mill is great,” she explains. “It presses the flavour from that and the skin, while at the same time separating them from the sauce base.”Mind you, that gel in which the seeds are suspended is watery, too, which is why Patel shuns it in the likes of tomato tarts: “You want to remove as much water as possible, because it will make the pastry soggy,” he says, so it’s best to deseed the tomatoes before slicing them uniformly. “Once baked, you get these lovely, almost semi-dried tomatoes.” And not a soggy bottom in sight.But it’s not just about the seeds. “The texture of the skin also messes things up sometimes, and it’s not that pleasant to pick out of your teeth, either,” Molyviatis says. But again, Roddy notes, to peel or not to peel generally depends on the dish and, “more importantly”, on the variety of tomato: “Thin-skinned toms aren’t a worry,” she says, “but thicker skins are not only pesky to eat, they can also twist into scrolls during cooking, and are very annoying in some sauces.”To peel her toms, Roddy plunges them first into boiling water and then into cold to loosen the skins; failing that, she passes them through – yes, you’ve guessed it – her trusty food mill. Patel, on the other hand, tends to rely more on a knife, especially if bull’s heart tomatoes are involved: “They’re so easy to peel with a serrated knife.” Sure, it’s a bit of a faff, but it’s worth the effort, he insists. “When you’ve paid good money for good ingredients, it’s always worth going the extra mile.”Got a culinary dilemma? title: José Pizarro’s recipe for grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche | Food | The Guardian
description: A winning combination of oily fish, sweet berries and a sharp dressing
Author: José Pizarro
Headline: A winning combination of oily fish, sweet berries and a sharp dressing
Content: José Pizarro's grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenJosé Pizarro's grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodJosé Pizarro’s recipe for grilled sardines with blackberry escabecheA winning combination of oily fish, sweet berries and a sharp dressingJosé PizarroTue 8 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of my favourite summer memories is makingcollares de morasas a child in Extremadura, which involved threading wild blackberries on to a piece of straw to make little necklaces. We’d always eat some too, of course, as well as wearing them, and we’d always come home with stained hands and big smiles. At the time, I never imagined that one day I’d be cooking sardines and pairing them with those same wild berries, but that’s the magic of food. The ingredients that filled my childhood with such simple joy have become part of the dishes I love creating today. Every time I make this recipe, it takes me straight back to those carefree summer days.Grilled sardines with blackberry escabechePrep10 minCook25 minMarinate1 hr+Serves43 tbsp olive oil2 banana shallots, peeled and finely sliced1 red or orange bell pepper, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely sliced4-5 fresh thyme sprigs2 tsp coriander seeds1 tsp black peppercorns1 small pinch chilli flakes(optional)200ml white-wine vinegar, or cider vinegar200ml white wine150g blackberries, washedSea salt and black pepper8 good-sized fresh sardines, butterflied (ask the fishmonger to do this for you, if need be)Heat a tablespoon of the oil, then gently fry the shallots and bell pepper for six or seven minutes, until lovely and tender. Add the thyme and spices, fry for a minute more, then add the vinegar, wine and 100ml water, bring to a simmer and cook until the liquid has reduced by about half. Stir in the blackberries, then take off the heat and leave to cool slightly.Meanwhile, put the rest of the oil in a large nonstick frying pan on a high heat. Season the butterflied sardines inside and out, then fry them skin-side down for three or four minutes, until golden and crisp. Flip over and fry for just a minute longer on the flesh side.Arrange the cooked sardines skin-side up and side by side in a suitable deep-sided dish, pour the warm escabeche all over the top, then leave to marinate and cool down for at least an hour. Serve at once, or cover and chill in the fridge until you’re ready to eat.Explore more on these topicsFoodFishFruitSeafoodAutumn food and drinkSpanish food and drinkMain courserecipesShareReuse this content

title: I paid my Ulez charge, but I am still receiving threats from TfL | TfL | The Guardian
description: Transport for London has fined me and warned that if I don’t pay it will possibly destroy my car
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: Transport for London has fined me and warned that if I don’t pay it will possibly destroy my car
Content: After paying the Ulez charge all signs pointed to a fine.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenAfter paying the Ulez charge all signs pointed to a fine.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAConsumer championsTfLI paid my Ulez charge, but I am still receiving threats from TfLTransport for London has fined me and warned that if I don’t pay it will possibly destroy my carAnna TimsTue 8 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI paid the £12.50LondonUlez charge on my Amex card within hours of driving through the zone. I was then fined £90 for non-payment. According to my card issuer, Transport for London (TfL) had failed to collect the £12.50.TfL’s letter threatened a £180 fine, rising to £360, and possible destruction of my car, if I did not pay. My appeal was rejected.As my wife and I are in our 80s and need a car for hospital appointments, I paid the £90 fine under duress.VR,Fleet, HampshireI’ve lost track of how often I have exposed TfL’s habit of fining fully paid-up drivers because of its own administrative incompetence.The process is always the same: the driver pays a Ulez/congestion/Dart charge within the deadline, but TfL, or its acquiring bank, omits to collect the money and refuses to accept evidence of the payment.I got £8,500 in Ulez fines after my car number plate was clonedRead moreYou submitted a screenshot from your banking app showing the payment was confirmed, and a letter from American Express stating it had authorised the sum but that TfL did not collect it. TfL ignored both, insisting that, as it had no record of the money it had failed to collect, you must take the rap. Back in 2019, it assured me it had changed its systems to prevent exactly this. It rang you the day after I challenged this latest lapse with an apology and a refund.It says: “Cases where payment is not taken are rare but we have established processes to ensure drivers are not issued with a fine. Unfortunately, they were not followed. We are reminding our contractor of the correct course of action if a case like this occurs.”We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. title: Houseplant hacks: can white vinegar or lemon juice clean leaves? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: Dust and hard water can leave deposits that slow photosynthesis, but don’t believe everything you read about using acids to remove them
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: Dust and hard water can leave deposits that slow photosynthesis, but don’t believe everything you read about using acids to remove them
Content: Will lemon juice dissolve the minerals left behind by hard water?Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWill lemon juice dissolve the minerals left behind by hard water?Photograph: Getty ImagesHouseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant hacks: can white vinegar or lemon juice clean leaves?Dust and hard water can leave deposits that slow photosynthesis, but don’t believe everything you read about using acids to remove themGynelle LeonTue 8 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 05.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe problemDusty leaves are more than a cosmetic problem. A film of dust blocks light, which slows photosynthesis and dulls the plant. Hard water makes it worse, leaving chalky white mineral spots on the foliage that a damp cloth simply smears around.The hackThe acids in white vinegar, or lemon juice, dissolve the mineral salts left behind by hard water – just wipe a very diluted solution over the leaves with a microfibre cloth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHouseplant hacks: should you always quarantine new plants to avoid pests spreading?Read moreThe methodThe popular version of this hack recommends a one-to-one mix of acid and water, which I think is far too strong and risks scorching your leaves. Instead, use roughly a teaspoon of white vinegar or two tablespoons of lemon juice to a litre of water. Mix it up, dip a microfibre cloth, hold the underside of the leaf with one hand and wipe gently with the other, top and bottom.The testI mixed a weak vinegar solution and used it on a peace lily blotched with hard water marks. The chalky spots lifted cleanly and left the leaves clean.The verdictThis one works, but the internet’s usual recipe could ruin your plant. Kept very dilute and used only occasionally when hard water marks build up, a weak acidic solution is a useful way to get leaves clean and healthy.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: This moorland needed rainfall – it got something even better | Rural affairs | The Guardian
description: Eyam Moor, Derbyshire: It’s a place that I treasure greatly, and now it has a change of ownership that is worth celebrating
Author: Ed Douglas
Headline: Eyam Moor, Derbyshire: It’s a place that I treasure greatly, and now it has a change of ownership that is worth celebrating
Content: View from Eyam Moor looking towards the Hope Valley.Photograph: Mark Titterton/AlamyView image in fullscreenView from Eyam Moor looking towards the Hope Valley.Photograph: Mark Titterton/AlamyCountry diaryRural affairsCountry diary: This moorland needed rainfall – it got something even betterEyam Moor, Derbyshire:It’s a place that I treasure greatly, and now it has a change of ownership that is worth celebratingEd DouglasTue 8 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 05.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan a landscape sigh with relief? It felt that way, pushing through bilberry and cowberry hung with pearls of overnight rain that soaked my lower legs.On the path, dry, dusty soil had reverted to reassuring gloop. I was thrilled, at one point, to step cautiously round a puddle. Overhead, a buzzard wheeled and a small gang of swallows skimmed across heather whose purple intensity was already fading, too soon it seemed to me. To the west, a kestrel was quartering the slopes ofWet Withens.View image in fullscreenHeather and Cowberry.Photograph: Ed DouglasThe downward curve of the moor steepens here, as it drops towards Highlow Brook, but before it does, there’s a bench, a flat space, which in the bronze age was used for a barrow. Next to it is a henge, with its circle of small stones, the most prominent of which was long ago dubbed “the chair”.I noticed that a raptor, perhaps the kestrel nearby, had recently been dismantling something small and furry on top of the chair, so I moved quickly on to the barrow.The view from here is among the best I know – evidence that our distant forebears had a grand feeling for landscape. I could see in the distance the spire ofSt Michael’s in Hathersage, its location no less harmonious, nestling in the crook of the hills opposite, ridgelines intersecting like arms round shoulders.The barrow itself is a jumble of stones, torn apart in the mid-18th century when the nearby turnpike was built and workmen came looking for material. This was decades before the commons were snaffled by acts of enclosure, in this case for the Duke of Devonshire. Later in the 19th century he turned it into a grouse moor.View image in fullscreen‘A henge, with its circle of small stones, the most prominent of which was long ago dubbed “the chair”.’Photograph: Ed DouglasThese twisting strands of deep history show how varied our uplands have been, from sacred space, to sheepwalk, to elite playground. Now this place has a new story. An anonymous benefactor haspresented Eyam Moor to the Derbyshire Wildlife Trustto be a haven for biodiversity, a gleam of light in a troubled sky.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsRural affairsCountry diaryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Skyscrapers and smokestacks: the grittier side of Georgia O’Keeffe | Georgia O'Keeffe | The Guardian
description: Beyond her famed paintings of flowers and landscapes, the American artist created stunning studies of urban architecture
Author: Veronica Esposito
Headline: Beyond her famed paintings of flowers and landscapes, the American artist created stunning studies of urban architecture
Content: Georgia O’Keeffe in 1932.Photograph: Alfred Stieglitz/APView image in fullscreenGeorgia O’Keeffe in 1932.Photograph: Alfred Stieglitz/APGeorgia O'KeeffeSkyscrapers and smokestacks: the grittier side of Georgia O’KeeffeBeyond her famed paintings of flowers and landscapes, the American artist created stunning studies of urban architectureVeronica EspositoTue 8 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorgia O’Keeffe is celebrated for her ethereal depictions of flowers, sunlight, landscapes and animal bones, their gracefully swooping forms dripping with organic curves and seemingly on the verge of melting before our eyes. Such an approach would seem to be quite at odds with the firm, straight lines of farmhouses and barns, to say nothing of the electrified skyscrapers of New York City – and yet that is exactly what is centered inGeorgia O’Keeffe: Architecture, a new show at the Detroit Institute of Arts (Dia).“I wanted to tell a new story about an artist who is so familiar,” said curator Ben Colman, who oversaw this collection of close to 40 works from the famed artist. “We can take a fresh look at works that O’Keeffe always considered essential and celebrate them in the way she wanted to.”The idea for the show emerged from O’Keeffe’s 1932 work Stables, which is the only piece on exhibition that is in the Dia’s collection. It’s a charmingly tranquil side view of the titular construct, dominated by bright green, rich burgundy and subtly textured eggshell white, made by O’Keeffe during one of her many travels through the rurals of upstate New York and far-out parts of eastern Quebec. The artist regularly adventured through these rough and remote lands before deciding to leave New York City and live full-time in New Mexico in 1949.View image in fullscreenGeorgia O’Keeffe, Stables, 1932.Photograph: The Detroit Institute of Arts/© 2026 The Georgia O’Keeffe Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New YorkColman explained that Stables gave him the inspiration to look at O’Keeffe’s work with fresh eyes and seek out other ways of exploring her subtle textures and studies in pure color. “Stables is very precise in its use of geometry, and for many people who know O’Keeffe also a bit unexpected,” said Colman.With his eyes attuned to the geometries of Stables, Colman began to seek out more and more of O’Keeffe’s architectural works. Among other things, this search let him put fresh eyes on to the artist’s New York City pieces, many of which she made from the vantage of her apartment window; she and her husband Alfred Stieglitz started on the 11th floor of the Shelton hotel in 1926, then moved up to the 28th, and finally the 30th floor out of 31. “It was likely the tallest residential building in the world at the time,” said Colman.‘She had this divine calling’: the incredible and transporting art of Minnie EvansRead moreThis high vantage let O’Keeffe create unprecedented cityscapes, among them a series of works depicting the gritty urban industrial life surrounding the East River. With smokestacks billowing out pollution and endless rows of nondescript urban buildings, it’s quite far from the works O’Keeffe is famous for, but according to Colman, in these pieces she’s honing her ability to represent the feeling of a place by the buildings that fill it, a talent that she would famously apply to New Mexico’s adobes in subsequent years.“She tried very hard to represent the spirit and character of these places,” said Colman. “So in my mind it connects an adobe church in New Mexico with a skyscraper in midtown Manhattan.”Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture also offers viewers a most remarkable depiction of the Brooklyn Bridge; verging on religious in its adoration of a beloved icon, it was made by the artist in 1949 as a sort of swan song as she was on her way out of New York. The piece is dominated by a flattened view of the bridge’s famous arches, bringing to mind the shapes of stained glass windows, framing gracefully swooping renditions of the bridge’s suspending cables. It neatly defamiliarizes the bridge, toying with abstraction while offering much to anchor the eye in reality.View image in fullscreenGeorgia O’Keeffe, Brooklyn Bridge, 1949.Photograph: Brooklyn Museum/© 2026 The Georgia O’Keeffe Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York“It’s a deeply personal painting,” said Colman, “documenting a moment of transition for O’Keeffe. It places our point of view into a moment of departure, and there’s a beautiful, poetic quality to how she uses light and variations of color, almost like looking through a stained glass window.”Another noteworthy aspect of Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture is that it brings together multiple depictions of a humble patio door, a beloved part of the artist’s home in Abiquiu, New Mexico. O’Keeffe bought the house in 1945, taking four whole years to restore it from the ruined state that she found it in. It became her permanent home in 1949, and she resided there until 1984, just two years before her death.The patio door paintings are a part of a suite of nearly abstract works centered around doors that O’Keeffe made during the 1940s and 50s, remarkable for the variety of colors that she brings to these simple, repeating forms. “Once she saw this patio door,” said Colman, “O’Keeffe decided that it was something that she needed to live with. She was inspired to paint it dozens of times, and it’s part of an extraordinary series of works, some of the most abstract in her career, but also so precisely anchored and placed.”Placing her alongside contemporaries such as Agnes Martin and Mark Rothko, these pieces are color studies formed out of minimalistic geometries, generally showing rectangles of color with minimal, if any, perspective. After viewing one of the patio door paintings, Martin wrote to O’Keeffe: “It was a joyous experience and afterwards I knew more about the possibility of human response.”View image in fullscreenGeorgia O’Keeffe, Black Door with Red, 1954.Photograph: Chrysler Museum of Art, Norfolk/© The Georgia O’Keeffe Museum/ Artists Rights Society (ARS), New YorkImmersive digital experiences offered at the exhibition let audiences actually feel what it’s like to be in some of the places that O’Keeffe inhabited while painting – the upper floors of the Shelton hotel and her beloved patio in Abiquiu. They offer a chance to slow down and let one’s senses take charge, as museum-goers take their shot at attending to the subtle details of place that O’Keeffe drank in as she attempted to capture the pure essence of a location.Colman is excited to be bringing O’Keeffe’s architectural works to light, a part of her career that is built on an entire social network of architects and designers that she had deep personal and creative relationships with. In his telling, it’s a story that has long resided in the archives, and now is the time to give it greater prominence in a celebrated artist’s career. “It’s a really exciting story,” he said, “to see these rich connections that inspired her to engage with the built environment for many years. I think visitors will be surprised that these works exist at all.”Georgia O’Keeffe: Architectureis on view from 11 September to 3 January at Detroit Institute of ArtsExplore more on these topicsGeorgia O'KeeffeArt (Education)PaintingArt (Art and design)ExhibitionsDetroitMichiganfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We have really cool sharks’: three-year project to lift lid on Britain’s little-understood species | Sharks | The Guardian
description: Anglers will help scientists investigate the porbeagle, tope and blue shark to boost knowledge and conservation
Author: Anna Turns
Headline: Anglers will help scientists investigate the porbeagle, tope and blue shark to boost knowledge and conservation
Content: A bue shark off the coast of Penzance, Cornwall. More than 40 species of shark occur in British waters.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyView image in fullscreenA bue shark off the coast of Penzance, Cornwall. More than 40 species of shark occur in British waters.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamySeascape: the state of our oceansSharks‘We have really cool sharks’: three-year project to lift lid on Britain’s little-understood speciesAnglers will help scientists investigate the porbeagle, tope and blue shark to boost knowledge and conservationSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentAnna TurnsTue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 00.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘We have really cool sharks,” says Dr Lucy Hawkes. She is not referring to animals in the rich coastal waters of South Africa or Mexico, but instead talking about the species that live around Britain. Hawkes, an associate professor at the University of Exeter, is co-leading a new three-year project to investigate the lives of three of England’s most vulnerable shark species.“I like the porbeagle, which looks like a baby great white shark,” she says. “Surfers could see one and absolutely poop their pants, but they’re not dangerous. It’s amazing that we share the water with some pretty exciting animals.”More sharks swim in British waters than you might expect. From small catsharks and deepwater dogfish to migratory blue sharks and huge filter-feeding basking sharks, there are more than 40 different types in these waters. Yet scientists know surprisingly little about most of them.Now, the lab that Hawkes and her colleague Dr Matthew Witt run at Exeter has beenawarded almost £1mby Natural England to collaborate with the Marine Biological Association, the Angling Trust and thePat Smith Database, a long-running online record of shark catches dating back to 1953.Together, they will use a mix of historical records, electronic tags and recreational sightings to find out more about where and when porbeagle, tope or school sharks, and blue sharks are feeding, mating and migrating. The project will also monitor how shark populations are changing in terms of numbers and distribution – helping determine how best to prioritise conservation efforts.View image in fullscreen‘The UK has a long history of recreational fishing for sharks and big fish like tuna’: Dr Francesco Garzon.Photograph: NOAAFish_NEFSCSightings from some of the nation’s3 million recreational anglersprovide crucial information.“The UK has a long history of recreational fishing for sharks and big fish like tuna,” says Dr Francesco Garzon, a marine biologist working alongside Hawkes. “It’s one of the best places to see sharks in Europe.”Recreational shark fishing in the UK is now “catch and release”, he explains. Angling clubs used to keep catch records based on weight once a dead fish was landed onboard the boat. Now, many fishers measure the length of live sharks in the water before releasing them. Tagging should reveal how sharks respond to catch-and-release practices.“Anglers are conservation-conscious,” says Garzon. “They can sometimes be ostracised but are usually just as passionate about protecting sharks as we are.”He adds that direct commercial fishing or accidental bycatch are the biggest threats for UK sharks.Hawkes likens shark anglers to bird ringers. “These people are so passionate about the marine environment; they want to spend thousands of hours just trying to see these amazing animals up close. They’re obsessed with sharks.”By reporting their catches to the Pat Smith Database, skippers and recreational anglers act as citizen scientists and help researchers find out where these species go.“Even if all the shark researchers in England got together, we just couldn’t have the same level of records,” says Garzon. “Angler records are an essential tool, helping us understand shark populations.”The shark scientists will also run in-person workshops and interview hundreds of anglers across the country, from the south-west to the north-east of England.View image in fullscreenThe Pat Smith Database is particularly interested in the underside of pups as it allows accurate ageing of the fish and a better understanding of how close the pupping occurred.Photograph: Pat Smith DatabaseThe mutual trust they have developed with the angling community is key to the success of the project. Over the years, the team have spent a lot of time on boats talking to fishers, while tagging pelagic species such as bluefin tuna. And it is entirely possible that porbeagles, for example, could swim halfway across the Atlantic, as bluefin tuna do.Forty tags, each worth £1,500, will stay on the fish for about 45 days. These tags should reveal how well sharks survive after being caught then released. According to Hawkes, even anglers want to know more about this so they can take measures to avoid harming the fish.“If tags show that sharks are travelling into waters where a particular fishery is permitted with a high rate of bycatch, that would be relevant to their conservation. It really depends on what the sharks tell us.”During tagging, the team plan to take DNA samples from the sharks. Usually that involves obtaining a tiny clip of skin from a fin, or swabbing a cotton bud on their skin. By doing this, scientists create a map of genetic connectivity.“We could work out whether a French blue shark is closely related genetically to an English blue shark,” explains Garzon. “They might be loners then aggregate in big numbers to mate, like tope sharks do in northern Scotland. We don’t yet know.”The team will also use another 30 more expensive tags, costing about £4,500 each, which last about a year. “These enable us to reconstruct a shark’s path and tell us how deep each shark has been diving and for how long,” says Garzon.Hawkes says people often recoil when she mentions sharks. “We scientists are the ones who say, ‘Shark! Where? Let me see!’ I’d love to change people’s minds about these beautiful animals. They totally belong here.”This story was produced in partnership withthe Conversation, whereAnna Turns is senior environment editorExplore more on these topicsSharksSeascape: the state of our oceansConservationWildlifeOceansEnglandAnimalsMarine lifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Princess’s story: the case that highlights scourge of illegal care provision | Social care | The Guardian
description: Child was sent to live in 11 different Airbnbs or hotels and two ‘barren and inhospitable’ houses, as companies profited
Author: Tom Wall
Headline: Child was sent to live in 11 different Airbnbs or hotels and two ‘barren and inhospitable’ houses, as companies profited
Content: A police officer said of conditions Princess was living in: ‘If she lived with her parents and I came into this house, I’d be removing her for serious neglect.’Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA police officer said of conditions Princess was living in: ‘If she lived with her parents and I came into this house, I’d be removing her for serious neglect.’Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesSocial carePrincess’s story: the case that highlights scourge of illegal care provisionChild was sent to live in 11 different Airbnbs or hotels and two ‘barren and inhospitable’ houses, as companies profitedCouncils pay more than £125m a year placing vulnerable children in illegal care homes in EnglandTom WallTue 8 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrincess had a hard start in life. Her father drank too much, and referrals were made to social services. As she got older, she started going missing, telling police officers she was being physically abused by her parents, who in turn claimed they could not manage her behaviour. She was eventually taken into care amid concerns about self-harm, aggression and exploitation outside the home.Even though social workers described her as a lovely child, they struggled to find her a permanent home capable of keeping her safe in England’sdysfunctional, largely outsourced residential care system.Her social workers were left with no lawful options. Instead, they placed her in hastily cobbled-together illegal provision. Princess was sent to live in a series of unregulated placements, including 11 different Airbnbs or hotel rooms and two “barren and inhospitable” houses, for the best part of a year.Councils pay more than £125m a year placing vulnerable children in illegal care homes in EnglandRead moreA safeguarding review last year found that the illegal homes could not meet her needs. She continued to self-harm and hurt staff. She sometimes lived in empty rooms, with as many as nine carers dressed in protective clothing. One police officer said: “If she lived with her parents and I came into this house, I’d be removing her for serious neglect.”Shocking though Princess’s situation was, similar scenarios play out hundreds of times a year in children’s services departments throughout the country. According to the children’s commissioner for England, Rachel de Souza, these children are being endangered by the continued use of illegal care homes, which, an investigation by the Guardian and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ) has found, have been paid £250m over the last two years by councils in England.De Souza said: “My previous research has uncovered [Princess’s] story is far from an isolated case. This investigation continues to raise serious questions about the millions spent by local authorities on placements when they cannot guarantee that vulnerable children are receiving the safeguarding and quality of care they need.”Councils are increasinglyturningto illegal provision because the mainstream,profit-drivencare market isfailingto accommodate rising numbers of vulnerable teenagers, with registered homes often too far away or incapable of meeting their needs. This has generated a growing shadow market for unlawful care, where huge sums are paid for unregulated placements.The safeguarding review into Princess’s case concluded she was harmed by the council’s failure to find a suitable placement for her. She told the review she hated her time in care and it made her issues worse.A Guardian and TBIJ investigation has established that the companies staffing the illegal homes where Princess lived for almost a year were paid more than £1m byPeterboroughcity council. The companies were not named in the review.Thornbury Nursing Services, which is based in Bristol, was paid £61,000 for staffing her unregistered placements. The company is ultimately owned by the Canadian private equity firm Onex via Acacium Group. Onex announced it had $275m available to distribute to shareholders in 2026.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCouncil payment records obtained as part of the investigation show Thornbury Nursing Services also received £3.8m from four councils for staffing five other illegal placements during 2024 and 2025.Thornbury said it complied with all relevant laws. It said it supplied healthcare staff when there were limited options but did not operate children’s homes, adding: “Responsibility for accommodation and placement decisions sits with the relevant local authorities.”Another agency, CAMHS Professionals, was paid more than £500m for staffing Princess’s unregistered placements. It said it supplied a large team of qualified nurses at short notice to a home commissioned by Peterborough council. “CAMHS Professionals did not provide the home for this young person,” it said.Peterborough council said it secured the properties but commissioned the companies to provide care and support for Princess. It said unregistered placements were only used when there were no regulated alternatives and were subject to monitoring visits.Explore more on these topicsSocial careYoung peoplePeterboroughChildrenfeaturesShareReuse this content
