title: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia | Somalia | The Guardian
description: US-Israel war against Iran and political instability in Somalia have led to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: US-Israel war against Iran and political instability in Somalia have led to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa
Content: The Indian Navy recaptures the MV Ruen, a Maltese ship, from Somali pirates off the Indian coast in March 2024, after a three-month hijacking.Photograph: Indian Navy X/AFP/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Indian Navy recaptures the MV Ruen, a Maltese ship, from Somali pirates off the Indian coast in March 2024, after a three-month hijacking.Photograph: Indian Navy X/AFP/AFP/Getty ImagesSomaliaHijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off SomaliaUS-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of AfricaMohamed Gabobe in Mogadishu andPeter BeaumontTue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability inSomalia.Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnightin August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has mainland Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage,netting $400m (£296m) in ransom paymentsfor the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.View image in fullscreenArmed Somali pirates guard the beach in Hobyo district, 540km north-east of Mogadishu, in 2008.Photograph: Badri Media/epa/CorbisThe hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents.Turkeyhas been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.View image in fullscreenMembers of Somalia Puntland maritime police force on duty in 2023.Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPAIn a comment for theCenter for Maritime Securityin July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser,warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn ofAfricadiverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.Areport by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in Mayreached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.View image in fullscreenYemenis protest against Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping. Experts warn that these attacks in response to the US-Israel war on Iran are allowing piracy to thrive.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyPiracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya bya previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.View image in fullscreenThe MV Sward, a cement carrier hijacked in April, was repurposed as a pirate mothership.Photograph: EU Naval Force Operation AtalantaOfficials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.View image in fullscreenResidents of Galkayo, Somalia, said money has begun to circulate in the local economy since the hijacking of the Lutuf.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverDuring the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.Writing inThe Conversation in May,the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.View image in fullscreenSomali pirates apprehended by French soldiers in the Gulf of Aden in 2009.Photograph: Sipa Press/Rex Features“What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”Explore more on these topicsSomaliaPiracy at seaAfricaUS-Israel war on IranTurkeyHouthisMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs take effect as trade dispute grows | Canada | The Guardian
description: Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
Content: Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks.Photograph: Ari Saperstein/EPAView image in fullscreenTensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks.Photograph: Ari Saperstein/EPACanadaCanada’s retaliatory US tariffs take effect as trade dispute growsCounter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goodsMaya YangTue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 19.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada’s retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports have come into effect, escalating atrade fightthat has been marked by intensifying tensions between the US president, Donald Trump, and the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney.The tariffs took effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, and range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering $20bn in imports from the US. The measures target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $20bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian governmentsaid.Carney said Tuesday thatCanadawould move faster to reduce its economic reliance on the United States. “In too many areas, they wanted dependency, not a true economic partnership,” said Carney. “We can’t let American goods into Canada tariff-free while they charge our companies to export to them.”Last month,Trump announceda new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”. The US tariffs hit items such as hockey sticks and cement, affecting about 5.5% of Canadian exports to the US.Since then, tensions between Canada and the US have intensified, with Carney last week urging theTrump administrationto “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” – whichCanadians have rejected.On Monday, Trump threatened to block sales of Canada’s Bombardier Aviation in the US, unless the Quebec-based plane maker moves manufacturing to the US.“No more selling Bombardier in the United States!” Trump posted in all caps on his Truth Social platform, though he did not specify how he would achieve a sales halt.Thousands of Bombardier aircraft currently operate in US airlines’ domestic fleets.In a statement on Monday, the aerospace company touted its creation of “tens of thousands of jobs across the United States”, with “direct employment” in more than 20 states including Kansas, Texas, Arizona and California.The company also noted that it spent more than $2.5bn annually with suppliers, and said its supply chain was “made up of approximately 2,800 American companies across 47 states”.Negotiations between both sides broke down on 21 August after days of meetings in Washington, with Carney saying at the time that the Trump administration’s terms were ultimately unacceptable and that US negotiators had introduced restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the 11th hour.US officials also made unacceptable“threats” to the French languageand “Quebec culture”, he added, referencing the French-speaking province in eastern Canada, with Carney saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut Trump’s top trade official Jamieson Greer later noted the US government was aware that French language protections were sensitive and important.“This is not something where we push hard, or condition, or red-line,” he told Canadian public broadcaster CBC last month.Polls show Carney has broad support from Canadians, but it could disappear within months as the consequences of the trade war sink in, according to political analysts.Just 20% of Americans approved of Trump’s ⁠tariffs on Canadian goods, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found.Carney said last week his government was ready ​to sign a trade deal that ​benefited both countries, but US media reports say there are currently no ongoing negotiations between the two sides.Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsCanadaTrump tariffsUS politicsTariffsAmericasTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I heard a lot of noise’: trial begins in Mexico for alleged killers of Australian surfers and American friend | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Bereaved mother Debra Robinson in court stares at three men accused of murdering Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in 2024
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bereaved mother Debra Robinson in court stares at three men accused of murdering Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in 2024
Content: Callum Robinson, 33, and his brother Jake, 30, from Perth, Australia, were camping in a remote beachside area when they were robbed and killed.Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenCallum Robinson, 33, and his brother Jake, 30, from Perth, Australia, were camping in a remote beachside area when they were robbed and killed.Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGEMexico‘I heard a lot of noise’: trial begins in Mexico for alleged killers of Australian surfers and American friendBereaved mother Debra Robinson in court stares at three men accused of murdering Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in 2024Agence France-Presse in EnsenadaMon 7 Sep 2026 22.00 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 13.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe suspected murderers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot have gone on trial, two years after the killings in a suspected robbery.Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state.They had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were allegedly attacked in April 2024.Their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft several days after they went missing. They had gunshot wounds to their heads. Three men are on trial over their killings.View image in fullscreenDebra and Martin Robinson arrive at court in Baja California on Monday.Photograph: Guillermo Arias/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings on Monday. Their mother, Debra Robinson, stared at the accused before bursting into tears in the courtroom.“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” her partner, Martin Robinson, had earlier told reporters. “We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why.”Authorities allege the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was found burned near their bodies.Three witnesses appeared before the court on Monday, including the stepson of one of the defendants, who described his stepfather as violent.Testifying from an adjoining room with his face concealed, he said he accompanied the accused to the crime scene, waiting nearby when the “commotion” began. “I heard a lot of noise,” he said, explaining that he had run away but rejoined the group after they called him.Parents of Australian brothers killed at Mexican surfing hotspot attend murder trial – videoHe said they warned him that “the same thing that happened to the gringos would happen to him” if he said anything.Tourist killings expose fragmentation of organised crime at the heart of Mexico’s extraordinary violenceRead moreThe crime sparked outrage and grief in Australia and the US, where the surfers’ friends and families galvanized a major search on social media for their bodies.Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad was killed a few months before he was set to marry.Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists.Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.Explore more on these topicsMexicoWestern AustraliaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tokyo tourist hotspot bans short-term rentals amid surge in complaints | Japan | The Guardian
description: Shinjuku ward targets accommodation in residential areas and near cultural sites as locals complain visitors disposing of rubbish improperly and being too noisy
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Shinjuku ward targets accommodation in residential areas and near cultural sites as locals complain visitors disposing of rubbish improperly and being too noisy
Content: Tokyo’s popular Shinjuku ward is introducing bans on short-term visitor accommodation such as Airbnb after complaints about tourists’ behaviour.Photograph: World Discovery/AlamyView image in fullscreenTokyo’s popular Shinjuku ward is introducing bans on short-term visitor accommodation such as Airbnb after complaints about tourists’ behaviour.Photograph: World Discovery/AlamyJapanTokyo tourist hotspot bans short-term rentals amid surge in complaintsShinjuku ward targets accommodation in residential areas and near cultural sites as locals complain visitors disposing of rubbish improperly and being too noisyJustin McCurryin TokyoTue 8 Sep 2026 03.43 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 01.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with foreign tourists will ban visitors from using thousands of short-term rental accommodations after a slew of complaints about behaviour.In the latest sign that Japan’s patience withmass tourismis wearing thin, Shinjuku ward – home to the notoriousKabukicho nightlife districtand the world’s busiest railway station – will prevent visitors from using private lodgings in residential areas and near schools and important cultural sites, Japanese media reported this week.The measure, to be introduced through a local ordinance, could encourage other local authorities to follow suit. Shinjuku, with a regular population of more than 350,000, is home to 3,775 private lodgings – orminpaku– the largest number anywhere inJapan.‘Fine for others to pay more’: can Japan attract more overseas tourists while charging them extra?Read moreWhile tourism has boosted sectors of Japan’s economy and raised the country’s profile overseas, thesurge in visitor numbershas created tensions with residents in popular destinations such asTokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.Shinjuku ward believes the measure will affect as many as 2,000 lodgings in residential areas – almost half the total, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. The number of minpaku residences in Shinjuku has almost tripled since 2022.Reports said officials had been forced to act after receiving more than 1,300 complaints from residents in the 12 months to March. Many cited disruption caused by visitors who did not dispose of their rubbish properly, made too much noise and smoked in areas where it is banned. There have also been reports of trespassing.Officials said temporarily revoking the licenses of renters whose tenants misbehaved would not address residents’ concerns. “Even if we crack down on badly behaved operators, the number of complaints remains the same,” a ward official told the Japan Times. “So we decided it’s better to change the ordinance.”Authorities did not single out particular operators for the ban. But it is likely to affect those using popular companies such as Airbnb.An Airbnb spokesperson told the Guardian: “Shinjuku has been an important partner to us, and we take residents’ concerns seriously. Home sharing works best when residents, hosts and guests can all live well alongside each other, and that is what we want to help the ward protect.“We would welcome the chance to work with the ward on measures that target the problem more precisely - a prohibition across residential zones would close thousands of registered homes affecting compliant and responsible hosts, while leaving untouched the unregistered operators behind much of the disruption residents describe.“We believe there is a version of this ordinance that protects residents’ quality of life without closing responsible, licensed hosts, and we want to help find it.”The ward will ask for members of the public to give their feedback on the proposal next month, with a view to submitting revisions to the ordinance in February. It also plans to reduce the number of days per year that minpaku in residential areas can be rented out from 180 to 120.Authorities in Kyoto – where tourists flock to view temples and shrines, rent kimono andphotograph traditional geisha entertainers– limit minpaku operations in residential areas to just 60 days a year, during the off-peak season between January and March.“Residents are concerned that their communities could be falling apart,” Kyoto’s mayor, Koji Matsui, said earlier this year. “We have strengthened the oversight of operators, but that is not enough. We need to go further,” the Asahi Shimbun quoted him as saying.Arecord 42 million peoplevisited Japan last year, spending a combined ¥9.5tn ($62bn) – also an all-time high. The government has set a target of 60 million visitors by 2030 – a goal critics say will exacerbate “tourism pollution”.Authorities nearMount Fujihave introduced climbing fees and imposed a daily visitor cap in an attempt to reduce overcrowding on Japan’s highest mountain. In February, the town of Fujiyoshida, a popular Fuji viewing spot, decided tocancel this spring’s cherry blossom festival, citing a rise in disruptive behaviour by tourists.The mayor, Shigeru Horiuchi, said the decision had been taken to “protect the dignity and living environment of our citizens”.Explore more on these topicsJapanOvertourismAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flushing the toilet can release a ‘plume’ of breathable pathogens – and closing the lid won’t stop their escape  | Australia news | The Guardian
description: New research shows turbulent flushes create toilet-generated aerosols that can transmit legionella, influenza and norovirus
Author: Tory Shepherd
Headline: New research shows turbulent flushes create toilet-generated aerosols that can transmit legionella, influenza and norovirus
Content: Flushing a toilet can release particles into the air that remain suspended for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found.Photograph: Naruecha Jenthaisong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFlushing a toilet can release particles into the air that remain suspended for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found.Photograph: Naruecha Jenthaisong/Getty ImagesAustralia newsFlushing the toilet can release a ‘plume’ of breathable pathogens – and closing the lid won’t stop their escapeNew research shows turbulent flushes create toilet-generated aerosols that can transmit legionella, influenza and norovirusFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTory ShepherdTue 8 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlushing toilets release particles into the “breathing zone” of adults and can remain suspended in the air for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found.And closing the lid might not be enough to avoid a “plume” of potential pathogens.Meanwhile, previous research has shown public toilets are an inescapable hotbed of microbes.The perfect flush: eight essential toilet tips – from closed lids to cleaningRead moreFlinders University researchers reviewed 22 studies of toilet-generated aerosols, publishing the results in theScience of the Total Environment journal.They found microbes from the water used for flushing or from contamination of the bowl ended up as aerosols, with more “turbulent” flushing releasing more particles.That included bioaerosols – aerosols that contain biological material and can transmit pathogens including legionella, influenza and norovirus. There are differing reports about whether Covid spreads through toilet aerosols.The researchers found higher levels of aerosols in the water and higher levels of turbulence during the flush increased the volume of particles suspended in the air, but the effects of bathroom ventilation and whether the lid was up or down were unclear.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailDespite that, lead author and PhD student Lira Adiyani said she would still recommend putting the lid down after using the toilet.“Toilet flushing creates turbulence that can release aerosols into the surrounding air,” she said.“Some studies detected these aerosols at adult breathing height, indicating a potential pathway for inhalation exposure.“The more microbes present in the toilet, the more bioaerosols may be released. Therefore, larger flush volumes generally produce more aerosols.”Adiyani said “based on the available evidence” she would still recommend closing the lid as a precautionary measure, “while recognising that it does not completely prevent aerosols from escaping”.In the report, the researchers wrote that the effects of indoor aerosols had been “understudied” despite the risk of infection. This had “important implications for risk assessment, building design, and infection control in an era of water security pressures and emerging infectious diseases”, they wrote.“Indoor aerosols influence air quality and human health as their small size allows them to penetrate deep into the respiratory tract when inhaled, providing a direct exposure pathway.”Co-author, environmental health professor Harriet Whiley, said people didn’t have to be worried in their own homes, unless someone in the house was immunocompromised.She said the team was working on “protecting the most vulnerable through good design” in places such as hospitals and aged care environments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey are increasingly concerned about “opportunistic pathogens” that can be present in water, particularly recycled or rainwater. “They don’t affect healthy people,” she said. “But if you’re immunocompromised you can get very sick, and it can be fatal.”So it’s about getting “an effective flush with less volume and less turbulence”, she said.Dr Lotti Tajouri, an associate professor in molecular genetics at Bond and Murdoch universities wasn’t involved in the research but warned bathroom dangers go well beyond the toilet.His own research is particularly focused on public toilets and mobile phone use in toilets.“As soon as you enter a toilet, consider everything contaminated,” he said.The door will have microbes on it, as will the floor – so you should never put anything on it, he said. Then you might touch the lid, after which you flush with the lid up or down.If it’s up, you get the “plume” effect, an “explosion or aerosols … you are literally sprayed [with]”.Flushing with the lid down might limit your exposure to the plume, but depending on the cleanliness of the toilet, previous users have left microorganisms on every surface anyway. “The roof, the walls, the floor,” he said.Then, you touch the toilet door again, before (hopefully) washing your hands. But you will probably touch the taps again, blow microorganisms around with the hairdryer, touch the exit door and then touch your phone.“Studies show between 50% and 80% of people use mobile phones in the toilet. For younger generations it’s almost 100%,” he said. “They will contaminate their phones and fingers with fecal microorganisms – salmonella, campylobacter, all sorts of bacteria and viruses.“The less contact you have, the better it is.”Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsMicrobiologyInfectious diseasesHealthHygienenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mother flagged faulty smoke alarms before house fire that killed father and five children, court hears  | Queensland | The Guardian
description: Pre-inquest conference into Queensland deaths hears witnesses did not hear any smoke alarms during 2023 fire
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Pre-inquest conference into Queensland deaths hears witnesses did not hear any smoke alarms during 2023 fire
Content: Emergency services at the scene of the Russell Island house fire. The blaze killed a father and five children.Photograph: Russell Freeman/AAPView image in fullscreenEmergency services at the scene of the Russell Island house fire. The blaze killed a father and five children.Photograph: Russell Freeman/AAPQueenslandMother flagged faulty smoke alarms before house fire that killed father and five children, court hearsPre-inquest conference into Queensland deaths hears witnesses did not hear any smoke alarms during 2023 fireGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAndrew MessengerTue 8 Sep 2026 05.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 05.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA landlord was repeatedly warned about improperly installed smoke alarms before a house fire that killed a father and five children inQueenslandin 2023, a coroner has heard.Deputy state coroner Donald MacKenzie held a pre-inquest conference into the Russell Island deaths on Tuesday.No witness recalls hearing the sound of an alarm during the blaze, it heard.The owner was fined $774 for improper installation in 2024, the maximum possible penalty under Queensland law. A conviction was not recorded.The fire in the two-storey wooden Queenslander broke out on 6 August 2023. The house had been moved to the island and then renovated in 2013 before being rented privately.Five children – two brothers aged four and others aged three, 10 and 11 – died in the blaze. Their father, 34, died after running into the fire to rescue them. None can be identified for legal reasons.The children’s mother and father had fallen asleep in a converted “chill out” area underneath the house.The father awoke to see thick black smoke and immediately raced upstairs, where the children were sleeping.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailHis partner also tried to get into the house, but was forced back by the fire. Another adult woman leapt off a balcony to safety and survived.The Queensland fire department does not have a station on Russell Island, and vehicles must be ferried over in an emergency, a process that takes about 45-60 minutes, the court heard.As a result, it was a paramedic who first arrived at the scene, arriving within minutes at about 6.26am.“He recalls that the fire’s heat was so intense that he could feel it through his vehicle window, and could see the flames coming from the roof and smoke in a mushroom formation,” counsel assisting Corinne Leach told the court.“[The children’s mother] was kneeling on the ground in complete distress with [the other woman] beside her. He asked if anyone else was inside, to which [the mother} replied: her five children, and lost all ability to communicate.”The paramedic also tried to get into the building but was halted by the intense blaze. He instead focused on evacuating neighbouring homes. Rural firefighters arrived at 6.35am.The court heard the home had poor wiring, an exposed electrical box and faulty power points, known to short out. It also had an extension cord running from a poorly operating power point in a child’s bedroom, from a double adapter, to the understory area.The home’s smoke alarms also had not been updated in compliance with 2017 laws that applied to any tenancy renewed after January 2022 imposing additional safety measures for alarms.The homeowner claimed not to have been aware of the legislative change, the court heard.“[The mother] says that she raised the issue of non-working smoke alarms with the home’s owner, but nothing was done about it,” Leach told the court.“No witness recalls hearing a smoke alarm sounding at all prior or during the fire.”MacKenzie has been tasked with investigating seven issues, including whether legally installed fire alarms might have prevented the deaths, and whether the emergency service response to the fire was adequate.He will also consider whether the presence of any additional emergency service resources located on the island could have prevented the deaths.Fire investigators have been unable to identify the cause of the blaze, and could not categorically rule out that it was lit deliberately, the court heard.The inquest has been listed to sit for 10 days in November, to hear from 16 witnesses.Explore more on these topicsQueenslandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Global reckoning for big tech’: Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithms | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Draft legislation enforces digital duty of care including limiting children’s exposure to misogynistic and eating disorder content
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Draft legislation enforces digital duty of care including limiting children’s exposure to misogynistic and eating disorder content
Content: Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said social media giants would be forced to provide an opt-out option for users under the duty of care legislation.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said social media giants would be forced to provide an opt-out option for users under the duty of care legislation.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesAustralian politics‘Global reckoning for big tech’: Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithmsDraft legislation enforces digital duty of care including limiting children’s exposure to misogynistic and eating disorder contentTom McIlroyandLuca IttimaniTue 8 Sep 2026 04.38 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 00.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety.Users over 16 years of age will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content, with platforms facing fines of more than A$100m for non-compliance.Under the plan – dubbed “my feed, my way” – users opting out of the algorithm will see content only from individuals and groups they have actively chosen to follow.Users would be asked what they want their default feed to be through a pop-up message provided on their platform of choice.New laws designed to provide a digital duty of care for social media users under 18 will also require services such as online games, apps and AI chatbots to protect children from specific harms.How much control should we have over the algorithm? - podcastRead moreThey will include pornography; content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; misogynistic content; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying.The regulator, the eSafety commissioner, will have the power to issue removal notices to social media companies, with platform operators required to document measures taken to address online harms.The prime minister,Anthony Albanese, is expected to highlight the plans at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month.“This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control,” he said.Albanese dismissed concerns of possible retaliation by big tech platforms, and their owners, many of whom have close relationships with the US president, Donald Trump.The Labor government will require the support of the Greens to advance the laws through parliament. The opposition Liberals and Nationals have flagged opposition, warning the governmentagainst efforts to censor the internet.“Of course there will be opponents, because what this is about is changing the power relationship,” Albanese said.“We’re taking power from big global tech companies and giving it to ordinary Australians. That is what we are doing. It’s the right thing to do.”The communications minister, Anika Wells, said tech companies had for too long been allowed to run real-time, unregulated product testing on Australian users.“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” she said. “And it started here in Australia, with the introduction of our world-leadingsocial media minimum age laws.”The legislation is expected to be introduced to parliament before Christmas, but will likely face a lengthy public inquiry and negotiations.Australia’s digital duty of care bill a ‘global reckoning for big tech’, minister says – videoThe Greens communications spokesperson, Sarah Hanson-Young, warned the draft legislation should have a lower threshold for harm, and penalties for platforms should be a percentage of their global revenue.“Opt out is not acceptable,” she said.“Opt out is a recipe for big tech to manipulate and to get around it. They’ve got a lot of money, and we know that big tech will be looking for every crack, every possible workaround. So we need to tighten this up and make sure it is watertight.”The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said Labor could not be trusted with “censorship powers”.“Rather than trying to rig the algorithm, the government should focus on fixing the problems of too high prices, too much tax and too much migration.”A spokesperson for DIGI, the lobby group representing tech companies including Meta, Snapchat and Google, defended algorithms as helpful to users seeking diverse content.“We also recognise there is community concern about how these systems work and DIGI welcomes the discussion on the role of recommender systems in online safety,” they said.“We support an approach that gives people meaningful choice and control over the content they see, while managing safety risks.”Campaigner Chanel Contos, founder of Teach Us Consent, called the draft laws a good first step by the government.“This reform sends the right message to Big Tech,” she said. “You cannot introduce harmful features into our digital lives without asking for our consent first.”Tom Mooney, campaign director for Democracy Counts, an alliance of organisations concerned about the function of democratic institutions in Australia, said common facts and diversity of opinion was essential.“Social media is where the majority of Australians get their news, where many people spend hours each day,” he said. “It is common sense to require platforms to give users choice over those experiences.”Countries including France, Britain and New Zealand are following Australia in implementing social media bans for children, even as expert research showed the systems put in place in Australia in Decemberis only partly effective.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsSocial mediaAnthony AlbaneseSocial media banSocial media bansnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK air traffic control problem strands hundreds of thousands of passengers | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: More than 1,000 flights cancelled as airlines call for overhaul of ATC system after third incident in just over three years
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: More than 1,000 flights cancelled as airlines call for overhaul of ATC system after third incident in just over three years
Content: People queue at check-in desks at Heathrow terminal 5 after large-scale disruption caused by an air traffic control system glitch.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople queue at check-in desks at Heathrow terminal 5 after large-scale disruption caused by an air traffic control system glitch.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesAirline industryUK air traffic control problem strands hundreds of thousands of passengersMore than 1,000 flights cancelled as airlines call for overhaul of ATC system after third incident in just over three yearsUK airport disruption: what are your rights?Gwyn TophamTransport correspondentTue 8 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 10.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of thousands of air passengers had flights delayed or cancelled after another UK air traffic control technical glitch kept planes grounded for hours on Tuesday.Airlines demanded action after a “technical issue” at the air traffic control services provider Nats caused the third large-scale stoppage in just over three years.Flight monitoring website Flightradar24 said more than 1,000 flights had been cancelled at UK airports by about 8pm in an incident that started at about 1pm and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports, including Heathrow and Gatwick.Nats said on Tuesday evening that work was continuing to assist airlines and airports recover from the disruption, adding: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.”By the time Nats said it had identified and implemented a fix to restart its flight processing system almost four hours later, most flights scheduled to depart from theLondonairports and others were yet to take off. The disruption had spread to include incoming flights to much of southern England.Cancellations and delays were continuing well into Tuesday evening, andBritish Airwayssaid disruption would affect operations through Wednesday at least, with passengers offered free rebooking until Friday.Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed and 50 flights cancelled. The knock-on effects hit flights across Europe, according to easyJet. Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely until the evening.All London airports, as well as Manchester and Birmingham, were among the most directly affected. Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted.According to the flight monitoring website FlightRadar24, easyJet had 137 flights cancelled, British Airways 111, KLM 26, Eurowings 22 and Ryanair 21 by 5pm.View image in fullscreenPassengers stranded at London Gatwick’s south terminal.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PANats initially announced at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”. It later identified the problem in its flight processing system, and announced at 4.40pm that it had implemented a fix.A spokesperson said the fault was not the same as the ones that caused previous outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.They said the system was only “starting to recover”.“We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery,” they said. “We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.”The chief executive of Nats, Martin Rolfe, expressed his “huge sympathies to everyone who has been caught up in today’s disruption”.“We absolutely take responsibility for this,” he told Sky News.“We never want this sort of thing to happen. I completely understand how frustrating it is for passengers.”He claims, however, “these things are relatively rare”.“We resolved it to get back to our systems operating normally,” he added. “But of course, there’s a huge amount of disruption that’s now built up in the system.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’re working very closely now with airlines and airports to try to work through the night to make sure that we can get as many people travelling as possible.”The air traffic control problems follow an“isolated event” a year agothat caused widespread disruption, although it so far appears less severe than the fullgrounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.However, British Airways said that “the severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact for customers and colleagues”.“We were forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday afternoon, inconveniencing tens of thousands of customers,” a spokesperson said.“This incident was entirely out of our control and incredibly frustrating for our customers and colleagues, with aircraft and crews ending up out of place.”Heathrow said late on Tuesday that departures had resumed with disruptions but arrivals had been suspended for the rest of the night.Airlines renewed calls for Nats to be overhauled after the third incident ascribed to its systems in as many years.Ryanair repeated its calls for Rolfe to resign. The Irish airline’s chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Families travelling on holiday, people travelling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for Nats’ abhorrent failure.”He said the government should “stop making excuses for repeated Nats failures and appoint a new leader capable of running the UK ATC system”.Wizz Air said: “A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. Nats is simply not fit for purpose in its current form.”The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “I’m aware of a technical issue impacting flights at airports including Heathrow and Gatwick. Technicians have identified the issue and are fixing it as we speak. I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry.“I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job.”Explore more on these topicsAirline industryHeathrow airportGatwick airportLondonAir transportStansted airportTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine’s prosecutor general quits after anti-corruption agents raid his office | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ruslan Kravchenko resigns over allegations some of his officials were engaged in large-scale money laundering
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Ruslan Kravchenko resigns over allegations some of his officials were engaged in large-scale money laundering
Content: Ukraine’s former prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, gives a press conference in Kyiv in July.Photograph: Thomas Peter/ReutersView image in fullscreenUkraine’s former prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, gives a press conference in Kyiv in July.Photograph: Thomas Peter/ReutersUkraineUkraine’s prosecutor general quits after anti-corruption agents raid his officeRuslan Kravchenko resigns over allegations some of his officials were engaged in large-scale money launderingLuke Hardingin London andAmy Hawkinsin KharkivTue 8 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine’s prosecutor general has resigned after investigators used ladders to raid his office in connection with a major corruption scandal that threatens to embarrass Volodymyr Zelenskyy.Ruslan Kravchenko quit his post on Monday after allegations that some of his officials were involved in large-scale money laundering. They received cash to protect call centres involved in illegal phone scams, it was claimed.Kravchenko, who denies wrongdoing, left his job after meeting Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s president also spoke to the heads of Nabu and Sapo, the two anti-corruption agencies that have uncovered a sprawling criminal scheme involving government officials.Zelenskyy described his conversation with Kravchenko as “fairly long” and said: “I’m sure you understand what we discussed.” The prosecutor’s resignation letter will be sent to Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, he said.Kravchenko is the latest member of Zelenskyy’s inner circle to be linked to corruption. The allegations involve so-called call centres operating in Ukraine. Employees pose as banks, law enforcement agencies or investment advisers, and persuade victims to transfer funds to accounts or crypto wallets under their control.Those targeted include Ukrainians, Russians and EU citizens. According to Nabu, a senior official inside the prosecutor general’s office protected the criminal network and helped it to launder its assets.Each “call centre” paid $7,000 (£5,200) a month in protection money, law enforcement sourcestold the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper. The bribes ran into millions of dollars, it said, with hundreds of centres believed to employ about 60,000 people across the country.Nabu investigators raided Kravchenko’s office on Friday. Staff refused to let them in so they used ladders to scale a metal gate. Kravchenko was not at work and had disappeared from his home, which was searched later that evening.The chief suspect was arrested in the western city of Lviv. Recordings of phone calls published by Nabu suggested he wasoverseeing repairs at Kravchenko’s homewhile simultaneously collecting bribes from the fraudulent call centres.Nabu released images over the weekend of a safe filled with bundles of dollar bills. It said it had uncovered five officials behind the scheme but did not name them. The cash was spent on real estate, jewellery and other valuables, it said,laying out its evidence in a 30-minute video.Zelenskyy tried to strip Nabu and Sapo of their independence last year, a move he reversed after protests in Kyiv and other cities. There are further claims that the prosecutor’s office subsequently spied on Nabu staff and tried to obstruct their work.The revelations come at a time when Ukraine is under day-and-night attack from Russian drones and missiles.Three people were killed and 19 injuredin overnight strikes on Kyiv that caused huge fires and left smoke hanging over the city.The onslaught marked the end of a three-day ceasefire in the capital after a visit on Sunday by Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. They visited Moscow on Saturday and met Vladimir Putin.Zelenskyy said the pair had brought some “very good, worthwhile ideas” for ending the war but gave no further details. He said he hoped to meet Trump in the next two weeks. Few expect a breakthrough, with the Kremlin claiming on Tuesday that its forces were close to victory.While Russia escalated its bombing, Ukrainians were talking about corruption investigations, posting numerous comments on social media, the transparency advocate Olena Tregub said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Society is shocked and appalled by government officials who are basically behaving as mafia,” she said. “It’s not even corruption. It’s organised crime, protecting illegal call centres that were scamming people, not only in Ukraine but inEurope.”She said anti-corruption investigations were different from previous ones because Nabu detectives were “very good technically”.“They are recording people in their homes, in their offices and over the phone,” she said. “They are outsmarting other law enforcement bodies fighting against them, and are able to tape people who think everything is discreet.”She said the high-profile raids were “changing the culture in Ukraine” and making society less tolerant of ill-gotten wealth.Zelenskyy’s former business partner fled the country last year after being implicated in a corruption casefeaturing the state nuclear energy company. Two ministerswere fired. The president’s powerful chief of staff, Andriy Yermak, also later resigned after being questioned. Both deny wrongdoing.Kravchenko rejected the allegations against him on Sunday, calling them “completely unsubstantiated”. A day later he said he did not want his office “to be used as a tool in political confrontation”.The deputy chair of parliament’s law enforcement committee, Andriy Osadchuk, said the ​scandal underlined the need to ‌reform the prosecution service ​and called for key posts ​to be filled through open competition. Fighting corruption was also vital to Kyiv’s bid for EU membership, he said.“It will be very difficult for Ukraine to move forward if we do not change the approach to selecting and appointing the prosecutor general and prosecutors at lower levels,” Osadchuk said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Remilitarisation and support for Ukraine must not slacken, US tells Europe | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Comments in virtual meeting aimed at securing 300 Patriot missiles for Kyiv come as UK commits £100m for Ukraine’s air defences
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Comments in virtual meeting aimed at securing 300 Patriot missiles for Kyiv come as UK commits £100m for Ukraine’s air defences
Content: People stand in front of a building hit during Russian missile and drone strikes in Kyiv on Tuesday.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople stand in front of a building hit during Russian missile and drone strikes in Kyiv on Tuesday.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersUkraineRemilitarisation and support for Ukraine must not slacken, US tells EuropeComments in virtual meeting aimed at securing 300 Patriot missiles for Kyiv come as UK commits £100m for Ukraine’s air defencesDan SabbaghandJamie GriersonTue 8 Sep 2026 12.57 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 03.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby, told European countries they “must not slacken” in their remilitarisation and their backing forUkrainein a virtual meeting aimed at securing 300 Patriot interceptors for Kyiv.The influential Pentagon official praised Ukraine’s recent “stout defence”, which he said proved thatEuropewas capable of leading the defence of its own continent from Russian aggression rather than relying on the US.“Support for Ukraine contributes to Europe’s security,” Colby said at the start of a 50-country virtual meeting of the Ukraine contact group, reflecting what appears to be a warmer tone from the US on Ukraine.It helped, he continued, “to rebuild Europe’s military strength and industrial capacity. But words are not enough. Real money and industrial capacity must be put to work. Again, I underline that this is happening, but we must not slacken.”Led by its president, Donald Trump, the US has been pushing for Europe to dramatically increase defence spending and pay to supply American weapons, such as Patriot interceptors, to Kyiv, via a scheme set up by Nato.The UK announced it had committed £100m to boost Ukraine’s air defences over winter by buying a package of US military equipment that will include urgently needed Patriot missiles, before the meeting had started.Ukraine war briefing: New political turmoil in Kyiv as prosecutor general resignsRead moreBoris Pistorius, the German defence minister, pledged in his opening remarks that Berlin would donate a number of older Patriot Pac-2 interceptors from army stocks, and urged other allies of Ukraine to follow suit.Ukraine is currently unable to prevent Russian ballistic missile attacks because of a shortage of Patriot interceptors, leading to attacks that havekilled civilians and destroyed food and logistics warehousesover the summer.Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said that Ukraine had been “pretty clear” about what it needed: “Three hundred Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability, $2bn for drones,” and continued contributions to other schemes.The UK did not say how many Patriots it would be able to buy, but the number is likely to be only a fraction of the number sought, given the cost of each interceptor is estimated at about $3m.Yevhen Khmara, Ukraine’s newly appointed defence minister, acknowledged that Ukraine’s “situation with ballistics is much more difficult” and which was “precisely down to a lack of Patriot missiles”. It was a situation, he added, that the Kremlin was aware of, and trying to exploit.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Ukrainian minister also said that Ukraine faced a defence budget gap of €23bn this year, and he hoped that countries would bring forward more funding so that its drone investment programme could continue uninterrupted. Kyiv hopes that the EU will bring forward some of a €90bn two-year loan to help plug the shortfall.An escalation of the long-range war has meant that the harm to civilians is increasing as Ukraine targets Russian oil refineries and warehouses, while Russian bombing has meant that civilian casualties in Ukraine are at their highest level since May 2022 amid near constant attacks on the country’s cities.On Sunday,US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time, to discuss peace proposals, though no breakthrough was made. A day earlier they had visited the Kremlin, which is still pressing for Ukraine to give up territory and make a string of concessions for ending the war.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Trump about the war on Monday, with the two agreeing on the need to “continue working towards a ceasefire that prevented more loss of life”.Explore more on these topicsUkraineForeign policyWes StreetingDefence policyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Artworks stolen from Renoir Museum on French Riviera in latest heist | Art theft | The Guardian
description: Thieves took four artworks but it is thought they dropped two in museum garden as they fled
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Thieves took four artworks but it is thought they dropped two in museum garden as they fled
Content: A composite of stolen the Renoirs: Young Woman ‌at the Well and Madame Colonna Romano.Photograph: Musée RenoirView image in fullscreenA composite of stolen the Renoirs: Young Woman ‌at the Well and Madame Colonna Romano.Photograph: Musée RenoirArt theftArtworks stolen from Renoir Museum on French Riviera in latest heistThieves took four artworks but it is thought they dropped two in museum garden as they fledJon HenleyandAngelique Chrisafisin ParisTue 8 Sep 2026 11.37 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 03.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench police are hunting two thieves who escaped with two Renoir paintings from a museum on the French Riviera after breaking in through a hole cut in its garden fence.Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, about 10 miles west of Nice, said the pair appeared to have been “well equipped and well informed” about the museum, which houses works by the French impressionistPierre-Auguste Renoirin his former home.The theft early on Tuesday is the latest in a string of recent museum heists in France and across Europe, including thebrazen break-in at the Louvre in Paris last October, when ⁠thieves stole crown jewellery worth €88m (£75m), including tiaras, a brooch, necklaces and earrings.Masson told the local broadcaster Ici Azur that the two thieves sliced through the museum garden fence with an electric knife or metal saw, entered the building through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames.View image in fullscreenThe mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, Bryan Masson, said his office estimated the stolen art was worth €9m.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesPolice arrived about five minutes after the museum’s alarm system went off at 5.48am, Masson said, which “forced the burglars to flee in haste and helped limit the scale of the theft”.Two of the four works taken were abandoned in the museum gardens during the getaway, the mayor, a member of the far-right National Rally (RN), said. His office estimated the value of the stolen works at €9m.The two stolen paintings were Young Woman ‌at the Well and Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano. Both were on loan from the Musée d’Orsay, in Paris. “They’re Renoirs … you cannot sell them like that,” Masson said.The paintings the thieves abandoned were both portraits: Portrait of Madame Pichon, and Coco Reading, a portrayal of Renoir’s young son Claude.The Renoir Museum was established in 1960 in the mansion where the painter ‌died aged 78 in 1919. It houses about a dozen of his paintings and about 40 sculptures, as well as photos, furniture and objects including his easel and wheelchair.View image in fullscreenRenoir’s study at the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer.Photograph: DEA/G Nimatallah/De Agostini/Getty ImagesMasson called for greater security for museums aroundFrance. “This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art,” the mayor said.An art theft expert, James Ratcliffe of theArtLoss Register, said thieves were increasingly targeting valuable artefacts. “Sadly, without further funding to improve museum security, we are likely to see an increase in the number of museum thefts,” he said.“Each time thefts occur, it draws yet more attention to the perception of these museums as relatively easy targets. That can only encourage some criminals to consider them as straightforward places to steal from,” he told the Associated Press.Europol, the pan-European police organisation,said last monthrobberies at European museums were becoming increasingly violent, with some thieves brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives.The Europol report suggested specialist property crime or art theft gangs, who usually avoid violence, were being replaced by “individuals who often have histories of involvement in other types of crime”, who were recruited through social media.The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the jewels they allegedly grabbed in the seven-minute heist have not been found. Two of the suspectshave reportedly told policethe mastermind behind the heist was disappointed by the haul and thought “they could have taken more”.Italian police recently recoveredpaintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m stolen from a museum in March. However, last month four of the most important works by the Renaissance masterAntonello da Messina were stolenfrom a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.Explore more on these topicsArt theftFranceArtPierre-Auguste RenoirEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing | Israel | The Guardian
description: Ed Miliband announces sanctions on trade with settlers as PM says in the Guardian it is time to act
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Ed Miliband announces sanctions on trade with settlers as PM says in the Guardian it is time to act
Content: Palestinian landowners, journalists and protesters run from teargas fired by Israeli security forces blocking a road leading to a newly built Israeli settlement near Dura in the West Bank in June.Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPalestinian landowners, journalists and protesters run from teargas fired by Israeli security forces blocking a road leading to a newly built Israeli settlement near Dura in the West Bank in June.Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelUK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backingEd Miliband announces sanctions on trade with settlements as PM says in the Guardian it is time to actI believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy BurnhamPippa Crerar,Jessica ElgotandKiran StaceyTue 8 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 08.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSettler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank,Ed Milibandhas said, in the UK’s starkest condemnation since the foundation of the Israeli state.Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued,writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.In the Commons, the foreign secretary said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of theWest Bankwas unlawful in its entirety, as he announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.The dramatic shift in the UK’s position comes after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank, which has resulted in 12 nations – including France and Canada – announcing they would impose sanctions.In a joint statement Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney said: “The time has come to take further action to uphold our commitment to protect the two-state solution, our interests and to stand up for our values, before it is too late.”In response, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Saar, announced the closure of the UK consulate in Jerusalem and that 12 British MPs and activists – including Jeremy Corbyn and Labour MP Diane Abbott – would be banned from enteringIsrael.Saar accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”. Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, warned that the US could take retaliatory action over trade.However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Washington would “obviously” not follow the UK’s course of action, and did not want to see the West Bank destabilised, but declined to comment further. Burnham had briefed Donald Trump on the plan in advance.In his statement to parliament, Miliband said the UK government would enact:An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories and a new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK.Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence.A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.1:59UK foreign secretary announces sanctions on trade with Israeli West Bank settlements – videoThe foreign secretary said the UK’s actions would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice, and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whosehomes had been destroyedand from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment.The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.Ministers expect the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months, although they could be subject to legal challenge, which would result in a delay.Graph of demolitions in the West Bank since 2023Miliband stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, as some on the left have demanded, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts, but that there was evidence of “war crimes”.Speaking in the Commons, he said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.“All too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians.“I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”Graph of Palestinian civilian killings in West Bank since 2020Miliband suggested that Keir Starmer had been reluctant to take action against West Bank settlers during his time as prime minister. “I’ll say very bluntly we should have acted earlier. And it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation,” he told MPs.Burnham, whoapologised for Labour’s stance on Gazawhen he became prime minister, attempting to shore up votes on the party’s progressive flank, also said the previous government had been too slow to act.Writing in the Guardian , he said: “We have called for years for a two-state solution in the Middle East, but we must recognise that those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action. For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel.”Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust. “I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said.“And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state ofPalestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.”The foreign secretary said that to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.The action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine, he said, one that not only condemned but took action. “Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.”Burnham wrote that the British Jewish community must not be blamed for the actions of the Israeli government. “[It] is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple,” he said.“I met with the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society.”Far-right Israeli minister outlines plan for removal of all Palestinians from GazaRead moreThe shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said “illegal settlements are wrong” but suggested that Miliband was introducing policies the Foreign Office did not believe would work. Whitehall insiders denied this was the case.The senior Conservative MP also said there was a risk of harming Palestinians who worked in the West Bank and that “the economies of Palestine and Israel were too interconnected” for a ban on goods for illegal settlements to work.But the veteran Tory MP Edward Leigh gave full backing to the sanctions. “I am proud to say as the longest serving member of the Conservative Friends of Israel that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and justice for all people in this world,” he said.The move forms part of a broader attempt by Burnham’s government to reset British policy towards Israel, in part to regain the trust among Muslim and progressive voters in the UK they lost in the early days of the conflict.It was overwhelmingly welcomed by Labour MPs, many of whom have been struggling with the issue in their constituencies, although some sounded a note of caution about the potential impact on local Jewish communities.Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the foreign affairs select committee, said: “At last! I am so very happy to see a British government – a Labour British government – finally doing the right thing and taking a strong stance … no longer a bystander wringing their hands.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelForeign policyEd MilibandWest BankPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel to close British consulate in Jerusalem after sanctions announced | Israel | The Guardian
description: Several MPs also banned from Israel after UK steps up condemnation of settlements and announces sweeping sanctions
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Several MPs also banned from Israel after UK steps up condemnation of settlements and announces sweeping sanctions
Content: An Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, said on Tuesday that the UK regards Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as illegal.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, said on Tuesday that the UK regards Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as illegal.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelIsrael to close British consulate in Jerusalem after sanctions announcedSeveral MPs also banned from Israel after UK steps up condemnation of settlements and announces sweeping sanctionsPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentTue 8 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael has ordered the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem in response to sweeping UK sanctions on goods from illegal settlements.Reacting to Ed Miliband’s description of violent Jewish settler activity on the occupied Palestinian West Bank as“ethnic cleansing” carried out with the tacit backing of the Netanyahu government, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced retaliatory measures including the closure of the consulate and entry bans on several UK MPs.It is the latest stage in a furious and escalating row between the countries in which diplomatic relations have hit rock bottom.12:01UK condemns Israeli settler ethnic cleansing in West Bank - The LatestThe consulate in the Sheikh Jarrah area of the city focuses on Palestinian issues in the occupied territories, including Gaza, theWest Bankand Jerusalem. The British embassy in Tel Aviv is where the UK’s ambassador to Israel is based.While most countries regard East Jerusalem as illegally occupied by Israel since the Six Day War in 1967, Israel says Jerusalem is its undivided capital.“United Jerusalem is the capital of Israel and is under its full sovereignty,” Sa’ar said. “Any foreign activity in the area must be conducted through accepted and agreed channels and without violating Israel’s sovereignty.”1:59UK foreign secretary announces sanctions on trade with Israeli West Bank settlements – videoSa’ar also announced entry bans on a number of mostly leftwing MPs including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, the Your Party MP Zarah Sultana, the Labour MPs Diane Abbott, Naz Shah, John McDonnell and Richard Burgon and the Green MPs Hannah Spencer, Carla Denyer, Siân Berry and Ellie Chowns.The Israeli government added that longstanding British involvement in the training of Palestinian security forces on the West Bank would be terminated. Britain will also be excluded from the US-led Gaza coordination mission, which is based in Israel.The British sanctions were coordinated with 11 other countries, including France and Canada.Sa’ar said: “The British move is morally distorted, ​and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process.”He added: “Israel has nothing against the British people. We know that we have many friends in Britain. Unfortunately, a hostile Labour government is in office, systematically acting against the state of Israel, and it has left us with no choice but to finally respond to its hostile actions.”View image in fullscreenGideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, described the UK’s actions as ‘morally distorted’.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPASa’ar said that he ​had coordinated ‌Israel’s response ​with the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Israel will hold an election in late October.Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, called the ban “a grave miscalculation, a decision that will fall on the wrong side of history”.“In the current context, it would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation,” he said. “Sanctions are not a solution – dialogue is. I say to all foreign governments: Stop. Step away from the dead-end of sanctions and boycotts, and turn toward constructive dialogue and toward cooperation.”Settlement building and settlement-related violence have increased under the auspices of far-right Israeli ministers in the Netanyahu government who have said publicly that they aim to “bury” a two state solution through their actions.Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s hardline public security minister and a settler leader, called on Netanyahu to recognise Argentina’s claim to the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory in the South Atlantic known in Argentina as Islas Malvinas.View image in fullscreenPalestinians attend the funeral on Monday of a young man who died after being shot in the head when Israeli settlers raided a village.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, a longtime supporter of the settlements, said the British sanctions were “discrimination against the Jewish people”.
