He said the UK could face “repercussions or retaliations” from the US.However, in a markedly more muted response, US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Washington would ‌not follow Britain, ​France and Canada in blocking ⁠imports from Israeli ​settlements in ​the Palestinian ​territory and did not want to see moves that would destabilise the West Bank.Israel has been under notice from successive British governments – both Conservative and Labour – for years over the risk of international isolation and potential sanctions related to continuing settlement activity in the occupied territories. These warnings have becomelouder in recent years as violent settler activity has escalated.The UK’s Labour government previously sanctioned some Israeli settlers and illegal outposts over violence against Palestinians and illegal development in the West Bank.In a change of Britain’s position, Miliband, the foreign secretary, said on Tuesday that the UK regards Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, and not just the settlements, as illegal.The tougher stance is likely to be welcomed by many Labour voters and lawmakers, who have urged the government to go further in sanctioning Israel and supporting Palestinians.Difficulties to establishing an EU-wide approach, coordinated with the UK, had led to countries making individual decisions on a widening sanctions regime that culminated in the joint statement by 12 countries that they were setting in train the process of far harder-hitting sanctions.Explore more on these topicsIsraelPalestineWest BankMiddle East and north AfricaForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: British family of man abducted by Saudi Arabia speak out over nine-year ordeal | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Mira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Mira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017
Content: Rami Naimi with his son, Ali, his wife, Mira, and his daughters, Saria and Noor, in 2016.Photograph: Bring Rami Home Campaign/PAView image in fullscreenRami Naimi with his son, Ali, his wife, Mira, and his daughters, Saria and Noor, in 2016.Photograph: Bring Rami Home Campaign/PASaudi ArabiaBritish family of man abducted by Saudi Arabia speak out over nine-year ordealMira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017Geneva AbdulTue 8 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 10.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British woman has spoken out for the first time about the alleged abduction, torture and coercion of her husband at the hands of Saudi authorities, after nine years of “failed” quiet diplomacy.The businessman Rami Naimi was first abducted in Dubai in 2017 on his return from a trip to Australia with his father. After being tortured, he was released the following year.The father of three, who is the son ofAli Al-Naimi, a former Saudi oil minister and head of the state oil company Aramco, was detained again in 2022 and held for two years. Last year he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial.He was initially detained alongside 400 of the kingdom’s most powerful people in an infamous round-upat the the Ritz-Carlton hotelin Riyadh, which became the biggest and most contentious purge in the modern kingdom’s history.Speaking out for the first time after years of what they described as a failed diplomatic process, his family has alleged abduction, disappearance, torture and coercion at the hands of Saudi authorities.Naimi now faces a second trial for allegedly following certain accounts on X critical ofSaudi Arabiaand for attempting to leave the country without permission – both of which he denies.“The first thing I wanted to do was speak out, but I was told no,” said his wife, Mira Lozi, speaking alongside her son at acampaign launch to bring Naimi homein London on Tuesday.Lozi, currently fighting cancer, fought back tears as she said she had been encouraged to keep silent since 2017 to help secure his release.“For nine years my children and I have lived through a nightmare,” she said. “Saying the truth today is like a liberation, enough is enough and we’re just hoping that we can end this nightmare and all the governments will be able to help us.”View image in fullscreenMira Lozi with her husband, Rami Naimi.Photograph: Bring Rami Home Campaign/PANaimi left Saudi Arabia aged 13 and travelled for years between the UK, US and Middle East as a businessman. His family claim he was abducted in Dubai in 2017 after returning home from a book tour trip from Australia with his father.They say he was blindfolded and forcibly taken by car to Abu Dhabi and then by private jet to Saudi Arabia. He was surprised to find himself with the others who had been rounded up, his family said, as he is not a journalist, activist or politician.His abduction in 2017 came as the kingdom’s elite were detained at a five-star hotel in Riyadh during a purge in which princes, tycoons and ministers were stripped of their fortunes. Accounts later surfaced detailing torture and coercion, and the event preceded the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, whoseassassination at the Saudi consulatein Istanbul in 2018 sparked revulsion around the world.Naimi was held at the hotel and tortured, electrocuted, waterboarded and psychologically abused for three months, his family said. He was told, falsely, that his father was being tortured next door. He was released in January 2018 after signing a “settlement agreement”.He was subsequently forced to sign a document pledging to surrender 5bn Saudi riyals, later “discounted” to 1bn riyals (£200m) – which the family says neither he nor they possess. Naimi was placed under electronic surveillance and banned from leaving the kingdom.His family said he was disappeared again for nearly two years in 2022, and subjected to further torture, and emotional and psychological abuse. They said they had no idea if he was alive or dead, and learned only through the help of his legal team and diplomats that he was being held in Saudi’s notorious Al Ha’ir prison.It was after his release in March 2025, with an electronic tag and subject to a travel ban, that he learned of charges against him claiming he had “exploited” his father’s official influence. Naimi faced allegations he acted as an agent for a US company in Saudi Arabia and helped Aramco to secure a contract to provide technology to prevent diesel smuggling.After seven years without charges, Naimi, an EU citizen, was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial. Now he is unable to leave Saudi Arabia and his communications with his family remain monitored. He has no idea, the family said, of their decision to go public with his case.“Until today we have no idea why Rami was targeted,” said Lozi, who is too frightened to return to Saudi Arabia or travel to the United Arab Emirates.“It really is something out of a movie. It’s shocking and we just want to end this nightmare,” said his 21-year-old son, Ali, who was 12 when his father was abducted.In recent years the UK’s relationship with Saudi Arabia has come under scrutiny over the flow of arms between the two countries, Riyadh’s use of public executions and targeting of exiled activists and dissidents.“Any family making a decision like this needs to be supported by the government,” said human rights lawyer Caoilfhionn Gallagher KC, who is leading the case.As the family hopes to meet the new prime minister and foreign secretary, Gallagher said the recent appointmentof a special envoy for Britons detained overseasdid not go as far as campaigners, experts andparliamentarians had called for.Gallagher described it as: “Tea and sympathy for a very limited group of people.”Last month the Guardianreportedthat X had become the latest US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.The UK Foreign Office declined to comment. The Saudi embassy in London has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricaHuman rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Trust deficit’: Why India’s economic data has sparked a furore | World news | The Guardian
description: India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous – that appears to have eroded
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous – that appears to have eroded
Content: Critics say the India government has changed methologies and suppressed findings about its GDP figures.Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCritics say the India government has changed methologies and suppressed findings about its GDP figures.Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty ImagesThis Is IndiaWorld news‘Trust deficit’: Why India’s economic data has sparked a furoreIndia’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous – that appears to have erodedDon’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNiha MasihTue 8 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 04.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher thanthe forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors.According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a morefundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.In November, theInternational Monetary Fundrated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.View image in fullscreenCritics say the government has hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesIndia’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019,a Business Standard journalist revealedthat the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commissionresigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only releasedmonths later.Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, wasdelayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician PronabSen havepointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young peoplehave taken to the streetsin frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.View image in fullscreenCockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke at a protest against leaked exam papers, as young people in India face soaring rates of unemployment.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesAlmost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed,a recent reportby Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktankreported last month.That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book,Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, theDaily FTnewspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenMumbai bound … British singer Olivia Dean is headed to Lollapalooza.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersLollapalooza| British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists onthe lineupinclude Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.The price of gold| Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again torefrain from buying goldand travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliancein May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.Census 2027| The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns,reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversialdue tofears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteView image in fullscreenBean-to-bar movement … artisanal chocolate is having a moment.Photograph: ManamSinger Prateek Kuhad(@prateekkuhad), whose latest album,Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenA controversial revision … one-third of the electorate in Delhi have been deleted from voter lists.Photograph: Reuters4,756,000One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.Vibe checkView image in fullscreenFirst of many mashups … Ismail Langa Group pose with a larger-than-life image of Shakira.Photograph: Ismail LangaEarlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group(@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way.Their mashupof the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us atthisisindia@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is IndiaIndiaSouth and central AsiaNarendra ModiInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)EconomicsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Nepal says big polluters must ‘wake up’ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disaster | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions
Content: A woman looks on as heavy machinery works in the aftermath of deadly flash floods and a mudslide near the Nepal-Tibet border.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/ReutersView image in fullscreenA woman looks on as heavy machinery works in the aftermath of deadly flash floods and a mudslide near the Nepal-Tibet border.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/ReutersNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepal says big polluters must ‘wake up’ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disasterForeign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissionsHannah Ellis-Petersenin KathmanduMon 7 Sep 2026 20.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.Scientists believe the climate crisishad a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminishedafter 12 days of rescue operations.A journey to the frontline of Nepal’s disastrous floods – podcastRead moreSpeaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods.Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average.In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on parwith the 2015 earthquakethat left much of the country in ruins.View image in fullscreenAn excavator repairs a damaged road in Nepal near the Trishuli River on Monday.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters“This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.”Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to theUN’s fund for responding to loss and damage– which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.“We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.”For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said.“The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.”Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher.Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground.While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.”View image in fullscreenDamaged buildings on the banks of the Trishuli River.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/ReutersHe emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”.After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districtsRead moreThe UN has admittedthe loss and damage fundis already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement.Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding.“Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly.He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk.Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region.“With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said.“But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterTibetNepalClimate crisisFloodingUnited NationsSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Two more people arrested over ‘mountain of illegal waste’ dumped in Oxfordshire | Waste | The Guardian
description: A total of six people apprehended as clean-up of rubbish stacked 10 metres high cost about £6m
Author: Charlie Moloney
Headline: A total of six people apprehended as clean-up of rubbish stacked 10 metres high cost about £6m
Content: Fly-tippers dumped hundreds of tonnes of waste in a field between the River Cherwell and the A34 near Kidlington, Oxfordshire, west of London.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFly-tippers dumped hundreds of tonnes of waste in a field between the River Cherwell and the A34 near Kidlington, Oxfordshire, west of London.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesWasteTwo more people arrested over ‘mountain of illegal waste’ dumped in OxfordshireA total of six people apprehended as clean-up of rubbish stacked 10 metres high cost about £6mCharlie MoloneyTue 8 Sep 2026 17.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men have been arrested after fly-tippers dumped a “mountain of illegal waste”, stacked 10 metres high, inOxfordshire.Hundreds of tonnes of rubbish appeared in a field between the River Cherwell and the A34 near Kidlington in November last year. The waste tip was so large that removing it could cost more than the local council’s annual budget, the area’s MP said.The clean-up operation, which concluded last month, took five months. An estimated 22,704 tonnes of rubbish were cleared, with the operation costing an estimated £6m.The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed on Tuesday that a 21-year-old man from Ashford in Surrey and a 43-year-old man from Stanwell in Surrey had been arrested.It brings the total number of people apprehended to six, after one arrest in February, two in January and one in November, the EA said.The watchdog shut down the Kidlington site in October after officers discovered continued criminal activity after the first report of dumping at the site in July 2025.Colin Chiverton, area environment manager for the Thames at the EA, said: “The dumping at Kidlington was abhorrent and had no regard for the local community.“We moved quickly to remove all illegal waste from the site and our teams continue to work tirelessly on this investigation. These arrests are another vital step in collecting new evidence and delivering justice for the residents of Kidlington.”Dame Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said: “This government said we’d take on waste criminals and that’s exactly what we’re doing.“These arrests are another step towards delivering justice for Kidlington residents, who have had to put up with the dumping of disgusting waste.“The years of waste crime being allowed to fester have ended. We are taking decisive action through our crackdown and putting more officers on the frontline to restore pride in our communities.”The two men have been released on conditional bail pending further investigations.The EA previously announced it was to spend millions of pounds to clear the enormous illegal rubbish dump, saying the waste was at risk of catching fire.Its policy is to refuse to clear up illegal waste dumps across the country, instead pursuing the perpetrators and landowners. But officials said they had taken the exceptional decision to clear up the waste outside Kidlington, which is next to the River Cherwell, because the scale of the fire risk set it apart from other illegal waste dumps in England and presented an overriding public imperative.The agency was given no extra money to clear the waste, and the EA said this would come from “making efficiencies in its operations”. The cost to the taxpayer would also include the payment of the landfill tax on the waste to the Treasury.The dumping in Kidlington took place under the noses of the EA, which was monitoring the site after being alerted to suspicious activity.Explore more on these topicsWasteEnvironment AgencyOxfordshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Far-right port protests: police told to improve intelligence gathering | Police | The Guardian
description: Whitehall officials ask why laws meant to clamp down on mask wearing at demonstrations were not used
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Whitehall officials ask why laws meant to clamp down on mask wearing at demonstrations were not used
Content: Anti-migrant protesters confront police at Portsmouth at the weekend.Photograph: Jamie Lashmar/PAView image in fullscreenAnti-migrant protesters confront police at Portsmouth at the weekend.Photograph: Jamie Lashmar/PAPoliceFar-right port protests: police told to improve intelligence gatheringWhitehall officials ask why laws meant to clamp down on mask wearing at demonstrations were not used​Vikram Dodd,Ben Quinn,Rajeev SyalTue 8 Sep 2026 15.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice have been told by the government they expect better intelligence gathering after masked far-right groups took to the streets at the weekend, the Guardian has learned, as the Kent force admitted mishandling warnings of potential trouble.Police in Kent on Saturday and thenPortsmouth, Hampshire, on Sunday said they were taken by surprise when hundreds massed to oppose what they say is illegal immigration via small boats.Both protests are believed by police to have been far-right inspired, with evidence emerging that those behind them were determined to avoid detection.Claims by Kent police since Saturday that they had no warning fell apart on Tuesday when the force admitted there werewarning calls to police on Friday eveningwhich were not acted upon.Kent police said: “The force had received non-emergency information late on Friday evening that a protest could take place in the town the following day. This information was not fully assessed.”The government’s view is that police actions once officers were faced by hundreds of men was reasonable.But there is dismay at how Kent police explained their decision-making afterwards, for instance viewing the gathered masked men outside the port of Dover as peaceful protesters, with one source describing it as “fucking crackers”.On Tuesday evening the prime minister, Andy Burnham, met police chiefs to discuss what had happened and preparedness for any further unrest.In Dover on Saturday, where hundreds of masked men in black converged undetected, police believe those taking to the streets used walkie-talkies to coordinate their actions.Police on the ground report the masked men had lawyers’ phone numbers and cited public order case law and were well briefed on how far they could go: “They toed the line perfectly to avoid arrest,” one source said.InHampshirepolice are investigating whether vehicles were deliberately left behind to block access roads.Police said the Dover gathering passed peacefully, while in Hampshire there were clashes, with the local Police Federation saying anger and violence was directed at officers.The Guardian understands that part of Hampshire police’s investigation will examine whether the gathering of 200 people was meant to harass or intimidate.A spokesperson added they are also hunting for those behind the violence, conducting “a thorough review of the body-worn video” to look for offenders.The protests are believed to have been coordinated on closed social media networks and not publicly advertised.Police are considering whether the threshold for warrants for covert tactics has been met, with one source warning that police were wary of criticism of using “police state tactics” against people portraying themselves as peaceful protesters motivated by a legitimate issue.The National Police Coordination Centre has intensified its monitoring.The action in Kent was organised by Daniel Thomas, a long-term associate of the far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known as Tommy Robinson. Thomas, who has established an umbrella grouping called Patriot Platform, was also linked to theblockade in Portsmouththe following day.Whitehall officials have asked police whytougher lawsin place since last year meant to clamp down on the wearing of face masks at protests were not used.The police view was that at Dover those gathered complied with requests from officers and dispersed after three hours. In Portsmouth, which was more heated, police prioritised a formal dispersal order which they think worked.Both police and government sources say the “optics” of masked men in black thronging the streets looked “intimidating”.Also on Tuesday it emerged that lifeboat staff who picked up 120 asylum seekers from a large dinghy in the Channel on Sunday were refused entry to two ports shortly before being harangued by right-wing protesters.Crew on two RNLI vessels were also threatened with legal action if they approachedSouthamptonPort and tried to bring the claimants ashore.They were forced to take the migrants several miles away to Eastney, where police, firefighters, Border Force and other officials faced protests by up to 200 people, most of whom wore balaclavas and black clothing.Peter Sparkes, the chief executive of the RNLI, said abuse of its volunteers is “wholly unacceptable in a civilised society”.He said recent protests had “generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding” about the charity, and condemned threats by “those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard”.Officials confirmed that a broadcast on an open marine VHF radio said Southampton Vessel Traffic Service and King’s Harbour Master Portsmouth denied the RNLI permission to enter their ports.The two RNLI rescue boats from Bembridge and Yarmouth had intercepted a “mega-dinghy” that had left Utah beach near Cherbourg in Normandy.A spokesperson for Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates the port of Southampton, said: “ABP did receive an enquiry about landing recovered migrants at the port of Southampton. We had to decline the enquiry as the port did not have suitable reception facilities available. If there had been a safety of life at sea issue where Southampton was the closest port or if we had received a formal direction from the relevant authority then we would have played a role. Neither was the case in this situation.”On Tuesday, anti-migrant protesters attempted to identify RNLI volunteers involved in rescuing those onboard the dinghy. Demonstrators named and shared pictures on X of two people they said were volunteers, claiming they had tracked down an address for one of the men.Sparkes’s words come after footage posted on social media showed volunteers labelled as “traitors”. In a statement issued on Tuesday, Sparkes said the misinformation led to “some of our volunteers and staff [being] the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse.“The RNLI’s people represent the very best in our society. They selflessly give up their time to keep others safe.“Yet they and their families are being threatened by those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard.“Their action, in contrast, is wholly unacceptable in a civilised society.“We will take whatever steps we can to care for and protect our people and their families.”Explore more on these topicsPoliceFar rightSouthamptonPortsmouthKentHampshireImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham says Britain will ‘continue to act in support of our values’ after UK launches sanctions on Israel – as it happened | Politics | The Guardian
description: Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Saar, earlier claimed that the UK was ‘systemically working against the state of Israel’
Author: Andrew Sparrow
Headline: Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Saar, earlier claimed that the UK was ‘systemically working against the state of Israel’
Content: 13.31 EDTBurnham: Britain will “continue to act in support of our values”Andy Burnham said Britain will “continue to act in support of our values” after his Government announced a raft of sanctions againstIsrael.The Prime Minister said: “In an increasingly volatile world, Britain must be willing to lead. The British people expect it, as do our international partners, and I am determined my Government will continue to act in defence of our values.“Today, we are bringing forward targeted measures aimed not at the Israeli people, but in support of the two-state solution – and the prospect of Israelis and Palestinians living side by side in peace.“The suffering of the Palestinian people is a scar on the conscience of the world. Innocent Palestinians, including children, continue to be killed inGaza. And there is still a humanitarian crisis, with far too little aid getting in”, Burnham said. “That’s why we are acting, and why Britain will continue to act in support of our values.”Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets with Jewish community leaders inside 10 Downing Street in central London on September 3, 2026.Photograph: Jack Taylor/AFP/Getty ImagesShare

title: Ed Miliband has overturned decades of Foreign Office inertia on illegal Israeli settlements | Israel | The Guardian
description: Foreign secretary ends UK’s feigned helplessness with sanctions and condemnation of ‘ethnic cleansing’
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Foreign secretary ends UK’s feigned helplessness with sanctions and condemnation of ‘ethnic cleansing’
Content: Ed Miliband said he would refuse to be a bystander to further suffering and the destruction of the two-state solution.Photograph: House Of Commons/ReutersView image in fullscreenEd Miliband said he would refuse to be a bystander to further suffering and the destruction of the two-state solution.Photograph: House Of Commons/ReutersIsraelAnalysisEd Miliband has overturned decades of Foreign Office inertia on illegal Israeli settlementsPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorForeign secretary ends UK’s feigned helplessness with sanctions and condemnation of ‘ethnic cleansing’Will UK sanctions have any impact on ‘settler terrorists’?Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe indefatigable ability of UK Foreign Office ministers over decades to issue boilerplate statements of concern about the extension of illegal settlements inIsraelhas long been a matter of ridicule.Even some of the Conservative ministers who issued them, notably Alan Duncan and Alistair Burt, have agreed. Duncan described the UK stance towards settlements as weak and naive, while Burt wondered at the ability of the Foreign Office to find new forms of diplomatic condemnation that never amounted to any specific action. Margaret Thatcher, often torn as prime minister between her natural sympathy for Israel and her fear of the Gulf states falling under the sway of the Soviet Union, similarly expressed her anger at the settlements.But in the face of the Israeli disillusionment with a two-state solution – to which the UK had been committed at the UN since 1946, if not before – the UK produced little practical policy to prevent the spread of Israel’s illegal settlements.The UK-Israel trade agreement prevented preferential tariffs applying to goods coming from territories brought under Israeli administration after June 1967. The business department also advised companies not to trade with the settlements – but many simply ignored the advice or, to secure the preferential tariff, relabelled their goods as from Israel. The then trade minister Chris Bryant told the business select committee in June it was very difficult to be certain of the origin of goods.At the same time, the legal advice was that the UK regime could place sanctions on entities only if they were linked to settler violence, but could not put a contractor under sanctions simply for working on settlements.View image in fullscreenYoung Palestinians look at a new Israeli settlement from the Palestinian village of Duma, near Nablus, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank in February 2026.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersIt was this unhappy moral and legal mess thatEd Milibandinherited. As soon as he took office as foreign secretary, he said he refused to be a bystander to further suffering and the destruction of the two-state solution that settlement expansion represented. In this he had the support of the prime minister, Andy Burnham.Above all, Miliband felt that the UK could not feign powerlessness, and to do so, or pay lip service to action, would prove disastrous to Israel’s own future. He was perhaps the only front-rank Labour politician who could push this argument through at such pace, overturning the inertia and caution built into Foreign Office legal advice.His Jewish heritage – his mother, Marion Kozak, was a Holocaust survivor who fled to Israel – his life growing up with the Palestinian question and empathy for those subjected to antisemitism put him in a near unimpeachable position to adopt the role of Israel’s critical friend.The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, might this week say the Labour government is gripped by Jew-hatred, a charge he laid at Miliband’s door knowing he is Jewish, but Miliband’s riposte is simple. The best route to Israel’s security lay in Palestinian self-determination and the introduction of the two-state solution in its fullest form. To equate Israel only with the current Likud-led government as too many Conservatives have been prone to do, was a category error, he said: “Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, plain and simple.”He is thus the first UK foreign secretary to describe what is happening in theWest Bank as ethnic cleansing, and in so doing to in effect to accuse Israel of turning a blind eye to acts that amount to war crimes.Miliband also ended the two years of delay in responding to the international court of justice advisory opinion in June 2024 that the occupation is unlawful. In what he admitted was an overdue statement of reality, he accepted the ICJ opinion that the occupation, and not just the settlements, were so designated. Accepting the ICJ opinion arguably places stronger obligations on the UK government to not assist the occupation. It may help to explain why the trade ban extends into services such as providing insurance for illegal settlements.View image in fullscreenMike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel and a steadfast supporter of the Netanyahu government, has previously claimed that Ed Miliband hates Jews.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe biggest diplomatic rabbit Miliband pulled from the hat was the agreement of France and Canada toimpose similar trade bans. France took the lead last year on recognition of Palestine; this year, it is the turn of the UK to lead on following through on the consequences of that recognition.Paris appears to have been persuaded by the UK to stop waiting for the EU to reach an agreement on collective action, since it seemed unlikely the opposition in Germany and indifference in parts of the European Commission would end. A group of countries imposing the trade ban together of course makes Israeli reprisals harder, and serves to underline Israel’s isolation.The perceived weaknesses are obvious.Miliband still left it to the international courts to determine whether a genocide occurred in Gaza, something that might not be adjudicated for at least five years. There was mounting evidence of ethnic cleansing in Gaza, he said, but again it was for the courts to determine if that was so.There is no pledge to protect the international court of justice or the international criminal court from the US drive to render them inoperable. As to a UK arms sales ban, an exemption continues for the sale of parts for F35 jet planes to the main US spares pool – all on the basis the F-35 jets “do not materially support the occupation” – the criteria the foreign secretary has set.Miliband specifically condemned the Boycott, Disinvestment and Sanctions movement because it targets the whole Israeli economy and not just the occupied territories. The secondary legislation required to make sanctions as wide as envisaged may take as long as nine months, contrasting with the speed with which sanctions were enforced against Russia over the annexation of Crimea.But to focus solely on what is absent is to miss the moment. Duncan, for instance, said: “At last, in the face of state-backed terrorism by illegal settlers, the British government has shown unprecedented moral courage.”There is a risk of a cascading backlash from the White House – but Trump, trapped in a political labyrinth after he was persuaded to attack Iran, has little reason to come to Benjamin Netanyahu’s aid. Miliband has taken a risk, but after more than 70,000 deaths in Gaza, and the two-state solution on life support, it may be time to dare.Explore more on these topicsIsraelEd MilibandWest BankPalestineForeign policyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: UK to force Apple and Google to block explicit images on children’s smartphones | Internet safety | The Guardian
description: Lisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthrough
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Lisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthrough
Content: Lisa Nandy says the government will start work on an act of parliament to prevent under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.Photograph: EMS-FORSTER-PRODUCTIONS/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLisa Nandy says the government will start work on an act of parliament to prevent under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.Photograph: EMS-FORSTER-PRODUCTIONS/Getty ImagesInternet safetyUK to force Apple and Google to block explicit images on children’s smartphonesLisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthroughDan MilmoandKiran StaceyTue 8 Sep 2026 14.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple andGooglewill be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said.The legislation commitment puts ministers on a collision course with two of the biggest players in Silicon Valley, months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s.Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, said the government would start work on an act of parliament to stop under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.Talks with Google andApple, whose operating systems dominate the smartphone market, had not reached agreement as a three-month deadline passed on Tuesday.Nandy told the House of Commons the tech companies could still reach a deal but it was “almost certain” groundbreaking legislation would be required.“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from some of the worst harms,” she said. “And to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace that we need it to, while harm is being done now.”The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the protections would be “built into the device and switched on by default”, and tech companies will be required to verify an adult user’s age before they are allowed to take, view or send nude images. The government also wants the restrictions to apply to apps used by children, which will require further legislation.Nandy said: “This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.”Sources familiar with progress in the talks have said there iwas a desire to reach a deal on both sides but significant hurdles remained including privacy concerns on the tech side.Jess Phillips, the Labour MP and former safeguarding minister, said the legislation would stop the UK from producing self-generated child sexual abuse material, where children are duped or groomed into sharing explicit images of themselves.However, she urged the government to ensure the UK was followed by other countries and to make sure that “while we lead the world, we’re not standing alone for too long”.Hannah Swirsky, head of policy at the Internet Watch Foundation, which monitors the online spread of child sexual abuse material [CSAM], said: “It is deeply disappointing that tech firms have failed to act in full, but we are pleased that the government is now taking decisive legislative action to keep children safe.”Last year the IWFsaid a quarter of the images or videos of CSAMit recorded were self-generated, representing more than 140,000 pieces of content over a 12-month period.One of Keir Starmer’s final acts as prime ministerwas to give Apple and Google three months to stop under-18s from generating, sending or seeing nude images on their devices, by activating built-in features on the hardware or other technological solutions. Between them, Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android smartphone operating systems dominate the mobile phone market.The nudity block implies the use of “client-side scanning”, where content is scanned by software on the device before it is encrypted or sent.“Client-side scanning is the least evil approach,” said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow in cybersecurity and privacy at Kings College London. “That said, it does put in place an infrastructure to scan content of messages.”Privacy campaigners have also warned that adults would have to verify their age before switching off any nudity-blocking features. In June, the government said the proposals would “not affect the use of devices owned and used by adults who verify their age”.Google said it was “pleased to have made progress” in talks with the government and was “fully committed” to working with legislators, experts, app developers and device manufacturers to “keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information”.An Apple spokesperson said the company was preparing to strengthen its “communication safety” feature, which warns children when they are receiving or sending nude images and videos.“We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen communication safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”Explore more on these topicsInternet safetySmartphonesGoogleAppleChildrenLisa NandynewsShareReuse this content

title: US bans Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles as trade war with longtime ally escalates | US news | The Guardian
description: The measure comes as Canada imposes $20bn in retaliatory tariffs and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney vows to reduce his country’s economic dependence on the US
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The measure comes as Canada imposes $20bn in retaliatory tariffs and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney vows to reduce his country’s economic dependence on the US
Content: The US and Canada have long sparred over trade, particularly Canada’s protected dairy market and its subsidies for producers of softwood lumber.Photograph: Saul Loeb,andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US and Canada have long sparred over trade, particularly Canada’s protected dairy market and its subsidies for producers of softwood lumber.Photograph: Saul Loeb,andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesUS newsUS bans Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles as trade war with longtime ally escalatesThe measure comes as Canada imposes $20bn in retaliatory tariffs and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney vows to reduce his country’s economic dependence on the USAssociated PressTue 8 Sep 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US is banning dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles fromCanada, the White House said Tuesday, as the trade war between the two neighbors and longtime allies escalates.The ban will take effect in three weeks and comes after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $20bn in US imports earlier Tuesday.Donald Trump also moved Tuesday to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term US government contracts as Canada’s retaliatory tariffs took effect and prime minister Mark Carney vowed to speed efforts to reduce the country’s dependence on the United States.The US president directed the General Services Administration to declare Canadian products ineligible for those contracts until Canada allows “full and fair reciprocity″ for American products.Carney said Tuesday that Canada’s strategy was about becoming more independent. “It’s about ensuring that no country can hold us hostage. And that we can live how we want to live.”The rupture has upended one of the world’s closest relationships. On 22 August, the US imposed 50% tariffs on about 5% of Canadian imports, charging that Canada had unfairly treated the American dairy, alcoholic beverage and auto industries.The US and Canada have long sparred over trade, particularly Canada’s protected dairy market and its subsidies for producers of softwood lumber. But they remained friends and staunch allies.Under Trump, US-Canada relations have deteriorated rapidly. In addition to imposing tariffs on Canadian products, Trump has repeatedly made inflammatory comments about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney came to power in a come-from-behind political victory last year by promising to stand up to him.Some Canadian provinces have banned the sale of US alcoholic products – a move that prompted the retaliatory US ban on Tuesday.How the trade war ends could carry consequences far beyond Canada, testing whether a smaller US ally can resist Trump’s economic pressure without being forced to yield.Earlier on Tuesday, a Canadian official said Ottawa did not intend to change course regardless of whether Trump responded with nothing or what the official called a “nuclear response”. The government’s strategy will remain focused on building more at home and diversifying trade abroad, the official said.The tariffs hit hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment, at rates of 15%, 25% or 50%. They cover about $20bn in American goods, roughly 6% of the $333.6bn the United States exported to Canada last year.Since Canada-US trade talks collapsed 21 August, Trump and his administration have imposed additional tariffs and issued a series of threats and attacks portraying Canada as weak and dependent.Trump’s trade war and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have fueled anger across the country. Canadians have sharply cut travel to the United States and boycotted US goods, moves Carney praised as signs of national resolve.Gabriel Brunet, a spokesperson for Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc, said officials from both countries remain in contact even though formal talks have not resumed.Explore more on these topicsUS newsCanadaDonald TrumpTrump administrationMark CarneyUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs take effect as trade dispute grows | Canada | The Guardian
description: Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
Content: Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks.Photograph: Ari Saperstein/EPAView image in fullscreenTensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks.Photograph: Ari Saperstein/EPACanadaCanada’s retaliatory US tariffs take effect as trade dispute growsCounter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goodsMaya YangTue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 19.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada’s retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports have come into effect, escalating atrade fightthat has been marked by intensifying tensions between the US president, Donald Trump, and the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney.The tariffs took effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, and range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering $20bn in imports from the US. The measures target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $20bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian governmentsaid.Carney said Tuesday thatCanadawould move faster to reduce its economic reliance on the United States. “In too many areas, they wanted dependency, not a true economic partnership,” said Carney. “We can’t let American goods into Canada tariff-free while they charge our companies to export to them.”Last month,Trump announceda new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”. The US tariffs hit items such as hockey sticks and cement, affecting about 5.5% of Canadian exports to the US.Since then, tensions between Canada and the US have intensified, with Carney last week urging theTrump administrationto “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” – whichCanadians have rejected.On Monday, Trump threatened to block sales of Canada’s Bombardier Aviation in the US, unless the Quebec-based plane maker moves manufacturing to the US.“No more selling Bombardier in the United States!” Trump posted in all caps on his Truth Social platform, though he did not specify how he would achieve a sales halt.Thousands of Bombardier aircraft currently operate in US airlines’ domestic fleets.In a statement on Monday, the aerospace company touted its creation of “tens of thousands of jobs across the United States”, with “direct employment” in more than 20 states including Kansas, Texas, Arizona and California.The company also noted that it spent more than $2.5bn annually with suppliers, and said its supply chain was “made up of approximately 2,800 American companies across 47 states”.Negotiations between both sides broke down on 21 August after days of meetings in Washington, with Carney saying at the time that the Trump administration’s terms were ultimately unacceptable and that US negotiators had introduced restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the 11th hour.US officials also made unacceptable“threats” to the French languageand “Quebec culture”, he added, referencing the French-speaking province in eastern Canada, with Carney saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut Trump’s top trade official Jamieson Greer later noted the US government was aware that French language protections were sensitive and important.“This is not something where we push hard, or condition, or red-line,” he told Canadian public broadcaster CBC last month.Polls show Carney has broad support from Canadians, but it could disappear within months as the consequences of the trade war sink in, according to political analysts.Just 20% of Americans approved of Trump’s ⁠tariffs on Canadian goods, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found.Carney said last week his government was ready ​to sign a trade deal that ​benefited both countries, but US media reports say there are currently no ongoing negotiations between the two sides.Agence France-Presse and Reuters title: Real Madrid somehow cling on to beat Inter on José Mourinho’s big night | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Two goals in the first 23 minutes secured Real Madrid a 2-1 victory against Inter, who had pulled one back through Carlos Augusto, in the Champions League
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Two goals in the first 23 minutes secured Real Madrid a 2-1 victory against Inter, who had pulled one back through Carlos Augusto, in the Champions League
Content: Fede Valverde (left) is congratulated by Kylian Mbappé after scoring Real Madrid’s second goal.Photograph: Juanjo Martin/EPAView image in fullscreenFede Valverde (left) is congratulated by Kylian Mbappé after scoring Real Madrid’s second goal.Photograph: Juanjo Martin/EPAChampions LeagueReal Madrid somehow cling on to beat Inter on José Mourinho’s big nightSid Loweat the BernabéuTue 8 Sep 2026 17.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes football is silly, sometimes it doesn’t make much sense, and sometimes it’s fun for it. On a night when there were 37 shots and the goalkeepers shared 13 occasionally absurd saves between them, José Mourinho’s current side beat his former team Inter on hisChampions Leaguereturn to Real Madrid. Just don’t ask exactly how. Except perhaps to cite Thibaut Courtois, whose astonishing 89th-minute stop from Henrikh Mkhitaryan explained much and allowed them, just, to hold on to the first-half lead they had been given by goals from Kylian Mbappé and Fede Valverde.Haaland double gives Manchester City ideal Champions League start in PortoRead moreBy Mbappé, Valverde, and Inter themselves, that is. You might be tempted to say the Italians had shot themselves in the foot, only if they tried Courtois would probably save that too. “If he wasn’t voted man of the match tonight, he never will be,” Mourinho said. It took 77 minutes for him to be beaten, Carlos Augusto’s goal giving this match a frantic last 15 minutes and Inter hope of justice, but it didn’t happen again. So a game that could have had any scoreline – “5-1 to us, 6-6, I don’t want to say they could have won,” Mourinho suggested – actually ended 2-1. Madrid’s manager called it “mad, and not a madness I like.”This wasn’t always good from Madrid, in fact at times it was terrible. There was a void where the midfield should be, Mourinho thanking Trent Alexander-Arnold for filling in a “specific” midfield role that’s not for him. The intensity in the press high up was matched by a passivity elsewhere. Inter played through and round them, clocking up twice as many attacks and passes. At the end the Santiago Bernabéu whistled; Vinícius Júnior in particular felt their frustration. Yet their team, who also could have won by more – Jude Bellingham said he had missed “two sitters” – have started with a win.View image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho makes his point against the team with whom he won the treble.Photograph: Diego Souto/Getty ImagesThe irritation had grown. When Madrid scored the first, this placed cheered but they might have laughed too. That Madrid led didn’t make sense; not when it came to the goal, not when it came to the game either. It had taken Madrid four minutes to get a meaningful touch, and by then Courtois had already made a superb save from Marcus Thuram. But this is Madrid in the Champions League and now somehow they led. Ninety minutes later, they still did, which didn’t compute either.Quick GuideDortmund's Karetsas taken to hospitalShowBorussia Dortmund's Konstantinos Karetsas was taken to hospital after slumping to the turf 25 minutes into his Champions League debut against Villarreal.“Konstantinos Karetsas had to leave the field due to circulatory problems,” Dortmund said in a statement. “Kosta is doing well under the circumstances and is on his way to the hospital for further tests.”The 18-year-old Greece international passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass. Karetsas was treated laying down then taken away on a stretcher. The score was 0-0 at the time.Dortmund went on to win 3-2 at home. Renato Veiga’s 53rd-minute own goal put the Bundesliga side ahead before Santiago Mouriño equalised in the 66th. Serhou Guirassy restored the lead in the 80th minute and scored the third with an 84th-minute penalty, before scoring an own goal in added time while trying to help in defence.Real Betistwice came from behind to beatLille3-2 away, ⁠with Marc Bartra scoring in the 34th and 49th minutes before Troy Parrott’s 54th-minute winner.Lille ​scored their opener in the 12th minute ‌and regained the lead through ‌Alexsandro in the 37th. The hosts later had Ethan Mbappé sent off for an elbow to ‌the face of an opponent.AEK Athens​made a winning start, beating the Austrian sideLASK1-0 in Greece thanks to Romanian midfielder Razvan Marin’s curling free-kick midway through the first half.AgenciesWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Inter had been playing with what looked like ease until suddenly even the simplest things looked complicated. Hakan Calhanoglu and Lautaro Martínez had just fired off the third and fourth shots without reward when it happened. Inter had enjoyed 65% of possession so far but gave it up in a way that was comic. Curtis Jones struggled with the first ball, playing to Yann Bisseck who fatally lost his bearing and his footing. Stumbling like someone attached his legs the wrong way round, he gave it to Brahím Diaz who sent Mbappé away to score.It was Madrid’s first shot and the opening goal. If that was silly, what came next was even more ridiculous. What is it Madrid do to goalkeepers in this competition? Receiving on his line, Josep Martínez saw Valverde steaming in and tried a drag back, which failed. A flick of the ankle and the Uruguayan had scored. Twenty-three minutes, two shots, 2-0. “That was not chance,” Mourinho said and the lead might have grown when another robbery saw Vinícius dashing away. Bissek, this time, made a fantastic saving challenge. For all the fortune this felt like a plan now: force the mistake, punish it. Madrid forced more too, which they didn’t punish.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKylian Mbappé opens the scoring for Real Madrid in the 14th minute.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersInter recovered and reasserted themselves, a calmness in possession at one end that contrasted with the calamitousness further back. Curtis Jones, Lautaro Martínez and Augusto virtually walked into the area, where Jones’ effort smashed the crossbar. Then another gift, from Benjamin Pavard, saw Madrid escape just before the break. Bellingham was denied by a wonderful stop from JosepMartínez and Díaz hit the post. Inter led 12-3 in shots, boasted 70% possession and had completed 125 final third passes to Madrid’s 13. Madrid, though, led.Those numbers evened as the game opened, the second half beginning with Josep Martínez coming out to stop Mbappé before Inter came back at them. Courtois saved from Jones, Nicolò Barella shot wide and Thuram scooped over. The roar that then greeted an outrageous Courtois double stop spoke of disbelief, although the flag was up. The feeling was similar when Josep Martínez scrambled across his line to stop Bellingham after Díaz’s glorious scoop over him and into the Englishman.A competition built between the keepers. Madrid could have killed this, many times. Inter could have revived it. Courtois saved from Alessandro Bastoni. Josep Martínez saved from Mbappé with his legs. That was 6-5 to Courtois. There were whistles, frustration, but chances too: the 20 seconds or so between Lautaro Martínez being blocked at one end and Díaz slotting wide at the other told a tale. Inter finally scored when another incisive exchange saw Lautaro Martínez pull back for Augusto to score. There were f15 minutes left and a game on, but that, somehow, was that. Which didn’t make sense either.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueReal MadridInternazionalematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Iowa marching band member taken off life support after collapse in extreme heat | College football | The Guardian
description: Third-year University of Iowa student suffered severe brain damage after collapsing shortly before marching band’s half-time performance
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Third-year University of Iowa student suffered severe brain damage after collapsing shortly before marching band’s half-time performance
Content: Members of the Hawkeye Marching Band perform before Iowa’s game against Minnesota at Kinnick Stadium in October 2025.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of the Hawkeye Marching Band perform before Iowa’s game against Minnesota at Kinnick Stadium in October 2025.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesCollege footballIowa marching band member taken off life support after collapse in extreme heatDerek Phillips suffered cardiac arrest at football gameTemperatures reached 94F in Iowa City on SaturdayUniversity has not said whether heat caused collapseGuardian sportTue 8 Sep 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA University ofIowamarching band member has been taken off life support after collapsing during extreme heat at the Hawkeyes’ season-opening football game on Saturday, his family said.Derek Phillips, a third-year student from Dubuque, Iowa, suffered a sudden cardiac arrest shortly before the band was scheduled to perform its half-time show against Northern Illinois at Kinnick Stadium, according to a messageposted to his Instagram accountby his family.Phillips was taken to University of Iowa Health Care, where he was treated in intensive care. His family said the cardiac arrest caused severe brain damage and that they made the decision to remove him from life support.“Derek is comfortable, surrounded by family, and enveloped in the music he loved so much,” the family said. “Thank you for every prayer, every shared experience, and every bit of love you’ve given to our boy.”Temperatures reached 94F (34C) in Iowa City on Saturday. It was 90F (32C) at kickoff, making it the fourth-hottest home football game in Iowa history, according to the university.The heat index made conditions feel hotter and Iowatook several precautionsahead of the game. Fans were permitted to bring water bottles into the stadium, while start times for several other athletic events over the weekend were changed because of the forecast.The marching bandalso wore alternate uniformsof shorts and T-shirts rather than its traditional wool uniforms. It performed its usual pre-game program but canceled its half-time performance.“The health and safety of our students, staff, and fans are our top priority,” the Hawkeye Marching Band said in announcing the cancellation Saturday. “Due to the heat, HMB will forego our halftime performance today.”The university has not said whether the heat caused Phillips’ cardiac arrest,according to KCRG, the ABC affiliate covering Iowa City.“The entire Hawkeye Marching Band family is thinking of Derek Phillips and his loved ones,” the university said in a statement. “We are grateful to his parents for providing regular updates to the students who love Derek. This is heartbreaking for everyone who cares for him. The university is in close contact and is offering support.”The university said counselors were made available this week to students in the marching band and School of Music.Phillips played horn in the Hawkeye Marching Band and studied business analytics and information systems at Iowa. He had spent the summer touring with a drum and bugle corps, according to his family.His family described him as someone who brought “so much light, humor and kindness into this world” and whose life revolved around music.“He was a phenomenal musician – whether he was playing jazz, singing his heart out, or marching under the lights, music was the language of his soul,” the family said.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballCollege sportsIowaUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy protection as it looks to ‘begin the next chapter’ | LIV Golf Series | The Guardian
description: Saudi investors stopped backing LIV Golf this year although top players like Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cam Smith are still involved
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Saudi investors stopped backing LIV Golf this year although top players like Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cam Smith are still involved
Content: Jon Rahm was one of LIV’s highest-profile recruits but his future on the breakaway tour has not been confirmed.Photograph: Justin Casterline/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJon Rahm was one of LIV’s highest-profile recruits but his future on the breakaway tour has not been confirmed.Photograph: Justin Casterline/Getty ImagesLIV Golf SeriesLIV Golf files for bankruptcy protection as it looks to ‘begin the next chapter’Saudi investors stopped backing LIV this yearRahm, DeChambeau and Smith among the creditorsAgence France-PresseTue 8 Sep 2026 17.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 20.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLIVGolf, the breakaway tour that spent billions of dollars luring top players away from the PGA and triggered bitter divisions within the sport, has filed for bankruptcy protection in the US.The filing at a New Jersey court indicates LIV, which abruptly lost its deep-pocketed Saudi investors earlier this year, intends to restructure and return in a new form.LIV Golf to lay off majority of staff amid ‘compressed timeline’ for new investorsRead moreBut documents show LIV owes between $500m and $1bn in estimated liabilities to at least 1,000 creditors, including star players like Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm and Cam Smith.The future of those popular players remains deeply unclear; they are now faced with deciding whether to remain with the tour in its new guise, or leave and attempt to pursue the millions of dollars they are owed in court.“This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf,” said the chief executive, Scott O’Neil, whose organisation had already laid off the majority of its staff this month.O’Neil said LIV still intends to return in a new form next year “built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem”. But “no definitive decisions regarding the 2027 schedule or individual events are being announced at this time,” the statement added.Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) had spent an estimated $5bn on the tour before abruptly pulling the plug this year. LIV Golf is also seeking recognition of the US bankruptcy filing in England and Wales to cover its international assets and operations.LIV officials have pledged that a “2.0” version of the tour will re-emerge under new investors next season, with a shorter schedule and reduced prize money. Much will depend on whether the top stars of the tour remain. Tuesday’s statement said “the company remains in advanced discussions”with players, including on “creating an ownership structure aligning players’ interests with the League’s long-term success”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWidespread reports have linked several LIV stars with returns to the PGA Tour and other series, though the PGA said it has no plans to offer LIV players a pathway back.Explore more on these topicsLIV Golf SeriesSaudi Arabia and sportGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fake wide receivers to undercover stings: did the 49ers have the wildest NFL preseason of all time? | San Francisco 49ers | The Guardian
description: A large part of San Francisco’s summer was a literal car crash. On the positive side, they have so far avoided their usual list of crushing injuries
Author: Melissa Jacobs
Headline: A large part of San Francisco’s summer was a literal car crash. On the positive side, they have so far avoided their usual list of crushing injuries
Content: 49ers owner Jed York was arrested last month in Ohio.Photograph: Getty Images49ers owner Jed York was arrested last month in Ohio.Photograph: Getty ImagesSan Francisco 49ersFake wide receivers to undercover stings: did the 49ers have the wildest NFL preseason of all time?A large part of San Francisco’s summer was a literal car crash. On the positive side, they have so far avoided their usual list of crushing injuriesMelissa JacobsTue 8 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Los Angeles Rams andSan Francisco 49ershave trekked to Australia for this week’s NFL season opener in Melbourne.
