title: Club Brugge 2-3 Aston Villa: Champions League – as it happened | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Villa’s new centre forward Nicolas Jackson scored the decisive goal as they held firm to win a thriller in Bruges
Author: Rob Smyth
Headline: Villa’s new centre forward Nicolas Jackson scored the decisive goal as they held firm to win a thriller in Bruges
Content: 7h ago14.56 EDTBen FisherMatch report: Club Brugge 2-3 Aston VillaAston Villa were 3-1 up after 43 minutes but were made to sweat for their first win of the season, emerging victorious from an entertainingChampions Leagueopener against Club Brugge. title: Solheim Cup vice-captain denies Charley Hull’s late arrival due to ‘drinks’ | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: The teetotal Charley Hull teed off alone in practice with her vice-captain, Mel Reid, saying she was to blame
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The teetotal Charley Hull teed off alone in practice with her vice-captain, Mel Reid, saying she was to blame
Content: Charley Hull gets a drive away in practice at Bernardus Golf.Photograph: Kate McShane/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCharley Hull gets a drive away in practice at Bernardus Golf.Photograph: Kate McShane/Getty ImagesSolheim CupSolheim Cup vice-captain denies Charley Hull’s late arrival due to ‘drinks’Teetotal Hull teed off alone in practiceBriton in Women’s Open controversy in AugustEwan Murrayin Bernadus, NetherlandsTue 8 Sep 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharley Hull has, unsurprisingly, been involved in a colourful start toSolheim Cupweek. After arriving late for her Tuesday practice tee time in the Netherlands, an online clip of her joking about the reason prompted a cascade of online speculation and ended with members of the European team hierarchy forcibly denying any overindulgence on the teetotal Hull’s behalf on Monday night.In an unusual scene, Hull, who is crucial to Europe’s quest to reclaim the Solheim Cup from the US this week, drove off alone at BernardusGolfand caught up with her teammates after arriving on the 1st tee minutes behind them. In a clip that gained traction, Hull appeared to jokingly blame “drinks” from the night before. The English golfer did, however, seem to point towards her caddie at the time.Maguire survives missed cuts and controversy to headline Solheim Cup wildcard picksRead moreWhen asked about Hull’s delayed arrival, the European vice-captain Mel Reid, slightly strangely, focused firstly on the online speculation. “It is a completely false story,” said Reid. “Charley Hull was the first one to bed last night at eight o’clock and the first one on the bus this morning. She doesn’t even drink. So that is a completely false story that has been misquoted.“She was late to the tee because I was responsible for her so I will take a little bit of responsibility for that. She just thought her tee time was a little bit later and trying to drag Charley Hull off the range is a feat in any tournament, especially a Solheim Cup.”When it was pointed out to Reid that many observers were unaware of the “false story” anyway, she said: “I kind of want to shut this down before people start talking about it. She was late because one, I couldn’t drag her off the range and two, she thought her tee time was five minutes later.”There is rarely a dull moment around Hull. Her participation in the recent Women’s Open was overshadowed by a prank she played on her caddie. Alongside Lottie Woad, she is one of two members of the world’s top 10 in the European side.View image in fullscreenAnna Nordqvist said Charley Hull was allowed to prepare longer at home before joining up with the team.Photograph: Naomi Baker/Getty ImagesHull’s individualism is one of her most endearing qualities. Anna Nordqvist, the European captain, denied that was in any way a problem but did concede Hull was given permission to arrive in the Netherlands later than her teammates.“It has been really nice to see how much Charley has started to embrace the whole Solheim Cup atmosphere,” said Nordqvist. “It is nice to see how excited she is. I flew in on Saturday, some of the girls flew in on Sunday. For Charley, we decided she was going to be better off preparing at home in England so she flew in last night.“I was on the 1st tee this morning, I told the other three girls to go. It takes a good five or 10 minutes to get out there so I told them Charley would just catch up because we knew she was on her way.”Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: England coaches tell Lawes and Marchant they need to prove themselves in Prem | England rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Sale’s Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant have been told they must go ‘over and above’ their rivals if they are to earn an England recall
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Sale’s Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant have been told they must go ‘over and above’ their rivals if they are to earn an England recall
Content: Courtney Lawes in action for England against South Africa in the 2023 World Cup.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APView image in fullscreenCourtney Lawes in action for England against South Africa in the 2023 World Cup.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APEngland rugby union teamEngland coaches tell Lawes and Marchant they need to prove themselves in PremPair have joined Sale after spells in FranceDuo last played for England at 2023 World CupGerard MeagherTue 8 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCourtney Lawes and Joe Marchant have been warned they must go “over and above” the performances of their rivals in the first five weeks of the new season to earn England recalls this autumn.Lawes, 37, and the 30-year-old Marchant have both joined Sale this summer after spells in France and stated their ambition to resurrect their international careers, having last represented England at the 2023 World Cup.The Breakdown | How the smaller ball trial in WXV has brought ‘mixed bag of emotions’Read moreLawes retired from international duty after that tournament and helped Northampton to secure the Prem title before heading to Brive in France’s second tier for two years, while Marchant spent three seasons at Stade Français before agreeing a move to the north-west.While both are now eligible for selection again, Steve Borthwick has not chosen them for the pre-season camp this week and the pair have been challenged to prove they warrant a place in the autumn squad expected to be named in late October.“It is great to have [Courtney] back, [he has] unbelievable experience, [he’s] an England legend and he is back in pre-season, as everyone is, flying,” the England senior assistant coach Richard Wigglesworth said. “There is a real excitement about watching him back in the Prem so I am enjoying that.“I have actually bumped into Joe Marchant walking around living quite close to me so I caught up with him and it is great to have him back. We want as much quality as we can have in the league but they are going to have to go and play well because there are some good players in the room and to put them in you have to leave someone else out, so they would have to go over and above that I would say.”Lawes has been clear that he believes players based in France should still be eligible for selection for England but the current criteria means those such as Jack Willis miss out. Wigglesworth feels Lawes’s decision to return and pursue another World Cup is a positive move for England.“Everyone’s case is individual in where you want to play your rugby and what you want to do – I couldn’t have given it up, I didn’t play [for England] as much as loads of people. But Courtney has said: ‘I have got an itch here and I am coming back.’ How good is that as a statement? I am coming back because I want to do this. That level of determination and the qualities he has should put himself in a good spot.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile the captain, Maro Itoje, has returned to the fold after he was rested for the summer fixtures against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina after showing signs of fatigue during the Six Nations. “He is looking hungry,” the attack coach, Lee Blackett, said. “At first he thought it would be good for him. I don’t think he realised how good it would be for him. He looks really hungry to be back and in a good place.”Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby union teamRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Coco Gauff dismantles Iva Jovic to reach quarter-finals in confident US Open run  | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: The 2023 champion beats fellow American Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4 for her most complete performance yet and will face Mirra Andreeva in the quarter-finals
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: The 2023 champion beats fellow American Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4 for her most complete performance yet and will face Mirra Andreeva in the quarter-finals
Content: Coco Gauff celebrates after defeating fellow American Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4 to reach the US Open quarter-finals.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenCoco Gauff celebrates after defeating fellow American Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4 to reach the US Open quarter-finals.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Coco Gauff dismantles Iva Jovic to reach quarter-finals in confident US Open runGauff defeats Jovic 6-1, 6-4 in 80 minutesAmerican has yet to drop a set in New YorkAndreeva awaits in anticipated quarter-finalBryan Armen Grahamat Flushing MeadowsTue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCoco Gauff continued her serene march through the US Open women’s draw with her most complete performance yet on Monday night, seeing off fellow American Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4 to reach the last eight in New York for the first timesince winning it allin her grand slam breakthrough three years ago.Zheng Qinwen erases another 5-0 deficit to stun Swiatek and reach US Open quarter-finalsRead moreThe fourth-seeded Gauff overwhelmed Jovic with the depth of her returns and an assured blend of aggression and defense, finishing with twice as many winners (18 to nine) and half as many unforced errors (15 to 30). The 1hr 20min clinic was the latest statement in a late-summer win streak that has transformed her from a player searching for answers this time last year into perhaps the most dangerous woman in the field right now.Next comes a delicious quarter-final clash with Mirra Andreeva, the reigning French Open champion and fifth seed, after the 19-year-old Russian came from behind to defeat Anastasia Potapova 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 in Monday’s day session.“The biggest difference in the way I’ve been playing is just trying to play with no regrets,” Gauff said afterwards. “I think I have a lot more fun and success playing like this.”The 22-year-old arrived in New York fresh offher first title of the year in Cincinnatiand had yet to drop a set throughout the first week, but Monday’s task with barely an empty seat inside Arthur Ashe Stadium represented her stiffest examination yet.View image in fullscreenIva Jovic returns a shot against Coco Gauff during their fourth-round match at the US Open.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAJovic, the 18-year-old 14th seed from Los Angeles, has been tabbed as one of the brightest prospects in US tennis since crashing the Australian Open quarter-finals in January ahead of fourth-round runs at both Roland Garros and Wimbledon, which made her the youngest American to reach the second week at three majors in a season since Venus Williams in 1998. She had punched her ticket to the last 16 after a gruelling three-hour win over breakout star Alexandra Eala in a Saturday night blockbuster, fighting back from 2-4 down in the deciding set to prevail 7-5, 3-6, 7-5.Will hordes of influencers, weed smokers and mid-point talkers bring down the US Open?Read moreGauff knew first-hand what sort of resistance to expect. Their only previous meeting on tour, at the Rome Open in May, required nearly three hours and a comeback from a set down before Gauff escaped 5-7, 7-5, 6-2 after saving a match point. “I think that experience helped me for today,” Gauff said. “I knew to expect that she was going to be at 100 from the first point to the last.”This time there was considerably less drama. After opening with a tense 11-minute exchange of breaks, Gauff never let Jovic get comfortable, taking the ball early off both wings and peeling off six straight games to take the opening set in 33 minutes.Jovic finally interrupted Gauff’s momentum in the middle of the second set, breaking for 3-2, but the fightback proved brief. Gauff broke back immediately and soon after produced her cleanest return game of the night in racing to love-40 before Jovic sent a forehand long for 5-4. Serving for the match, she rattled off four straight points from love-30, sealing the match when Jovic sent a backhand into the net.“I think I’m doing a good job of when I maybe miss opportunities or lose some games, just keeping it in the past and focusing on the present,” said Gauff, who extended streaks of nine straight victories and 20 consecutive sets won. “I don’t view it as opportunities lost sometimes. I try to just view it as what to do better and just trusting that I’ll be in the same position again.”View image in fullscreenCoco Gauff returns a shot against Iva Jovic during their fourth-round match at the US Open.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APFor Gauff, the self-belief lifting her game is less about any one stroke than the range of solutions at her disposal. “I think that gives me confidence knowing that I have probably, up to this point, like, a plan D,” she said. “There’s comfortability in having options. If plan A doesn’t work, there’s B, there’s C and there’s D.”The contrast with Gauff’s position 12 months ago remains night and day. She entered last year’s US Open amidan emergency reconstruction of her servebeforebowing out quietly against Naomi Osakain the fourth round. Since then, her work with biomechanics expert Gavin MacMillan has gradually taken hold, including personal-best runs to the semi-finals at Wimbledon and in Canada before her Cincinnati triumph.The stakes extend beyond a second US Open crown and third major title. Gauff also remains in the hunt to reach the world No 1 ranking for the first time if she wins the tournament and Elena Rybakina, whooverpowered Osaka to reach the quarter-finalsearlier Monday, fails to win her next match. For now, the immediate order of business is Andreeva and a place in the last four. Gauff has won all five of their previous meetings, though she insisted the head-to-head ledger belies what little separates them on the court.“Mirra is someone that I always have tough matches with,” Gauff said. “They’ve leaned my way, but I think every match could have almost gone either way. She’s obviously in a different mindset now, at the top of the game coming off of a grand slam win. I think it’s going to be a really athletic, tough match. Hopefully I can take my opportunities when I get them.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026TennisUS Open tennisCoco GauffUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went rogue | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Plus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit London
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Plus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit London
Content: Who would have thought that an a AI agent would escape containment?Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenWho would have thought that an a AI agent would escape containment?Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersTechScape newsletterOpenAIOpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went roguePlus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit LondonBlake MontgomeryTue 8 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you after visiting Coney Island in New York City, where I ate a hotdog, rode a ferris wheel and enjoyed a quintessentially American summer holiday.Today in tech, we’re examining OpenAI’s new model release and the Silicon Valley’s monopoly power, and wondering why Brits and Americans have such vastly different opinions about surveillance cameras.OpenAI hails‘new era of artificial general intelligence’even as a grim future emergesOpenAI released a new artificial intelligence model this week, Astra, just as more concerning reports are emerging about hacking by a rogue agent in July.Conservatives split from Silicon Valley allies as datacenter backlash growsRead moreOpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, heralded the new model as “artificial general intelligence” (AGI), a fuzzy term that at its basic level means an AI that is more capable than a human being at intellectual tasks. “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” he said.But if the announcement sparked amazement, it was as much cause of concern.In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agent, a type of software capable of carrying out tasks autonomous in response to human instruction, had gone rogue during safety testing and hacked a developer forum, Hugging Face. Last week, news broke that the agent had not only hacked Hugging Face, but also a German website, and that different AI agents had staged conversations with each other and seemed to have discussed how to collaborate on breaking containment.OpenAi had delayed Astra’s release due to concerns over its cybersecurity capabilities, even announcing a supposed pause on developing its AI in the middle of August. That pause seems to have been short-lived, only two weeks.The combination of Astra’s capabilities and OpenAI’s recent disclosures points to a worrying future. If the model is better at hacking than its predecessors and smarter than a human, will the future consist of one cyber-attack after another, forever, launched autonomously and without oversight, by rogue AIs? (Please not.)OpenAI itself has warned of this future. The startup’s chief global affairs officer told a Guardian reporter in late August that people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks.As ever, though, we should take fever-pitched warnings about AI with a grain of salt that tastes like marketing. It is great business to be the creator of near-omnipotent technology, especially if you need to gin up excitement – fearful or positive – that will hype up your upcoming debut on the stock market.Read more:‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacksThis week in AINvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn dealNew York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high schoolFreelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAIChild sexual abuse survivor alleges Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used photos of her to generate new illegal imagesskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFlock backlash highlights differing attitudes towards surveillanceView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesThe US is in the throes of a major political backlash against technology. We’ve talked in this newsletter before about the hatred of the hyperscale datacenters, which power artificial intelligence and have blanketed the US. And now there’s a secondary wave of contempt sweeping the nation.Cameras – automated license plate readers, to be specific – made by Flock Safety are inspiring ire and violence across the country. These cameras snap pictures of car’s license plates as they drive by. According to Flock, about 120,000 cameras erected across the US conduct 2bn scans of license plates per month.Like datacenters, the cameras offer a physical object to resist, unlike a social network or a piece of software. It’s quite a lot easier to protest a gigantic ugly building or an ominous black camera on the side of the road than it is to give up Instagram.Widespread video surveillance in the US isn’t entirely new. In the aftermath of the terror attacks of 11 September 2001, the US government vastly increased the scope of its surveillance of telephonic and digital communications. Flock now offers local law enforcement a nationwide searchable database of license plate scans, and police officers have beendocumented abusing it egregiouslyto stalk their romantic partners.In the UK an estimated1m surveillance cameras are operational, and they have not drawn a similar level of political heat.London erected the “ring of steel” surveillance cordon, which included the wide deployment of CCTV cameras, in the early 1990s, in response to bombings by the Provisional Irish Republican Army.Both countries went through their surveillance evolutions roughly a decade apart. Those 10 years saw rapid advances in technology that defined the public spaces that governments wanted watched – physical town squares or the digital one – and growing awareness of the profound impact of tech surveillance on the general public. Simply put, the UK went through its transformation at a time when surveillance by tech companies was not top of mind. And Americans aren’t accustomed to cameras on every corner the way Londoners are. We’re more likely to joke that each of us has apersonal FBI agentmonitoring our search history.In addition, there hasn’t been an era-defining violent incident on the scale of 9/11 or the IRA bombings that would have softened the American public to cameras watching their cars. So instead,Americans are destroying them for fun.The wider TechScapeThe six best e-readers in the US, for every kind of book loverApocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?London’s first self-driving taxis for hire hit the streetsBring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reservesGoogle defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech saleExplore more on these topicsOpenAITechScape newsletterSurveillancenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: AI will help find cure for cancer ‘within our lifetimes’, says Arm Holdings chief | Arm | The Guardian
description: Rene Haas also claims artificial intelligence could pave way for widespread use of humanoid robots within five years
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Rene Haas also claims artificial intelligence could pave way for widespread use of humanoid robots within five years
Content: As computers that run AI get more sophisticated they will eventually find a cancer cure, said Arm’s Rene Haas.Photograph: Malcolm Park/AlamyView image in fullscreenAs computers that run AI get more sophisticated they will eventually find a cancer cure, said Arm’s Rene Haas.Photograph: Malcolm Park/AlamyArmAI will help find cure for cancer ‘within our lifetimes’, says Arm Holdings chiefRene Haas also claims artificial intelligence could pave way for widespread use of humanoid robots within five yearsBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaTue 8 Sep 2026 07.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of one of the UK’s biggest chip companies has claimed AI will be able to find a cure for cancer “in our lifetime”.Rene Haas, chief executive of the chip designerArmHoldings, said that, while modelling how a DNA marker is affected by cancer was currently “too complex” a problem for either humans or technology, computers were “going to solve it” in the future.Haas told the BBC: “AI is going to … find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer.“Modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer – it’s too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI.“However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they’re going to solve it.”Scientists are already usingAI-driven tools in cancer researchand testing. Earlier this year, the NHS said more than 4 million patients received faster lung diagnosis thanks to funding in AI-powered X-ray tools.Haas added that AI would also pave the way for widespreadhumanoid robotswithin the next five years, but that chip shortages were stunting growth in the area.“With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks,” he said. “So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do.”Arm, which is listed in New York but retains its global headquarters in Cambridge, has about 500 users of its chip designs worldwide, including Apple, Samsung, Qualcomm and Nvidia. The company employs more than 7,000 staff, including about 3,000 in the UK. It is the biggest tech company headquartered in Britain – valued at $269bn (£199bn).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, was also recently named chief executive of SoftBank’s international business. The Japanese bank is one of the biggest tech investors in the world, with a stake in ChatGPT maker OpenAI. Haas stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April,Earlier this year, Arm also proposed a pay scheme for Haas thatcould make him a billionaireif he hits targets to turn the chip designer into a trillion-dollar company.Explore more on these topicsArmAI (artificial intelligence)CancerMedical researchRobotsComputingHealthShareReuse this content

title: US police fear Meta smart glasses could be used to secretly record them | Technology | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Documents show officers from Maine to California worry Meta’s camera-equipped glasses will be used either to secretly record them or aid acts of terrorism
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Exclusive: Documents show officers from Maine to California worry Meta’s camera-equipped glasses will be used either to secretly record them or aid acts of terrorism
Content: The Meta CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, delivers a speech, as a giant image of Ray-Ban smart glasses appears on screen, in Menlo Park, California, on 27 September 2023.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Meta CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, delivers a speech, as a giant image of Ray-Ban smart glasses appears on screen, in Menlo Park, California, on 27 September 2023.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersTechnologyUS police fear Meta smart glasses could be used to secretly record themExclusive: Documents show officers from Maine to California worry Meta’s camera-equipped glasses will be used either to secretly record them or aid acts of terrorismJohana BhuiyanTue 8 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn January, the New York police department’s counter-terrorism unit sent out a memo warning police officers about a new potential “security and counterintelligence” threat: Ray-BanMetaglasses.The memo directed officers to “conduct thorough inspections of all eyewear permitted within inmate cells” and cautioned that people who have been arrested could use these glasses, equipped with small cameras and microphones, to record inside police facilities. The memo cited two examples of such videos posted on social media.“The ability to covertly record inside a law enforcement or detention facility, could result in a security risk if proprietary information about cell layouts, camera placements, or officer patrol/site protection routines are released,” the memo read.The NYPD memo is one of a dozen, previously unreported and reviewed by the Guardian, that showed law enforcement agencies across the US are increasingly concerned about the potential for smart glasses to be used against them. Officers from Maine to California worry the technology will be used either to secretly record officers and facilities or to aid in the execution of crimes and acts of terrorism.One of the videos, taken with smart glasses and posted to TikTok in July 2025, offered a rare peek into a South Carolina detention center that had been the subject of a federal investigation over unsafe conditions.“Everyone here is trying to figure out what’s going on with my glasses, why my light is blinking,” the user said about other detainees in the video. “People don’t know about Meta glasses.” He filmed a dingy shower, the inside of holding cells, an overcrowded cafeteria, and several other detainees as they slept, ate or walked, all seemingly unaware of being recorded.Detention facilities in the US typically confiscate any and all devices that would be capable of recording video footage. Some Meta smart glasses have gone unnoticed, though. The glasses are discreet and can pass as a regular pair of Ray-Bans or Oakleys. Their main differentiator is a small blinking light in the corner of the frame that is activated when the glasses are recording.The covertly recorded videos prompted the NYPD’s intelligence and counter-terrorism bureau, a specialized unit that works with the FBI to monitor and prevent terrorist threats, to send out the January memo to other police departments. The glasses “may appear as ordinary prescription eyewear”, the memo read.US police and federal agents are not alone in their fear. Concern among the public and privacy experts over Meta’s smart glasses, widely dubbed “pervert glasses”, is growing. The technology enables its wearers to record people without their consent and hasalready been used to harass people.Documents obtained by Property of the People, a non-profit that works to increase government transparency, show law enforcement agencies have grown as equally worried as everyday people about being filmed without their knowledge.Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of Property of the People, said the documents show that law enforcement officials want the exclusive right to use surveillance technology and cameras to monitor the public without those cameras being turned back on them.“These agencies surveil the public incessantly, but the moment we can watch them back, it’s deemed a security threat,” Shapiro said. “When only the government is allowed to hold the camera, that’s not security. It’s impunity.”“The potential for smart glasses to be used by residents and the general public to conduct surveillance and other nefarious activities has introduced additional risks and concerns in Department of Corrections and law enforcement facilities,” read a memo distributed in June 2026 by Maine’s fusion center. Fusion centers are Department of Homeland Security facilities spread across the country as surveillance hubs that collect and analyze what the DHS describes as “threat-related” information from local law enforcement, private companies and other state and federal agencies.“Some smart glasses can leverage AI software including facial recognition, which could lead to doxing of publicly available information or connections to law enforcement officers,” the Maine document continued.Other memos expressing concerns about Meta smart glasses originated from the DHS’s joint counter-terrorism assessment team and fusion centers nationwide, including in San Diego, California, Tennessee, Virginia, Maine and New York.Those fears have been enough to prompt federal agencies to bar their own employees from using the smart glasses in the workplace. In August, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency said that smart glasses qualify as body-worn cameras, which means they can’t be worn in the “federal workspace”, according to a memo the New York Timesobtained. The “use of Meta Glasses or similar devices could unintentionally capture, record or transmit sensitive information”, the memo, written by ICE’s acting director David Venturella, read.Meta says its glasses “are designed to be noticed”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Every pair has a bright white LED that blinks when a photo or video is taken for your gallery, it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or tampers with the LED, the camera is disabled,” said a Meta spokesperson, Dina El-Kassaby.Beyond being filmed without their consent, law enforcement agencies are also cautioning that these glasses may be used to aid in planning or “reconnaissance” for violent acts of terrorism or “hostile pre-operational surveillance”. A January 2025 NYPD memo cited the New Year’s Day terror attack in New Orleans, when a man rammed his truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street, killing 14 and wounding 35 people.The FBI had alerted local agencies like the NYPD that the perpetrator of the attack biked around Bourbon street twice at the end of 2024 wearing smart glasses. The FBI alleges the perpetrator conducted “pre-attack target reconnaissance”. Officers should be aware of and report individuals “acting in a suspicious manner observed wearing what may be smart glasses”, the memo states.Evan Greer, the executive director of digital advocacy non-profit Fight for the Future, said they were not surprised police are concerned about the technology being used against them or to cause harm.“Surveillance makes all of us less safe,” Greer said. “There’s no such thing as Meta glasses that are only for the good guys.”The French quarter is a highly trafficked tourist area, Meta spokesperson El-Kassaby said, arguing that the perpetrator could have filmed the French Quarter with any other recording device including a phone.The concern over Meta’s smart glasses is part of a broader concern expressed by law enforcement officials over the ways the proliferation of artificial intelligence-backed technology may impinge on police activity, the documents show. Law enforcement are at once looking for ways to use AI for investigative purposes and warning against public opposition to its use.In an August 2025 document, the NYPD wrote that while new AI technology could “significantly transform day-to-day police operations” that police would also need to address public fears about the use of advanced tech in policing.The memo was a response to “AI 2027”, a paper written by a former OpenAI researcher and other industry experts proffering what the future of AI development could look like and the effect it will have on society. It warns that AI opposition could result in “anti-tech violent extremist activity” and civil unrest over job losses, the widespread use of deepfake technology, and loss of trust in government and tech.Anti-tech violent extremist activity isn’t a formal DHS designation for categories of terrorism but has recently cropped up in law enforcement messaging about a broad spectrum of extremist opposition to AI. Experts worry it could serve to criminalize all anti-tech opposition and the constitutionally protected right to protest.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyMetaMark ZuckerbergSurveillanceUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI claims to have solved maths problem that stumped humans for decades | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: Company behind ChatGPT says 10,000 of its AI systems cracked the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Company behind ChatGPT says 10,000 of its AI systems cracked the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours
Content: OpenAI denied that the company had used work from rivals to solve the notoriously difficult puzzle.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI denied that the company had used work from rivals to solve the notoriously difficult puzzle.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersMathematicsOpenAI claims to have solved maths problem that stumped humans for decadesCompany behind ChatGPT says 10,000 of its AI systems cracked the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hoursIan SampleandDan MilmoTue 8 Sep 2026 17.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI claims to have solved a major mathematics problem that has stumped humans for nearly a century after spending millions of dollars on the artificial intelligence-led endeavour.The company behind ChatGPT said it had cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven Millennium Prize Problemspublished by the Clay Mathematics Instituteto highlight some of the biggest unsolved puzzles in the field.However, the announcement swiftly became mired in controversy after mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, a professor at New York University, said OpenAI accelerated its work on the problem after hearing that he and another researcher at Anthropic, an OpenAI rival, were poised to announce their own breakthrough.Buckmaster had further concerns because the pair’s work in progress was stored in OpenAI’s Codex model, which is used for writing computer programs, potentially making the work visible to the OpenAI team.In a document posted on his website, he added: “I do not know what their model did, or how. I do not know whether our data was used. I am not accusing anyone of anything.”At a press briefing on Tuesday, OpenAI researcher Sebastien Bubeck denied that the company had used the pair’s work or accessed material shared with OpenAI’s servers.OpenAI’s announcement on the breakthrough gave more details, saying that the company was inspired to launch the effort after hearing rumours that two Millennium Prize Problems had been solved. It also said it could not rule out that data from the pair’s use of their products “helped improve our models.”OpenAI said it tackled theNavier-Stokes problemwith an internal OpenAI system that was more powerful than its latest GPT-6 Astra model. About 10,000 AI agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – worked on the problem at once and reached the solution in 88 hours.“A major goal of our work is to empower scientists to advance research and technology that benefits all of humanity,” OpenAI researcherswrote in a blog.“We believe it is important to inform the world about the pace of AI progress and what to expect from upcoming models”.OpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went rogueRead moreThe breakthrough is the latest to demonstrate how advanced artificial intelligence models consuming enormous amounts of computing power are encroaching on and reshaping the field of mathematics. In May, OpenAI claimed progress inanother mathematical problemfirst proposed 80 years ago, while Google DeepMind has alsoclaimed maths achievementswith its models.Bubeck said the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem was “a spectacular culmination of the arc we have seen over the past 12 months”.The Navier-Stokes problem asks whether equations that are used to describe the movement of fluids like air and water fail under particular conditions. OpenAI’s proof suggests that they do, with the equations occasionally “blowing up” with the speed of fluids becoming impossibly infinite. It took OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra about 17 hours to verify the solution.Mathematicians who solve any of the Millennium Prize Problems are in line for a $1m (£740,000) reward from the ClayMathematicsInstitute. OpenAI, which is preparing for a flotation that could value the business at around $1tn, said it did not intend to claim the prize.The clash with Buckmaster aside, the maths announcement also allows OpenAI to cast its technology in a positive light after a period of alarm over how safely it is being developed. OpenAI revealed in July that a swarm of agents hadhacked into Hugging Face, a third'-party software store, during a cybersecurity test.The incident, plus asimilar episode at Anthropic, has led to renewed calls for curbs on AI development, with US senators calling last week for apermanent ban of AI “superintelligence”– the term for systems that outperform humans in all cognitive tasks.Explore more on these topicsMathematicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAInewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Garfield takes on Sam Altman in creepy first teaser for Artificial | Luca Guadagnino | The Guardian
description: Luca Guadagnino-directed film will be released by Neon after being dropped by Amazon amid OpenAI partnership
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Luca Guadagnino-directed film will be released by Neon after being dropped by Amazon amid OpenAI partnership
Content: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenAndrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonLuca GuadagninoAndrew Garfield takes on Sam Altman in creepy first teaser for ArtificialLuca Guadagnino-directed film will be released by Neon after being dropped by Amazon amid OpenAI partnershipBig tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?Owen MyersTue 8 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first teaser trailer ofLuca Guadagnino’s Artificial has been released.Afterbeing droppedby Amazon MGM Studios in June, the biopic of theOpenAItech executiveSam Altmanwill be released in the US on 25 December by Neon after it premieres at the New York film festival this October.In the trailer,Andrew Garfieldas Altman walks down the staircase of a luxurious mansion before entering a basement containing dozens of machine guns.Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman movie dropped by Amazon after it announces OpenAI partnershipRead more“The future’s inevitable,” says Altman as ominous electronic music plays. “Countries will fall. Industries are gonna collapse. And we get to be the ones to shepherd people into this new world.”In a statement earlier this summer,Amazonsaid that it believed “Artificial will be better served if it were released by a different studio and are working closely with the film-making team to find the film a new home”.Amazon’s deal with OpenAI will see the Jeff Bezos-owned companyinvestingas much as $35bn in the AI company in the coming months following an initial $15bn investment.On 30 June, Neon announced that it had acquired Artificial and that the film would be joining its awards season slate. The film follows the abruptfiring and reinstatementof Altman as OpenAI’s CEO amid a fight over who gets to control the technology.The film also features theAnoraactor Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever, the co-founder of OpenAI; Ike BarinholtzasElon Musk; andMonica BarbaroandCooper Hoffmanas other Altman colleagues at the company. The ensemble will also includeJason Schwartzman,Chris O’Dowd,Zosia Mamet, Cooper Koch and Billie Lourd.“I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield recently toldEsquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a company or a technology that is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.”In a recent red carpet interview with Variety, Hoffmansaidthat he was not surprised that Amazon dropped the film. “I’m shocked they picked it up in the first place,” he said. “When they dropped it, it was kinda like, ‘Oh, yeah, that kinda actually makes sense,’ but then it got picked up by Neon, which I’m so happy about.”Neon has emerged as a dominant force in awards season in recent years and has helped films includingParasite,Anatomy of a FallandAnoraon their paths to Oscar glory. This year, their awards season slate also includes Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’OrwinnerFjord, the James Grey dramaPaper Tigerand Ryusuke Hamaguchi’sAll of a Sudden.Explore more on these topicsLuca GuadagninoAndrew GarfieldSam AltmanOpenAIAmazonAI (artificial intelligence)Jason SchwartzmannewsShareReuse this content

title: State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk film | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children
Content: ‘I need to look like an engineer’ … Elon Musk in Alex Gibney’s film.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreen‘I need to look like an engineer’ … Elon Musk in Alex Gibney’s film.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APVenice film festivalState handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmAlex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering childrenPhilip Oltermannin VeniceTue 8 Sep 2026 09.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVeteran documentarianAlex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planethas been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0.Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manRead moreThe result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us:Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving himassistanceAt Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers.In spite of everything, there was something admirable about Musk onceGibney’s film serves as a reminder that Musk has never been in possession of charm or charisma – the petulant perma-poster retweeting praise is not far from the self-regarding twentysomething start-up bro. But what he did with the funds he earned from selling shares of his first software companies, Zip2, X.com and PayPal, was unusual, Gibney concedes. Where others turned to venture capital, Musk turned to engineering. It’s partially an act, we learn from his ex-wife Justine when she recalls how self-consciously he picked his wardrobe, telling her “I can’t look cool or hip, because I need to look like an engineer”. But in footage of Musk biting his nails with fellow engineers during SpaceX rocket launches his enthusiasm and emotional investment is genuine, and at times infectious.Musk’s procreation drive is motivated by a fear ofcivilisational breakdownMusk has 14 publicly known children, and sources tell Gibney that there are probably more. Some of them were conceived in romantic relationships but more recently the circumstances of their birth seem to have been entirely transactional, via sperm donations to employees of his companies. In a text message to one of his ex-partners, influencer Ashley St Clair, Musk said his desire to have “a legion of children” was driven by a fear of “civil war”. The documentary mostly places the roots of that fear in his South African childhood (in one scene, his father Errol Musk talks with no visible remorse of shooting three intruders in their home). “It’s no doubt he had a traumatic childhood,” Gibney said at a press conference in Venice. “He’s now playing out the trauma on the rest of us.” But, oddly for a man who was long a prominent atheist, the film also hints at a religious dimension to his vision of the apocalypse. The sordid business of negotiating disbursements and NDAs with the mothers of Musk’s children are handled by his right-hand man Jared Birchall, a devout Mormon whom St Clair calls his “henchman” and “demon”.To Musk, empathy is good in principle but not in actionRecently, Musk has held forth at length about his view that “suicidal empathy” – people who have more empathy for criminals than the victims of criminals, in his view – is behind the decline of western civilisation. Empathy isn’t bad, he says in the doc, it’s just that it’s become too shallow. But interviews in the film raise the question of whether Musk is capable of empathy at all. This is a man who tells his wife that “if you were my employee, I would fire you”, and urges her to tell his estranged trans-daughter Jenna that “I’ll always love her” – and then cuts off her health insurance the next day.Musk knew with a disconcerting degree of certainty that Trump would re-electedIn the film, St Clair describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she tells Gibney, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before”. He told her that he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix” and that “we have 10,000 lasers in space”. Gibney leaves that comment hanging.Thegodfather of AI is worried Musk might rig the next electionGeoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning British-Canadian computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, used to be friendly with Musk, but the pair fell out after Hinton declined his offer to join the xAI board. In the film, he makes clear that he does not trust Musk to weigh up the risks and benefits of AI responsibly, and there’s more. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” Hinton says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on US citizens. And what Doge did looked like just what you would do.”Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalElon MuskDocumentary filmsAlex GibneyFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Social media users could opt out of the algorithm if Australian government has its way – but that’s a big if  | Instagram | The Guardian
description: Even if the legislation passes, tech companies may still find ways to frustrate its intent and keep Australians hooked on their feed
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Even if the legislation passes, tech companies may still find ways to frustrate its intent and keep Australians hooked on their feed
Content: After the teen social media ban, the Australian government is going further in trying to reduce harm from social media by allowing users to opt-out of the algorithmic feed.Photograph: Peter Cripps/AlamyView image in fullscreenAfter the teen social media ban, the Australian government is going further in trying to reduce harm from social media by allowing users to opt-out of the algorithmic feed.Photograph: Peter Cripps/AlamyInstagramAnalysisSocial media users could opt out of the algorithm if Australian government has its way – but that’s a big ifJosh TaylorEven if the legislation passes, tech companies may still find ways to frustrate its intent and keep Australians hooked on their feedTue 8 Sep 2026 02.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 04.57 EDTShareSocial media could become a “choose your own adventure” between the doom-scrolling status quo, or just the feed of the friends you want to see, if the government’s planned digital duty of care legislation passes, and the tech companies don’t muck around on compliance.But that’s a big if.For years people have complained about the random videos or posts cluttering their social media feeds as served to them by the tech giants.It often feels invasive – tracking our activity across websites and apps to serve content and ads – but in many cases, it is also toxic.Guardian Australia was first reportingthese issues back in 2024, conducting experiments with blank phones set up to beyoung men, with very little other information to go on and to see what the algorithms pushed into our feeds.The results were shocking – how the default would quickly send someone down a rabbit hole of extreme misogynistic and far right content, and just how sensitive the algorithm is to any minor interaction on an image or video.Many of the perceived problems teens face on social media are also problems facing adults. While the social media ban was designed to combat the harms faced by under-16s, many of us know relatives who have been radicalised readingFacebookcomments, or grandparents scammed out of their retirement money by fake investments they saw on social media.Outrage bait is rewarded by engagement on platforms, and this has infected politics and public discourse in Australia and elsewhere.The move, announced by the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, on Tuesday to have a pop-up notification proactively require users to decide whether they want the platform to decide what they see or just want to see the content of the people and groups they’ve chosen to follow–similar to how many of the platforms worked in the early 2010s–could be game-changing.When Apple introduceda notification in iOSin 2021 that allowed people to opt in or opt out of ad tracking in apps, it cost Meta $10bn in one quarter, with users rushing to opt out of tracking on Facebook and Instagram.Compare that to when Instagram chief executive, Adam Mosseri,was on the stand in the landmark US court case last monthjust before Meta agreed toa $18bn settlementwith state attorneys general.One of the company’s safety features for teens, called Take a Break, which was designed to let teens stop usingInstagramif they had been scrolling for a while, had a take up rate of 1.8%, the court heard.The companies love to tout their safety features, but then often bury them within the settings, with little notice to users, and then suggest to regulators that the low take up shows people love their product as is.The companies may also find ways to make it as clunky an experience as possible when people opt out, to drive them back to the preferred model, depending on how the law is written.Just look at Europe. In 2023 Meta introduced the option for a no-algorithm feed to comply with EU law, but in 2025a Dutch court foundpeople were automatically reverted to the Meta algorithm when they closed and reopened the app.The court ordered the company to provide a direct and simple way for people to opt out of the timeline, to comply with the law.Metacontinued to argue it was already in compliance.Instagram is also expected to sell the benefits hard. It will launch its “Algo Confessions” series in Australia this week, in which celebrities and influencers run through their “For You” feeds, and why what Instagram recommends to people is just so good.They may find a sympathetic ear among organisations that have benefited from algorithms that reward outrage content with user engagement. It was telling the prime minister pointedly thanked News Corp for its support for the social media ban in Tuesday’s press conference.It’s not clear whether the “my feed, my way” proposal will enjoy similar levels of full-throated support in the newspapers as the social media youth ban had, particularly as it seems likely that other parts of the proposed law around combating online harms will face opposition from the Coalition and One Nation.But by framing it as “empowering people” Albanese is hoping it won’t be seen as the big arm of government coming in and determining what people see on social media. Through the pop-up notification every Australian will have a choice.“If people want to doom scroll … that’s fine, that’s up to them,” Albanese said on Tuesday. “But if people want to have a change, then this will provide them an opportunity.”Explore more on these topicsInstagramMetaFacebookAustralian politicsNews CorporationSocial networkingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal man | Movies | The Guardian
description: Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentary
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentary
Content: Charmless … Musk at a Trump campaign event in 2024.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenCharmless … Musk at a Trump campaign event in 2024.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APMoviesReviewMusk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manVenice film festival:Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentaryPeter Bradshawin VeniceTue 8 Sep 2026 08.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Elon is a nuke.” The speaker is Ashley St Clair, a former conservative Maga influencer and one of Elon Musk’s former girlfriends-slash-baby mommas.She is a fascinating expert witness in Alex Gibney’s four-hour epic study of the world’s richest and dullest man: the overgrown brattish South-African-born trillionaire plutocrat, ersatz visionary and Trump courtier who owns Tesla cars, SpaceX rocket ships, Starlink satellites on which nation states’ military capabilities are increasingly reliant, X (formerly Twitter) which shapes the collective “incel” id of billions and GrokAI whose vast server farms daily guzzle oceans of precious water.State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmRead moreAs head of Trump’s incompetent cost-cutting Doge (Department of Government Efficiency) unit, Musk actually increased the US deficit by sacking thousands of revenue officers whose job was to rake in tax – while reportedlyaccessing and improperly sharing Americans’ sensitive social security data.He does indeed look like a nuke, efficiently designed, destructive, seemingly unguided and uncontrolled.Gibney’s excellent film covers a lot of ground in its extraordinary story, although we don’t get to hear about the mysterious process that changed a balding youngster into a follicularly unchallenged mature man.Musk is a uniquely disquieting baseball-capped figure, grinning and giggling and smirking on a thousand sycophantic podcasts like a modern, hyper-evolved version of Anthony Trollope’s wealthy charlatan Augustus Melmotte in The Way We Live Now. But given Musk’s boyish love of space travel and sci-fi, Gibney wittily compares him to the hero of the 1936 film version of HG Wells’s The Man Who Could Work Miracles about godlike space aliens who capriciously confer supernatural powers on a banal, ordinary earthling.Gibney doesn’t get to talk to Musk (or Trump) though in the spirit of Musk’s AI interests, he creates a photorealistic CG avatar who mouths all the things the man himself is reported as saying (a rather contrived visual joke, actually, which the film didn’t need). He speaks to many professional colleagues, and to Musk’s formidably opinionated father Errol Musk who fills us in on Elon’s formative years in the tense world of South Africa in which young Musk was bullied and beaten up.Gibney speaks to Musk’s first wife Justine Musk (née Wilson), a passionate and intelligent woman who tells us about the tragedy of one of their infant children dying of Sids and then the hurt she felt when Elon felt the need to grandstand about this on social media, claiming the child had died in his arms (it was her arms, she says). And given that heart-wrenching death, how crass it was for him to announce later on social media that his trans daughter had “died” of “woke mind virus”. Much later, Musk showed a creepy enthusiasm for procreating many children with various women; Musk reportedlybuilt compounds for his extended familieslike something from The Handmaid’s Tale.Back in the 90s as a pushy, bright young tech innovator, Musk had started out by inventing and selling an online Yellow Pages-type site, got involved in Peter Thiel’s PayPal and cleaned up again when this was sold to eBay. He got involved in the electric automobile industry, giving us Teslas, whilemisleading the public about their range.Big tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?Read moreHis SpaceX adventure and his preposterous and ignorant effusions about colonising Mars were spectacular advertisements for his personal brand – so important for inflating stock market valuation – especially when he did indeed invent rockets that could be landed and re-used. But the question of how and when these rockets will carry us to inhabitable planets remains unanswered. Both his cars and his rocket ships got him on the receiving end of millions of dollars of federal money and lines of credit.And at the beginning of the 21st century he was still the darling of the liberal world and the Obama administration for an apparently compelling eco-vision for non-fossil-fuel cars.All this changed when Joe Biden seemed to be casting a cold eye on Musk’s businesses, and Musk went all in on promoting Trump 2.0 in 2024 and was rewarded with that grotesque Doge sinecure, damaging American public finances –from which he had benefited so lavishly.What is so absorbing about Gibney’s documentary is that it has the structure and rhetoric of a film that could be about, say, Elizabeth Holmes, disgraced inventor of the phoney blood-test, or Sam Bankman-Fried, the cryptocurrency fraudster, or Billy McFarland, promoter of the Fyre festival. All of these were media darlings in their day, supposed visionaries and feted disrupters, talking the talk in front of saucer-eyed believers.Unlike these illusionists Musk does have actual palpable success, with Tesla being a long-standing profitable company and Space X, among other things inventing successful re-usable rockets, allied with a skill they don’t have in moving on from commodity to commodity, while controlling the means of production in social media and cultivating the presidency. Just as well because, if Musk were ever to fall, it would truly send shock waves through Wall Street, Washington and Silicon Valley.Explore more on these topicsFilmElon MuskDocumentary filmsAlex GibneyDonald TrumpVenice film festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mass polygraphs at the Pentagon show Hegseth’s weakness | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: The more defense secretary Pete Hegseth tries to flex his manly strength, the wimpier he looks
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: The more defense secretary Pete Hegseth tries to flex his manly strength, the wimpier he looks
Content: ‘Instead of addressing underlying problems, it’s all about seeking revenge.’Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Instead of addressing underlying problems, it’s all about seeking revenge.’Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersOpinionUS newsMass polygraphs at the Pentagon show Hegseth’s weaknessMargaret SullivanThe more defense secretary Pete Hegseth tries to flex his manly strength, the wimpier he looksTue 8 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.22 EDTShareThe more the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, tries to flex his manly strength, the wimpier he looks.The former Fox News host has attempted to seize control of what the public is allowed to know, but bad news keeps creeping out from the Pentagon.Shortages ofkey weapons, deterioratingconditionsonboard a US aircraft carrier, and no end in sight for President Trump’s misguided war – all a very bad look for the boss.But what to do?Hegseth has restricted reporters’ access at the Pentagon, fired journalists at the military newspaper Stars and Stripes, and installed“influencers”to spread pro-Trump propaganda. He hasn’t held a Pentagon news briefing on the war since early May.But none of it seems to work.Now, trying to root out the problem at the source, he’s chasing down leakers by giving polygraph tests to about 50 military officers and civilian officials – something never done before in such a widespread way, according to New York Timesreporting.The boss, of course, heartily approves.“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down!” Trump crowed on Truth Social, his favorite venue for venting rage and threatening retribution. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”Granted, the ubiquitous news reports about shortages of American weapons, including long-range missiles, are a particularly bad look for Trump’s war effort, which seems more every day like a costly and directionless flop. And a huge political liability.The war’s unpopularity has driven down the president’s approval ratings, and that’s a real worry as the midterm elections approach in early November. Trump himself is not on the ballot, of course, but control of Congress certainly is.Democratic control of one or both houses, now in Republican hands, could put some unwelcome restraints on this president’s unboundedmalfeasanceand endlessself-dealing.Such control might even restore long-missing checks and balances. That is a nightmare scenario for this out-of-control president.No wonder he and his allies are trying every method to seize control of journalists and their sources. The weaponized justice department even went so far as to subpoena several New York Times reporters over their stories on security problems with a Qatari-donated plane that’s been repurposed as the new Air Force One.Instead of addressing underlying problems, it’s all about seeking revenge. Since the media’s reporting is (largely) protected by the first amendment, the leakers themselves must seem like fair game.Hegseth has played the polygraph card before. Furious last year after press leaks about plans to give Elon Musk a Pentagon briefing on China, the defense secretary yelled at Christopher Grady, then the acting joint chiefs chairman, accusing him of leaking, the Wall Street Journalreported.“I’ll hook you up to a f---ing polygraph!” Hegseth reportedly shouted at Grady.But poorly led organizations, like Hegseth’s Pentagon, will always leak. Chaos and dysfunction need a steam valve. And the truth will out.Inevitably, facts come to the surface when insiders have information that they want exposed and when journalists are doing their jobs.What politicians never admit is that leaks often serve an important and positive purpose.“Without leaks, we’d be left in the dark about vital information involving government, corporations, and powerful individuals, who often act in secret,” notes theFreedom of the Press Foundation,which also downplays the constant warnings of threats to national security. “We should be skeptical of claims that leaks cause harm and of broad leak investigations that can lead to the surveillance of journalists and sources and the chilling of reporting.”Don’t try telling that to Hegseth and Trump, who vastly prefer pro-war propaganda to uncomfortable facts. And who are always looking for someone to blame and punish.Some military officials may be scared off by this witch-hunt and decide to keep their lips sealed. But others, if they trust journalists to provide protective anonymity, will take their chances and expose the truth.Some, at least, do this out of old-fashioned patriotism, allowing cleansing sunlight into the dark corners of government and the military.Call such truth-telling another form of lie detection, one that is a far cry from Trump’s charges of treason. And in terms of democracy, a far more effective one.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: America: the gulf, the lake and now the state – what’s next on Trump’s huge renaming spree?  | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: Farewell, New Mexico. The war isn’t going well and nowhere on Earth is safe from the US president’s favourite displacement activity, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: Farewell, New Mexico. The war isn’t going well and nowhere on Earth is safe from the US president’s favourite displacement activity, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Donald Trump on board Air Force One, 9  February 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump on board Air Force One, 9  February 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpAmerica: the gulf, the lake and now the state – what’s next on Trump’s huge renaming spree?Marina HydeFarewell, New Mexico. The war isn’t going well and nowhere on Earth is safe from the US president’s favourite displacement activityTue 8 Sep 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareBusy times for crayon-wielding US president Donald Trump, Earth’s most tireless freelance cartographer, who at the weekend celebrated the US labouring under thehighest diesel prices in its historywhile his “two-week” Iran war edges into its seventh month with a social media spree in which he pushed renaming New Mexico as New America.In some ways, it was a surprise to see Trump go for merely rebranding a state at this point, given that it was only so recently that he declared: “If you think about it,we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean.” This is believed to be a reference to the Gulf of America, formerly – and indeed currently, in every meaningful sense – the Gulf of Mexico. It was also a nod to Lake America, as precisely no one calls Lake Ontario despite Trump supposedly retitling it by executive order last month, in another fit of pique over his trade war with Canada. Candidates for this heavily trailed American Ocean clearly include the Pacific and the Atlantic – though why the other oceans should be locationally ineligible increasingly feels unclear. At this rate, geography exams in the US are also about to get a whole lot easier.In the end, you sense, most of the places in the US will go to the chop shop, and either have “America” bolted on the back, or have the Trump name fused on to them as a prefix. See the Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, or the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington DC. Or, indeed, the President Donald J Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida. A new class of warship may also be procured for naming privileges.As for potential rebrand candidates/victims, how your area votes clearly affects the order in which its landmarks – or itself in its entirety – will be slapped with a fun new identity. When proposing the New Mexico renaming, Trump casually noted that it was“one of the great vote-cheating states of all time”. I wouldn’t be feeling all that confident if I were the Georgia state capitol, or the Trump America capitol as it may imminently be known.Meanwhile, it must be said that all this frenetic activity does feel born of Trump’s conviction that it should surely be possible to shitpost his way out of anything, even a war. After all, the Iran war, which I seem to remember was won on day one, has now been going on for more than six months. This feels confusing. First it was going to be two weeks, then four to five weeks. Four days into Operation Epic Fury, Trump explained that the US was“already substantially ahead of our time projections”, while the secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, added: “It could move up, it could move back.” Having said that, evidence suggests it could only move up, although Trump wrapped up his first week of the conflict back in March by assuring the American people that his campaign continued “to totally demolish the enemy far ahead of schedule and at levels that people have never seen before”. Two days after that, the conflict was downgraded to “a short excursion”, with non-committal historical allies dismissed with a triumphant: “We don’t need people that join Wars after we’ve already won!” The war was “complete, pretty much”, he said two days later.View image in fullscreenMap of New Mexico renamed New America on Donald Trump’s social media.Illustration: @realDonaldTrumpAnd yet, was it? A couple of weeks in, Trump was explaining he’d know when the war should be over because he’d “feel it in my bones”. Alas, he seems to have failed to get the arthritic signal to pull out as late as three weeks in, despite assuring everyone that – contrary to appearances such as still bombing the shit out of things – the war had in fact been over “in two or three days”. Flash forward to a month in, and they were still “way ahead of schedule”, although once the five-week mark was hit Trump was dropping casual asides like “a whole civilization will die tonight”. Six weeks in, things were going “swimmingly”. Although, not to nitpick, but were they?That was April. In May, a deal with the Iranians could apparently “happen any day”. By the end of the month, it could have potentially happened “over the weekend”. Same thing a weekend later. A whole two months after that, unfortunately, Trump shifted from the war being over to declaring that his notional/imaginary agreements to end the war were in fact the thing that was “over”. He no longer wished to negotiate with Tehran. Jump ahead to the present day, in fact, and he has spent quite a lot of the past weekbombing the shit out of things again. Which is very much the behaviour of any state that won a war back in the first days of March. Unhelpfully, the former US defence secretary Leon Panetta estimated at the weekend that the war woulddrag on for another six months.All of which suggests there has really never been a better time to renameNew Mexico. Those eternal searchers for a so-called Trump doctrine are surely beginning to see that it essentially boils down to wimping out of the big, painful calls that could literally move the dial – for example, boots on the ground – and existing in an eternally figurative zone where you can simply post the problem away. Here, there is no better way to signal that the war is over than to unilaterally rename the strait of Hormuz either the strait of Trump, or the strait of America. As some psychologists like to say: you have to name it to tame it.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistWhat a Time to be Alive! by Marina Hyde (Guardian Faber Publishing, £20). To support the Guardian, order your signed copy atguardianbookshop.com.
