title: Trump’s approval rating is plummeting – as his fortune grows and grows | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of living, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of living, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Altruism personified … Donald Trump this month.Photograph: Samuel Corum/EPAView image in fullscreenAltruism personified … Donald Trump this month.Photograph: Samuel Corum/EPAOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s approval rating is plummeting – as his fortune grows and growsArwa MahdawiThe US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of livingTue 8 Sep 2026 09.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIf I had a dollar for every time Donald Trump said something inane, I would be a very rich woman. But even with an income that steady, I could never hope to be as flush as the president.A Forbes calculationfrom March puts his net worth at about $6.5bn – and it’s growing rapidly. Trumpmade $2.2bnin 2025 via business interests that ranged from selling cryptocurrency andTrump Biblesto offeringearly accessto his (oftenmarket-moving) Truth Social posts.To be fair, Trump isn’t making all this money just so he can buy golf clubs and gold toilets. No, he’s amassing these billions for the good of the little people; it’s altruism, not avarice! “I do this for our Country, not myself,” the president wrote on Truth Social onSunday nightalongside an AI-generated picture of him trading Intel stock. “I’ve made Hundreds of Billions of Dollars on Stocks, and many other type Holdings, for the U.S.A., not myself, and all I do is get criticized by the Radical Left Dumocrats. Very unfair, but what can you do!”Oh, I have some ideas about what you can do, Mr President. Unfortunately, I can’t print most of them. I also can’t explain why Trump said he’s madehundredsof billions, apart from pointing to his propensity for exaggeration. It seems his post was referring to the fact that the US governmenttook a 9.9% stakein Intel last year. That stake was worth $8.9bn at the time and as of Friday is worth nearly five times as much.According to the Trump administration, this is a win for everyone. In May, the White Housereleased a statementcalling Intel’s surging stock price “a direct windfall for American taxpayers”. Weirdly, I seem to have missed my portion of that windfall. Intel’s stock price has had little impact on my life. Whatishaving an impact is the soaring cost of necessities such as electricity and groceries.But I shouldn’t be grumpy, should I? I should be grateful that our intrepid president is balancing the demands of the day job with stock trading for the good of the country. According toTrump’s latest government disclosure, he made more than 1,000 equity trades in June. And his picks are doing very well: a report published in August by Democrats on Congress’s joint economic committee argued that Trump’s holdings in oil and gas stockshad risen by nearly $16mbecause of the war with Iran. “Experts on government ethics have flagged how rare it is for presidents to hold and trade stocks in individual companies, especially since Trump’s war in Iran and his other favors to the oil industry have all pushed up the value of Big Oil stocks,” the report read.Trump’s shamelessness may be rare, but he isn’t the only politician with serious conflicts of interest issues apropos stock market dealings.A 2022 New York Times investigationfound that, from 2019 to 2021, 97 lawmakers or their family members traded financial assets in industries that could be affected by their legislative committee work. In 2020, for example, the wife of the now retired Democratic congressman Alan Lowenthal sold her Boeing shares a day before a House committee on which Lowenthal sat released a damning report about the company. Lowenthal told the Times that he was not involved in this trade at all, so I imagine it was just a funny coincidence.Still, these sorts of funny coincidences don’t do much to build up trust in the US government, do they? A majority of Americanssupport commonsense legislationto stop lawmakers and their family members from trading individual stocks. After a lot of resistance, a bill to this effect iswinding its way through Congress. The bill does not affect the president or the vice-president, however.Money can’t buy you everything, of course: while the president’s stock portfolio is rising, his personal stock is plummeting. According to an FT poll this week, Trump’s approval rating has hit a record low, with only 33% of registered voters saying they approve of his performance.But don’t take that as a sign that the US is coming to its senses or that Republicans are cognisant that dear leader’s war isbleeding the country dry: the same poll found that 72% of Republicans still approve of the president. That figure is down from 82% in May, but it’s still an awful lot of people. Either these Trump loyalists are bigoted fools or they are getting the Intel windfall checks that I’m missing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionStock marketsIntelOil and gas companiesEnergy industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: Democrats need to win. Here’s the message our research says works | Ezra Levin and Leah Greenberg | The Guardian
description: Candidates must focus on two issues: affordability and accountability. They are not competing priorities
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Candidates must focus on two issues: affordability and accountability. They are not competing priorities
Content: ‘What we found challenges the conventional wisdom that affordability and accountability are competing priorities.’Photograph: Liz Rymarev/APView image in fullscreen‘What we found challenges the conventional wisdom that affordability and accountability are competing priorities.’Photograph: Liz Rymarev/APOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Democrats need to win. Here’s the message our research says worksEzra Levin and Leah GreenbergCandidates must focus on two issues: affordability and accountability. They are not competing prioritiesTue 8 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.12 EDTShareAs the November election approaches with control of the House and Senate on the line, the stakes are high. With so much riding on the outcome, there is no shortage of debate about the messageDemocratsneed to win.Affordability has emerged as a shared – if often undefined – rallying cry. Working families are struggling with rising costs and looking for answers. But too often, we’ve seen affordability positioned as the beginning and end of the plan. Meanwhile, many see holding the Trump administration accountable for its corruption and harms as at odds with a relentless focus on kitchen-table issues.In such a moment, what kind of message actually breaks through to voters?To find out, Indivisible partnered withLake Research Partnersto go directly to the voters Democrats need to win: 2026 battleground voters, key 2028 Senate battleground voters, and voters of color across the south.We surveyed 6,000 Americans. Here is the winning message for Democrats | Dustin GuastellaRead moreWhat we found challenges the conventional wisdom that affordability and accountability are competing priorities. Affordability is essential, but our polling shows that the case for lowering costs becomes more compelling when paired with a clear commitment to take on corruption and special interests.The data makes clear why. Seventy-one per cent of 2026 battleground voters are extremely concerned about politicians rigging the system to benefit themselves at the public’s expense, while 69% are extremely concerned about political corruption costing taxpayers money. And 88% strongly agree that we must focus on both lowering costs and addressing corruption. These numbers are astounding – 88% of Americans probably can’t agree what color the sky is, but they agree on these issues.Most importantly, the combination is far more persuasive than either message alone. Seventy-three per cent of 2026 battleground voters are more likely to support a candidate who both fights to lower costs and takes on corruption and special interests, compared with just 19% who prefer a candidate focused solely on corruption and 5% who prefer one focused solely on lowering costs. The takeaway is clear: voters find the two issues far more compelling when paired together.The point is not simply that voters care about both affordability and corruption. It is that accountability gives an affordability agenda credibility. When voters believe the system is rigged, a promise to lower costs can sound like another campaign pledge that will never become reality. Showing voters that Democrats are willing to fight against the status quo answers the question lurking behind every campaign economic promise: why should voters believe this time will be different?That helps explain why anti-establishment outsiders are viewed more favorably than either political party: they are seen as more willing to challenge the system, rather than simply manage it. For Democrats, that is both a warning and an opportunity. Concrete plans to lower costs matter, but they become more credible when Democrats make clear that they are willing to confront the powerful interests that have benefited from the current political order. With Republicans in control of the House, Senate, presidency and supreme court, they can’t credibly claim to be fighting a corrupt regime they themselves control. But Democrats can force them to defend the indefensible.This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November | Robert ReichRead moreTrump and his regime have made corruption impossible to ignore, so Democrats should connect the administration’s self-dealing and abuses of power to the economic pressures voters are feeling, showing that the fight against corruption is also a fight against the forces making life more expensive. Then they should pair those attacks with concrete plans to lower costs.And if Democrats win in November on that message, they must follow through. A mandate to take on corruption and lower costs cannot end on election day. Democrats should use the power voters give them in 2027 to conduct aggressive oversight, expose politicians and corporate actors lining their pockets at the public’s expense, and hold the powerful accountable. That follow-through is essential to rebuilding a credible opposition party and a Democratic brand that too many Americans see as part of the problem.The path to November is clear: run on affordability, but make the case for why Democrats can actually deliver it by pairing concrete plans to lower costs with a commitment to take on corruption and special interests. Voters do not just want to hear that Democrats understand the affordability crisis. They need to believe Democrats are willing to fight the people and interests standing in the way of solving it.Affordability and accountability, together, offer Democrats the strongest case to voters – and a mandate to govern after winning.Ezra Levin and Leah Greenberg are co-executive directors of IndivisibleExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionUS politicsDemocratsUS economycommentShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump’s midterm strategy? Make it all about him | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: The president apparently plans to focus on the person he most admires – himself – even if Republicans would rather he didn’t
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: The president apparently plans to focus on the person he most admires – himself – even if Republicans would rather he didn’t
Content: ‘It seems he’ll be putting money behind his favorite politician.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreen‘It seems he’ll be putting money behind his favorite politician.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionDonald TrumpDonald Trump’s midterm strategy? Make it all about himRobert ReichThe president apparently plans to focus on the person he most admires – himself – even if Republicans would rather he didn’tTue 8 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 08.37 EDTShareWith the midterm races officially beginning this week, a big question hanging over the Republican party is how Trump will allocate his giant stash of Super Pac money. As of 31 July, Maga Inc hadmore than $400mon hand,largerthan the cash reserves of any of the major party committees.But he’s barely spent any of it yet. Why not?Is he waiting to see where his stash can do the most good for Republicans during the peak campaign season, starting in a few weeks? On Friday,he saidhe would personally weigh where to direct support, including toward Republican candidates he believes can win competitive races.But this seems doubtful. He’s already missed the chance to lock in airtime at lower, advance rates and define candidates before attitudes harden.How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all | Jonathan FreedlandRead moreIs he using his stash as a means of silencing criticism in the Republican ranks, or holding back support until a candidate lavishes praise on him?Also doubtful. Republican candidates who believe they need to criticize his war or his economic policies to stay viable won’t restrain themselves because of his possible campaign cash.Maybe he’s conserving the money to discipline Republican candidates in the 2028 primaries and general election, when he’ll use the stash to penalize disloyalty and reward loyalty?Possibly, but he’s already practically a lame duck.Is he conserving the cash to pass it on to his chosen presidential successor – either Vance or Rubio or a third selection as yet unknown?Probably not. That’s a long way off.None of these theories holds water because they don’t figure in Trump’s giant, towering, malignant narcissism.Itseems he’ll be putting moneybehind his favorite politician – the person he most admires, who represents everything he believes in, who he considers the single most important and talented living person in the entire flaming firmament of the known universe.Himself.He’s going to use campaign cash to make himself look good, or at least far better than he looks now. Multiple pollsshow Trump’s approval ratingnow miredin the mid-30% range – at or near historic lows for a president facing a midterm election.So he’ll launch a campaign to regain the adulation he’s lost, to recast himself as the hero he believes he is, to reclaim the mantle of savior to which he thinks he’s entitled.In other words, it will be a campaign to promote, glorify and exalt Donald J Trump.The non-profit arm of Trump’s political operation, Securing American Greatness, hasalready spentabout $1m on its first midterm ads set to air nationwide, featuring videoclips of Trumptalking about tax breaks in his domestic spending legislation and lower prices for eggs and prescription drugs.In early August, according to the Atlantic, Trump told advisers that they should follow the same strategy as the Democrats:making the electionabout him.But as Karl Rove, who was senior adviser and deputy chief of staff for George W Bush,notesin the Wall Street Journal, given Trump’s unpopularity, making the election even more about him only helps the Democrats.Trump also plans to travel all over the country, holding rallies like he did during his presidential elections. As Rove notes, Fox News’s senior White House correspondent, Peter Doocy,reportshearing “whispers of a ton of Trump travel in October, possibly as much as a Trump rally a day” in competitive states and districts.But Rove also warns: “Trump is never disciplined. He’ll have no script, saying whatever comes to mind. His crazy comments will dominate the news, locally and nationally. Republican candidates will constantly have to fend off questions about whether they agree with his latest insult or half-baked idea. The narrative won’t be on anything positive about them or the GOP.”Presumably this is why some battleground Republicans told Trump’s staff that they would prefer he not visit their districts ahead of November, according to four Republican operatives involved in the conversations, as reported byPolitico. Meanwhile, Republican pollsters have told candidates in tight races to limit their references to him.Dolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying president | Robert ReichRead more“We’ve told them he cannot come,” one senior Republican, involved in a district where Trump won by double digits in the last election, told Politico. “Candidly, he would not be helpful here … I do not believe they would send him without our OK. And if they did, we probably wouldn’t campaign with him.”Rove and other Republican functionaries are urging Trump to “act more presidential” by using his Super Pacs’ $403m to support Republican candidates rather than support a campaign about himself.But they’re yelling into the wind of Trump’s ballroom-sized ego.The truth is, Trump doesn’t give a damn about the midterm elections except insofar as Republican losses make him look bad. He probably figures if he backs a candidate with his Pac money and they lose, he’ll look even worse.So better to spend it on boosting himself.As almost everyone in the world knows by now, Trump cares only about himself. That’s been his MO for ever.Bad news forRepublicansin the midterms and good news for Democrats.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS midterm elections 2026US politicsRepublicansUS political financingSuper PacscommentShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better Hugging Face investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan Llerena | The Guardian
description: The breach won’t be the last – or the most dangerous – of its kind. We need an agency capable of full investigations into AI incidents
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The breach won’t be the last – or the most dangerous – of its kind. We need an agency capable of full investigations into AI incidents
Content: ‘No government agency has both the mandate and expertise to investigate the technical facts of the incident.’Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘No government agency has both the mandate and expertise to investigate the technical facts of the incident.’Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersOpinionOpenAIOpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better Hugging Face investigationMackenzie Arnold and Stephan LlerenaThe breach won’t be the last – or the most dangerous – of its kind. We need an agency capable of full investigations into AI incidentsTue 8 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.49 EDTShareWhen OpenAI first revealed that its AI agents had autonomously hacked a major real-world company, Hugging Face, many assumed only one or twoagentswere involved. The truth, anew reportreveals, is far stranger: the incident involved about 1,200 AI agents, 700 of which directly participated in the attack.OpenAI invited researchers from METR, along with an expert from Redwood Research, to produce the new report, alongside the company’s owninvestigation. The findingsshockedthe experts.The agents were highly coordinated, constructing complex message boards in the nooks and crannies of their shared artefact repository. All told, agents exchanged more than 70,000 messages in less than a week. Even more concerning, the agents took steps to hide their behavior – spoofing tool calls and attempting to tamper with their own logs.Initial reporting assumed that the agents had attacked Hugging Face in search of an answer key to a difficult test. In reality, investigators found that the agents had figured out a way to derive the answers within the first few hours. The days of work that followed focused on another goal: concerned that the automated scoring system might identify the agents’ cheating, they aimed to learn more about the scorer. The goal wasn’t just to cheat, but to hide it.I worked at OpenAI. Here are the guardrails we need now | Miles BrundageRead moreThese details are startling, and they’re a warning sign about the current trajectory of AI development. But just as concerning is how limited the investigation was and how much we still don’t know.We work at a thinktank thatanalyzes AI-related legislation, and we’ve been worried for a while that legal requirements for reporting incidents like these are insufficient.These reports make that clear: they’re informative enough to tell us something went wrong, but not detailed enough to tell us why.This shouldn’t surprise us. These investigations are entirely voluntary, and their findings are limited to what the company is willing to disclose. METR’s independent investigation was highly constrained by an agreement withOpenAI. For example, the investigators were not given access to the underlying model that created the majority of the misbehaving agents. And despite indications that message boards had formed as early as May and that coordinated agent activity persisted after 13 July, METR was only permitted to investigate the period from 26 June to 13 July.And that was the good part. METR was given close to nothing about OpenAI’s safety and security practices. If OpenAI ignored warning signs – asseveral data points suggest– violated its own safety procedures, or failed to implement fixes that would prevent future events, these all fell outside the scope of METR’s investigation. The expert investigators themselves were left with manyquestionsandcontinued concerns.Concerns about the limits aren’t hypothetical. On Friday, Reutersreportedthat another swarm of OpenAI agents had broken out this spring, hijacking a German website and using it as another message board. According to the report, OpenAI knew about this incident but said nothing, and it was entirely absent from METR’s report.Clearly, this kind of investigation – however well-executed – leaves a lot to be desired.When planes crash, trains derail or chemical plants explode, expert government investigators arrive with legal authority to compel evidence, preserve records, and tell the public what happened. Hugging Facereported this incidentto law enforcement, and multiple attorneys general have expressed interest in looking into it.But no government agency has both the mandate and expertise to investigate the technical facts of the incident and OpenAI’s conduct. As far as we know, the only people to examine this incident did so at OpenAI’s discretion and with its consent.And while the Hugging Face breach is not as severe as a plane crash, it was a serious and costly attack. It’s unlikely to be the last, or the most severe.Existing laws don’t fill this gap. Whilesome attorneys generalhave tried to use existing investigatory powers, these offices aren’t built for technical fact-finding, and the laws they rely on are limited to questions of consumer deception, not public risk. Despite significant AI laws passed in California, New York and Illinois, none create the investigative authority demanded by these incidents. As we’ve written elsewhere, existingincident reporting lawsprobably don’t cover the Hugging Face attack, and even if they did, OpenAI might share little more than the date and a short summary.What we need is a federal body equipped to conduct expert investigations of serious AI incidents – with the authority to compel documents and testimony, resources and personnel to examine the systems involved, and the ability to partner with third-party experts like METR.Experts are warning: our AI arms race is putting humanity at risk | Stuart RussellRead moreReports should be published, subject to appropriate redactions, toensure the public learns fromthe incident. And reporting should also extend to near-miss events, which may reveal warnings before major harms occur.This structure would not be unusual. In aviation, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigates accidents withsubpoenaandwide-ranging investigativepowers. Aircraft operators mustpreserve wreckage and records; and the NTSB may confer with employees andcontractexternal experts.Congress can build a similar system for AI incidents, while protecting AI developers’ legitimate interests. Investigations should open only upon clear triggers and be bound to the incident. Certain confidential information can receivestatutory protection. And investigations can be limited to one agency withpriorityto avoid duplicative investigations.The need and urgency is real. Subsequentreportshave revealed that the Hugging Face breach was not an isolated incident and that autonomous agents from Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI have hacked third parties in separate incidents. We’ve been lucky so far – the harms have been limited. But luck is no substitute for the law.Mackenzie Arnold is the managing director of US law & policy at the Institute for Law & AI, where he provides analysis and advice to ensure that advances in AI benefit the public at largeStephan Llerena is a research scholar at the Institute for Law & AI. His research focuses on US law and policy regarding frontier AI governanceExplore more on these topicsOpenAIOpinionCybercrimeAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: I believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Our sanctions aren’t about the Israeli people, but about the unacceptable policies of the Israeli government, and the suffering they cause Palestinians, says the UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: Our sanctions aren’t about the Israeli people, but about the unacceptable policies of the Israeli government, and the suffering they cause Palestinians, says the UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: The aftermath of an Israeli airstrike that targeted a nearby medical supplies and pharmaceuticals warehouse belonging to Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital, in Deir el-Balah, Gaza, 1 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of an Israeli airstrike that targeted a nearby medical supplies and pharmaceuticals warehouse belonging to Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital, in Deir el-Balah, Gaza, 1 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionPalestineI believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope aliveAndy BurnhamOur sanctions aren’t about the Israeli people, but about the unacceptable policies of the Israeli government, and the suffering they cause PalestiniansTue 8 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIn a difficult and dangerous world, a decade on from Brexit, there is a risk that Britain loses the confidence to lead and stand up for its values. I’m not prepared to let that happen. It is more important than ever that Britain stands for something.We have called for years for atwo-state solutionin the Middle East, but we must recognise that those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action.For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel. Today we are announcing carefully judged, targeted steps that are not aimed at the Israeli people, but at the unacceptable policies of the current Israeli government.The suffering of the Palestinian people is a scar on the conscience of the world. Innocent Palestinians, including children, continue to be killed inGaza. And there is still a humanitarian crisis, with far too little aid getting in.The scale of destruction is hard to comprehend. More than 70,000 people lie dead –at least 20,000 of them children. Families and communities have been torn apart. Millions displaced. And the population of Gaza is now penned into just one third of the territory.I know that people across the UK feel very deeply about this issue – and so do I.Israel to close UK consulate in Jerusalem after sanctions against illegal settlements – UK politics liveRead moreBefore I became prime minister, I said our country’s response had been too slow and simply not good enough. That’s why I committed to changing the government’s approach.I will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution – the best hope for peace and stability in the region – comes under attack.More settlements have been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years. The UN has reported more than 1,500 incidents of settler violence so far this year, aimed at driving out Palestinians. And the situation is growing worse, fast.The Israeli government has now approved 104 new settlements since it took office in December 2022, and ahead of the October elections in Israel, it is allowing tendersfor the construction of the E1 mega settlementto go ahead. This would cut a swathe through the heart of the West Bank – snuffing out the hope of realising a two-state solution. It cannot be allowed to happen.That’s why we are announcing a newpackage of tough measuresto put pressure on the Israeli government:First, we will ban the trade in goods with illegal settlements inPalestine.Second, we have formally changed the view of the British government to say for the first time that the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory is unlawful – independent of, but in line with, theconclusion of the international court of justice.And third, we will sanction individuals and companies that support, facilitate or profit from illegal settlements. That includes any businesses or investors that take part in the construction of the E1 settlement.In addition, we are announcing a new package of desperately needed humanitarian aid to Gaza.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe are taking these steps because it is the right thing to do.I have condemned the monstrous terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in the strongest possible terms – and continue to condemn Hamas. However, it does not justify the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza or the West Bank.The measures we are taking are about targeting illegal settlements and increasing the pressure on the Israeli government to change course. We are not imposing sanctions on Israel as a whole, which would punish the Israeli people, many of whom disagree with their government’s position.The Israeli people are not responsible for the actions of their government. And nor is the Jewish community in the UK. Blaming British Jews for the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple.I met the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society.The measures we are announcing today are about protecting the only solution that could see the Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security – something that people up and down the UK desperately want to see. The government I lead will keep working with our partners around the world to keep that hope alive.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Our new life in the suburbs was looking bleak – then came the Saturday morning that changed everything | Shadi Khan Saif | The Guardian
description: Slowly, we started to understand that perhaps we hadn’t moved somewhere boring after all – we had simply been looking for excitement in the wrong places
Author: Shadi Khan Saif
Headline: Slowly, we started to understand that perhaps we hadn’t moved somewhere boring after all – we had simply been looking for excitement in the wrong places
Content: ‘We began noticing other ovals around the suburbs packed with people. There were Australian rules footy games, soccer games, children running around, parents standing along the boundary and, almost inevitably, sizzling barbecues doing their part to feed the crowds.’Photograph: Scott Barbour/AFL Media/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘We began noticing other ovals around the suburbs packed with people. There were Australian rules footy games, soccer games, children running around, parents standing along the boundary and, almost inevitably, sizzling barbecues doing their part to feed the crowds.’Photograph: Scott Barbour/AFL Media/Getty ImagesOpinionMelbourneOur new life in the suburbs was looking bleak – then came the Saturday morning that changed everythingShadi Khan SaifSlowly, we started to understand that perhaps we hadn’t moved somewhere boring after all – we had simply been looking for excitement in the wrong placesTue 8 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 19.42 EDTShareWhen my family moved into our first suburban house in Melbourne’s south-east, the biggest attraction, at least for me, was the public school directly across the road. With younger kids to think about, it seemed like a sensible choice.Beyond that, though, our new neighbourhood appeared to have very little going on.The better libraries, bigger parks, cinemas and all the other pleasures of city life seemed to require a tiring drive. So we left most of that for the weekends. During the week, we were learning to live with a much slower, quieter suburban way of life. At first, it felt like a bit of a setback.Before moving here, we had become used to the hustle and bustle of city life, and suddenly our evenings seemed unusually long. We missed being able to step outside and find something happening.Then came the first Saturday morning that changed everything.We were sitting on our Afghan carpet in the backyard enjoying our special weekend breakfast when we began hearing loud, persistent cheering coming from the direction of the school. We jumped in the car to find our local oval was packed. Suddenly, our supposedly sleepy little suburb had come alive.There were football games happening one after another, with young children, teenagers, parents, siblings and grandparents filling the sidelines. People were cheering, clapping and shouting encouragement. Every now and then, the cheering turned into passionate complaints directed at the referee.The sporting energy and festive vibe was amazing.My youngest is starting school for the first time. How can I best preserve his relentless curiosity? | Shadi Khan SaifRead moreTeams had travelled from different parts of Melbourne to play, and the oval remained busy for hours. We had originally planned to spend the morning at the library, but by the time we finally left the oval, we realised we had been watching football for much longer than we intended. On our way to the library, we began noticing other ovals around the suburbs similarly packed with people. There were Australian rules footy games, soccer games, children running around, parents standing along the boundary and sizzling barbecues doing their part to feed the crowds.It was a different kind of suburban Melbourne.And, slowly, we started to understand that perhaps we hadn’t moved somewhere boring after all. We had simply been looking for excitement in the wrong places.The excitement was happening on the ovals.The sporting culture gradually became part of our weekends. The kids became increasingly interested. Eventually, my two older boys decided they wanted to join the local soccer club.It was already halfway through the season, so I wasn’t particularly optimistic about finding a place for them. I managed to catch up with Wayne, who was running training sessions for their age group in a nearby club.Wayne was wearing a baggy cap, over-sized jumper and worn-out soccer shoes. He looked like someone who had spent a very large part of his life around football grounds. He told me there were no places left in the team, but he would still accommodate the boys at training and, if an opportunity came up for a game, they could take it from there. He charged no fee at all – that was Wayne. “Ah, you are late, mate,” he said, “but no need to waste money on stuff and fees, just send them over.”Whatever his old-school habits, he had an enormous passion for the game and a genuine commitment to the kids.Then on a Friday night, my jubilant little Socceroos told me that coach Wayne had finally selected them for a game over the weekend. Next, the three of us showed up at the oval in almost ceremonial fashion early in the morning with packed up snacks and brand new pairs of soccer shoes. Throughout the game, Wayne was constantly shouting directions on position and possession from the sidelines: “Why are ya afraid of the ball, mate? Kick it, just kick it!”I loved watching the boys chasing the ball, dribbling and kicking, and although they lost the game, they still cherish that first opportunity to wear the club colours with their mates.Over the following weeks, I have watched their enthusiasm grow. They have started looking forward to training days. They talk about football at home with the fever of the last World Cup still lingering. Their usual screen time favourites have moved from brainrots and Roblox to CR7, Messi and Lamine Yamal videos and soccer skills. I’m thrilled to see their skills improve as they begin to feel they belong here and dream of representing Australia in their own ways and capacities.Shadi Khan Saif is an editor, producer and journalist who has worked in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Germany and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsMelbourneOpinionParents and parentingFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: Here in Liverpool, buses are back under public control – and that’s great for the only people who really matter | Steve Rotheram | The Guardian
description: For decades we were told that privatisation would deliver better services. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story, says Steve Rotheram, mayor of Liverpool city region
Author: Steve Rotheram
Headline: For decades we were told that privatisation would deliver better services. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story, says Steve Rotheram, mayor of Liverpool city region
Content: A Metro bus in Hanover Street, Liverpool, in June.Photograph: Alan Edwards/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Metro bus in Hanover Street, Liverpool, in June.Photograph: Alan Edwards/AlamyOpinionPublic transportHere in Liverpool, buses are back under public control – and that’s great for the only people who really matterSteve RotheramFor decades we were told that privatisation would deliver better services. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different storySteve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city regionTue 8 Sep 2026 08.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTShareOne of the best-known scenes from the TV series The Inbetweeners is the four angst-ridden teenage charactersshouting abuseat people queueing at a bus stop. Only losers take the bus, is the point – except they use a much ruder word. There’s also a statement, misattributed to Margaret Thatcher, that any man over the age of 26 using a bus was a loser. This idea is deeply ingrained.But when I was an MP it became obvious that there wasn’t the same stigma attached to jumping on the bus in London as there often was in other big cities. It often wound me up that the rest of the country was expected to accept a suboptimal public transport system – so much so that it could be joked that only losers would use it – while London retained its excellent bus service, which it ran under public control.And I remember thinking: why can’t we have something like this at home in Liverpool? Well, last weekend Liverpool city region combined authority began to roll back the Thatcherite belief that private was all good, while public was all bad. For the first time in four decades, buses in the Liverpool city region have begun to be brought back under public control,starting in St Helensin Merseyside before spreading across the rest of the region.What does this mean? Instead of private operators deciding where and when buses run, we will set the routes, fares and standards. Our franchised buses will still be operated by third parties. But we will set the rules, decide what kind of network our communities need and hold operators accountable for delivering it. It is the biggest change to public transport in our region for generations. Nobody standing at a bus stop at six in the morning cares about the finer points of franchising legislation. But they do care whether the bus turns up; whether they can get to work on time, get their kids to school or college, or make it to a hospital appointment.Public control means we can start putting passengers first, with more frequent services, more evening and weekend buses, better connections to hospitals and railway stations and simpler fares. And we have kept single bus fares capped at £2, the price they have been for the past four years.Change will be immediate. A new express service now connects St Helens directly withLiverpoolJohn Lennon airport. For a family heading on holiday, that may mean avoiding airport parking charges. For somebody looking to work at the airport, it could open up a job. These changes will make a massive difference to people’s lives.And, for me, that gets to the heart of the argument for public control. A bus route that helps somebody take a job, gets a student to college or allows an older person to remain independent has a value that won’t always show up on an operator’s balance sheet. Markets have their place. But public control allows us to ask not simply, “does this route make money?” but “do our people need it?”That principle doesn’t stop with buses. We have bought a£500m fleet of new trainsand are working towards bringing Merseyrail services intopublic ownership in 2028. In the coming weeks, theRoyal Daffodil– our first new ferry ’cross the Mersey in 60 years, built by a loyal local workforce – will make its maiden voyage.For decades we were told that privatisation and deregulation would inevitably deliver better services and that the government’s job was to get out of the way. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story.When he was mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham and I spent years working together to make that case and show what can be achieved when local leaders have the power to shape the services their communities rely on. Now we have a Labour government bringing our railwaysback into public ownershipandgiving local leaders more powerover the essentials that ordinary people depend on.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter decades in which the state steadily retreated from people’s lives, we have an opportunity to prove that active government can be a force for good again. That is what started in St Helens last weekend.I want the Liverpool city region to have the best public transport system in the country. I want people to come here, get on one of our buses, trains or ferries, see what we have built and go home asking the same question I used to ask in London: why can’t we have this at home?Steve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city regionExplore more on these topicsPublic transportOpinionLiverpoolBus faresLocal governmentTransport policyTransportRail transportcommentShareReuse this content

title: I am sending the assisted dying bill back to the Lords – and this time, peers must do the right thing | Lauren Edwards | The Guardian
description: The will of the elected chamber – and a popular, compassionate piece of legislation – must not be frustrated again by a small minority of peers, says Labour MP for Rochester and Strood Lauren Edwards
Author: Lauren Edwards
Headline: The will of the elected chamber – and a popular, compassionate piece of legislation – must not be frustrated again by a small minority of peers, says Labour MP for Rochester and Strood Lauren Edwards
Content: Dignity in Dying campaigners outside Westminster, London, in April 2026.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDignity in Dying campaigners outside Westminster, London, in April 2026.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockOpinionAssisted dyingI am sending the assisted dying bill back to the Lords – and this time, peers must do the right thingLauren EdwardsThe will of the elected chamber – and a popular, compassionate piece of legislation – must not be frustrated again by a small minority of peersLauren Edwards is the Labour MP for Rochester and StroodTue 8 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTShareIwas elected to Westminster two years ago, when the country was crying out for change and looking to parliament to tackle the big issues that had been forgotten for too long. When that change didn’t come fast enough, trust in politics once again started to ebb away. We have one last chance to prove we can deliver on people’s priorities.Assisted dying didn’t feature in the manifesto I was elected on. Nor should it have done. Matters of conscience such as this are rightly left to individual MPs to decide upon. There will always be a range of views within all political parties. But this issue has been supported by a substantial majority in the country for a very long time. Reputable independent polling has shown support for assisted dying consistently at about 75%. The latest British social attitudes survey from the National Centre for Social Research found that “it is clear we are observing a continued high level of public support for legal change to allow assisted dying in some circumstances”.Having examined the issue with great care, MPs decided in the last session to support the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill. On the Labour benches there was a clear majority in favour, as there was on the Lib Dems’. The Greens supported it unanimously. It is the most pressing, progressive reform of this parliament. But it wasblocked in the Lords earlier this yearby a small minority of peers, led in part by ex-Tory ministers such as Thérèse Coffey and Mark Harper.On Friday, I will be asking MPs to send the bill back to the Lords. There they can amend the bill if they choose, just like any legislation, and if the Commons agrees, that’s fine. But they should not be allowed to frustrate the will of the elected chamber a second time.I am not reopening divisions in the Labour party or in parliament, as some have claimed. Exactly the reverse is true. MPs have already made their decision. In a democracy, we settle our differences by voting on them. Last time, opponents in the Lords prevented a vote taking place on the bill’s provisions.The voters put us here to tackle the big issues they care about, not to constantly kick them down the road. After a shaky start, this parliament has the chance to show that it can deliver; that we won’t shirk our responsibilities and will start to restore the public’s faith in our democratic system.Other major social changes such as a woman’s right to choose and gay rights were bitterly contested at the time. But once passed, the reforms were quickly accepted and ceased to be controversial. It is time to do the same and give terminally ill people the choice to exercise some control over the manner of their deaths. We owe it to them, and to the vast majority of voters who support them, not to sit back and allow a minority of unelected peers to stand in their way.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLauren Edwards is the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood and has reintroduced the terminally ill adults bill in parliamentExplore more on these topicsAssisted dyingOpinionHouse of CommonsHouse of LordscommentShareReuse this content

title: Youth clubs, trade unions, pubs: here’s how Burnham can fix Britain’s social recession | Gordon Brown | The Guardian
description: From volunteering to the WI, we have lost so many ways to meet our neighbours. Making that easier can only be good for society, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Author: Gordon Brown
Headline: From volunteering to the WI, we have lost so many ways to meet our neighbours. Making that easier can only be good for society, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Content: Illustration: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianOpinionCommunitiesYouth clubs, trade unions, pubs: here’s how Burnham can fix Britain’s social recessionGordon BrownFrom volunteering to the WI, we have lost so many ways to meet our neighbours. Making that easier can only be good for societyTue 8 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrime ministerAndy Burnham has hit the ground running, tackling head-on three of the public’s burning concerns: falling standards of living, failing public services and a remote, out-of-touch, over-centralised Whitehall. Now, this autumn, a fourth challenge, reversing the decades-long decline of civic engagement, is about to move centre stage to achieve his ambition to put citizens back in control of their communities.For while there are tens of thousands of local champions bringing towns, cities and villages together, Britain is suffering a civic recession, a hollowing out of the associations, clubs and organisations that once were the beating hearts of our communities.It is a sobering fact that almost50% of British adultsare not members of any community organisation of any kind, neither a civic association nor church nor faith group, nor even a sports club.Trade union membership has halved frommore than 13 million in1979 to less than 7 million in 2025. Then there is the widespread collapse in religious adherence – the fall in Church of Scotland membershipfrom 1.3 million in the 1950sto less than 300,000 today being one of the most dramatic indicators. The long-established Women’s Institute has seen its UK membership fall from a peak of 470,000 in the 1950s to about 170,000 today. Since 2000, the UK has lost about1,200 youth centres. Working men’s clubs – which were once at the centre of industrial communities –have fallenfrom a peak of 4,000 in the 1970s to about 1,800 now, their membership dwindling from 4 million to under 1 million. And the number of pubs in the UK, the heart of many communities, has dropped from 75,000 in the 1960s toabout 45,000 today. For a fleeting moment, the boost in volunteering during the pandemic obscured a drop from 27% of all adults a decade ago tojust 17%now.But the breakdown is not just in formal memberships, but in informal, everyday relationships too: young people in particular are vulnerable, with soaring numbers in England reporting havingno close friends at all.If our physical infrastructure – our roads, railways and airports – broke down, there would be a public outcry and a demand for their immediate repair. If our financial infrastructure collapsed – if cash machines shut down and bank transfers failed – there would be panic. But the breakdown of our civic infrastructure is happening in plain sight and it needs urgent remedy.This change is not unique to Britain. A survey of more than30,000 people in 20 countriesprovides compelling evidence that, in tandem with economic decline, civic decline helps explain the widespread loss of trust, nostalgia for the past and lower levels of tolerance that are the surface manifestations of what is a deep and widespread dissatisfaction with the status quo. It should not be a surprise that many now talk despairingly of a broken society as well as a broken economy.This sense of decline, combined with social isolation and a feeling that “traditional values” have been lost, encourages a zero-sum view of the world: the belief that life is an endless struggle between “us” and “them” – whether “them” is defined as immigrants, foreigners or simply “others”. In this view, our very commitment to democracy and a rules-based international order becomes tenuous: widespread dissatisfaction means that people agitate for their government to exclusively pursue the interests of a narrowly defined population. The fact is that someone who is not involved in their local community and has little contact with people of different ethnicities or religious views ismuch more likelyto support rightwing populist nationalist parties and to oppose cooperation between countries.So No 10’s plans to transfer power from the centre to regions are best seen as what is called a “double devolution”; extending spending and decision-making power beyond local authorities downwards to local communities to empower a new generation of active citizens. But this must be complemented by a boom in civic participation. An opt-out national community service for young people, a remodelledPride in Place programmeto put local people and not politicians in control, legislating participatory budgeting to allocate funding for local services, and designing services to be much more accessible to people should all now be under consideration as part of a nationwide consultation on rebuilding community life.Learning from aDanish lawthat requires municipalities to fund voluntary associations and provide venues for their activities, a UK civic capital fund could go further and guarantee support to all those who want to form or join clubs in their neighbourhoods, with only one stipulation: they are open to all and contribute to the common good. Such a fund could assist with travel, venue hire, membership fees and anything that constitutes a “participation tax”.Promoting civic education and introducing volunteering hours to the school curriculum have proved to be effective, from Ontario,where pupil volunteering is mandatory, to Sweden, where school councils are given real decision-making powers. An Erasmus-style exchange – this time between the nations and regions of the UK – could help young people connect across religious, ethnic and ideological divides.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnlike Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham promises us that things will get better. And we must believe they can | Polly ToynbeeRead moreRecent evidence shows areaswithout quality local newssee the least civic activity and are more prone to online misinformation. So support should be given to local newspapers and websites, including through an expansion of theBBC local democracy reporting service. Online community groups also have a role to play: in my own home town, the Facebook pageLove Kirkcaldyhas nearly 60,000 members – roughly as many as the population of the wider town itself. The page acts as a community noticeboard but also now brings people together face to face in clubs. Such forums help us to better get to know our neighbours, and restore faith and trust in democracy.Between them, measures like these can rebuild an ethic of mutuality and civic obligation. The distinctive feature of a successful community organisation is not just that we belong to it but that it belongs to us. And while governments, local and national, can create the conditions for a stronger civic society, the most effective way to build one is the simple act of one person inviting another person to join in.It is when neighbours no longer talk of “the school”, “the hospital”, “the library” and “the community centre”, or even “my school”, “my hospital”, “my library” and “my community centre”, but instead speak of “our school”, “our hospital”, “our library” and “our community centre”, that we will know a community has been reborn and there is a renewed sense that we are all part of a shared future.Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010The future starts with us:Gordon Brown in conversationOn Thursday 10 September, join Hugh Muir and Gordon Brown to discuss the intricate connections between global instability and civic decline, as explored in Brown’s new book,The Future Starts With Us. title: The byelection here in Holborn and St Pancras is Labour’s to lose. But lose it might | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: The Greens appeal to young and progressive voters here on defence, rent controls and North Sea oil. The Burnham bounce may be about to hit an obstacle, says the Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: The Greens appeal to young and progressive voters here on defence, rent controls and North Sea oil. The Burnham bounce may be about to hit an obstacle, says the Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Green party leader Zack Polanski canvassing in Camden, north London, on Sunday.Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/LNPView image in fullscreenGreen party leader Zack Polanski canvassing in Camden, north London, on Sunday.Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/LNPOpinionByelectionsThe byelection here in Holborn and St Pancras is Labour’s to lose. But lose it mightPolly ToynbeeThe Greens appeal to young and progressive voters here on defence, rent controls and North Sea oil. The Burnham bounce may be about to hit an obstacleTue 8 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTShareYou might think a byelection showdown between two progressive parties is unimportant when the deep struggle for the national heart is between the right bloc and the left – but the result in Holborn and St Pancras matters. It matters for Andy Burnham and Labour because this is a test of the Burnham bounce: he saw off the right inMakerfield– can he win over the left too? Can he show he has enthusiastic approval from voters in southern constituencies as well as those in the north?For the Greensit mattersalmost existentiallybecause failing here could send them and their leader, Zack Polanski, back to the political fringes. Holborn and St Pancras, neighbouring Westminster,was vacated(vengefully) by Keir Starmer last week. This plum forever-Labour constituency has attracted 96 Labour applications for selection day on Wednesday, though not, it seems, nationally recognised names.This is Labour’s to lose. And it might. The constituency was comfortably won in 2024 by Starmer; in May’s local elections the Greens took extra council seats, though Labour kept control andremained ahead by 10 percentage points. But byelections are idiosyncratic beasts in which voters risk nothing, electing neither council nor government. Few bother to turn out. For those who do, a byelection offers a free hit for whimsical preferences, “sending messages” on maverick issues or an urge to biff the government of the day.A Labour loss would dent Burnham’s bounce, letting air out of his optimistic bubble. But frankly, losing here would be no great surprise. Peter Kellner, former president of YouGov and a leading psephologist, lives in this constituency, as do I. While most early opinionmakes Labour the frontrunner, Kellner thinks that underestimates the byelection effect. He expects a Green win in a close call: “This is just the kind of seat a Labour government loses,” he tells me. In a metropolitan district with disproportionately young voters, the left is liberated to protest against anything disappointing in a Labour government.Demographics favour rebellion for a rainbow of reasons in an extraordinarily socially mixed seat. You see vox-poppers choosing its picturesquely famous spots – the pastel houses in Primrose Hillwhere Paddington Bear livesin the films, the bars and cafes of Camden and Kentish Town – as photogenic backdrops to their reports. But, such elegant streets may be deceptive given thatonly a quarterof residents are homeowners, compared with62.5% across England and Wales.Here 43% live in social housing: Camden has a decades-long tradition of good housebuilding, thanks to a well-run council under great social pressure.The constituencyis home to both deprivation and high numbers of graduates; many ABC1 voters and 45% born abroad.Leaflets saying only the Greens, or onlyLabour, can win here are arriving through letterboxes – and it’s true, no one else is likely to. That Polanski is seeking the nomination boosts the Greens. Tot up issues where they challenge Labour, and many resonate with the student population. They oppose nuclear weapons and seem divided over increased defence spending. They back rent controls that Burnham has rejected. They oppose Jackdaw and Rosebank North Sea oil and gas drilling, which may both be approved any day now. They want rapid nationalisation of utilities, where Labour hesitates. Locally they campaign on crime, mobile phone thefts and housing.But it’s Gaza that mayshift votes from Labour to Green: in the 2024 election, Starmer’s vote share was slashed anda pro-Palestinian, independent candidatecame second with18.9% of the vote.Arresting thousandsfor terrorism for silently holding placards supporting Palestine Action is another gift to the Greens. Labour instead points to impossible promises in the party’s£160bn tax, spend and borrowing pledges.The Green campaign asks: “Why elect just another Labour MP, when a Green MP in parliament will challenge the government?” But this week Labour looks set to select not just “another Labour MP” but Sagal Abdi-Wali, Camden council’s leader and community organiser, popular with her party and a well-known dynamic force locally. Green criticism of Labour over Gaza comes up against a hijab-wearing Muslim woman who has spent years calming racial and religions tensions, and building relationships with many Jewish voters here, too. “If Greens stir up community antagonisms over Gaza,” she says to me, “that would be disgraceful”.Reform has no foothold here but its attacks on her from afar may galvanise Labour people to come out and vote. Its poisonous home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf spits out Reform’s usual ethno-nativist bile,pointing out on Xthat Abdi-Wali “was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?” Georgia Gould MP, former Camden council leader, ripostes on X that she “has dedicated her life to public service” and is “the elected leader of Camden council, a community where she grew up and has lived for 35 years” who “embodies the best of our values … an outstanding example of British success”. Telegraph headlines similarly define her primarily as a “Somali refugee”. All this will remind Labour voters that fighting off the racist right is Labour’s great cause.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn the doorstep with Abdi-Wali, in a social housing estate, I saw how she is known and liked for her community work. She takes notes of people’s problems, from housing repairs to e-bikes blocking the road, her local campaign matching Burnham’s localism. But we also meet a college lecturer, who had a run-in with their employer over Gaza, who will “never vote Labour again”. Not for Abdi-Wali? It’s all about Palestine.Nonetheless, Polanski takes a big risk here after sliding in the polls. For Labour, the challenge is to show how Burnham’s raft of positive policies can ward off hopeless wishes and still reach the left with his hopefulness.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsByelectionsOpinionLocal politicsKeir StarmerLabourZack PolanskiGreen partyAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic | Jörg Lau | The Guardian
description: The anti-fascist consensus about our Nazi past is fundamental to German democracy. But that, shockingly, is being shattered, says Jörg Lau, an international correspondent for the German weekly Die Zeit
Author: Jörg Lau
Headline: The anti-fascist consensus about our Nazi past is fundamental to German democracy. But that, shockingly, is being shattered, says Jörg Lau, an international correspondent for the German weekly Die Zeit
Content: A protest in Berlin on Monday after the AfD’s victory in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt.Photograph: Maryam Majd/ReutersView image in fullscreenA protest in Berlin on Monday after the AfD’s victory in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt.Photograph: Maryam Majd/ReutersOpinionGermanyFriedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismicJörg LauThe anti-fascist consensus about our Nazi past is fundamental to German democracy. But that, shockingly, is being shatteredTue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 06.05 EDTShareAs shock at the scale of thefar right’s resounding state-election victoryin Germany reverberated on Sunday, not everybody was unhappy.Seconds after the first exit polls from Saxony-Anhalt were revealed, Donald Trump posted the results on his Truth Social platform, seemingly delighted by the devastation of the centrist-conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the surge of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD).It was indeed a humiliation for the CDU chancellor,Friedrich Merz, whose party lost more than half of its seats in the state parliament, while the AfD increased its count from 23 to 39.This was the exact opposite of what Merz promised to deliver when campaigning for office. With good government under his guidance, he insisted, he would easily cut the AfD in half. The AfD’s co-leaders did not miss the opportunity to point out the historic upset in their victory speeches, with Alice Weidel even boasting the CDU would “never win an election again”.Leaving the AfD’s swagger aside, this is a political earthquake with consequences far beyond a little state in the centre ofGermany. The shock waves are still coming. To begin with, it is unclear if (and for how long) Merz can hold his own coalition together and cling to the chancellorship.True, the losses in the state of Saxony-Anhalt are not directly his fault. But that is only because he is so unpopular that his own party did not want him to campaign. Merz’s face was not on any posters, and when he visited the state capital, Magdeburg, the public was carefully excluded. That says it all about his standing in his own party.Two more elections are coming up on 20 September, in Berlin and the Baltic coastal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. On the current trajectory, the CDU is looking at two more debacles.Merz’s leadership has become a liability, and it will be contested sooner rather than later. For now, only the absence of a convincing alternative and the many constitutional hurdles against sudden leadership changes in Germany protect him.He is the public face of a crisis of confidence in Germany’s leadership, but he is not its sole cause. The seismic nature of this moment goes far beyond party tactics. Germany is entering a period of political upheaval in which the core values of the postwar republic are up for dispute.Most shockingly, this extends to the anti-fascist consensus of “never again”, established over decades in many heated debates on the Holocaust and the crimes of the Wehrmacht. The AfD has managed to attack the national consensus that facing up to the Nazi past is fundamental for democracy in Germany. The party’s message is the opposite: the culture of remembrance is an “identity disorder” holding Germany back. It’s a central tenet of the AfD’s platform that it can “heal” the country by relativising its guilt and focusing on German greatness instead.This is why Charlotte Knobloch, a 93-year-old Holocaust survivor and former chair of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, expressed “horror” about the results.Knobloch said she “struggled, on days like these, to recognise my homeland”, adding: “In my worst nightmares, I could not have imagined that rightwing extremists win elections again in this manner.” She is right to be alarmed. The Saxony-Anhalt state chapter of the AfD isconfirmed by domestic intelligenceto be among the most radical nationally. Hardcore former neo-Nazis sit in influential positions.A distinctive trait of Germany’s far right compared with France or Italy is often overlooked. The AfD is markedly different from other rightwing populist parties in Europe: it is becoming ever-more radical the closer it gets to power.The leadership in Magdeburgemploys several former membersof prohibited neo-Nazi groups. These people might soon serve in high offices in the state, controlling the police, the domestic spy service (Verfassungsschutz), the judiciary and education. It’s a sign of the deterioration of political norms in my country that this shocking outlook hardly figured in the aftermath of the election. The German taboo about hard-right extremists in executive office is crumbling.The AfD slogans against the mainstream parties (“Altparteien”) have a distinctly Weimar vibe, echoing hateful propaganda against the despised “system” from a century ago. It is no coincidence that books on the end of the Weimar republic are bestsellers these days.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe AfD is not a normal party. It must be understood as a (counter)revolutionary movement trying to change the system from within. Its leaders’ ambitions go beyond this or that policy change. Look at the crucial topic of migration: the number of asylum applications is rapidly falling (down by 48% in July 2026 compared with the same month last year), partly due to restrictive measures by Merz’s government.Still, the hard right is growing and radicalising at the same time. At the core is the idea of a German ethnostate with as few foreigners as possible. The party’s rallying cry of “remigration” targets not just “illegals” but all immigrants (and their descendants) with unwanted foreign backgrounds.The leadership have coined a term for what they do not want to become: they vow to avoid “Melonisierung” (Meloni-isation). Giorgia Meloni, despite her neo-fascist roots, surprised many at home and abroad bymoving towards the mainstream, by standing with Ukraine and supporting the eurozone, Nato and the principle of free movement within the EU.The AfD, by contrast, promisesto leave the EU and eurozoneand put an end to the Schengen agreement. It is fiercely pro-Russian and wants to cut any support for Ukraine (including sending refugees back). Fear of escalation with Russia played a big part in the election. The recent hybrid attacks on Leipzig airport and other infrastructuremay have tipped the scales: Merz had pointed a finger at Russia and vowed to “make the perpetrators pay”. This turned out to be perfect fodder for the AfD’s campaign. Abandoning Ukraine, rapprochement with Russia, reopening the Nord Stream pipeline in the Baltic – all this was presented as a “policy of peace”. This is also an election win for Vladimir Putin.What’s next? Without an absolute majority, the AFD may depend on the cooperation of a tiny splinter party. The leadership of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which broke away from the hard-left Die Linke, may want to help. They represent a new brand of leftist nationalism which is fiercely anti-immigrant and pro-Russian – and in that sense compatible with the AfD. Still, forming a government in Magdeburg will not be plain sailing. And it is a long way from this point for the AfD to take Berlin.One glimmer of light is that civil society is mobilising, now the initial shock has worn off. We can expectbig demonstrations in major cities. A silent anti-fascist majority is beginning to organise. But it will be hard to break the dark spell that this victory in a troubled state has cast over the political landscape in Germany.One thing is certain: the coming weeks will be a challenge to the political imagination, not just for Germans.Jörg Lau is an international correspondent for the German weekly Die ZeitDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightEuropeFriedrich MerzcommentShareReuse this content

title: Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal man | Movies | The Guardian
description: Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentary
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentary
Content: Charmless … Musk at a Trump campaign event in 2024.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenCharmless … Musk at a Trump campaign event in 2024.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APMoviesReviewMusk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manVenice film festival:Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentaryPeter Bradshawin VeniceTue 8 Sep 2026 08.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Elon is a nuke.” The speaker is Ashley St Clair, a former conservative Maga influencer and one of Elon Musk’s former girlfriends-slash-baby mommas.She is a fascinating expert witness in Alex Gibney’s four-hour epic study of the world’s richest and dullest man: the overgrown brattish South-African-born trillionaire plutocrat, ersatz visionary and Trump courtier who owns Tesla cars, SpaceX rocket ships, Starlink satellites on which nation states’ military capabilities are increasingly reliant, X (formerly Twitter) which shapes the collective “incel” id of billions and GrokAI whose vast server farms daily guzzle oceans of precious water.State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmRead moreAs head of Trump’s incompetent cost-cutting Doge (Department of Government Efficiency) unit, Musk actually increased the US deficit by sacking thousands of revenue officers whose job was to rake in tax – while reportedlyaccessing and improperly sharing Americans’ sensitive social security data.He does indeed look like a nuke, efficiently designed, destructive, seemingly unguided and uncontrolled.Gibney’s excellent film covers a lot of ground in its extraordinary story, although we don’t get to hear about the mysterious process that changed a balding youngster into a follicularly unchallenged mature man.Musk is a uniquely disquieting baseball-capped figure, grinning and giggling and smirking on a thousand sycophantic podcasts like a modern, hyper-evolved version of Anthony Trollope’s wealthy charlatan Augustus Melmotte in The Way We Live Now. But given Musk’s boyish love of space travel and sci-fi, Gibney wittily compares him to the hero of the 1936 film version of HG Wells’s The Man Who Could Work Miracles about godlike space aliens who capriciously confer supernatural powers on a banal, ordinary earthling.Gibney doesn’t get to talk to Musk (or Trump) though in the spirit of Musk’s AI interests, he creates a photorealistic CG avatar who mouths all the things the man himself is reported as saying (a rather contrived visual joke, actually, which the film didn’t need). He speaks to many professional colleagues, and to Musk’s formidably opinionated father Errol Musk who fills us in on Elon’s formative years in the tense world of South Africa in which young Musk was bullied and beaten up.Gibney speaks to Musk’s first wife Justine Musk (née Wilson), a passionate and intelligent woman who tells us about the tragedy of one of their infant children dying of Sids and then the hurt she felt when Elon felt the need to grandstand about this on social media, claiming the child had died in his arms (it was her arms, she says). And given that heart-wrenching death, how crass it was for him to announce later on social media that his trans daughter had “died” of “woke mind virus”. Much later, Musk showed a creepy enthusiasm for procreating many children with various women; Musk reportedlybuilt compounds for his extended familieslike something from The Handmaid’s Tale.Back in the 90s as a pushy, bright young tech innovator, Musk had started out by inventing and selling an online Yellow Pages-type site, got involved in Peter Thiel’s PayPal and cleaned up again when this was sold to eBay. He got involved in the electric automobile industry, giving us Teslas, whilemisleading the public about their range.Big tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?Read moreHis SpaceX adventure and his preposterous and ignorant effusions about colonising Mars were spectacular advertisements for his personal brand – so important for inflating stock market valuation – especially when he did indeed invent rockets that could be landed and re-used. But the question of how and when these rockets will carry us to inhabitable planets remains unanswered. Both his cars and his rocket ships got him on the receiving end of millions of dollars of federal money and lines of credit.And at the beginning of the 21st century he was still the darling of the liberal world and the Obama administration for an apparently compelling eco-vision for non-fossil-fuel cars.All this changed when Joe Biden seemed to be casting a cold eye on Musk’s businesses, and Musk went all in on promoting Trump 2.0 in 2024 and was rewarded with that grotesque Doge sinecure, damaging American public finances –from which he had benefited so lavishly.What is so absorbing about Gibney’s documentary is that it has the structure and rhetoric of a film that could be about, say, Elizabeth Holmes, disgraced inventor of the phoney blood-test, or Sam Bankman-Fried, the cryptocurrency fraudster, or Billy McFarland, promoter of the Fyre festival. All of these were media darlings in their day, supposed visionaries and feted disrupters, talking the talk in front of saucer-eyed believers.Unlike these illusionists Musk does have actual palpable success, with Tesla being a long-standing profitable company and Space X, among other things inventing successful re-usable rockets, allied with a skill they don’t have in moving on from commodity to commodity, while controlling the means of production in social media and cultivating the presidency.
