Just as well because, if Musk were ever to fall, it would truly send shock waves through Wall Street, Washington and Silicon Valley.Explore more on these topicsFilmElon MuskDocumentary filmsAlex GibneyDonald TrumpVenice film festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A constipated baby and a kid that looks like Boris Johnson: why would anyone bother stealing a Renoir? | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The chocolate boxiest of all the impressionists has long had his haters – even Manet thought he was rubbish. Little surprise then that the thieves ditched two works on the way out
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: The chocolate boxiest of all the impressionists has long had his haters – even Manet thought he was rubbish. Little surprise then that the thieves ditched two works on the way out
Content: ‘For the most part, the haters are right’ … Coco Lisant, 1905, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘For the most part, the haters are right’ … Coco Lisant, 1905, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: AlamyArt and designA constipated baby and a kid that looks like Boris Johnson: why would anyone bother stealing a Renoir?The chocolate boxiest of all the impressionists has long had his haters – even Manet thought he was rubbish. Little surprise then that the thieves ditched two works on the way outEddy FrankelTue 8 Sep 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStealing from the Louvre you can understand. I mean, who wouldn’t want a Géricault or Leonardo to hang in the downstairs loo? Same for the Musée d’Orsay too, even the Pompidou – they’re French museums absolutely rammed full of stunning art, all just begging to be audaciously heisted. But the Renoir Museum? It’s hard to see why anyone would bother.As French art fans reel at the news thattwo Renoir paintings were stolen from the Cagnes-sur-Mer museumthat bears his name this week, the rest of the art world has been saying really? Him? Renoir? He’s … awful. It’s like doing a heist of flares in the era of skinny jeans.Did the thieves know something the rest of us don’t? Or was this just a crime of opportunity, taking advantage of a regional art museum with shonky security?View image in fullscreenShonky security … police outside the gates of the Renoir Museum.Photograph: MAXPPP/AlamyPierre-Auguste Renoir was one of impressionism’s head honchos, a leading figure in one of 19th-century art’s most important movements. But time hasn’t been too kind to poor old Pierre. Where his contemporaries like Monet, Cézanne and Degas have been heralded as modernist revolutionaries, artists who shaped the future of western painting and helped set the path that all of their successors would soon follow, in recent years Renoir has been denigrated, mocked, protested and hashtagged.In 2015, a group who called themselvesRenoir Sucks at Paintingpicketed the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, and then protested outside the Met in New York, with placards that read “God Hates Renoir” and “ReNOir”, demanding the museums remove his work from display. And they had their sympathisers: the hashtag #RenoirSucksatPainting trended soon after, they sold hundreds of anti-Renoir T-shirts, and their Instagram was full of photos of people giving the finger to Renoir paintings or pretending to vomit in front of them.View image in fullscreenKitsch and chintziness … Renoir.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesAnd his crime? Kitsch and chintziness. His work is soft focus and gentle, his figures are plump and joyful, it’s all happy haze and night-time revelry. He lacks the hard-edged absolute dedication to angular, prismatic experimentation that made the impressionists so famous. He is the safest of the group, the chocolate boxiest, the easiest, the horniest. And that has made him the most hated.It’s not a new thing. Even his contemporaries disliked him. Édouard Manet said he had “no talent” and Mary Cassatt described his paintings of women as “the most awful of all”. Add to all of that a hefty dose of antisemitism (he refused to take part in exhibitions that featured Jewish impressionist Camille Pissarro), a big pinch of misogyny, and you’ve got a recipe of aesthetic distaste that can last centuries.However in PR terms, the timing of this latest in a long string of French art robberies couldn’t be better. The National Gallery is opening their majorRenoir and Loveexhibition next month, a show they hope will have the same blockbuster success it had at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris this summer.I want to defend Renoir, if only for the sake of debate, but I’ve hated his work for decades. I like him when he’s weird, when his nudes look like a super-psychedelic, ultra-horny version of Rubens with endless, surreal, undulating rolls of pink flesh. And I like a lot of his hazy, strange landscapes, though not as much as the work of any other impressionist. But for the most part, the haters are right.View image in fullscreenSoft focus … left, detail from Madame Colonna Romano; right, detail from Jeune Femme au Puits.Composite: Musée d’OrsayI mean look at the works the thieves made off with after cutting through the fence with bolt cutters in the early hours of the morning. The first isPortrait of Madame Colonna Romano, her tiny head dwarfed by shoulders so vastly broad she could play rugby for Saracens, all watched over by a tiny painting-within-a-painting of a constipated looking baby. The other,Jeune Femme au Puits, is an unfinished smudge of a woman pulling a bucket out of a well. An art detective said the thieves would “have no idea what to do” with the paintings, well, they probably have some idea, and it involves the dustbin.The best bit about this week’s heist on the Côte d’Azur is that the thieves actually took four paintings, but decided to leave two behind as they ran for it, including a portrait of a little boy who looks almost exactly like Boris Johnson. In all my years as an art critic, I’ve never managed a piece of criticism as incisive, cutting and direct as a bunch of criminals looking at a painting that they’d already nicked and thinking “leave it – it’s not worth it”.Explore more on these topicsArt and designArtPierre-Auguste RenoirArt theftFranceEuropeMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mr T: I Pity the Fool review – a rare chance with an electrifying star … and they blew it  | Television | The Guardian
description: The former A-Team legend tells his extraordinary story with endless charisma, but this show is so rushed that they even misspell his name. No wonder he isn’t happy with it
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The former A-Team legend tells his extraordinary story with endless charisma, but this show is so rushed that they even misspell his name. No wonder he isn’t happy with it
Content: A-Team player … Mr. T: I Pity the Fool.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenA-Team player … Mr. T: I Pity the Fool.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewMr T: I Pity the Fool review – a rare chance with an electrifying star … and they blew itThe former A-Team legend tells his extraordinary story with endless charisma, but this show is so rushed that they even misspell his name. No wonder he isn’t happy with itLucy ManganTue 8 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere’s a question: when was the last time you had as good a time as when you were watching The A-Team as a child? I know.Many of the best moments of the wholly unexpected documentary Mr T: I Pity the Fool recall his legendary turn as the soldiers of fortunes’ genius engineer, pugilist and instant fan favourite (not that we used the phrase then) BA Baracus. According to Mr T, the show was built around him; when you see now how well it plays to his talents and charisma – a proper tough guy, but shot through with warmth and humour, giving a perfectly outsize performance and never overplaying his hand – it makes a lot of sense, however much it would annoy George “Hannibal” Peppard to hear it.Mr T is now 74. Iknow. He looks a bit older, but the charisma is absolutely intact. He sits alone in a darkened room, occasionally being played old footage of his career’s highlights and lowlights, dressed in a stars-and-stripes boiler suit and bandana. You cannot take your eyes off him.Watch the trailer for the documentary.He has done very few public interviews since his heyday, but the clips they show from that period are electrifying, especially his thrillingly uncompromising one with David Letterman in which he unsmilingly explains his look to the increasingly cowed host. The Mohawk-style haircut and feathered earrings honour his African Mandinka warrior heritage. The gold chains are a transmutation of the shackles his ancestors were put in. He doesn’t get involved in “Black exploitation movies – no dope-dealing movies, no pimp roles … Give me the type of role you’d give Charlton Heston.” The audience laughs, not uneasily, missing and making his point.At the same time, his rise to fame and riches has an inescapably “only in America” feel to it. He was born Laurence Tureaud (spelled Tero throughout the documentary), one of 12 children to his loving and beloved mother Willa Lee, and brought up in an impoverished housing project in Chicago. He and his brothers worked on their fitness together – by the time he was 15, he already looked like an athlete-cum-bodybuilder.He renamed himself Mr T “so that the first word out of people’s mouths was always ‘Mister’”, after watching his father and brothers – including a Vietnam veteran – being habitually addressed as “Boy”. When his mother was robbed by local “thugs”, he went looking for them; although the story is left unfinished, it is implied that he carried out some serious physical damage. If so, it was a rare lapse in what seems to have been an otherwise hugely disciplined life.‘I don’t chase the dollar. I never did’: the astonishing hidden life of Mr TRead moreHe worked three manual jobs until bouncing gave way to bodyguarding and an entree into the world of television, which led to him being spotted by Sylvester Stallone and cast as the antagonist Clubber Lang in Rocky III. He turned up word-perfect to the audition – discipline again – met the ad-libbing requirements and worked on the accent the part originally required. The film was a hit – and so was Mr T.Then came The A-Team, enormous popularity and wealth (Mr T commercials and merch was everywhere), an almost inevitable inflation of ego – and then, in the mid-90s, a cancer diagnosis that, along with his increasing demands, caused his star to wane. Since then, he has become a man of God and finds fulfilment in good works and preaching.That, at least, is how the documentary tells it. In the accompanying publicity tour, Mr T has made clear that he finds the filmdishonest and unfair. He says that he wasn’t forced but chose to step out of the limelight, having fulfilled his ambition to set his mother up in comfort for the rest of her days. As a child, he had promised her a house and pretty dresses. “If that’s the lord’s willing,” she replied.Other objections include the time given to his former agent Peter Young (whom he says he had to sue and who is the main contributor of claims about Mr T’s diva behaviour and “bad decisions” professionally) compared with his longtime pastor, the Rev Henry Hardy, and the omission of counterweights to the hardman narrative.It is certainly a small, slight documentary. In a 50-minute runtime, some omissions are to be expected, but even without knowing about its subject’s resulting displeasure, the emphasis on the violent incident reads oddly and the misspelling of his name raises questions about the quality of the research. There is a sense of eagerness with which the picture of Mr T as a monstrous egomaniac is painted. At best, it feels like a rushed job. At worst, it feels like the imposition of another negative narrative on a Black man by fools who are more to be censured than pitied.Mr T: I Pity the Fool is available on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We all have an expiry date’: Kimberly Akimbo, the achingly funny musical about a teen with a 64-year-old body | Musicals | The Guardian
description: The uplifting, award-winning show about a girl aging four times too fast electrified New York. As it hits the UK, co-creator Jeanine Tesori talks about being inspired by the Aids crisis and all her friends who died young
Author: Emma John
Headline: The uplifting, award-winning show about a girl aging four times too fast electrified New York. As it hits the UK, co-creator Jeanine Tesori talks about being inspired by the Aids crisis and all her friends who died young
Content: ‘Your one wild and precious life?’ … Maria Friedman and Gilli Jones in Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreen‘Your one wild and precious life?’ … Maria Friedman and Gilli Jones in Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerMusicalsInterview‘We all have an expiry date’: Kimberly Akimbo, the achingly funny musical about a teen with a 64-year-old bodyEmma JohnThe uplifting, award-winning show about a girl aging four times too fast electrified New York. As it hits the UK, co-creator Jeanine Tesori talks about being inspired by the Aids crisis and all her friends who died youngTue 8 Sep 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJeanine Tesori is thinking about her mother back home in the US. “She’s 95,” says the composer, “and she’s not been well. But she would look in the mirror and be like, ‘I can’t believe I’m old.’ It’s always a surprise, always. There’s an interiority about ageing, especially as women. You stay playful and you stay curious, but the world has other ideas.”Ageing – and growing up, which is not necessarily the same thing – are a central consideration in the musical that Tesori has been rehearsing. Kimberly Akimbo, which the composer developed with David Lindsay-Abaire from his play, follows a teenage girl with a rare genetic condition that causes her to age at four times the normal rate. Its London debut stars the 66-year-old Maria Friedman as Kimberly. “And she has such a bright young energy,” says Tesori as we chat in a rough-and-ready rehearsal room in London, “that she doesn’t have to do anything to play 16.”double quotation markMy dad was a man of science who really wanted to be a fisherman. He wanted sons and got daughtersIf a story about a girl with a life-shortening condition sounds like a tragedy, don’t be fooled. Kimberly Akimbo is a comedy about a chaotic family (from a hypochondriac mother to a criminal aunt) and a tender teenage romance. Uplifting and achingly funny, the original New York production was the biggest winner of the 2023 Tony awards. Tesori watched the London cast rehearse its bittersweet ending with her lips zipped firmly shut: “David and I know the show so well that we have to just let people interpret it their own way.”For Tesori, a protagonist who knows she may not reach adulthood raises the question of how we use our time. “We all have an expiry date,” she says, recalling the line from Mary Oliver’s poem, The Summer Day:what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life? “I lost so many friends during the Aids crisis. I’m from that generation of watching these incredible people, mostly men, disappear. You become aware of how you live.”At 64, her own life looks a fulfilled one: mother, teacher, legend of her industry. Her compositional dexterity and range, combined with an extraordinary ability to turn playwrights into lyricists and librettists, has produced everything from fun-packedBroadwayshows (Thoroughly Modern Millie, Shrek), to complex, thought-provoking musicals (Soft Power, Caroline, or Change) and avant garde operas about police racism, drone pilots, and Eugene O’Neill’s marital rows.“Everybody knows she’s a brilliant composer,” says Lindsay-Abaire, when he swings by rehearsals during lunch. “But she’s also one of the most insightful dramatists – she understands story structure and character and things that not all composers do or are even interested in.”What Tesori’s projects have in common is her laser-sharp focus on emotional truth, be it in the powerfully orchestral blues and spirituals of Caroline, or Change – or the intimately interwoven harmonies and counterpoint of the three-handed chamber piece, Fun Home. Aproductionof that last one – an adaptation of Alison Bechdel’s celebrated autobiographical graphic novel – ran at Manchester’s Royal Exchange Theatre this summer and its director, Sarah Frankcom, calls it “a masterpiece”, adding: “Jeanine is able to express moments of profound change in people, in what is a very spare musical. The motifs coalesce and consolidate and lead you towards a last 15 minutes that are absolutely shattering.”View image in fullscreen‘We both like inappropriate comedy’ …Jeanine Tesori and David Lindsay-Abaire during rehearsals for Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerTesori admits she’s drawn to dad-daughter stories, which are at the heart of Fun Home, Caroline, or Change and Kimberly Akimbo. Her own father died more than 20 years ago, but “the story lives on, and I think it helps me process – you try to answer the unanswerable question. My father was a very complicated man: a man of science who really wanted to be a fisherman. He wanted a simple life and he got anything but; he wanted sons and he got daughters.”Tesori’s upbringing in a chaotic, multi-generational Italian family helped inspire some of Kimberly Akimbo’s scenes. (Her three sisters sound a hoot: not long ago one of them stole a picnic table from a park in broad daylight to prove that older women are invisible). It also played its part in her musical development. Tesori’s grandfather was a band arranger and violist who emigrated from Sicily – she still has his baton – and one of her sisters played piano while another had a vast record collection. “We listened to everybody from Stevie Wonder and Aretha Franklin to the Stones and the Beatles, Led Zeppelin, Carole King. Cat Stevens was huge in our house.”That breadth of repertoire – encouraged by her first piano teacher – led Tesori outside the confines of classical academe, and fostered a musical versatility that has become the hallmark of her career. A recent trip to Jesus Christ Superstar blew her away, although she says it can be hard to relax and enjoy musical performances because her brain insists on analysing the scores. Instead, she has spent these weeks dipping into plays and comedy in off-West End and fringe venues: “That’s my favourite kind of theatre, to go in not knowing anything and just discover it.”View image in fullscreen‘Jeanine is able to express moments of profound change in people’ … Harriet O’Shea and Alex Young in Fun Home.Photograph: Johan PerssonWhat about Broadway, whichAndrew Lloyd Webberrecently pronounced to be “in dire danger”? Tesori says she finds the capitalisation of its business models “scary” and feels a responsibility to find solutions for its increasing costs. “My job is to make things work better than when I leave – that’s the job of everybody who has been rewarded by the industry. When I started doing shows they were tearing Broadway houses down, because there were not enough shows to fill them. So I’ve always heard this chorus of ‘Broadway’s in trouble’, but for different reasons.”She is a dedicated mentor (“I take that job seriously”) at a time when performing arts space in the US is being threatened and politicised. “It’s really frustrating,” she says, “and it’s very easy to feel hopeless. But I don’t. You could throw up your hands – but our job is to write.” She typically has three to four projects on the go, and has recently been researching a story in Naples, but never writes music for anything she doesn’t believe in. “Any show I do is going to be five years of concentrated work. That’s like graduate school plus a year. If I don’t understand it, I can’t say yes to it.”She adds: “I love working with playwrights who are looking at the global conversation.” And her deep friendship with Lindsay-Abaire is obvious. “We both have a similar sense of humour,” he says. “We like dark, inappropriate comedy, which is why this show is funny and sad at the same time.”Kimberly Akimbo is atHampstead theatre, London, until 7 NovemberThis article was amended on 8 September 2026. In an earlier version, the recent production of Fun Home at Manchester Royal Exchange was referred to as the first time it had been performed in the UK. In fact, it was performed at the Young Vic, in London, in 2018.Explore more on these topicsMusicalsTheatreBroadwayWest EndHampstead theatreAgeinginterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cantona’s a Kwengletarian!’ Inside the maximalist, magical mentality of rising London Irish rapper Kibo | Music | The Guardian
description: The masterful ​Harrow MC behind the year’s funniest, most inventive UK rap debut explains how his parents sparked his ravenous outlook – and why he’s wrestling his peers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The masterful ​Harrow MC behind the year’s funniest, most inventive UK rap debut explains how his parents sparked his ravenous outlook – and why he’s wrestling his peers
Content: ‘I ain’t fucking bluffing / You’re not a bad boy, you’re an Egg McMuffin’ … Kibo.Photograph: SwurlaView image in fullscreen‘I ain’t fucking bluffing / You’re not a bad boy, you’re an Egg McMuffin’ … Kibo.Photograph: SwurlaMusicInterview‘Cantona’s a Kwengletarian!’ Inside the maximalist, magical mentality of rising London Irish rapper KiboHugh MorrisThe masterful ​Harrow MC behind the year’s funniest, most inventive UK rap debut explains how his parents sparked his ravenous outlook – and why he’s wrestling his peersTue 8 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 12.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew Guinnesses into an interview in his local Irish boozer, and 26-year-old Harrow rapper Kibo is cooking. We’re talking football. As a kid, he preferred playing Fifa Street – where ordinary players backflip off walls to score incomprehensible bicycle kicks – to regular realistic Fifa. “If I’m gonna play a video game, I want to do some shit I can’t do in real life,” he says. He’s drawn to similarly miraculous footballers:Balotelli, Drogba in his Chelsea days, Ronaldinho and his dad’s favourite, Eric Cantona: “Oh God, with his collar popped, looking like Kanye West?” Kibo then recites Cantona’s2019 Uefa president’s award speech– a mash-up of King Lear and philosophical musings on war and science – to near perfection.Magic is at the heart of Kwengletarianism, “the idea of being in a place that’s very grey, and trying to find a prismatic iridescence in it”, that underpins Kibo’s sensational album Kwengletaria: Ragamyff. (Cantona? “He’s a Kwengletarian to the nth degree.”) During his long rise through London’s rap scene, canonised by co-signs from Skepta, JME and Dave, Kibo has become a rare MC from Harrow, the town that produced Kate Nash and Jai Paul but no rappers of note. “It’s awesome,” he says of its lack of rap tradition, “a complete blank slate” to be as imaginative as he wants. Kwengletaria finds the myth in the mundane: on the track Bakerloo Dragon, a normal tube journey becomes a cruising broken-beat roller aboard a fire-spitting Bakerloo line train. I tell him my train to Harrow was one of these flame-graffitied dragons. “But did you get any sparks?” he asks enthusiastically. “You get sparks after Stonebridge Park!”We meet midweek, and Kibo tells me he’s heading to a wrestling match in Dublin at the weekend. I ask him who he’s watching. “No,I’mwrestling,” he fires back: he’s up against Irish rapper Lil Skag, “to see who really is ready to hold the responsibility of being the champion of Ireland”. Kibo is 6ft 4in tall, possessing Irish heritage, a goatee, a mane of hair straight from a fantasy film, and a sackful of devastatingly rude bars: “I’ll take your mum Butlin’s / And I ain’t fucking bluffing / You’re not a bad boy, you’re an Egg McMuffin.” You’d back him to win a match on aura alone.Add in references to anime, Pokémon, chicken shops and X-wing fighters, combine it with 16 producers making beats spanning garage, R&B, donk, grime and jungle, and you get a sense of Kwengletaria: Ragamyff’s scale. “I’m quite a maximalist guy, and a lot of the artists that I gravitate towards – Ghostface Killah, MF Doom, Yung Lean – it’s all about asking, how much can you stuff into one thing?” he says.The all-you-can-eat impulse comes from growing up online – “I was a kid with a million tabs open, trying to speak with a level of eloquence” – and the Kwelengletarianism concept stems from when Kibo’s schoolmates began trading pirated Yu-Gi-Oh! cards. “They would slap even more glitter and shine on it, to make it look like it was the most valuable shit ever,” he says. “Like, I know this is fake, but this shit looks awesome. It’s the first thing I remember in my life where I was looking at something and knowing it was valuable.”Kibo nods to his grime forebears on the album, sampling from Dizzee Rascal’s Boy in da Corner on closer Our War Game. “My absorption of grime was very retroactive,” he says. “Going back into Dizzee, Flirta D, Skepta, and D Double E … even though it was very local, it felt like discovering Three 6 Mafia, or old Memphis rap: like, this is awesome, but it’s nothere.” Where those older acts felt remote to Kibo, Novelist, the Lewisham MC behind grime’s modern resurgence and Kwengletaria’s only guest, was “the first time I was able to tune into grime sets live and feel like I was present for this thing,” Kibo says. “It’s always felt like he was bringing grime backandpushing it forward.”View image in fullscreen‘Charm from ma, swag from dad’ … Kibo.Photograph: SwurlaWhat’s impressive is how clear, satisfying and relentlessly funny Kibo’s path through the melee is. He shouts out Fiona Templeton, an academic at Brunel University (where he got a first in film, drama and media) for giving him a word for what he was doing: hyperdiction. “It was like someone showed me a brain scan,” he says. These collisions – of genres, references and words – create a new meta-language of smashed together non sequiturs in his work, such as “Courvoir-Sierra Leone”, or “Dimitar Burberrytov”. They’re also stamina-boosting power-ups. On Chancer, the album’s midpoint mellow grime flexer, Kibo’s criss-cross patterns unfold over three beat switches and five relentless verses.On Bakerloo Dragon, Kibo says he gets the “charm from ma, and the swag from dad”. Eileen of Limerick fell swiftly in love with John, a drummer from Harrow, when he was over in Ireland for a holiday. They navigated a two-year long-distance relationship before she moved to England. “There was one phone box in her whole village, so it would be like, ‘You must be here at 7 o’clock.’ My dad used to work at the BT phone line so he was able to wrangle a few things.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I’ve rebranded as a stoic. It’s my ting now!’ The crime and punishment of Pozer, UK rap’s fastest, fiercest talentRead moreIt made Kibo a true believer in romance. “It’s Kwengletarianism!” he says. “You’ve got to believe in something, you’ve got to believe there’s light at the end of the tunnel.” Kibo is a third generation member of Harrow’s Irish community, and there’s a distinctly Irish feeling to a project about belief, myths, good craic and finding the magic in ordinary objects.Kwengletaria: Ragamyff is about celebrating where you’re from, but it’s also about feeling stuck in a place that, once the iridescent sheen has faded, is still grey and boring. Off the back of the album, and a medley of viral live clips, Kibo has his sights set beyond Harrow. “I feel like I finally got a grip of London. [The track] Red Starz is like, I’ve completed London, right? It’s almost like the post-credit scene is Ryanair: oh shit, there’s 200 other countries? Damn. There’s a crunch point there, between leaving home and returning. But if you find the magic and the pride in your base, you can always come back to that and recharge. Home is like your charging point.”Kibo plays Bristol (28 October), London (30 Oct) and Manchester (1 November)Explore more on these topicsMusicRapinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Monty Don is quitting Gardeners’ World – and you’re right to be devastated about it | Factual TV | The Guardian
description: Handsome, charming and vulnerable, the host made horticulture TV hotter than ever. What a huge hole he will leave
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Handsome, charming and vulnerable, the host made horticulture TV hotter than ever. What a huge hole he will leave
Content: The best to ever do it … Monty Don on Gardeners' World.Photograph: BBC StudiosView image in fullscreenThe best to ever do it … Monty Don on Gardeners' World.Photograph: BBC StudiosFactual TVMonty Don is quitting Gardeners’ World – and you’re right to be devastated about itHandsome, charming and vulnerable, the host made horticulture TV hotter than ever. What a huge hole he will leaveStuart HeritageTue 8 Sep 2026 08.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter 23 years at the helm, Monty Don has announced that he is leaving Gardeners’ World at the end of the series. All said, you are right to be distraught about it.Gardeners’ World is a show with a long history – it was commissioned by David Attenborough as a way to showcase the potential of colour television – but Don arguably did the show better than anyone. Under his watch, the show and the host managed to mesh perfectly. He became it and it became him.Don’s strength was that he approached the show as a self-taught gardener. This meant that it suddenly became more welcoming to newcomers and outsiders who had possibly been a little intimidated by the show.Monty Don steps down from BBC’s Gardeners’ World after 23 yearsRead moreThis was a masterstroke. Previously, watching an episode could be like trying to download a horticulture encyclopedia all in one go, but Don – who always primarily viewed himself as a writer – was able to talk about gardening in more emotional and philosophical terms. Under him, the “why” of gardening became more important than the “how”.Nevertheless, it took a while for him to bed in. After a minor stroke took him out of action after five years in the job, he returned having made the decision to present from his own home, Longmeadow in Herefordshire. This changed everything. It meant that, instead of seeing gardening happen in the abstract, we watched it happen to him. Over the years, audiences saw Longmeadow develop season after season. Sometimes the garden flourished. Sometimes it failed. But whatever happened, it strengthened the bond between viewer and host immeasurably.A lot of this is down to Don’s presence as a host. Much has been made about how handsome and charming he is – when I met him last year,during the recording of an AI Michael Parkinson podcast that bewildered us both, there was no denying that he was either – but as he grew older, it was Don’s vulnerability that appealed the most. He became more used to silence, and was unafraid to express his uncertainties. Under his watch, Gardeners’ World became a programme about patience and resilience. Little wonder it surged in popularity during the pandemic.View image in fullscreenHe became it and it became him … Monty Don in his cottage garden at Longmeadow.Photograph: BBC StudiosNeedless to say, talk will soon turn to Don’s successor. This is a role that needs to be chosen carefully, because this is a job for as much of your life as you are willing to give it. Although some presenters have enjoyed shorter stints – the original host Ken Burras lasted one year, while Arthur Billett managed three in the 1970s – Gardeners’ World is a programme that is at its best when it is given the space to unfurl according to the sensibilities of the person in charge.Nobody typifies this more than Don, who took a show that had subtly increased in pitch and frequency under Alan Titchmarsh and went about making it earthier and ever so slightly more romantic. Before Titchmarsh, of course, the show had been in the hands of Geoff Hamilton, who lasted almost as long as Don did.Fortunately, Gardeners’ World isn’t Top Gear. The BBC will be keenly aware that the last thing it should do is hand the programme over to someone big and starry, who’ll get bored and drift away after a few months.The better bet is to recruit from within. Adam Frost has already presented episodes by himself, and is now in the middle of creating a garden from a blank canvas on the show. Then there’s Frances Tophill, who could approach from a more explicitly conservation-based approach. There is also Jamie Butterworth, who last year got called “the Jamie Oliver of gardening” and “Monty Don’s protege” in the space ofa single headline. All would be worthy replacements.But that is all to come. For now, it is time to herald Don, and the hole he leaves. The good news is that in no way did Don’s announcement signal a full-blown retirement. “There are more books to write, more programmes to make,” he said.This is heartening news. Outside Gardeners’ World, Don has made some fine gardening travelogues – taking him to Italy, Spain, Japan and the US, among others – which fits, since he got his TV break in the 1990s on holiday programmes. More of these would be most welcome, as would anything else he chooses to do, quite frankly. He remains the best to ever do it.Explore more on these topicsFactual TVTelevisionGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I suggested maybe a lighter touch’: William Shatner on Star Trek at 60 | Star Trek | The Guardian
description: The actor and others involved with the phenomenon speak about the legacy and progressivism of a much-loved science fiction TV series as it reaches an important milestone
Author: David Smith
Headline: The actor and others involved with the phenomenon speak about the legacy and progressivism of a much-loved science fiction TV series as it reaches an important milestone
Content: William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy in Star Trek.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyView image in fullscreenWilliam Shatner and Leonard Nimoy in Star Trek.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyStar Trek‘I suggested maybe a lighter touch’: William Shatner on Star Trek at 60The actor and others involved with the phenomenon speak about the legacy and progressivism of a much-loved science fiction TV series as it reaches an important milestoneDavid Smithin WashingtonTue 8 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 08.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘The mystery of time,” musesWilliam Shatner, and for a moment we are back on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise listening to one of Captain Kirk’s philosophical tag-line speeches. “Not just the passage of time and our perception of it, but what is time? What does 60 years mean? It really is meaningless, isn’t it, 60 years, in terms of what time is? On the other hand, Dolly Parton just died. It brings up the whole concept of the passage of time and what that means.”Seam me up, Scotty! After 60 years, Star Trek has had a muppet takeover. About time tooRead moreIn an episode called The City on the Edge of Forever, Shatner’s Kirk travelled back in time and fell in love with a pacifist (Joan Collins) only to discover that she must die to prevent Nazi Germany winning the second world war. Such ethical quandaries help explain why Star Trek willcelebrate its 60th anniversaryon 8 September not just as a force in US culture but a mirror held up to the country’s politics.Born in the idealism of the 1960s, the show offered a utopian vision of the future in which humanity sought to explore rather than conquer. Diversity, empathy and reason had triumphed over tribalism, superstition and greed. Big government and big tech were liberators from scarcity and inequality. Star Trek’s fans includedMartin Luther Kingand his wife, Coretta, who said it was the only programme they allowed their little children to stay up and watch.But six decades on, the Enterprise is encountering some cosmic turbulence. Donald Trump’s America is convulsed by polarisation, culture wars and the retreat of liberal democracy, along with anxiety over artificial intelligence and climate catastrophe. Paramount,merged with Skydance Mediafor $8bn, promptly cancelled the latest Star Trek series amid claims that it was too “woke”.The rightwing complainers yearn for a return to the days of Iowa-born Captain Kirk, who fits their conceit of an all-American hero, even though Shatner is Canadian. When he was hired in 1965 after NBC rejected Jeffrey Hunter’s dour pilot performance asCaptain Pike, he brought an athletic, theatrical charisma that lifted the cerebral storytelling.“I saw the film and I thought it was really interesting, a little ponderous,” Shatner, a sprightly 95, recalls of the original pilot via Zoom from his home in Los Angeles, with his dogs sleeping nearby. “So I suggested maybe a lighter touch, and we made another pilot and it sold.”That lighter touch did not prevent Shatner from making history. In 1968, he and Nichelle Nichols, who played Lt Nyota Uhura, shared television’s first high-profile scripted interracial kiss in the episodePlato’s Stepchildren. Was he aware of its groundbreaking importance?View image in fullscreenLeonard Nimoy, DeForest Kelley, Nichelle Nichols and William Shatner.Photograph: Paramount/Sportsphoto/Allstar“I was told,” he says, sounding reluctant to be cast as a civil rights activist. Shatner muses about “infrequent hates” that are “dramatised by documentary filming” to shock audiences and contends: “The vast majority of us just want to live and have your barbecue and live in peace and quiet and go do what you want to. You believe what you wanna believe and, if you don’t bother me, I won’t bother you. I think most people want to do that and if we could elevate those people to express themselves more, we’d discover that humanity really just wants to be human.”Star Trek is still pushing boundaries, much to the chagrin of unlikely fan Stephen Miller, the deputy White House chief of staff and driver of Trump’s extremist immigration policy. In January Miller cited a social media account called End Wokeness that mocked the newest Star Trek series, Starfleet Academy, as “Beyond parody”.Miller himself wrote: “Tragic. But it’s not too late for @paramountplus to save the franchise. Step 1: Reconcile with @WilliamShatner and give him total creative control.”Shatner laughs at the idea of White House aides spending their days picking holes inStar Trek. “Can you imagine they’re watching TV, criticising TV. I mean, it’s bizarre! I don’t understand it. I don’t know why they don’t – I don’t want to be political. I’m Canadian in America but it’s enthralling.”He rejects Miller’s notion that Star Trek’s inclusiveness has gone too far. “I don’t know what going too far is. Where’s the demarcation line? Who drew that line? ‘Now you’ve gone too far.’ Excuse me, I didn’t realise that. Where should I have stopped? And by the way, what is ‘woke’?”In creator Gene Roddenberry’s 23rd-century vision, nation-states no longer exist and planets have banded together to form a sort of United Nations in space. Poverty, disease and hunger have been eradicated, currency has largely disappeared from Federation life and citizens pursue self-improvement rather than private accumulation. To some, it might sound likeJohn Lennon’s Imagine. But others would rather not imagine it.In 2017 the billionaire investor Peter Thieltold Maureen Dowdof the New York Times: “I like Star Wars way better. I’m a capitalist. Star Wars is the capitalist show. Star Trek is the communist one. There is no money in Star Trek because you just have the transporter machine that can make anything you need. The whole plot of Star Wars starts with Han Solo having this debt that he owes and so the plot in Star Wars is driven by money.”Shatner, whotravelled into space for real aged 90, sounds wryly amused. “Peter Thiel must be a very bright, creative man, full of opinions and he’s made a lot of money which should indicate he’s very self-sufficient and has ideas. He talked about money. Well, that’s one aspect. You need money to live. But you need other things as well and the other things are represented by Star Trek. I’d love to talk to him. I’d love to get into a discourse on the differences between Star Trek and Star Wars.”One difference has been articulated by Shatner’s friend, the astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson,who argues that Star Trekadheres more closely to real science. Another can be traced to the franchises’ origins: whereas Star Wars draws on the classic hero myth outlined by scholar Joseph Campbell, Star Trek was forged in the horrors of the mid-20th century.Roddenberrywas a decorated second world war bomber pilot who later survived a harrowing commercial plane crash in the Syrian desert. His writing partner Gene Coon had served in the marines and received training as a war reporter during the Korean war era.View image in fullscreenJoan Collins and William Shatner in Star Trek.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesMark Altman, co-author of The Fifty-Year Mission and director of a new documentary,The 60-Year Mission, says via Zoom from Los Angeles: “Their approach to Star Trek was they had lost a lot of friends and had seen war up close and they didn’t romanticise it. They knew the cost of war. They weren’t changing the name of the Department of Defense to the Department of War. They loathed war.“That’s something I find shocking, these deeply conservative fans like Stephen Miller say, ‘I’m a huge fan of Star Trek.’ How is that possible? Did they miss the memo thatin reality, Star Trek abhorred war, and it always said that talking is the way to resolve conflict?”Nowhere was that clearer than in the1967 episode Arena, in which Kirk refuses to execute the monstrous Gorn that has obliterated a Federation outpost. “Kirk makes this decision not to kill this alien creature that has annihilated our base and killed his friends,” Altman notes. “Some people look at it and say, ‘Oh, it’s this goofy monster in a suit.’ But there’s a reason an episode like that becomes so iconic: it’s the message as well as the visuals.”Viewers in the late 1960s were accustomed to all-white TV westerns. On Star Trek, they encountered a meritocracy: an African American woman, Nichols’s Uhura, answering communications with unflappable authority (she was poised to quit after one season butKing persuaded her to stay); George Takei’s Sulu piloting the flagship barely two decades after Japanese Americans had been interned; and an alien second-in-command, Leonard Nimoy’s Mr Spock, acting as what Altman calls “the ultimate immigrant”.Altman points out that this integration extended beyond the main bridge crew: “What about the diversity in the guest characters? In one episode you have Captain Kirk answering to his superior, Commodore Stone, played by the latePercy Rodriguez. Many years before Colin Powell, Kirk is answering to an African American who’s his boss. That stuff resonates too.”The original series ran from 1966 to 1969, crashing headlong into the Vietnam war, racial violence and the assassinations of John F Kennedy, King and Robert F Kennedy. Animated seriesand films followed. Then came The Next Generation (1987–1994), starring the Shakespearean actorPatrick Stewartas Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Deep Space Nine (1993–1999), Voyager (1995–2001) and several subsequent iterations.View image in fullscreenThe cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation.Photograph: Cine Text/Sportsphoto/AllstarAltman regards Kirk as an analogue for John F Kennedy, the young president who had pledged to reach the moon before the decade was out. “The final frontier isthe New Frontier. Kirk is very much a Kennedy-esque liberal. He’s liberal on social issues but more hard-nosed on defence. It’s more of a traditional moderate than what we see with democratic socialists today. It’s a meritocracy; it believes everybody needs to start from the same starting line but then it’s about your gifts and you have ability.“But if you look atThe Next Generation, it’s a very George HW Bush vision: consensus-building, a thousand points of light. Kirk has a line: ‘When this becomes a democracy, I’ll let you know.’ Picard was more of a consensus builder who had a lot of meetings to get a lot of input from people. It was more of an HW Bush thing.“You can extend that to a lot of Star Trek shows which were clearly influenced, if not necessarily by the president, by the tenor of the times.Deep Space Ninewas heavily rewritten in the aftermath of the Los Angeles riots and the beating of Rodney King. It was all about rebuilding and asking, can’t we all just get along? It has one of the great Star Trek quotes: ‘It’s easy to be a saint in paradise.’ When you’re on a starship and everything’s great, it’s easy to be a saint in paradise. But on a station, there’s more of a struggle and more conflict.”The latest series,Starfleet Academy, starred Oscar-winner Holly Hunter as the captain and a chancellor alongside Paul Giamatti as its central antagonist. The show boasted the largest and most expensive physical set in the franchise’s history. Set in a distant future where young cadets rebuild the Federation following an apocalyptic event, it was designed as an allegory for institutional renewal.But following Paramount’s merger with Skydance, which is led by David Ellison, who is the son of Trump ally Larry Ellison,Starfleet Academy was cancelled,with its forthcoming second season set to be its last. Miller had been joined by tech billionaire Elon Musk in a Maga pile-on denouncing the show’s alleged wokeness.View image in fullscreenPaul Giamatti and Holly Hunter in Star Trek: Starfleet Academy.Photograph: Brooke Palmer/ParamountAltman is scathing of the rightwing crusade. “How can you criticise Starfleet Academy on the ground that it’s too diverse? It’s absolutely ridiculous, and particularly if you’re someone who’s claiming to be a Star Trek fan who needs to understand that diversity is in the DNA of Star Trek.“Diversity as a strength is something that’s celebrated as a through-line in all the Star Trek series. The series can be very different but one thing that has never changed from 8 September 1966 is the value of diversity in making these crews stronger. If they were all homogeneous, they would not be able to as effectively deal with the challenges they face in the cosmos.”That sentiment is shared by the veteran actorRobert Picardo, who spent seven seasons playing Voyager’s Emergency Medical Hologram and reprised his role in Starfleet Academy. Speaking by phone, the 72-year-old does not mince words: “Let’s face it: when someone that high up in the administration and also Elon Musk piled on the same day, do I think it’s a coincidence that the new owners of Paramount cancelled our show the first moment they could have? We did not get a fair shake.We were killed in the cradle.”Picardo adds: “Yes, there was the fact that we hada gay Klingon. Did a lot of people get over-exercised about that? My feeling is, get over yourself! There seems to be a movement to drive us back to the 1950s. Star Trek is all about the future, not about returning.“In that climate the core values of Star Trek – science and also diversity and inclusion – are going to get lumped in with what is under attack. Some people say, do you feel that it was at all current politics that had to do with your cancellation? If we caught the same flu thatStephen Colbertand the editorial freedom of CBS 60 minutes caught then we’re in excellent company.”If Star Trek’s social politics were prescient, its engagement with science and technology was frequently uncanny. Decades before smartphones, tablets, automated doors and voice-activated digital assistants, the Enterprise was operating with personal access display devices, communicators and talking mainframes. But it also interrogated the ethics of innovation.View image in fullscreenRobert Picardo in Star Trek: Starfleet Academy.Photograph: Miller Mobley/ParamountFor Picardo, who spent seven years embodying a holographic doctor wrestling with sentience and civil rights on Voyager, current debates aroundSilicon Valley’s generative AI boomfeel oddly familiar. “The explosion of the technology and the pace at which it is happening is something nobody could have predicted.“It’s a useful tool but it’s raised all sorts of issues. We actually did episodes on Star Trek where my character wrote a book and then there was the question of whether an artificial intelligence could have intellectual property rights. We did the whole issue of whether an artificial intelligence can have an original idea or if it can only slice and dice human ideas scraped from the internet, from everything ever written.”Sixty years on, Star Trek’s faith in a United Federation of Planets that has outgrown bigotry, racism and nationalism feels perversely quaint in an era that has seen Trump champion “America first”,deride the UNand denigrate the very concept of empathy. The show, whose future is uncertain as Paramount’s new owners focus on a proposed $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros, offers utopia in a time of dystopia.Picardo observes: “Post-9/11, a lot of science fiction has become very apocalyptic. It’s in some hellscape future with a few straggler survivors and Star Trek is the opposite of that. But to me, the biggest damage that’s been done in current politics is the destruction the idea of truth or that there is such a thing as a fact and our word does matter. I worry about Star Trek’s survival in a post-truth, post-literate world.”Explore more on these topicsStar TrekWilliam ShatnerUS televisionScience fiction TVTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Monty Don steps down from BBC’s Gardeners’ World after 23 years | Factual TV | The Guardian
description: Final series hosted by ‘utterly unique’ presenter will continue to be broadcast until later this year
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Final series hosted by ‘utterly unique’ presenter will continue to be broadcast until later this year
Content: Monty Don said it was ‘the right time to change’ and he will continue working with the BBC on other programmes.Photograph: BBC StudiosView image in fullscreenMonty Don said it was ‘the right time to change’ and he will continue working with the BBC on other programmes.Photograph: BBC StudiosFactual TVMonty Don steps down from BBC’s Gardeners’ World after 23 yearsFinal series hosted by ‘utterly unique’ presenter will continue to be broadcast until later this yearRachel HallandHelena HortonTue 8 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 08.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMonty Don, the longest serving head gardener on the BBC’s Gardeners’ World programme, will step down at the end of the current series.After 23 years leading the show, which he has hosted alongside his dogs from his own garden in Herefordshire since 2011, Don said it was “the right time for a change”. He will continue working with the BBC on other programmes, as well as pursuing his own projects, such as writing books.“Throughout that time – and around 700 programmes – I have had the privilege of sharing my own abiding passion for gardens and gardening with an equally passionate, and often equally knowledgable, audience,” Don said.Monty Don is quitting Gardeners’ World – and you’re right to be devastated about itRead more“That connection with millions, not just in Britain but across the world, who share a love of gardens, plants and the natural world is something I have always treasured and which I increasingly believe to be at the heart of a life well lived.”The final series hosted by Don will continue to be broadcast from Longmeadow until later this year. It is understood that he will shortly begin filming a travel programme for the BBC, named IslandGardens.Kate Phillips, the BBC’s chief content officer, said Don was “utterly unique, a wonderfully engaging broadcaster with a soothing, calm presence who has inspired so many with his passion for gardening”.In reference to Don’sfrankness about his experience with depression, she added: “I would like to thank Monty personally for his honesty and kindness, which has seen him open up about his own personal struggles and the power of the natural world to improve mental health. We will miss him on the show hugely.”Sharon Fisher, BBC Studios’ series editor for Gardeners’ World, who has worked with Don for the last 20 years, described his contribution as extraordinary.“Through his warmth, wisdom and deep love of gardening, he has inspired millions to discover the pleasure and purpose that getting your hands into the soil can bring,” she said.“I have seen first-hand the care, integrity and generosity he brings to everything he does. His departure marks the end of a remarkable chapter in the programme’s history.“All of us on the Gardeners’ World team will miss him enormously, but we celebrate everything he has given to the programme, the gardening community and the audience, who have welcomed him into their homes every week for over two decades.”A Gardeners’ World source said Frances Tophill, a presenter on the show, “has been tipped as his successor for a while”. At the RHS Chelsea flower show this year, Tophill co-designed a garden with David Beckham and King Charles.View image in fullscreenFrances Tophill at Powderham Castle in Devon for Gardeners’ World in 2024.Photograph: BBC Studios“She is incredibly popular, excellent on-screen and a brilliant gardener,” the source added.Tophill’s Chelsea flower show garden included an area for natural and homeopathic remedies in a shed, requested by the king, and bee-friendly features requested by Beckham.She has deputised for Don when he has been unavailable, and when asked by the Sunday Times this year if she had designs on Don’s job, she said: “I hope [Don] never leaves.”Explore more on these topicsFactual TVTelevisionBBCGardening adviceEducational TVGardensShareReuse this content

title: Glastonbury tickets break £400 for first time as on-sale date is announced | Glastonbury festival | The Guardian
description: Tickets set to cost £408 at return for Somerset festival after a fallow year, a jump from £378.50 in 2025
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Tickets set to cost £408 at return for Somerset festival after a fallow year, a jump from £378.50 in 2025
Content: Glastonbury’s Pyramid stage, pictured in 2023.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGlastonbury’s Pyramid stage, pictured in 2023.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianGlastonbury festivalGlastonbury tickets break £400 for first time as on-sale date is announcedTickets set to cost £408 at return for Somerset festival after a fallow year, a jump from £378.50 in 2025Ben Beaumont-ThomasTue 8 Sep 2026 13.58 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a fallow year in 2026,Glastonbury festivalfans can start to get excited – and nervous – about tickets for 2027’s event going on sale.The price breaks £400 for the first time, at £408 including a £5 booking fee, a rise from the 2025 cost of £378.50. The usual scramble to acquire them – with all the attendant frantic spreadsheets and WhatsApp groups – will begin at 9am on Sunday 4 October.To encourage festival-goers to take more environmentally sound coaches rather than cars, tickets bundled with coach travel go on sale earlier, at 6pm on Thursday 1 October.Harry Styles is already much rumoured to be headlining, with the likes of Taylor Swift, Fontaines DC, Sabrina Carpenter and Fred Again among others mooted by the bookies.Organiser Emily Eavis scotched rumours that Madonna would play, saying: “No, it’s definitely not Madonna, I’ll tell you that. But we have got three [other] headliners and we’re very excited about it – it’s all coming together really well.”In 2025, the festival was headlined by the 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo, with the latter described as “the weekend’s best big set” in a five-star Guardian review.There were also secret sets from Pulp, Skepta, Haim and more, and acclaimed turns from Doechii, Alanis Morissette and others. But there was controversy around Kneecap’s appearance at the festival, as well as the act that preceded them:Bob Vylan, who led a chantof “death to the IDF”. Then-BBC director general, Tim Davie, said “I deeply regret that such offensive and deplorable behaviour appeared on the BBC,” and the furore led to an internal investigation.Since that previous edition, Eavis’s father, Michael, who founded the festival in 1970, has turned 90. Speaking to the BBC in October, he said: “It’s all been a long story of excitement. That’s probably what’s keeping me going.”He added: “I was always at war with the council and the village and the local magistrates and the police”, as he turned the festival from a gathering on his Somerset dairy farm into arguably the world’s greatest music festival. “And it came good. Which is extraordinary, really. The fight was really what made it work, there’s no doubt about that. It was certainly worth it.”The 2027 festival takes place between June 23-27. Anyone wanting to buy a ticket must register with the festival by 5pm BST on Friday 25 September. Tickets can be paid for in full or with a £100 deposit, with the rest paid off in the first week of April. Under-13s attend for free.Explore more on these topicsGlastonbury festivalFestivalsMusic festivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Richard Alston, trailblazer and guiding light of British dance, dies aged 77 | Richard Alston | The Guardian
description: Akram Khan among those paying tribute to ‘pioneering’ choreographer of intense musicality and grace who inspired generations of dancers
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Akram Khan among those paying tribute to ‘pioneering’ choreographer of intense musicality and grace who inspired generations of dancers
Content: He took contemporary dance into new directions with his elegant and intelligent creations … choreographer Richard Alston in 2008Photograph: Linda Nylind/the GuardianView image in fullscreenHe took contemporary dance into new directions with his elegant and intelligent creations … choreographer Richard Alston in 2008Photograph: Linda Nylind/the GuardianRichard AlstonRichard Alston, trailblazer and guiding light of British dance, dies aged 77Akram Khan among those paying tribute to ‘pioneering’ choreographer of intense musicality and grace who inspired generations of dancersChris WiegandStage editorTue 8 Sep 2026 07.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSir Richard Alston, the British choreographer and teacher who took contemporary dance into new directions with his elegant and intelligent creations, has died at the age of 77. A former artistic director of Rambert and the Place, where he made more than 50 pieces for theRichard Alston Dance Company, he was celebrated for lucid, emotionally attuned work that was often as graceful as it was rigorous.His death was announced on Monday by theRichard Alston Foundation, which was established in 2021 to promote contemporary dance and preserve his work. “It is with deep sadness that we have to report the death of Sir Richard Alston,”said the statement. “After a period of ill-health, and despite exceptional treatment at the Royal Free Hospital in Hampstead and the support of his closest friends, he passed away peacefully at his home on 7 September. While Richard is best known for his extraordinary career and contribution to contemporary dance, we will also remember him for his wit, warmth and generosity of spirit.”Akram Khan was among those paying tribute to Alston. “Like so many of us, I grew to know Richard as a student, looking up to him as I began to find my own way in contemporary dance,”wrote Khan, who called him “a pioneer” and praised his kindness and encouragement. “It is now our collective responsibility to ensure that the legacy of these great leaders of British contemporary dance continues to inspire and is passed on.”View image in fullscreenAlston, centre, with dancers after a performance of Voices and Light Footsteps at Sadler’s Wells, London, in 2020.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianAlston’s eye for movement was matched by an ear for all kinds of music from around the world. “Why dance to Britten?” hewrote in an article for the Guardianin 2013, before his company’s performances with the Britten Sinfonia. “The simple answer is that his music breathes. It rises and falls, often with the voice, in lucid phrases that have a palpable sense of physical movement.” Astatement from Rambert dance companypraised his “extraordinary musicality” and said he had “shaped generations of dancers”.The Place’s tributesaid his “lifelong conversation with music” shaped “every dance he ever made”. It continued: “His legacy cannot be measured by honours or dances alone. It lives in the dancers who still carry his movement in their bodies. In the students who continue to discover that music can be seen as well as heard. In the generations of artists who inherited from him an uncompromising belief in clarity, craftsmanship and beauty.”Alston was born in Sussex in 1948 and educated at Eton. He left at 16 to study fine art and theatre design at Croydon School of Art. When he saw Frederick Ashton’s ballet La Fille Mal Gardée in the mid-60s he knew his future was in dance. He joined the nascent London School of ContemporaryDance(which became London Contemporary Dance School at the Place), choreographed his first work, Transit, in 1968 and formed a trailblazing experimental group, Strider, in 1972. That decade he also studied in New York under Merce Cunningham who would become a huge influence on him.View image in fullscreen‘Clarity, craftsmanship and beauty’ … dancers in Proverb from Mid Century Modern at Sadler’s Wells, London, 2018.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianIn 1980, Alston became resident choreographer at BalletRambert. He then ran the company as artistic director from 1986 to 1992 during which time it dropped the “ballet” from its name. He created 25 works for Rambert, which is marking its centenary this year. “Richard stands among the defining artists of our 100-year history,” said the company, calling him “an artist whose vision helped shape Rambert’s identity, its evolution and its future”.Richard Alston Dance Company rehearsals – in picturesRead moreIn 1994, he launched Richard Alston Dance Company when he became artistic director of the Place in London. He received a knighthood for services to dance in 2019. The following year, his company closed due to funding difficulties and itsfarewell performancesincluded a new work, Shine On, its title capturing the undimmed commitment of Alston, who mentored many in the dance community.“I’ve never wanted to make loud statements,”he told the Guardian in 2008. “What I believe in is the amazing power and complexity of the human body in steps, in rhythm and music. And that doesn’t change.”Explore more on these topicsRichard AlstonDanceRambertThe PlaceAkram KhannewsShareReuse this content

title: Artworks stolen from Renoir Museum on French Riviera in latest heist | Art theft | The Guardian
description: Thieves took four artworks but it is thought they dropped two in museum garden as they fled
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Thieves took four artworks but it is thought they dropped two in museum garden as they fled
Content: A composite of stolen the Renoirs: Young Woman ‌at the Well and Madame Colonna Romano.Photograph: Musée RenoirView image in fullscreenA composite of stolen the Renoirs: Young Woman ‌at the Well and Madame Colonna Romano.Photograph: Musée RenoirArt theftArtworks stolen from Renoir Museum on French Riviera in latest heistThieves took four artworks but it is thought they dropped two in museum garden as they fledJon HenleyandAngelique Chrisafisin ParisTue 8 Sep 2026 11.37 EDTFirst published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 03.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench police are hunting two thieves who escaped with two Renoir paintings from a museum on the French Riviera after breaking in through a hole cut in its garden fence.Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, about 10 miles west of Nice, said the pair appeared to have been “well equipped and well informed” about the museum, which houses works by the French impressionistPierre-Auguste Renoirin his former home.The theft early on Tuesday is the latest in a string of recent museum heists in France and across Europe, including thebrazen break-in at the Louvre in Paris last October, when ⁠thieves stole crown jewellery worth €88m (£75m), including tiaras, a brooch, necklaces and earrings.Masson told the local broadcaster Ici Azur that the two thieves sliced through the museum garden fence with an electric knife or metal saw, entered the building through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames.View image in fullscreenThe mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, Bryan Masson, said his office estimated the stolen art was worth €9m.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesPolice arrived about five minutes after the museum’s alarm system went off at 5.48am, Masson said, which “forced the burglars to flee in haste and helped limit the scale of the theft”.Two of the four works taken were abandoned in the museum gardens during the getaway, the mayor, a member of the far-right National Rally (RN), said. His office estimated the value of the stolen works at €9m.The two stolen paintings were Young Woman ‌at the Well and Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano. Both were on loan from the Musée d’Orsay, in Paris. “They’re Renoirs … you cannot sell them like that,” Masson said.The paintings the thieves abandoned were both portraits: Portrait of Madame Pichon, and Coco Reading, a portrayal of Renoir’s young son Claude.The Renoir Museum was established in 1960 in the mansion where the painter ‌died aged 78 in 1919. It houses about a dozen of his paintings and about 40 sculptures, as well as photos, furniture and objects including his easel and wheelchair.View image in fullscreenRenoir’s study at the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer.Photograph: DEA/G Nimatallah/De Agostini/Getty ImagesMasson called for greater security for museums aroundFrance. “This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art,” the mayor said.An art theft expert, James Ratcliffe of theArtLoss Register, said thieves were increasingly targeting valuable artefacts. “Sadly, without further funding to improve museum security, we are likely to see an increase in the number of museum thefts,” he said.“Each time thefts occur, it draws yet more attention to the perception of these museums as relatively easy targets. That can only encourage some criminals to consider them as straightforward places to steal from,” he told the Associated Press.Europol, the pan-European police organisation,said last monthrobberies at European museums were becoming increasingly violent, with some thieves brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives.The Europol report suggested specialist property crime or art theft gangs, who usually avoid violence, were being replaced by “individuals who often have histories of involvement in other types of crime”, who were recruited through social media.The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the jewels they allegedly grabbed in the seven-minute heist have not been found. Two of the suspectshave reportedly told policethe mastermind behind the heist was disappointed by the haul and thought “they could have taken more”.Italian police recently recoveredpaintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m stolen from a museum in March. However, last month four of the most important works by the Renaissance masterAntonello da Messina were stolenfrom a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.Explore more on these topicsArt theftFranceArtPierre-Auguste RenoirEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Freiburg Baroque Orch/Rattle/Faust review – ‘problem’ Schumann works shine in exceptional evening | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Simon Rattle, guest conducting the period instrument ensemble, brought insights and detail to these three lesser known works by Schumann. Isabelle Faust was a spirited and graceful soloist in the Violin Concerto
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Simon Rattle, guest conducting the period instrument ensemble, brought insights and detail to these three lesser known works by Schumann. Isabelle Faust was a spirited and graceful soloist in the Violin Concerto
Content: Isabelle Faust and Simon Rattle with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou /BBCView image in fullscreenIsabelle Faust and Simon Rattle with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou /BBCProms 2026ReviewFreiburg Baroque Orch/Rattle/Faust review – ‘problem’ Schumann works shine in exceptional eveningRoyal Albert Hall, LondonSimon Rattle, guest conducting the period instrument ensemble, brought insights and detail to these three lesser known works by Schumann. Isabelle Faust was a spirited and graceful soloist in the Violin ConcertoClive PagetTue 8 Sep 2026 08.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSimon Rattle sure loves a challenge. This all-Schumann evening featured three “problem” works: the overture to a failed opera, a violin concerto deemed sufficiently disappointing that the composer’s executors ordered it locked away for a century, and a symphony written in the depths of depression. What’s more, he was conducting the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra in an acoustic hardly conducive to the soft-grained tones of period ensembles. In the event, we needn’t have worried, but you have to admire his pluck.The overture to Genoveva got off to a moody start. Rattle and the Freiburgers drew the listener in by tapping into the musical storytelling – the quartet of horns was especially striking – rather than relying on sheer volume. Closer to Mendelssohn than Wagner, it must have felt old hat in 1848, but here came up bristling with romance and chivalry.Isabelle Faust was the soloist for only the sixth Proms performance of Schumann’s Violin Concerto (by comparison,the previous nightsaw the 103rd outing for Dvořák’s New World Symphony). Conducting without a podium, Rattle was an attentive partner, leaning into the first movement’s dark urgency while deftly shadowing Faust whose subtle rubato afforded a degree of flexibility to her otherwise determined sense of the work’s thematic architecture. Dynamic shading and delicate trills decorated the line as she calmly overcame a host of technical challenges. Sailing through the Elgarian central movement, she slid gracefully into a spirited yet wistful account of the polonaise finale. Rattle and the orchestra accompanied her with elfin lightness.Schumann’s Second is the Cinderella among his four symphonies. Rattle didn’t shy away from the opening movement’s gloomier moments, or indeed its turbulence, but on the whole, this was a crisp reading where sunshine outweighed the showers. In the scherzo, conductor and orchestra highlighted the obsessive nature of the nagging principal theme, which in turn emphasised the Jekyll and Hyde nature of the contrasting trio. The slow movement, an endless flow of melody, exuded a noble melancholy before the curiously structured yet ultimately celebratory finale carried all before it. Exceptional playing, insightful and affectionate conducting, and not once did the period-instrument blend blur or smudge.Available onBBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicPromsSimon RattlereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Goodbye, Colin from Accounts: how TV’s loveliest comedy stuck the landing | Colin from Accounts | The Guardian
description: For a show that started with a screech of car brakes and a wounded dog, Brammall and Dyer steer the finale home as if rolling comfortably down a familiar road
Author: Walter Marsh
Headline: For a show that started with a screech of car brakes and a wounded dog, Brammall and Dyer steer the finale home as if rolling comfortably down a familiar road
Content: Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer say Gordon and Ashley aren’t entirely based on their own love story, but their chemistry is, without question, the secret sauce in Colin from Accounts.Photograph: Lisa TomasettiView image in fullscreenPatrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer say Gordon and Ashley aren’t entirely based on their own love story, but their chemistry is, without question, the secret sauce in Colin from Accounts.Photograph: Lisa TomasettiColin from AccountsGoodbye, Colin from Accounts: how TV’s loveliest comedy stuck the landingFor a show that started with a screech of car brakes and a wounded dog, Brammall and Dyer steer the finale home as if rolling comfortably down a familiar roadWalter MarshTue 8 Sep 2026 02.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 04.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe streaming age has no shortage of will-they-won’t-they romances – the good, the bad, the cosy, the smutty, the made-for-the-algorithm. How did Colin from Accounts manage to rise above the tropes? How, in just a few years, has Patrick Brammall’s overseas profile gone from asolid but largely ignored cop comedy,to getting headhunted to woo Anne Hathaway in The Devil Wears Prada 2?When I think of howColin from Accountsfirst won me over in 2022, a moment in the first episode comes to mind. Two strangers, pub owner Gordon (Brammall) and med student Ashley (Harriet Dyer) sit in a cafe, making awkward small talk as they wait for the veterinary clinic next door to tell them whether the small runaway dog they’ve accidentally maimed will pull through.Suddenly, the barista relays sad tidings phoned in from the vet: the dog has died. Or rather,adog has died. It soon becomes clear multiple diners are anxious pet owners killing time, and a Mexican wave of shock and grief envelopes the cafe as they try to figure out whose beloved pet carked it.As far as meet-cutes go, it’s more of a meet-cringe. But, having just spent an awful lot of time and money in vet clinics – where the cute chaos of untrained puppies often shares a waiting room with tearful customers about to leave empty-handed – I found it perfectly relatable, and perfectly ridiculous. My partner and I laughed through tears (neither of our cats survived, FYI).Such a tableau shows why Colin from Accounts is such a charming watch. It’s grounded in its absurdity, self-assured in its delivery, distinctly Australian but never panders to a preconceived idea of what that means. For me, its winning blend of caustic discomfort and a big heart also evokes that other great TV love story: Tim and Dawn in the original UK run of The Office.The real love story behind Colin from Accounts: ‘I wouldn’t want to write with anyone else’Read moreThere’s also the couple themselves. Brammall and Dyer say Gordon and Ashley aren’t entirely based ontheir own love story, but their raw chemistry is, without question, the show’s secret sauce. Like Australia’s elderly millennial answer to Zendaya and Tom Holland, there is something magnetic about watching these two cook on and off-screen, from the way their comic sensibilities sync as writers, to how they make that writing crackle for the camera.This third and final season opened with a gambit: having ended the previous season on what seemed like a narrative point of no return (an ill-judged marriage proposal from Gordon, humiliatingly shot down on the spot by Ashley) the show jumped ahead three years. We find Ashley and Gordon after years of radio silence, both now in well-established new relationships. The reasons they didn’t work out the first time are still there, but then, so are the reasons they often did.We meet their respective new partners and immediately know it isn’t going to work. It’s not because David, a handsome but hopeless trout farmer played by Thomas Cocquerel, or Nikki Shiels’ Chelsea, a corporate she-EO way past ready to move in and unfreeze her eggs for Gordon, are bad people. They’re just not right for our heroes.Equally, this final season has taken plenty of opportunities to count the ways Ashley and Gordon aren’t always good or likable either – sometimes, not even to each other. But they are, for better or worse, each other’s kind of person. They’re good for each other. They make each other laugh.For a show that started with a screech of car brakes and a wounded dog, Brammall and Dyer steered the finale home as if they were rolling comfortably down a familiar road. Like the standout finale of Hacks earlier this year, the showrunners knew exactly where to leave their onscreen counterparts without overstaying their welcome or over-egging the pudding (notwithstanding a Christmas theme that makes one wonder if international streaming schedules had derailed a planned December release, like the original Office finale).For a pair brought together by a chance collision, the finale also delivered some poignant reflections on leaving your happiness to fate, or trusting your own gut. But it also wore its finality lightly, making time for scene-stealing cameos from Broden Kelly and Mark Trevorrow, a police chase, and a pretty funny handjob joke.Without spoiling anything, they also brought us back to that fateful vet’s office. “Please calm down,” a terse receptionist reminds them. “I see a lot of highly emotional pet owners every day and I can’t remember them all.”Watching Ashley and Gordon’s final scenes from our sofa, with our new rescue cat curled up between us, happily dozing, it was a perfect callback. Life, love and pet ownership can be a mess, but if it feels right, it feels right.Explore more on these topicsColin from AccountsAustralian televisionTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

Plus: David Attenborough goes for the double at the National Television Awards.
