title: The Castle by Jon Ronson review – bizarre tales of modern masculinity | Society books | The Guardian
description: A journalist embarks on a wild goose chase that might – or might not – be informative about the male condition
Author: Anthony Cummins
Headline: A journalist embarks on a wild goose chase that might – or might not – be informative about the male condition
Content: Chris Mark’s castle in Woodstock, Connecticut.Photograph: Tyra PachecoView image in fullscreenChris Mark’s castle in Woodstock, Connecticut.Photograph: Tyra PachecoSociety booksReviewThe Castle by Jon Ronson review – bizarre tales of modern masculinityA journalist embarks on a wild goose chase that might – or might not – be informative about the male conditionAnthony CumminsTue 8 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 05.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRecovering from surgery at home in upstate New York in 2023,Jon Ronsonawoke to a string of texts from his adult son about a weird evening he just had at a stranger’s castle in Connecticut. Having gone along with a friend who’d been invited to a party there, he arrived to find a few lost-looking young women with the sixtysomething host, Chris Mark, a steel heir filming a reality show about “101 princesses” whose first rule was “Never say no to King Chris”.As a parent, Ronson is worried; as a reporter of more than 30 years on the cranks-and-crooks beat, he’s already on the clock. After trawling online whispers of sinister goings-on at the castle, he decides to pay a visit to Mark, who proudly shows off the stalactites and waterfall in his “cave-themed” bedroom before explaining how he picks up women on dating apps to “adapt” them to life as “princesses”. “The only girls that really work are drug addicts ... they don’t know what’s going on,” he says. Almost touchingly, Mark asks Ronson to sign an NDA, and the book describes Mark flooding his phone with threats when he declines.Ronson knows he has a story on his hands; but what is it? A disenchanted associate leaks Mark’s private messages, revealing plans for a $2,500-an-hour floating brothel lit up in purple LEDs, and suggesting that Mark once paid for a woman to fly into the US from Poland, only for authorities to send her home in fear for her safety. Further dirt is dished by an ex-fiancee after Ronson two-facedly tells her he’s “really, really sorry” their relationship collapsed (he already told us “a break-up can be good news for a journalist”). As allegations mount, he imagines – perhaps even hopes – that Mark murdered his own father, who drowned in a boating accident in 2009.While Ronson ends up satisfied Mark didn’t do that, the author’s willingness to guy his own ego – he wants “to be better than every other nonfiction writer” – adds a vital measure of comic charm to this creepy wild-goose chase. But gonzo sleuthing is only one ingredient of The Castle: the subtitle, Adventures in a World of Unravelling Men, hints at its ultimately piecemeal nature, as Ronson zigzags around case studies designed to illustrate the plight of the post-industrial male, simultaneously exhorted to open up and be vulnerable while pressured to avoid giving women “the ick” by snoring or failing to spot a beard crumb.Boo hoo, one might counter, yet Ronson is persuasive on the problems of casting masculinity as original sin. He talks to an Australian man whose teacher rounded up every boy in his school to make them “apologise for rape”, and meets a lone father courted by YouTube for the lucrative videos he posted of his daughters’ food fights, then dropped when online Sherlocks wrongly accused him of kidnap.Ronson makes these and other bizarre tales feel emblematic of topsy-turvy times, but when he says Chris Mark is just one of many men “discovering there were things they’d once done that they couldn’t do anymore”, you sense an over-caffeinated logic at work. “I was reminded a little of America in Iraq,” he tells us, when Mark can’t decide what to do with his castle, torn between housing OnlyFans models or setting up an orphanage. Mark’s “insatiable ... self-gratification” prompts a segment on the controversial actor Armie Hammer, seemingly mentioned only so Ronson can let us know Hammer gave him a tell-all scoop interview he didn’t publish.Ronson’s reflexive parallels don’t always help us understand his slippery subjects. Mark also puts him in mind of the Father Ted co-creator Graham Linehan, an ex-friend whose online posts about transgender people Ronson compared to bullying, whereupon, he tells us, Linehan began subjecting him to multiple abusive messages. Ronson interviews him to try to fathom what fed his obsession, but it’s typical of The Castle’s jittery analytical style that Ronson’s eventual summing-up rests less on their six hours of video calls than on a tenuous analogy he detects in the tragic case of Brandi Bragg, a West Virginian teenager who fatally overdosed in 2004 after a lottery win plunged her into paranoia.Near the end, he recounts thefatal shootingof Renée Good by an ICE agent who muttered “fucking bitch”. It isn’t clear why he brings this up, until he notes that Linehan – the only man in the book described as “unravelling” – apparently took to X to repost a tweet that called her “the face of chaos” and “the epitome of the modern-day liberal white woman”. “Graham’s plummet into disinhibition, his obsessive anti-wokeness, had evidently become so overwhelming it eclipsed his role as a self-appointed defender of women.” The gotcha, slipped into a footnote seven pages from the end, leaves you wondering if The Castle has been constructed not simply as an exploration of 21st-century maleness but as an act of slow-brew payback – though maybe it tells us something about men either way.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The Newer World by Sebastian Barry review – a near-miracle of storytelling | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The third in a loose American trilogy follows the epic journey of a formerly enslaved man in the aftermath of the civil war
Author: Sara Collins
Headline: The third in a loose American trilogy follows the epic journey of a formerly enslaved man in the aftermath of the civil war
Content: Unrelenting lyricism … Sebastian Barry.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The ObserverView image in fullscreenUnrelenting lyricism … Sebastian Barry.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The ObserverBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Newer World by Sebastian Barry review – a near-miracle of storytellingThe third in a loose American trilogy follows the epic journey of a formerly enslaved man in the aftermath of the civil warSara CollinsTue 8 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 02.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBut is not the story as good as the truth?” asks Tennyson Bouguereau, the narrator of Sebastian Barry’s The Newer World. Tennyson, a formerly enslaved man in post-civil war America, recounts his life story in ways that call to mind the age-old debate about whether it’s better to get our history from novelists or historians. While historians might argue that there is no contest, the question hints knowingly at the novelist’s counter-argument. It sent me searching for a line from Barry’s 2008 Costa-award winning novel,The Secret Scripture, in which the narrator describes history as “a fabulous arrangement of surmises and guesses held up as a banner against the assault of withering truth”.In her Reith Lectures, Hilary Mantel suggested that history is “what’s left in the sieve when the centuries have run through it”, but I tend to think of it as more of a butterfly net. Historians chase after and capture the things they deem significant. They leave things out, often deliberately. Barry’s entire body of work is a prime example of fiction’s ability to fill history’s gaps, merging personal tragedies with national ones in ways that (dare I say) demonstrate the supremacy of the form – especially for those of us descended from people for whom history never cared one whit. I was therefore intrigued to learn that he had set out to write the story of a man like Tennyson. Barry’s earlier novels refracted Irish history through the lens of two fictional Irish families, the Dunnes and the McNultys. His first foray into this period of American history inDays Without End, for which he won his second Costa award, also followed one of the McNultys – Thomas McNulty flees the Irish famine for America, where he finds himself drawn into the genocidal work of clearing Native Americans off their land, and then, together with his lover and fellow soldier, John Cole, adopts a Lakota girl, Winona, whose family they have helped slaughter. Barry picked up Winona’s story inA Thousand Moons, published in 2020, which follows her fortunes as she, Thomas and John settle on the same farm outside Paris, Tennessee that is occupied by Tennyson and his twin sister Rosalee among others.double quotation markIn Barry’s hands, language attains registers that can only be described as soaring; a vertiginous high wire of proseWith the publication of The Newer World, it seems a loose trilogy has taken shape, hinting at possibilities for future expansion: the authorial hand nudging Tennyson from the background into centre stage and for the time being leaving the McNultys behind. This passing of the storytelling baton – an Irish refugee ceding the floor to a Native American woman, who then does the same in favour of a formerly enslaved man – feels as urgently contemporary as the best historical fiction always does, relevant to “the writer’s now”, to borrow John Fowles’s phrase. So too does the description of a postbellum Tennessee landscape in which the Confederates may have been defeated but their ideologies are still virulently alive: “All their intent was to shove us back into the hog pen and put the hasp on tight as they could, against any further straying”.Part Bildungsroman, part picaresque, Tennyson’s account of himself moves from the American civil war, when “the end of the world had come”, to its immediate aftermath, “a time of guns and watchfulness”. He describes himself and Rosalee, enslaved orphans in childhood, “freed but not free” in adulthood, as “nothing people”. It’s reminiscent of Winona’s description of herself as “just the cinders of an Indian fire”, and Thomas’s of the ships bringing “ruined people” from Ireland to Canada: “The point is, we were nothing. No one wanted us.” The thing I like best about a Barry novel is how he gives a voice to the “nothing people” of history. It’s like pulling up a rocking chair on a shaded porch and listening as the narrator, usually in retrospective mode, attempts to reckon with what they did and what was done to them. It’s an astonishing effect, especially when you consider the near-miracles Barry performs with language. In his hands it attains registers that can only be described as soaring; a vertiginous high wire of prose. Here, for example, is Tennyson describing a reunion with his sister at sunset, after many years: “The harbour of my brave sister. The darkness growing in courage and, since it met no enemy, having its little victory everywhere. Pleasing darkness, in its way. There was bliss in those long moments”.Putting this kind of arresting language into the mouths of “nothing people” makes it impossible to overlook them, as if only in fiction can they be given their due. And there is also a compelling point in using language from the poetic realm to reveal rather than cloak atrocities, its rhythms building to an unrelenting lyricism, a juggernaut that gains power precisely because it is not just set alongside brutality but entwined with it. Here is a siege, after Tennyson has enlisted in the army: “Men cried out as the life was lifted from them. All in the cruel dark.” Cruelty is endured and inflicted by the same people. In Days Without End, Thomas McNulty, an Irish famine victim, takes part in slaughtering Indigenous Americans; in The Newer World, Tennyson, an African American victim of enslavement, does the same. It is “never enough for Americans to live in their American paradise. There had to be blood and chaos all the while too.” What does it mean to be part of a “killing machine” where “[e]ven one death was a personal matter”?I can think of no other writer who could, as Barry does, describe blood and chaos in language that reaches for such a high register, as if at the same time invoking paradise, in an attempt to answer that question. I can also think of few whose natural writerly empathy, evidenced by such an impressive body of work, pre-empts the otherwise inevitable discussion about cultural appropriation. Any writer has the right to imagine any point of view, but few truly earn it.The Newer World by Sebastian Barry is published by Faber (£20). title: Runner review – Alan Ritchson and Owen Wilson thriller is serviceable B-movie camp | Movies | The Guardian
description: Impressive stunts and tongue-in-cheek flourishes elevate Scott Waugh’s silly Aussie action flick
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Impressive stunts and tongue-in-cheek flourishes elevate Scott Waugh’s silly Aussie action flick
Content: Owen Wilson and Alan Ritchson in Runner.Photograph: Courtesy of Angel StudiosView image in fullscreenOwen Wilson and Alan Ritchson in Runner.Photograph: Courtesy of Angel StudiosMoviesReviewRunner review – Alan Ritchson and Owen Wilson thriller is serviceable B-movie campImpressive stunts and tongue-in-cheek flourishes elevate Scott Waugh’s silly Aussie action flickAdrian HortonTue 8 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCredit where credit is due: of the many, many variations on the hammy late-summer action romp, very few have applied the gonzo B-movie treatment – physics-defying car chases, knee-smashing violence and the like – to the practice of organ transportation.Donor delivery is not the direction you think things are going in upon first meeting Hank Malone, Alan Ritchson’s outlandishly muscled fixer, of sorts, in Runner, the latest attempt from faith-based distributor Angel Studios to enter the market of more straightforward base entertainment.Embodying the term “ex-military” in appearance and vibe (we get an early and ominous “I don’t hurt people any more” proclamation), this “big American Wario” – so says his phone-only handler – seems more suited for high-stakes extractions and special-op missions than life on a houseboat in Australia. There, he Duolingos French in between AA meetings and runs bespoke errands up to and including exotic bird delivery. But Runner, directed by action film veteran Scott Waugh (6 Below,Need for Speed) from a script by Miles Hubley and Tommy White (and not to be confused with Gal Gadot’s comparatively drabTheRunner, also out this month), possesses enough unpretentious humor and B-movie sensibility to approach camp.The Runner review – Gal Gadot stumbles through derivative high-speed, low-rent thrillerRead moreAnd thus, a seemingly straightforward assignment – drive a donated liver from the airport in Brisbane to the little girl with cancer and her frazzled mother (Leila George) languishing in Gold Coast children’s hospital – goes terribly, and dare I say enjoyably, awry. For one, the liver comes accompanied byOwen Wilson, going through the motions as Ben Bishop, a folksy bon vivant in a fedora with an annoying tendency to refer to himself in the third person. For another, there’s a seemingly endless series of cartel hitmen who, like the infamousdog who ate the ill-fated heartin One Tree Hill, are inspirationally absurd, singularly focused on the valuable organ at hand and largely mute.View image in fullscreenWilson and Ritchson in Runner.Photograph: Courtesy of Angel StudiosOne may ask, as Ben Bishop does: “What is the cartel doing in Queensland, Australia?!” Little clarity is provided, other than that rare blood-type livers apparently go for upwards of a million dollars on the black market. But no matter – Runner soon offers reason enough, along with the requisite B-movie pleasures: multiple telenovela-worthy plot twists; Ritchson coolly delivering lines such as “I’m the only one we can trust right now” while flexing his jaw; a steady escalation of gun size and hand-to-hand combat (why is the Colombian cartel reliant on Aussie biker gangs? Who knows!); the opportunity for the non-Aussie viewers among us to learn the approximate geography of the space between Brisbane and the Gold Coast; a battle of Range Rovers propulsive enough to keep one on the hook for a respectable 98 minutes. And chiefly, the deliciously sinister Rodrigo Santoro as an open wound of a cartel boss known as Damian, so in touch with his molten core, for reasons to be revealed, that he appears to be on the verge of tears in every shootout.As former stuntman, director Waugh knows his way around a jam-packed action sequence, careening the camera around a car chase or a six-versus-one beatdown with the panache of a sports star. There’s a vertiginous video-game logic to Runner’s shin-splitting, anvil-heavy violence that at once unites the film with its innumerable Netflix brethren and also distinguishes it from them. That our POV sometimes resembles a (glorious) death spiral is perhaps for the best, as there’s little else to back it up. Though both are playing squarely to type, Ritchson and Wilson’s chemistry is at best serviceable, at worst an (admittedly soapy) distraction from the cartoonish antics at hand. Attempts at big feelings to accompany the big biceps – yes, the big American Wario has a tragic backstory – have the emotional heft of checking a box. In the film’s meta battle between action camp and sincerity camp, the former is winning by a bro-country mile – and yes, you get that needle drop, too – though I do appreciate any movie where grown men cry.I’m reluctant to value brawn over everything else, but given the ignominious glut of straight-to-streaming background noise, it’s hard to root against a theatrical release that, knowingly or not, lands some truly cataclysmic punches with enough over-the-top silliness to force a smile. That some heart got lost in transit is, in this case, just fine.Runner is out in Australia on 10 September and in the US and UK on 11 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmOwen WilsonAction and adventure filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Don’t Forget Me review – Eddie Cochran bio-doc boasts top-notch roster of talking heads  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Kirsty Bell alternates archival footage with tacky dramatised filler, but it’s the breadth of appreciation, from Keith Richards to Kiefer Sutherland that impresses
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Director Kirsty Bell alternates archival footage with tacky dramatised filler, but it’s the breadth of appreciation, from Keith Richards to Kiefer Sutherland that impresses
Content: Big fan … Keith Richards in Don’t Forget About Me.Photograph: Goldfinch FilmsView image in fullscreenBig fan … Keith Richards in Don’t Forget About Me.Photograph: Goldfinch FilmsMoviesReviewDon’t Forget Me review – Eddie Cochran bio-doc boasts top-notch roster of talking headsDirector Kirsty Bell alternates archival footage with tacky dramatised filler, but it’s the breadth of appreciation, from Keith Richards to Kiefer Sutherland that impressesLeslie FelperinTue 8 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo one could argue that rock’n’roll legend Eddie Cochran isn’t worthy of a birth-to-untimely-death bio-doc; it’s almost shocking that this is the first one to be made. But if truth be told, director Kirsty Bell’s effort is stretched so thin to make a feature-length running time you can practically see through the screen. Also it’s so old-fashioned in its structure it plays almost like a tongue-in-cheek parody.The film deploys just about every scrap of archive material featuring Cochran that the budget could afford (which means we see precious little of his performance in The Girl Can’t Help It), plus scads of rostrum-mounted newspaper articles. That’s still not enough to make more than a long short film, so Bell has inserted endearingly tacky dramatic recreations with actors playing Cochran and his mother, whom the rocker reportedly phoned regularly while on tour. In these performed conversations Cochran confides to mom about, for instance, his fears that he’ll die an early death like his friend Buddy Holly. (And sure enough he did, in 1960 in a car accident on the road between Bristol and Heathrow.)Luckily though, someone connected to the production has top-notch persuasion skills and/or fantastic connections because the lineup of talking heads willing to wax lyrical about Cochran really is impressive and charmingly eclectic; these include famous fans such asKeith Richards, Rod Stewart, Roger Daltrey and Tim Rice (and that’s just the Brits). More unexpected contributions come from the likes of a typically wry yet well-read John Waters, effervescent guitarist and one-time TV presenter Brix Smith and, most randomly of all, Kiefer Sutherland – who was once attached to an Eddie Cochran biopic that never got made but has ever since retained a deeply informed knowledge of Cochran’s musical technique.By the time an hour has passed, Cochran’s life story has ended with his death but Bell and her interviewees keep going for another 30 minutes or so, discussing his legacy and the many covers of hits such as C’mon Everybody and Summertime Blues. But credit where credit’s due, the old guys in scarves are willing to get into the details of pickups and string choices, and the significance of Cochran’s 1955 Gretsch 6120 Chet Atkins hollow body guitar; it’s delightful to listen to, like an audio version of one of those guitar-geek magazines. Bio-docs about musicians never have nearly enough space allocated to the nuts and bolts of what makes the music itself so great, and too much to the gossip. This feature is a welcome exception, though perhaps erring a little too much the other way, heavy on the side of appreciation at the expense of lowdown.Don’t Forget Me is in UK cinemas from 11 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMusic documentaryPop and rockKeith RichardsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Knightfall review – low-rent gender-flipped Bond knock-off swaps Aston Martins for Minis | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jeanine Nerissa Sothcott’s no-nonsense spy heads a game cast that includes Ian Ogilvy and Roger Moore’s son Geoffrey, but this austerity actioner lacks tension
Author: Mike McCahill
Headline: Jeanine Nerissa Sothcott’s no-nonsense spy heads a game cast that includes Ian Ogilvy and Roger Moore’s son Geoffrey, but this austerity actioner lacks tension
Content: Nostalgic charm … Ian Ogilvy and Jeanine Nerissa Sothcott in Knightfall.View image in fullscreenNostalgic charm … Ian Ogilvy and Jeanine Nerissa Sothcott in Knightfall.MoviesReviewKnightfall review – low-rent gender-flipped Bond knock-off swaps Aston Martins for MinisJeanine Nerissa Sothcott’s no-nonsense spy heads a game cast that includes Ian Ogilvy and Roger Moore’s son Geoffrey, but this austerity actioner lacks tensionMike McCahillTue 8 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProceeding from an old-school title pun – yes, the heroine goes by the name Ros Knight – the latest from resourceful microbudget producer Jonathan Sothcott surely has one optimistic eye on filling the void left by the withdrawal of 007 from public life. Here is the gender-flipped Bond some have been seeking: the adventures of a no-nonsense, tough-talking security operative (Jeanine Nerissa Sothcott) who is tasked with recovering a lethal bioweapon pilfered from a scaled-down Porton Down during the prologue. Everything, in truth, proves a bit reined-in. This austerity actioner spends less on its set pieces than the Broccolis typically did on keeping one Aston Martin refuelled; the Sothcotts’ car of choice, emblematically, is the dinkiest of Minis.In essence, it’s Bond without the attendant glamour, hanging around drizzly marinas and parky-looking country lanes, in dim light that hopefully obscures some of the more obvious budget limitations. What money there is here has wisely been spent on human resources, faces who might still look good on the promotional material: a cameoing Michael Paré as a shady Felix Leiter type, Roger Moore’s son Geoffrey as our gal’s understandably worried-looking lover, Nick Moran giving cut-price Colin Firth as a meddling bureaucrat. The pick of the players is a spry, characterful Ian Ogilvy as Ros’s estranged father, helpfully identifying where the real power lies on a chessboard and generally steadying scenes whenever matters get a bit too threadbare.Despite the brassy parps of Logan Jones’s score, there’s nothing much here to give Eon sleepless nights. Director Ben Fortune keeps his careworn world-domination plot moving and just this side of coherent, but the action scenes don’t build tension so much as deconstruct the very idea of it, setting Sothcott and Ogilvy plodding around the garden in the dead of night, taking out the gunmen behind the polytunnel; the grand finale involves a Mexican standoff in someone’s front room. What would already have seemed antiquated circa Bourne risks redundancy in the Slow Horses era, where the tattiness is fully costed and integrated. Still, Knightfall holds a certain nostalgic charm; a bizarro-world vision of Bond in severely straitened circumstances, armed only with a licence to kill time.Knightfall is on digital platforms from 14 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmThrillersAction and adventure filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Better Go Mad in the Wild review – boozing, bantering hermits impart their spiritual wisdom | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Miro Remo journeys deep into the Czech countryside to find two brothers living an isolated life filled with quixotic wisdom in this surreal documentary
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Director Miro Remo journeys deep into the Czech countryside to find two brothers living an isolated life filled with quixotic wisdom in this surreal documentary
Content: No BS … Better Go Mad in the WildView image in fullscreenNo BS … Better Go Mad in the WildMoviesReviewBetter Go Mad in the Wild review – boozing, bantering hermits impart their spiritual wisdomDirector Miro Remo journeys deep into the Czech countryside to find two brothers living an isolated life filled with quixotic wisdom in this surreal documentaryPhil HoadTue 8 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 02.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNarrated by a slaughtered bull, this extraordinary film takes the less-travelled path in charting the daily life of a pair of Czech twins a long way off conventional routes themselves. František and Ondřej Klišík are slowly going mad – or maybe closing in on enlightenment – in a cabin in the Šumava mountains and, extrapolating a short story about the brothers by Aleš Palán, director Miro Remo succumbs productively to the prevailing cabin fever – not only egging these longbeards on in their squabbling and loopy philosophising, but pitching in with his own fabulism and surrealism.Closing on 60, “Franta” and “Ondra” still farm their smallholding with the help of Nandy, a mutinous bull ill-chosen as a draught animal. In their downtime, they booze, banter and bicker, lament their lack of prospects with the fairer sex, and blow off steam in epic arm-wrestling bouts. Despite an arm lost to a sawmill accident, it’s Franta who’s usually the victor; he is also possessed by a quixotic streak absent in his bluff sibling. Letting loose streams of poetry into the air like bunting, wishing “joy to all conscious beings”, he is also constructing his own Da Vinci-style perpetual flying machine. “Your aversion to my perpetuum is a little annoying,” he informs the exasperated Ondra.The Klišíks are definitely not “boring cunts”, as they dub 99% of humanity (including Vladimir Putin). They were decorated by the Czech state for their anti-Soviet activism, but that engagement seems to have waned, and Remo follows them away from the political deep into the personal and spiritual. In an intense communion with nature, including the animals they kill, they seem to inhabit a strange prelapsarian haven, inside which discord is continually bubbling up. Franta slates Ondra for his alcoholism, into which he is drawn; they differ on which one of them is Cain and which is Abel. In the end, they settle: they’re both Abel.As these spats recur and resolve themselves in kitchen-table laughter, it’s like watching some natural dialectical process in motion; a dishevelled but beautiful ying-yang cohabitation. The twins are ready collaborators in their own mythologisation, participating in Remo’s more leftfield plays, such as sequences where Ondra sledgehammers through the spiral mural on the wall between their rooms, or a dream featuring a levitating Franta. But shortly after the film won the Grand Prix at Karlovy Vary film festival last year, Franta died in a village pond. This took self-mythologisation too far, but his mystical remit still stands though; there is copious wisdom regarding family, nature, interdependency and love in this rowdy, rapturous and brilliant film.Better Go Mad in the Wild is in UK and Irish cinemas from 11 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsCzechiaFilm adaptationsEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not good to walk through the world feeling like prey’: Thelma & Louise’s writer on turning a movie classic into a musical | Musicals | The Guardian
description: It was her very first film and it won her an Oscar. But can Callie Khouri now make it work on stage with songs? She talks about the outrages that made her write it – and how little has changed since
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: It was her very first film and it won her an Oscar. But can Callie Khouri now make it work on stage with songs? She talks about the outrages that made her write it – and how little has changed since
Content: ‘Nothing’s ever come as easily’ …Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis in the 1991 film.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Nothing’s ever come as easily’ …Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis in the 1991 film.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyMusicalsInterview‘It’s not good to walk through the world feeling like prey’: Thelma & Louise’s writer on turning a movie classic into a musicalLyndsey WinshipIt was her very first film and it won her an Oscar. But can Callie Khouri now make it work on stage with songs? She talks about the outrages that made her write it – and how little has changed sinceTue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Ihave a world-class case of beginner’s luck,” says Callie Khouri, who won an Oscar for her very first screenplay,Thelma & Louise. She also scored a hit with her first TV series,Nashville, which lasted six seasons. And at 68, she is taking on another first by penning a musical theatre version of Thelma & Louise, hoping her luck hasn’t run out. “I hope that this is not the end of that streak,” she laughs. “That I don’t hit a wall here and slide down it like Wile E Coyote.”Thelma & Louise isn’t an obvious bet for a musical. A story that features an abusive marriage, attempted rape, murder and double suicide doesn’t scream “jazz hands”, and Khouri had turned down offers before. “My agent said, ‘There’s a guy who wants to meet you to talk about doing Thelma as a stage musical,’” says Khouri. “And I just thought, ‘Well, that’s nuts!’” But the iconic 90s film – starring Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis (and a young Brad Pitt) – is an ultimately triumphant piece of cinema: a feminist road movie driven by the power of female friendship, which still captures imaginations. Khouri was eventually convinced. It’s been a decade in the pipeline, but things took off when uber-producer Sonia Friedman came on board, and now it has premiered at London’sYoung Vic, starring Rachel Tucker and Amy Lennox.double quotation markScenes would wake me up in the middle of the night – it was the easiest job I ever didI meet Khouri at a south London studio during one of the summer’s heatwaves. She is dressed in airy, white cotton, looking like an elegant lady who might be tending her garden in the American south – which is what she spends a lot of her time doing these days at home in Nashville, Tennessee, with husbandT-Bone Burnett. When Khouri floated the idea for the musical at home, it was record producer Burnett who immediately suggested a composer, the American singer-songwriterNeko Case.View image in fullscreen‘It’s a completely different telling’ … Amy Lennox as Thelma and Rachel Tucker as Louise.Photograph: Tea Films“As soon as he said it, I heard this giant click,” says Khouri. “I love her music so much and it’s such a different approach to a musical. She is truly a poet, but her songs are very tactile – I don’t know exactly the right word – and she’s got this voice that’s like a clarion call.” Choreography is by Bobbi Jene Smith with her husband Or Schraiber, whose dance you could also describe as tactile – and sensuous, mercurial, deeply feeling. “I’m on my knees with gratitude that Bobbi’s part of our team,” says Khouri. The director is Trip Cullman, whoseBecky Shawplayed on Broadway earlier this year.The musical version of Thelma & Louise is being tweaked to suit the 21st-century stage, but it’s not set in the modern day: no mobile phones, Khouri tells me. “It’s a completely different telling of this same story,” is how she puts it. There are scenes that are from the movie and new ones that aren’t, but Khouri is reluctant to give much more away. “I don’t want to reveal magic tricks,” she says. “One of the things I really enjoyed about the movie was that people walked in having no idea what to expect, and I think that’s still really important for this story.”It’s true that back in 1991, when the film was released, nobody had any expectations of Khouri, a complete unknown who was living in Santa Monica working in production on music videos for big-haired rock bands. She had studied theatre at university but didn’t want an actor’s life, as “I didn’t like being looked at”, she says. “I just kept thinking, ‘There’s something I’m supposed to be doing and this is not it.’” It was the beginning of the MTV era and there was “a lot of really intense talent” making music videos, including Hollywood-bound directors such asDavid Fincher. “There was also a lot of not really intense talent,” she says – guys who were writing scripts and getting jobs who didn’t seem much smarter than she was, which is what gave Khouri the confidence to have a go.View image in fullscreen‘I had friends who had bad experiences’ … Khouri with Davis and Sarandon at a 30th-anniversary screening of the film in 2021.Photograph: Amy Sussman/Getty ImagesAt 29, she began the script for Thelma & Louise in secret between freelance jobs. “You know, while I was writing it, scenes would wake me up in the middle of the night. It was the easiest job I ever did,” she says. “Nothing’s ever come as easily.” She showed it to a friend, and via a chain of friends and colleagues the script eventually got into the hands ofRidley Scott, who decided to direct it himself. “It was really such an improbable journey every step of the way,” says Khouri.Khouri never would have thought she’d still be talking about this story 35 years later. In the film, a girls’ weekend spirals out of control when Louise shoots Thelma’s would-be rapist and the pair end up on the run. Inspiration came in part from Khouri’s own experiences, having twice been mugged in LA, once at gunpoint. “When you feel your life being threatened …” she starts. “It’s not a good feeling to walk through the world as a prey animal, which is how you start to feel. I had friends who had really bad experiences – I feel like I was one of the lucky ones.”There is sadness in her voice that the elements of the film, from casual sexism to serious assault, seem just as prevalent all this time later. “I wish so much that it wasn’t,” she says. “Honestly, I wish the world had made that shift to be a more hospitable place for women, and especially for young women. I think our expectations got really high, and they rolled the clock back. We’ve lost rights in the States, and it’s dangerous.” She calls the rollback of abortion rights in the US “barbaric”.She does think her own industry is more welcoming to women than it used to be. “But then you look at the backlash from #MeToo and that’s real,” she says. “The Epstein files have not been fully released. Bill Cosby’s out of jail.” Did she think #MeToo was going to make a genuine change in Hollywood? “I never feel like anything’s going to make a tectonic shift. I know how slow change is,” she says. “To me, equality is the obvious goal for all of society, but there are a lot of people that don’t think that, and they don’t want to let go of it, and they’ll fight. And so will we.” She is as incensed by the deaths of young men in “wars that are fought over money” as she is about the assault on women’s rights. “It seems like the world keeps giving way too much power to psychopaths.”View image in fullscreen‘I was called to tell this story’ … rehearsals for the musical.Photograph: Helen MurrayKhouri may rage at the state of the world, but in her own little horticultural corner of it she has “a beautiful life”. She got into Gardeners’ World during the pandemic. “That’s my crack,” she says with relish. And she has nothing to prove these days. “I still have to work,” she says, “but I like to work.” And she is finding this foray into theatre “so much fun”, especially compared with her usual beat. “The film and television business has gotten really hard,” she says. “Everybody feels like we’re working for an algorithm. It’s not about original ideas as much as it once was. It’s a lot about IP and sequels and tent-poles [the blockbuster franchises that prop up the studios], and those aren’t really the kind of movies I’m interested in, especially at this age.”Thelma & Louise at 30: a groundbreaking road movie that still strikes a nerveRead moreOf course, you could say Thelma & Louise is a powerful piece of IP, on which Khouri is still trading. She has written other films, and directed too (Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood; Mad Money), but never topped her first time. “It’s always lucky when you get called to something, and I feel very much like that’s what happened,” she says. “I was called to tell this story and I didn’t really have a great desire to tell it again. But once we started the musical, I could see a whole new way. Everybody – Neko, myself, Trip – we are all finding ways to elevate it to being worthy of being on a stage.”Thelma & Louise is at theYoung Vic, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicalsTheatreYoung VicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger: what we learned from the year’s biggest rockumentary | Oasis | The Guardian
description: Capturing the band’s 2025 global comeback tour, this two-hour film reveals the tense first rehearsal with Liam, Noel being a big softie and the Gallaghers’ politics – just don’t expect any mention of ticket prices
Author: David Renshaw
Headline: Capturing the band’s 2025 global comeback tour, this two-hour film reveals the tense first rehearsal with Liam, Noel being a big softie and the Gallaghers’ politics – just don’t expect any mention of ticket prices
Content: Liam and Noel Gallagher backstage in a scene from Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Simon Emmett/PAView image in fullscreenLiam and Noel Gallagher backstage in a scene from Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Simon Emmett/PAOasisOasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger: what we learned from the year’s biggest rockumentaryCapturing the band’s 2025 global comeback tour, this two-hour film reveals the tense first rehearsal with Liam, Noel being a big softie and the Gallaghers’ politics – just don’t expect any mention of ticket pricesDavid RenshawMon 7 Sep 2026 22.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 07.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was the reunion that many thought would never happen: Oasis re-forming for a series of sold-out live shows, their first since Noel andLiam Gallaghersplit acrimoniously in 2009. For those who managed to get tickets last year, the performances were a celebration of one of Britpop’s finest bands and a chance to live through a night of 90s nostalgia. For the millions who missed out, be it due to demand or budgetary restraints, the tour represented a generational Fomo moment.Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger review – mammoth tour movie brings the joy and poignancy of reunionRead moreLuckily, the directors Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern were embedded within team Oasis throughout the whole thing, alongside the Peaky Blinders creator, Steven Knight: the result isOasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger, a two-hour concert film that hits cinemas around the world this week. Whether you were on the front row at Manchester’s Heaton Park, doing the Poznan in Seoul or stuck at home watching it all online, Don’t Look Back in Anger captures the Oasis Live ’25 Tour for posterity. Here’s what we learned.The tension of the long-awaited first meetingRecorded by cameras hidden around the band’s practice room, Don’t Look Back in Anger opens with footage ofOasisrehearsing together before their first show in Cardiff. Initially it is just Noel and the rest of the band running through the music, with Liam due to join them after a couple of weeks. The younger brother breaks the ice immediately upon arrival, telling Joey Waronker that part of his drum kit is “giving me the hump” before stepping behind the mic and letting rip. The second he finishes his work for the day Liam walks straight out the door and heads home. His bandmates keep playing while laughing. With that, Oasis are back in business.Noel the softie?It’s notable how at ease Noel appears in Don’t Look Back in Anger. Perhaps it’s age – he turns 60 next year – or just the achievement of reuniting a band whose absence shadowed him for more than a decade, but he is positively soppy at points. He admits to being nervous before opening night and in tears before a show in Ireland.The death of Stone Roses bassist, Mani, has him questioning his own mortality. Seeing fathers and sons embracing in the crowd gets him, too. “I had to turn my back on the audience a lot,” he says.View image in fullscreen‘It takes a lot of caring to not give a fuck’ … Liam Gallagher on stage in a still from the filmLiam remains a singular presence …Despite the nonchalant confidence, Liam seemingly went into the tour with a point to prove. Avoiding both cigarettes and alcohol, he is in athletic form while remaining quick-witted (a joke about Mick Jagger providing one of many laugh-out-loud moments) and vocally stronger than he has been in years. We learn that he turned up to the Principality Stadium in Cardiff 20 minutes before the band stepped on stage. As he puts it: “It takes a lot of caring to not give a fuck.”… but both are obviously on their best behaviourNoel and Liam appear throughout the film, first in separate on-camera interviews and later in a joint chat. Liam mentions letting music “be the superhero”; the songs don’t belong to them but to the fans. It’s clearly true – the film pulls at an interesting thread about the new generation of Oasis fans who have emerged in the band’s absence – but it also feels as though the documentary is avoiding the elephant in the room. For more than a decade these brothers were sworn enemies; Noel at one point says he “never forgives”. And yet, by the end of the film, he claims that “all was forgiven without a word”. The fact that money isn’t mentioned once as a motivating factor for the tour, even in jest, doesn’t feel true to a group who never previously shied away from the financial benefits of being the biggest band in the world.Don’t expect any mention of the ticket pricesThe joy and euphoria across the faces of every fan in Don’t Look Back in Anger makes it clear people could have paid double and still got value for money watching Oasis – but that doesn’t mean they should have been forced to pay through the nose. In one throwaway moment Liam refers to the people in the cheap seats, before adding: “Actually there are no cheap seats, sorry about that.” Funny, but it would have been nice to hear someone justify Ticketmaster using “tiered” pricing that led to some tickets advertised at £148.50 ending up costing more than £350.View image in fullscreen‘Songs are bellowed by a choir of fans swaying on top of loved ones’ shoulders’Don’t call Oasis rightwingThe Gallagher brothers’ political views have always been hard to pin down. Noel famously backed Tony Blair in 1997 and has previously stated that an “invisible force field” would stop him from voting Tory. But, like many men in their late 50s, his views have become more reactionary over time. In 2018 he claimed that he would reform Oasis to stop “communist” Jeremy Corbyn from being elected prime minister then, a few years later, said an increasingly politicised Glastonbury was“getting a bit woke now”.Noel is not asked about his views in the film but he and Liam reject any notion that they stand for anything but unity between people. “The media never understood what Oasis are,” he argues at one point. “I know what it isn’t. It’s not a rightwing thing. All are welcome. It’s we and us. ‘We will find a brighter day.’ [The songs] are about us.”The concert footage is electricWith imagery from a team of cinematographers including Lol Crawley, known for his Oscar-winning work on The Brutalist – plus seriously loud sound design by Moonage Daydream’s Samir Foco, mixed by The Zone of Interest’s Tarn Willers and James Mather – Don’t Look Back in Anger is an impressive piece of work. Guitars ring out with a muscular heft and songs are bellowed by a choir of fans swaying on top of loved ones’ shoulders. Anthemic songs are used as a thread between tour dates: Rock’n’Roll Star in Los Angeles, Wonderwall in Buenos Aires and Some Might Say back in Dublin.The tour was a true family affairNoel and Liam can’t party like they did in the 90s – but their kids can. The fact that the siblings had not spoken in a decade and a half is underlined by a discussion about their four sons (aged 15, 18, 25 and 26) meeting for the first time during the tour. Donovan, Noel’s oldest, is given the dubious honour of the story of his night getting “absolutely spangled” and puking in a taxi being shared with millions. Thanks, Dad.The Gallagher brothers have a group chatAmazingly, it’s also revealed that the brothers now text each other “like fucking mates” and are “in touch way, way, way, way more” than they used to be. Their texts largely consist of silly videos and opinions of people on TV. Maybe their Reels-based relationship is the strongest sign yet for fans hoping to see a fresh batch of dates announced for 2027.Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger is released 9 September in the UK, 10 September in Australia and 11 September in the USExplore more on these topicsOasisMusic documentaryDocumentary filmsLiam GallagherNoel GallagherPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘So big and so close’: spotting endangered bears on a trip to northern Spain | Spain holidays | The Guardian
description: Conservationists have helped Cantabrian brown bears claw their way back from the edge of extinction in the beautiful mountains of Asturias – and carefully controlled nature tourism allows visitors to see them
Author: Stephen Phelan
Headline: Conservationists have helped Cantabrian brown bears claw their way back from the edge of extinction in the beautiful mountains of Asturias – and carefully controlled nature tourism allows visitors to see them
Content: A Cantabrian brown bear in Somiedo natural park in Asturias.Photograph: Lucas Vallecillos/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Cantabrian brown bear in Somiedo natural park in Asturias.Photograph: Lucas Vallecillos/AlamySpain holidays‘So big and so close’: spotting endangered bears on a trip to northern SpainConservationists have helped Cantabrian brown bears claw their way back from the edge of extinction in the beautiful mountains of Asturias – and carefully controlled nature tourism allows visitors to see themStephen PhelanTue 8 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnce upon a time, in the woods outside Pola de Somiedo, lived a family of Cantabrian brown bears. The villagers reported sightings of a mother bear who had lost a leg to a hunter’s trap, her two cubs and two adult males, either of which might have been the father. In those days, at the end of the 1980s, they seemed to be the last of their kind in this part of Asturias. Meanwhile, the wider population dropped to about 60 bears across the surrounding Cantabrian mountain range that gave the species its name.They have since clawed their way back from the edge of extinction here in northern Spain, and nature guide Luis Frechilla believes their numbers may now be upwards of 500 again. “They’re still classed as endangered,” he tells me, until the official count hits 1,000. But relative abundance makes them much easier to see today inSomiedo natural park– one of Spain’s first such protected areas, established in 1988.View image in fullscreenSomiedo natural park.Photograph: Biosphoto/AlamySetting his scope on a tripod in a steep-angled pasture, Frechilla spots a bear almost as soon as we start looking. A juvenile, apparently, which means the animal is old enough to be foraging alone, but it’s still too small, and too far away, for him to tell if it’s a male or female. Another bear-spotter standing near us seems more willing to take a guess.“Ooh, look at his little ears,” she says delightedly, beaming behind binoculars. No expert myself, I watch that distant fuzzy shape move across the viewfinder and along the sharp ridges opposite, blinking in and out of sight like a cursor on the trend line of a graph. I’m not sure that we are close enough to call this an encounter, but it is an experience.double quotation mark‘They can’t be too heavy because they have to climb,’ says our guide. Their paw prints look big enough to meThe sun drops behind the peaks; the birds sing a dusk chorus in the birches and oaks; cowbells ring through the valley from the dairy herds that help this region of so-called “Green Spain” look and sound like the Swiss Alps. It gets cold at night up here, and it’s been known to snow in summer, though my own visit in late spring sees the mountaintops looking whiter than anyone around here can remember so deep into May.That weather, and the sheer calorific spend of living and working at a median altitude of 1,300 metres, has made the traditional cuisine much sturdier here than elsewhere in Spain.Down at the village inn,Casa Miño, we share a bottle of regional cider and acachopo(beef fillet topped with serrano ham, peppers and goat cheese, and pounded into a single solid unit the size of a solar panel). I wantfabada,too, the famous Asturian stew of white beans, pork belly and blood sausage. Frechilla says it’s a winter dish, customarily eaten for lunch – too heavy for the body to process later in the day. But I would orderfabadaat midnight in a heatwave, and keep eating it even while they loaded me into the ambulance.View image in fullscreenThe Lake of the Valley.Photograph: Manu Garcia/AlamyThe bears, meanwhile, don’t have much to feed on at the moment. They only woke from hibernation a few weeks ago, explains Alicia Madrid the next day, on a forest trail above the century-old hydroelectric power station at La Malva. A biologist with the conservation groupFundación Oso Pardo, Madrid tells me that Cantabrian bears don’t hibernate as long or deeply as other brown bears and are generally smaller and lighter than American grizzlies.“They’re adapted to this terrain, and they can’t be too heavy because they have to climb a lot,” she says. Their paw prints in the mud look big enough to me, and the bite marks where they chewed clumps of long grasses, and the hairs shed where they scratched their backs against trees. Madrid shows us, too, the hefty rocks they overturned looking for insects. Further into the summer, there’ll be plenty of berries, acorns, chestnuts and maybe some meaty carrion to fatten them up.The foundation has played a major role in the regrowth of bear populations, building bio-corridors with strategic placements of trees and bushes full of all the things they like to eat. Another key factor is the hunting ban, introduced in 1973. The trick now, says Madrid, is coaxing isolated cohorts to breed with other groups and boost genetic diversity.double quotation markEveryone is watching a large male bear as he lopes across a meadow to take a splash in the riverAlso: managing the tourists who come to see them, and balancing ecological imperatives against financial incentives. Later, after a long hike through the Valley of the Lake to reach the aptly named Lake of the Valley, I overhear Frechilla fielding the related concerns of two local women. Against a backdrop of blue sky, bright wildflowers and silver waters, the women seem to argue that conservation efforts amount to commercial exploitation. Frechilla gently insists that Somiedo natural park is a model of good practice in Spain. Much of the bears’ territory is closed to the public, and spotting expeditions are only permitted in the company of licensed guides. Nature tourism, he says, keeps villagers in jobs where farming culture cannot, and is proving vastly more sustainable than hunting bears for sport. As for protecting humans, there has been only one bear attack in recent memory, on an elderly lady whose evening stroll led her between a mother and cubs. She survived.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor now, at least, most residents seem willing to share the bears with outsiders. That evening, a small crowd gather by the side of a winding back road near Saliencia, some sitting comfortably on camping chairs with spotting scopes in their hands. Everyone is watching a large male bear – so big and so close that they don’t need the viewing equipment – as he lopes across a meadow to take a quick splash in the river. Another male is spotted in the treeline above, and the two circle each other at a distance for a while. There is some speculation that they might fight for this turf, and a man with two leashed greyhounds seems ready to take bets on it. Frechilla shakes his head.“Maybe later in the season, when they’ve gained enough weight.”View image in fullscreenA bear in Somiedo  natural park.Photograph: Lucas Vallecillos/AlamyThese bears are doing better now, but it’s still a tough life. The reality of their ongoing baby boom is that only 30% of juveniles will survive on their own, after a year of maternal supervision. This is surely why I find it so moving when we follow reports of another sighting in the twilight: a mother and her two young cubs have been seen climbing a slope called El Diente,or “The Tooth”.It’s getting dark and cold, but we can see them through the scopes, about a mile away from us across the high mountain pass at La Peral. I watch the mother bear waiting and cajoling as needed while the siblings struggle up the vertical planes of rock like toddlers trying to climb a baby gate. On the ridgeline, they turn to silhouettes, play-fighting against a white sky.They disappear over the far side, but then a little one comes back, seeming to wave goodbye with both front paws in the air. I remember a story I read to my daughter once, which put a poignant time limit on the usual fairytale ending: “And they all lived happily together, for as long as they could.”The trip was provided by theSpanish Tourist Office,Turismo AsturiasandCasa Miñoin Pola de Somiedo. Bear-spotting tours with nature guide Luis Frechilla can be organised throughWild Spain Travel. For more information on the Cantabrian brown bear and related conservation efforts, visitFundación Oso PardoExplore more on these topicsSpain holidaysEurope holidaysWildlife holidaysWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why bother deseeding tomatoes? | Chefs | The Guardian
description: It all depends on the variety of tomato and the dish you’re making, says our panel of experts
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: It all depends on the variety of tomato and the dish you’re making, says our panel of experts
Content: More often than not, a pasta sauce will work better if the tomatoes are deseeded.Photograph: Dan Matthews/The Guardian. Food styling: Lola Faura @ Style Department.View image in fullscreenMore often than not, a pasta sauce will work better if the tomatoes are deseeded.Photograph: Dan Matthews/The Guardian. Food styling: Lola Faura @ Style Department.Kitchen aideChefsWhy bother deseeding tomatoes?It all depends on the variety of tomato and the dish you’re making, says our panel of expertsAnna BerrillTue 8 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy do recipes often say to deseed tomatoes? Isn’t that where the flavour is,especially since the seeds don’t make much difference to a sauce’s texture?Catriona, by email“It all depends on the variety of tomato,” saysthe Guardian’s Rachel Roddy, “because some are much seedier than others. Sicilian varieties that require little watering, for example, have loads of little bitter seeds, which do need flicking or sieving out.” If, however, Catriona had some vesuvio tomatoes destined for a salad, Jay Patel, co-owner of Italian restaurantLegarein London, wouldn’t bother: “Those are generally pretty meaty and don’t have many seeds, so I’d just slice and dress them generously with olive oil and salt, and you’ll have something pretty special.” And that’s the crux of the matter: as well as the type of tomato, the answer hinges on what you’re planning to do with them, too. “If you’re making a salad with watery winter tomatoes, say, there’s a purpose for those seeds,” Patel adds, “because they provide a lovely pop as well as acidity.”The most common deseeding scenario is for pasta sauces, but even that comes with a caveat, Patel says: “If I’m going for a slow-cooked sauce, it’s tinned chopped tomatoes, seeds and all. But if I’m after a lighter, fresher tomato sauce, I’ll quickly blanch, peel and deseed fresh tomatoes myself.” Nick Molyviatis ofZyliain London, meanwhile, scoops out the seeds with a teaspoon or he grates his tomatoes instead – “the skin acts as a protector, a glove” – while Roddy’s “best defence against seeds” is a food mill: “Seeds don’t contain flavour as such, but the fleshy gel around them does, which is why a food mill is great,” she explains. “It presses the flavour from that and the skin, while at the same time separating them from the sauce base.”Mind you, that gel in which the seeds are suspended is watery, too, which is why Patel shuns it in the likes of tomato tarts: “You want to remove as much water as possible, because it will make the pastry soggy,” he says, so it’s best to deseed the tomatoes before slicing them uniformly. “Once baked, you get these lovely, almost semi-dried tomatoes.” And not a soggy bottom in sight.But it’s not just about the seeds. “The texture of the skin also messes things up sometimes, and it’s not that pleasant to pick out of your teeth, either,” Molyviatis says. But again, Roddy notes, to peel or not to peel generally depends on the dish and, “more importantly”, on the variety of tomato: “Thin-skinned toms aren’t a worry,” she says, “but thicker skins are not only pesky to eat, they can also twist into scrolls during cooking, and are very annoying in some sauces.”To peel her toms, Roddy plunges them first into boiling water and then into cold to loosen the skins; failing that, she passes them through – yes, you’ve guessed it – her trusty food mill. Patel, on the other hand, tends to rely more on a knife, especially if bull’s heart tomatoes are involved: “They’re so easy to peel with a serrated knife.” Sure, it’s a bit of a faff, but it’s worth the effort, he insists. “When you’ve paid good money for good ingredients, it’s always worth going the extra mile.”Got a culinary dilemma? title: José Pizarro’s recipe for grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche | Food | The Guardian
description: A winning combination of oily fish, sweet berries and a sharp dressing
Author: José Pizarro
Headline: A winning combination of oily fish, sweet berries and a sharp dressing
Content: José Pizarro's grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenJosé Pizarro's grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodJosé Pizarro’s recipe for grilled sardines with blackberry escabecheA winning combination of oily fish, sweet berries and a sharp dressingJosé PizarroTue 8 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of my favourite summer memories is makingcollares de morasas a child in Extremadura, which involved threading wild blackberries on to a piece of straw to make little necklaces. We’d always eat some too, of course, as well as wearing them, and we’d always come home with stained hands and big smiles. At the time, I never imagined that one day I’d be cooking sardines and pairing them with those same wild berries, but that’s the magic of food. The ingredients that filled my childhood with such simple joy have become part of the dishes I love creating today. Every time I make this recipe, it takes me straight back to those carefree summer days.Grilled sardines with blackberry escabechePrep10 minCook25 minMarinate1 hr+Serves43 tbsp olive oil2 banana shallots, peeled and finely sliced1 red or orange bell pepper, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely sliced4-5 fresh thyme sprigs2 tsp coriander seeds1 tsp black peppercorns1 small pinch chilli flakes(optional)200ml white-wine vinegar, or cider vinegar200ml white wine150g blackberries, washedSea salt and black pepper8 good-sized fresh sardines, butterflied (ask the fishmonger to do this for you, if need be)Heat a tablespoon of the oil, then gently fry the shallots and bell pepper for six or seven minutes, until lovely and tender. Add the thyme and spices, fry for a minute more, then add the vinegar, wine and 100ml water, bring to a simmer and cook until the liquid has reduced by about half. Stir in the blackberries, then take off the heat and leave to cool slightly.Meanwhile, put the rest of the oil in a large nonstick frying pan on a high heat. Season the butterflied sardines inside and out, then fry them skin-side down for three or four minutes, until golden and crisp. Flip over and fry for just a minute longer on the flesh side.Arrange the cooked sardines skin-side up and side by side in a suitable deep-sided dish, pour the warm escabeche all over the top, then leave to marinate and cool down for at least an hour. Serve at once, or cover and chill in the fridge until you’re ready to eat.Explore more on these topicsFoodFishFruitSeafoodAutumn food and drinkSpanish food and drinkMain courserecipesShareReuse this content
